The Living World

Biology from the dry seed to the thinking brain. Sixteen chapters on how non-living atoms organize into cells, steal energy from sunlight, copy a four-letter code, and evolve—and how we know.

Written for Kym

Start reading

A letter to Kym

Dear Kym,

I should tell you something first: I am not a biologist. I don’t know much biology at all. What I have tried to do is make the book I would have loved to read when I was your age: one that tells you who found each idea and how, that lets you try things in the kitchen, and that never just hands you a Latin word to learn by heart. Much of what is in here was new to me too. I also had help: I made this book with the help of AI, which searched out the research, wrote the chapters to my design, and then checked them. The explanations draw on the free courses and books that MIT and OpenStax share with the world, and on what researchers have learned about the ideas students most often get wrong. Every fact, date and number was checked against reliable sources, more than once, by checkers whose only job was to find mistakes, and every number was worked out again from scratch. Even so, a few mistakes may have slipped through. If something here doesn’t match what you find somewhere else, or what your teacher says, or an experiment you do with your own hands, don’t simply trust the book: tell me, and we will find out together which is right. And where the people who really know biology still argue about something, the book says so.

Go into the kitchen and hold a dry green moong bean in your palm. It feels like a tiny green pebble. It does not move. It does not breathe measurably. If you leave it in a closed glass jar on the shelf for five years, it sits there as still as a stone. Now think of a candle flame on a birthday cake. A flame moves, flickers, grows, takes in oxygen, gives out carbon dioxide and heat, and can even start new flames. By almost every everyday test, the flame looks alive and the dry bean looks dead.

Yet the flame is not alive, and the bean is. Drop that dry pebble of a bean into a bowl of tap water on a warm Mumbai evening, and by tomorrow night a white root has cracked the green coat and pushed out into the dark. Give it soil, air and sunlight, and it builds leaves, flowers and dozens of new beans. Somehow, inside that dry speck, a four-billion-year-old set of instructions was waiting—along with the microscopic machinery to read it.

Biology is the investigation of how non-living atoms—the very same carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and phosphorus atoms you met in chemistry, obeying the very same laws of force and energy you met in physics—organise themselves into things that are alive. It asks how a hundred-tonne banyan tree at Horniman Circle builds almost its entire solid body out of thin air, how mangroves along Carter Road drink salty seawater that would kill a garden plant, why your idli batter rises overnight, how thirty trillion cells in your body work together without a boss, and how a four-letter chemical code inside a microscopic nucleus can build both a leopard in Sanjay Gandhi National Park and the brain you are reading this sentence with.

For a long time, biology in school has been taught backwards: as a giant dictionary of Greek and Latin names to memorise for a test. Memorising names in biology is like reading the last page of a detective novel—it spoils the mystery without letting you see how anyone solved the case. In this book we follow Richard Feynman’s rule: see the thing first, understand how the mechanism works, and only then learn its name.

Almost every section starts with an idea that sounds completely sensible—and turns out to be wrong. Clever people once believed that rotting meat turns into maggots on its own, that trees eat soil to grow heavy, that your lungs are where respiration happens, and that bacteria mutate on purpose to beat antibiotics. Before each experiment, the book will ask you to predict first. Please really pick an answer before you read on. Discovering where your intuition gets tricked is how a detective learns to see.

The heroes of this story are real people: a Dutch cloth merchant who pointed a tiny glass bead at rainwater and tooth scrapings, a Flemish doctor who weighed a pot of dirt for five years, an Indian biochemist from Andhra Pradesh who discovered the rechargeable battery inside every living cell, a woman in London whose X-ray photograph revealed the twisted ladder of DNA, a botanist from Kerala who sweetened India’s sugarcane by counting chromosomes, and a ten-year-old boy in Bombay whose curiosity about a yellow-throated sparrow launched conservation across India.

With love,

Amar

P.S. This is the third book in your series. Whenever living machinery meets atoms and bonds, we link across to Book 1, The Invisible World (chemistry). Whenever it meets forces, pressure, heat, optics or electricity, we link across to Book 2, The Moving World (physics).

How this book works

This book is one continuous detective investigation. It follows people across four centuries—from a physician in Florence covering jars of meat with fine veil, to a friar in Brno counting twenty-eight thousand pea plants, to scientists in Calcutta, Madras, Coimbatore and Mumbai working out how plants send electrical signals, how proteins fold, and how nerve cells fire. Each of them was asking the same two questions you will ask on every page: how does this living machine work, and how do we know?

There are four volumes and sixteen chapters, starting at Chapter 0 because every detective needs a toolkit before entering the crime scene. Each chapter opens with a biological paradox, follows the wrong turns and forensic experiments that cracked it, and builds the real mechanism from the ground up.

As you read, you will meet a few kinds of boxes. Each one has one job.

Story links
Some words in the text are marked like this. Each one opens a longer story beside the page: the historical adventure of how that discovery was made, told step by step. They are collected in Stories behind the ideas, and The adventure in time puts them in order.
The cast
Biology was built by real people: a cloth merchant grinding lenses in Delft, a monk with a garden notebook, a biochemist from Bhimavaram isolating the cell’s fuel, a cell biologist in Parel setting up India’s first tissue-culture lab. Their names are story links too. The cast introduces them all.
Scenes
A small pin with a place and date, like Florence, summer 1668 or Sanjay Gandhi National Park, Mumbai, June, takes you somewhere real. Every scene sits on the adventure map.
Margin notes
After you have seen how something works, its technical name is marked like this and defined in the margin (along with where the Greek or Latin word came from). Every term goes into Words worth knowing at the back.
Predict first
A question with a few choices, placed right before the decisive experiment. Commit to one before you reveal the answer; your notebook remembers what you picked.
Careful
A common-sense idea ("the Red Herring") that tricks most people—and often tricked scientists for centuries—together with the exact evidence that disproves it.
Understand it
Knowing a biological word is not the same as understanding the mechanism. Every central concept gets unpacked into five core questions (what it is, why it is called that, what problem it solved, why it works, and how it helps), three folded go-deeper questions, and a space to explain it back in one sentence.
Try it
A quantitative puzzle or spatial comparison tied to the investigation.
Try it at home
A safe "Kitchen Forensics" experiment using everyday things in a Mumbai flat: dry moong beans, raw potato strips, salt, yeast or idli batter, dish soap, a banana, a hand lens or your phone camera.
Watch and play
Every figure starts as a still, engraved scientific drawing that works on paper and without JavaScript. Tap the button beneath a live figure to launch an interactive 2D particle workbench or a 3D Three.js molecular and cellular model you can turn with your finger.
At school
Your "Cambridge Decoder Ring": one or two sentences showing how Cambridge Lower Secondary, IGCSE Biology (0610), and IB MYP word the same concept—and which phrasing traps examiners penalise.
Check yourself
One question at the end of each section. The full reasoning sits at the back of the book.
Back from Chapter N
An earlier misconception returning in a brand-new biological disguise, so you can test whether the real mechanism stuck.
Case file
An end-of-chapter forensic mystery where you use the chapter’s clues to crack a real-world biological case.

Four full-page explorers sit at the front of the book for structures you will return to again and again: Powers of Ten in the Living World (from a water molecule to the biosphere), The 3D Cell & Nanocity Explorer (interactive 3D animal, plant and bacterial cells), The Master Code: 3D DNA to Protein (helix, codons and 3D protein folding), and the adventure map.

Numbers in this book are real measured quantities. A millimetre (mm) is $10^{-3}\text{ m}$, athousandth of a metre. A micrometre ($\mu\text{m}$) is $10^{-6}\text{ m}$, a thousandth of a millimetre—the scale of cells and bacteria. A nanometre ($\text{nm}$) is $10^{-9}\text{ m}$, a thousandth of a micrometre—the scale of DNA, proteins and cell membranes.

Five ideas that run through everything

Biology can look like a vast museum of separate creatures, organs and Latin names. It is not. Almost everything in the living world grows out of five connected ideas, working together across every scale from a molecule to a rainforest.

  1. Life is a rebellion against chaos, paid for continuously with energy.Left to themselves, complex things fall apart into random thermal disorder: a dead leaf crumbles, a warm cup of chai cools to room temperature. A living cell is made of ordinary atoms, but it stays alive by continuously capturing energy from its surroundings—sunlight in a green leaf, chemical fuel in food—and spending that energy via a tiny rechargeable molecule called ATP to pump ions, repair damage and build order against the tide of decay.
  2. In the molecular world, 3D shape is how machines do work.Inside a cell there are no eyes or hands to recognise molecules. Instead, long chains of amino acids fold into exact three-dimensional pockets, motors and gates. An enzyme speeds up a chemical reaction a millionfold because its pocket fits one specific molecule like a lock that bends a stick; an antibody grabs a virus, and a receptor catches a hormone, by matching its physical shape and electric charges.
  3. Every living cell carries and copies a digital four-letter recipe book.Inside a dry moong bean, a bacterium and your own brain cells sits the same chemical storage tape: DNA, written in an alphabet of just four letters (A, T, C, G). Cells copy that tape when they divide, and tiny molecular printers called ribosomes read the letters three at a time to build every protein machine the organism needs.
  4. Random copying glitches plus a survival filter create all adaptation and diversity.No organism ever mutates "in order to" solve a problem, and no species plans ahead. When DNA is copied, tiny random typos inevitably happen. Most do nothing or cause harm, but occasionally a typo alters a protein in a way that helps its owner survive and leave more offspring in that environment. Over millions of generations, that simple filter—natural selection—turned ancient ocean microbes into banyan trees, flamingos and humans.
  5. Atoms loop forever through the biosphere, while energy flows one way.Earth is a closed box for matter and an open window for energy. Sunlight streams in, drives photosynthesis in green leaves and ocean algae, passes through food webs, and ultimately radiates into space as low-grade heat. Meanwhile, the actual carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and phosphorus atoms are never used up: they cycle endlessly between air, soil, water and living bodies.

And underneath all five is the detective’s cardinal rule: never confuse a label with a mechanism, and never trust a common-sense guess until a controlled experiment has tried to prove it wrong.

Chapter 0

The detective’s lens

The big questionWhen maggots appear on rotting meat, or a muddy Mumbai monsoon puddle turns bright green overnight, did living things spring out of non-living matter by themselves?

  1. 0.1The maggot red herring
  2. 0.2The cloth merchant’s glass bead
  3. 0.3The swan-neck trap
  4. 0.4The ladder of biological size

Imagine walking into a room where a crime began four billion years ago. There is no police tape and nobody left an instruction manual on the desk. Yet every corner of the room is packed with clues. On your windowsill in Mumbai, a green money-plant leaf is quietly turning sunlight and invisible air into solid sugar. Inside your chest, a fist-sized muscular pump is beating about seventy times a minute without your having to remind it. And if you scoop a single drop of rainwater out of an old flowerpot saucer after a June shower and hold a strong lens to it, you will find thousands of tiny creatures darting, spinning and hunting in a world you never knew was there.

Before we can investigate how living things work, we have to learn the detective’s first skill: how to look at a puzzling clue without letting our own common sense trick us. For more than two thousand years, some of the cleverest people on Earth looked at rotting food, stagnant puddles and dusty grain tins and came to an obvious conclusion that turned out to be completely wrong. How a handful of stubborn experimenters proved them wrong is the story of how biology became a science.

0.1The maggot red herring

Florence, summer 1668

Open an old tin of rice or atta that has sat at the back of a warm Mumbai kitchen cupboard through the monsoon, and you may find tiny brown beetles crawling through the grain. Leave a piece of raw fish on a plate in July heat, and within two days pale, legless maggots are wriggling over it. Where did they come from?

Spontaneous generation

The old, mistaken belief that living organisms (such as maggots, beetles or microbes) regularly spring to life out of non-living matter like rotting meat, mud or broth.

For centuries, the answer seemed too obvious to question: they grew out of the food itself. Aristotle taught that frogs and eels form out of pond mud, fleas out of dust, and maggots out of decaying meat. Even Jan Baptista van Helmont—a brilliant seventeenth-century doctor whom we will meet again in Chapter 5—wrote down a recipe for making mice: stuff a dirty shirt into a pot of wheat grains, wait twenty-one days, and mice will appear. The idea was called spontaneous generation: the belief that living creatures can arise directly and regularly from non-living muck or food.

Notice why that wrong idea lasted so long. Every time someone left meat out, maggots really did appear. Observation alone was not enough, because two completely different stories fitted the same observation:

  1. Story A (Spontaneous generation): Rotting meat chemically transforms itself into maggots.
  2. Story B (Hidden parents): Adult flies land on the meat, lay microscopic eggs too small to notice at a glance, and those eggs hatch into maggots.

In the summer of 1668, an Italian physician and poet named Francesco Redi decided to force those two stories into a contest where only one could survive. If Story B was right, he reasoned, then keeping adult flies away from the meat should stop maggots from ever appearing. So he placed identical pieces of meat—snake, fish and veal—into two sets of wide-mouthed glass jars. He left the first set open to the room, and sealed the second set tightly with paper and wax. Within days, flies buzzed in and out of the open jars and maggots swarmed over the meat. In the sealed jars, the meat rotted just as foully, yet not a single maggot appeared.

Case closed? Not quite. Put yourself in the shoes of a stubborn defender of spontaneous generation. What objection would you raise against Redi’s sealed jars?

Predict first

A critic looks at Redi’s sealed jars—where no maggots grew—and says: “Your experiment is unfair! You didn’t just block the flies; you also blocked something else that rotting meat needs to generate life.” What did the sealed lid block?

  1. Fresh air
  2. Gravity
  3. Room warmth

What happens

Fresh air. A sealed jar blocks both flies and the free circulation of air. As long as Redi changed two things at once (flies and air), critics could claim that fresh air was the missing ingredient for spontaneous generation. To clinch the case, Redi needed a third jar that let fresh air flow freely while still keeping flies out.

Redi saw that objection himself, and his answer was a masterpiece of detective work. He set up a third group of jars covered not with solid lids, but with fine velo di Napoli—delicate Naples gauze, like mosquito netting. Air passed straight through the mesh. The smell of rotting meat drifted out into the room. Attracted by the scent, adult flies landed on top of the gauze and laid their tiny white eggs right on the cloth, where Redi could see them with his own eyes—unable to reach the meat a few centimetres below. Inside the gauze-covered jars, the meat stayed completely free of maggots.

How do we know? Redi’s Esperienze intorno alla generazione degl’insetti 1668

Redi did not trust a single trial. Across dozens of flasks in Florence, he tested snake meat, river fish, eels and milk-fed veal under open, sealed and gauze-covered conditions. He also caught the maggots from the open jars, watched them harden into oval pupae, and waited until adult flies crawled out—showing that the maggots were simply the young stage of the very flies buzzing round the room.

Controlled experiment

A test in which only one factor (the independent variable) is deliberately changed while all other conditions (controlled variables) are kept the same, so that any difference in the outcome (the dependent variable) has only one possible cause.

What Redi invented in those three jars is what scientists today call a controlled experiment. When you want to test whether one specific factor (say, access by flies) causes an outcome (maggots appearing), you change only that one factor—the independent variable—while keeping every other condition (type of meat, jar size, temperature, access to fresh air) the same. Those kept-the-same conditions are your controlled variables, and the outcome you measure or count is the dependent variable. Without the open jar as a control group to show that the meat could support maggots in that room, or without the gauze jar to keep air constant, Redi would have been fooling himself.

Understand itControlled experiment

What is it?

A side-by-side comparison where you change only the one suspected cause you are testing, while holding every other condition identical between the test group and the control group.

Why is it called this?

From the medieval French contrerolle, a duplicate ledger roll kept to check whether the first tax collector’s scroll had errors. In science, the control jar is your duplicate scroll: it shows what happens when you do not make the change.

What problem did it solve?

Living things are sensitive to dozens of things at once—temperature, moisture, air, light, contamination. If you change two things together, you cannot tell which one caused the result.

Why does it work?

By making the test jar and the control jar identical in every way except one, any difference in the outcome must come from that single difference.

How does it help?

It is how we test whether a new vaccine protects children (Chapter 10), whether plants need carbon dioxide to make starch (Chapter 5), and whether bacteria come from dust in the air (Section 0.3).

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Whenever an experiment omits a proper control—like Redi’s first sealed jar that cut off both flies and air—rival explanations survive until a tighter control eliminates them.

What it isn’t

It does not mean “controlling” the result to get the answer you want; it means holding background conditions steady so nature’s answer cannot be misread.

Where does it stop working?

In whole ecosystems—like removing leopards from Sanjay Gandhi National Park—you cannot put two identical forests in glass jars, so ecologists use natural comparisons and long-term tracking instead (Chapter 15).

Your turn

Explain Controlled experiment to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“Weevils appear inside a sealed plastic packet of rice or besan that came straight from the shop, so they must have grown out of the grain!”

Look closely with a hand lens at grains of rice or wheat before they are packed. Female rice weevils (Sitophilus oryzae) chew a microscopic pinhole into a grain, lay a single egg inside, and seal the hole with a gelatinous plug you cannot see with the naked eye. Weeks later, in your warm kitchen cupboard, the larva finishes eating the inside of the grain and chews its way out as an adult beetle. The egg was already inside the packet before it was sealed.

At school

Cambridge Lower Secondary and IGCSE Biology (Paper 6, Alternative to Practical) test three variable names on almost every paper: the independent variable (what the investigator changes, plotted on the horizontal x-axis), the dependent variable (what is measured, plotted on the vertical y-axis), and controlled variables (conditions kept constant so the test is fair).

Check yourself

Suppose a student wants to test whether light is needed for moong seeds to germinate. She puts Dish A on a sunny windowsill in wet cotton wool, and Dish B inside a dark cupboard in dry cotton wool. Only Dish A sprouts, so she concludes that seeds need light to sprout. Why is her conclusion invalid, and how should she fix Dish B?

Answer at the back of the book

0.2The cloth merchant’s glass bead

Delft, the Netherlands, September 1674

Redi settled the question for flies and maggots. Seven years later, however, a cloth merchant in the Dutch town of Delft opened a trapdoor beneath everyone’s feet—and made the spontaneous generation mystery ten times harder.

Cell

The smallest unit of life that can carry out all the processes of a living thing, bounded by a membrane and containing genetic instructions and molecular machinery. Coined by Robert Hooke in 1665 after looking at dead cork chambers.

Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was not a university professor. He sold linen and cloth, and to check the thread count of his fabrics he learned to make his own magnifying lenses. In London, a few years earlier (1665), Robert Hooke had used a compound microscope—a leather tube with two lenses—to look at a razor-thin slice of bottle cork. Hooke saw rows of tiny empty boxes separated by thin walls; they reminded him of the bare rooms (cellae) where monks slept in a monastery, so he called them cells. What Hooke was actually looking at were the dead, empty wooden walls left behind after the tree bark cells had died.

Leeuwenhoek found a simpler, shrewder way to build a lens. By melting a slender filament of soda glass in a flame until it pulled into a tiny, near-spherical bead less than 2 millimetres across—and mounting that single glass bead between two brass plates with a screw to hold the specimen right up against the lens—he achieved magnifications of up to $270\times$, far sharper than Hooke’s big two-lens tubes, which suffered from blurry colour fringes.

In September 1674, Leeuwenhoek filled a thin glass tube with greenish water from a lake called Berkelse Mere and held it to his brass lens. He saw green spiral ribbons (the alga Spirogyra) and thousands of tiny creatures darting, spinning and tumbling through the water. He called them dierkens—“little animals”, translated into English as “animalcules”. Nine years later, on 17 September 1683, he scraped a speck of white plaque from between his own front teeth, mixed it with clean rainwater, and looked again. Inside his own mouth were darting rods, spinning spirals and clusters of tiny spheres: the first human sight of bacteria.

The story behind this

The cloth merchant who found an invisible kingdomA Dutch draper with no university degree ground tiny glass beads that beat every compound microscope in Europe and revealed bacteria in his own teeth.

How do we know? Leeuwenhoek’s Letter 39 to the Royal Society 17 September 1683

Leeuwenhoek sketched the exact shapes of the bacteria from his teeth—rods (bacilli), spheres (cocci) and spirals (spirilla)—along with dotted tracks showing how the rods tumbled and swam. He noted with delight that “there are more animals living in the scum on the teeth in a man’s mouth than there are men in a whole kingdom”—and observed that when he drank scalding hot coffee, the creatures on his front teeth stopped moving, while those sheltered between his back molars kept swimming.

Leeuwenhoek’s discovery stunned Europe—and breathed new life into spontaneous generation. Nobody believed anymore that full-grown mice or flies popped out of dirt. “But surely,” people argued, “these microscopic specks—so simple, so tiny, appearing by the million whenever a bowl of soup or meat broth sits warm for two days—must form by themselves out of the broth!”

0.3The swan-neck trap

Paris, 1859

For nearly two centuries after Leeuwenhoek, naturalists fought over where the microbes in spoiled broth came from. If you boiled meat broth in a flask to kill everything inside and left the flask open, it turned cloudy and teamed with swimming bacteria within forty-eight hours. If you boiled the broth and melted the glass neck shut, it stayed crystal clear—but critics gave the exact same reply they had given Redi: “By sealing the glass, you ruined the fresh air that spontaneous generation needs!”

In 1859, the French Academy of Sciences offered the Alhumbert Prize to anyone who could settle the question with a clean, decisive experiment. The chemist Louis Pasteur took up the challenge. Pasteur suspected that ordinary room air is full of invisible floating dust, and riding on those dust specks are dormantly waiting bacterial spores and yeast cells. What he needed was a flask that stayed wide open to fresh air, yet trapped every speck of dust before it could reach the boiled broth.

Predict first

Pasteur pours nutrient broth into a glass flask, heats the glass neck in a flame, and pulls it out into a long, downward-curving S-bend—like a swan’s neck—leaving the tip of the neck completely open to the room. He boils the broth until steam shoots out of the open tip, then lets it cool slowly. What will happen to the broth over the next month?

  1. It will turn cloudy within days, because fresh outside air can still flow freely down the open tube
  2. It will stay crystal clear, because heavy dust and microbes settle in the bottom dip of the curved neck while clean air passes over them
  3. It will stay clear only for a day, then grow mould from the oxygen in the air

What happens

It stays crystal clear—for months, and in fact for more than a century! As the flask cools, outside air is drawn gently in through the open tip, but dust particles and the microbes riding on them settle by gravity onto the damp glass walls at the bottom of the U-bend. Air reaches the broth; dust does not.

How could Pasteur prove that the boiled broth inside his swan-neck flask was still perfectly capable of supporting life, and hadn’t been chemically ruined by boiling? He didn’t even need a second flask. He simply took a swan-neck flask that had sat clear and sterile on his shelf for weeks, tilted it sideways so a splash of clear broth ran down into the dusty U-bend and back into the bulb, and set it upright again. Within forty-eight hours, the broth was cloudy with millions of multiplying bacteria.

Pasteur’s swan-neck flasks established one of the foundational laws of biology: Omne vivum ex vivo—all life comes from pre-existing life, and every cell comes from an existing cell dividing into two. There is only one exception in the entire history of the Earth: the very first transition from non-living chemistry to the first primitive cell nearly four billion years ago, a cold case we will investigate in Chapter 15.

The two-glass broth test (with an adult)

Dissolve half a spoon of dal water (the clear starchy liquid from boiling toor or moong dal) or a pinch of sugar and a drop of milk in half a cup of water. With an adult’s help, boil it in a small steel pan for 3 minutes to sterilise it, then pour equal amounts into two clean glasses rinsed with boiling water. Cover Glass A tightly with cling-film or aluminium foil right away while it is still steaming; leave Glass B uncovered on the kitchen counter, or stir it once with an unwashed finger. Put both glasses in a warm corner for 48 hours and look at them sideways against a torch beam (do not taste or smell close up; pour both down the sink with dish soap when done). Glass B turns cloudy as airborne microbes multiply; Glass A stays much clearer.

0.4The ladder of biological size

Once Hooke and Leeuwenhoek opened the microscopic world, biologists needed a new set of rulers. Everything you hold in your hands—a pencil, a moong bean, your own thumb—is measured in metres ($\text{m}$) or millimetres ($\text{mm}$), where $1\text{ mm}$ is one thousandth of a metre ($10^{-3}\text{ m}$). Look at the finest millimetre ticks on your geometry-box ruler. Your naked eye can just make out an object about $0.1\text{ mm}$ across—roughly the width of a human hair or a large human egg cell.

To step down into the world of cells, bacteria, viruses and molecules, biologists divide the millimetre by a thousand, and then by a thousand again:

Micrometre and nanometre

A micrometre ($\mu\text{m}$) is one thousandth of a millimetre ($10^{-6}\text{ m}$), the scale of cells and bacteria. A nanometre ($\text{nm}$) is one thousandth of a micrometre ($10^{-9}\text{ m}$), the scale of viruses, ribosomes, membranes and DNA.

  • 1 millimetre ($\text{mm}$) $= 10^{-3}\text{ m}$: A small mustard seed (rai) is about $1\text{–}2\text{ mm}$ across; a dry moong bean is about $4\text{ mm}$ long.
  • 1 micrometre ($\mu\text{m}$) $= 10^{-3}\text{ mm} = 10^{-6}\text{ m}$: Divide a single $1\text{ mm}$ gap on your ruler into one thousand equal slices. That is the scale of cells. A human red blood cell is about $8\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ across; a typical plant cell in an onion skin is about $50\text{–}100\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ long; a rod-shaped E. coli bacterium in your gut is about $2\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ long.
  • 1 nanometre ($\text{nm}$) $= 10^{-3}\text{ }\mu\text{m} = 10^{-9}\text{ m}$: Divide one micrometre into one thousand slices again. That is the scale of viruses and biological molecules. A coronavirus or bacteriophage is about $100\text{ nm}$ across; a ribosome (the cell’s protein printer) is $25\text{ nm}$ wide; a cell membrane is $8\text{ nm}$ thick; the DNA double helix is $2\text{ nm}$ wide; and a single water molecule is $0.28\text{ nm}$ across.

You can explore this entire ladder interactively—zooming continuously from a single ATP molecule up to a banyan tree and Sanjay Gandhi National Park—in Powers of Ten in the Living World.

Whenever a biologist draws a cell or takes a photograph through a microscope (a photomicrograph), they state its magnification: how many times wider the drawing or image ($I$) is than the real object ($A$). The rule is simple division, provided both lengths are written in the same unit (usually micrometres or millimetres):

$$\text{Magnification } (M) = \frac{\text{Image size } (I)}{\text{Actual size } (A)}$$

Suppose you look at a pond-water Paramecium through a microscope and draw it in your notebook. Your drawing ($I$) is $54\text{ mm}$ long. The real Paramecium ($A$) is $200\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ long. What is the magnification of your drawing?
1. Convert both measurements to the same unit ($\mu\text{m}$), using $1\text{ mm} = 1,000\text{ }\mu\text{m}$:
$$I = 54\text{ mm} \times 1,000\text{ }\mu\text{m/mm} = 54,000\text{ }\mu\text{m}$$
2. Divide image size by actual size:
$$M = \frac{54,000\text{ }\mu\text{m}}{200\text{ }\mu\text{m}} = \times 270$$
Your drawing is magnified $270$ times ($\times 270$), the exact power of Leeuwenhoek’s best brass lens.

Careful

“Atoms, molecules, viruses, bacteria and human cells are all just ‘microscopic specks’ of roughly the same size.”

In surveys of twelve- and thirteen-year-olds, more than half guess that a protein molecule is bigger than or the same size as a cell! In reality, the gap between a water molecule ($0.28\text{ nm}$) and a human cell ($20\text{ }\mu\text{m}$) is a factor of nearly 100,000 in width—the same ratio as a $2\text{ cm}$ marble compared with a $2\text{ km}$ stretch of Marine Drive. A cell can hold trillions of molecules because molecules are tens of thousands of times smaller than cells.

At school

On Cambridge IGCSE Biology exams, always convert ruler measurements from millimetres ($\text{mm}$) to micrometres ($\mu\text{m}$) by multiplying by $1,000$ before using $M = I \div A$ (or $A = I \div M$), and write a multiplication sign in front of a magnification ($\times 270$), never a unit like $\text{mm}$.

Check yourself

A photograph of a chloroplast in a textbook measures $36\text{ mm}$ across. The caption says the magnification is $\times 6,000$. What is the actual width of the real chloroplast in micrometres ($\mu\text{m}$)?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 0

The cloudy soup in the monsoon kitchen

On a warm July afternoon in Mumbai, two identical bowls of clear vegetable broth are boiled for five minutes. Bowl 1 is placed inside a clean plastic box whose lid has a tiny, long S-shaped drinking straw glued through a hole in the top (open to the air at both ends). Bowl 2 is placed in an identical plastic box with a wide, straight $2\text{ cm}$ hole in the top lid. After three days on the kitchen counter, Bowl 2 is cloudy and sour, while Bowl 1 is still clear. On Day 4, someone picks up Box 1, shakes it vigorously so the broth splashes against the inside of the lid and straw, and puts it back down. By Day 6, Bowl 1 is cloudy too.

Use the clues from this chapter to explain: (a) why Bowl 2 turned cloudy while Bowl 1 stayed clear for the first three days even though both boxes were open to the air, and (b) why shaking Box 1 on Day 4 made it turn cloudy by Day 6.

Show the solution

(a) Boiling killed the existing microbes in both bowls. In Box 2, dust particles carrying airborne bacteria and fungal spores fell straight down through the wide hole into the broth. In Box 1, the long S-shaped straw acted just like Louis Pasteur’s 1859 swan-neck flask: air could move in and out, but airborne dust and microbes settled on the inner walls of the curved straw and could not fall into the soup. (b) When Box 1 was shaken on Day 4, liquid broth splashed against the trapped dust inside the straw and lid, picking up dormant bacterial cells and carrying them back into the bowl, where they multiplied over the next 48 hours.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

Now that we have a lens to see the invisible and a rule for testing our guesses without fooling ourselves, we are ready to step into the main mystery of the book. Hold a dry green moong bean in one hand and look at a flickering candle flame in the other. What makes one of them alive and the other just a chemical fire?

Where this chapter comes from

1

Chapter 1

The seed and the flame

The big questionA candle flame moves, grows, consumes fuel, takes in oxygen, and releases carbon dioxide. A dry moong bean in your kitchen cupboard does none of those things. Why is the bean alive and the flame not?

  1. 1.1The first rains in June
  2. 1.2The flame and the bean
  3. 1.3Paying for repairs, and SubbaRow’s ₹10 coin
  4. 1.4Seven processes in a living system
  5. 1.5The outlaw at the border

In Chapter 0 we saw that every living creature on Earth today—from a bacterium in a drop of puddle water to a banyan tree—comes from an existing living parent. That raises an immediate, sharper question. What is “being alive”?

If you ask ten people on the street how to tell whether something is alive, they will give you a sensible-sounding list: living things move, breathe, eat, grow, and respond when you poke them. Yet nature loves to embarrass a hasty list. A candle flame moves, grows, consumes wax fuel, takes in oxygen, gives out carbon dioxide and heat, and can even “reproduce” by lighting a second candle—yet a flame is not alive. Meanwhile, a dry green moong bean sitting in a glass jar in your kitchen is as hard, cold and still as a pebble—yet it is alive. Why? Cracking that paradox takes us straight to the first principles of all biology: water, energy, molecular machines, and a digital code.

1.1The first rains in June

Sanjay Gandhi National Park, Mumbai, early June

Walk up the basalt trail towards Kanheri Caves in the last week of May, before the monsoon arrives. The hillsides look dead. The grass is brittle straw; the earth is baked into cracked brown brick; the rock pools are bone-dry dust. If an alien landed on those hills in late May, it might conclude that almost nothing on the ground was alive.

After the first heavy rains, brown hillsides begin turning green. Shoots emerge and pools refill. Different organisms return in different ways: seeds germinate, some tiny aquatic animals hatch from resistant resting eggs, and frogs breed in the new water. Tadpoles develop from frog eggs, not from dry mud cysts. There is no single timetable or survival mechanism for the whole hillside.

Where was the next generation of grass hiding through the dry weeks? Much of it was inside seeds. Pick up a dry green moong bean (Vigna radiata), a chickpea or a mustard seed. A viable seed contains a living embryo, stored materials and machinery that can resume development when conditions permit.

As many desiccation-tolerant seeds dry, their cell contents become extremely viscous and can form a sugar-rich biological glass, a change called vitrification. Molecular movement is greatly restricted, and metabolism slows enormously. Not every motion or chemical change stops: dry seeds can still deteriorate. Water content, temperature and the seed’s composition affect this state. A seed that looks unchanged is not guaranteed to remain viable forever.

Adding water softens this crowded interior and allows the reactions needed for germination to resume. Water uptake is called imbibition. Water can enter through permeable regions of the coat; a single pore is not a universal explanation for all seeds. Once hydrated, the embryo can use stored nutrients in respiration, supplying ATP for growth even in darkness.

Predict first

Two batches of viable moong beans are kept in darkness, one dry and one moist with access to air. Which observation would best support resumed metabolism rather than water absorption alone?

  1. Increased wet mass immediately after soaking
  2. Sustained oxygen uptake accompanied by carbon dioxide release
  3. Droplets on the glass beside wet cotton

What happens

The second observation. Absorbed water increases wet mass, and wet cotton can supply water vapour without respiration. Sustained gas exchange under suitable controlled conditions supports metabolic activity. Our home activity observes swelling and germination; it does not measure those gas rates.

Here is a chosen mass-accounting example, not a measured soaking result. Start with 50 g of seeds containing 10% water: 5 g water and 45 g other material. If they absorb 55 g water, total mass becomes 105 g, of which 60 g is water. That is 57.1% water. The model keeps the 45 g of other material fixed to isolate hydration; during real germination, respiration also changes the material account.

Investigation 1.1

Open the hydration workbench. Predict the total mass at 65% water before moving the slider. Compare that mass with the 105 g example above. Changing the slider changes a model state, not elapsed time. The moving dots illustrate restricted versus greater mobility; they do not measure ATP production or oxygen uptake.

Kitchen forensics: The waking bean

Use two clean small jars, cotton wool and whole moong beans sold for sprouting. Put two tablespoons of dry beans on dry cotton in Jar A. Soak another batch for about six hours, drain it, and place it on damp, not flooded, cotton in Jar B. Cover loosely so air can enter. Keep both together out of direct sunlight; inspect after a night and again the following day.

If you have a kitchen scale, weigh the same batch before and after soaking, draining and blotting consistently. Record the actual gain. Sketch any white embryonic roots, called radicles. Different seeds take different times, and some will not germinate. Swelling alone does not establish that a seed is alive. Droplets do not establish respiration, and a small batch need not feel warm.

Do not eat these experimental sprouts. Clear them away within two days, sooner if mould appears; do not sniff mouldy material. Wash hands, jars and surfaces. This comparison tests the effect of water availability on visible germination, not the rate of respiration.

Check yourself

A seed gains wet mass before a root appears. Does that prove it has built new living material? What later observation strengthens the evidence that it was viable?

Answer at the back of the book

1.2The flame and the bean

Now that you have watched a dry bean wake up, let us put it side by side with our rival suspect: a burning candle flame.

Look at why the candle flame fools so many people at first glance. A candle is made of solid hydrocarbon wax—chains of carbon and hydrogen atoms storing chemical potential energy, very much like the starch and fat stored inside a seed. When you touch a match to the wick:

  • The flame consumes fuel (melted wax drawn up the wick).
  • It takes in oxygen ($\text{O}_2$) from the room air and releases carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) and water vapour ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$)—the exact same gases a sprouting bean or a running human exchanges!
  • It moves and responds to a draught of air, bending away from a breeze.
  • It grows larger if you feed it more wick, and can start new flames if touched to another candle.

So why is the candle flame not alive, while the bean is?

To see the real difference, we have to zoom down to the nanometre scale—where chemistry and physics meet biology.

In the candle flame, vaporised wax reacts with oxygen through a network of reactions called combustion. Chemical changes transfer energy to the surroundings as heat and light. The flame has no cells, inherited instruction system or machinery that couples these reactions to cellular maintenance and reproduction. Many-step chemistry alone is not a test for life.

Now zoom inside a single cell of your soaked moong bean at $28^\circ\text{C}$. The bean is also reacting sugar with oxygen to make $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$! If you burned a spoonful of glucose sugar in a flame and let a bean cell oxidise the exact same spoonful of glucose, the total energy released from start to finish would be identical (recall from Book 2, The Moving World, Chapter 7, that energy is strictly conserved).

The difference is how the energy is released and what it is coupled to:

In the bean cell, enzymes, biological catalysts, help reactions proceed at ordinary cellular temperatures. The pathways connect nutrient breakdown to other reactions, including the formation of ATP. ATP-dependent reactions can in turn be linked to transport, repair and building cellular material. This physical connection between reactions is called coupling. Simply warming the cell would not provide the same organised chemical connections.

Predict first

A germinating seed in darkness develops a longer root while its total dry mass falls. Which account reconciles those observations?

  1. The growing root gains material transferred from reserves, while some reserve material leaves as respiration products
  2. Growth creates matter, so the dry-mass measurement must be wrong
  3. A longer root must mean the entire seed has gained dry mass

What happens

The first. Stored materials supply the developing root. Some fuel is also oxidised, and carbon dioxide leaves. A growing part can gain material while the whole seed loses dry mass. There is no claim here about equal gas quantities from wax and carbohydrate, or a fixed four-hour growth result.

Check yourself

Could a non-living chemical reaction release heat and carbon dioxide? Which additional features distinguish the viable seed from the flame?

Answer at the back of the book

1.3Paying for repairs, and SubbaRow’s ₹10 coin

Boston & Bhimavaram, 1929

A cell can build an organised structure while releasing heat and changing its surroundings. That fits the second law of thermodynamics: the total entropy of an isolated system does not decrease. A cell is an open system, exchanging matter and energy with its surroundings. Looking only at its internal organisation leaves part of the account out.

In his 1943 Dublin lectures, Erwin Schrödinger asked how living things maintain organisation. The useful question for our bean is concrete: how do reactions using stored nutrients help build and maintain its cells? A temporarily inactive dry seed can retain the machinery to resume. Irreversible loss of that capacity is different from a pause in activity.

Metabolism

All the enzyme-controlled chemical reactions taking place inside a living cell or organism—both those that break down fuel molecules to release energy and those that build up complex molecules for growth and repair.

All the hundreds of chemical reactions running inside a cell in growth, maintenance and energy transfer have a single name: metabolism (from the Greek metabolē, “change”). Metabolism has two halves that work like a demolition crew and a construction crew: - Breaking down fuel (like oxidising glucose in cellular respiration) to release stored chemical energy; and - Building up parts (like stitching amino acids into proteins, or glucose units into cellulose walls), which costs energy.

Breaking down fuel and building a cell must be physically connected. One important connection uses a small molecule: ATP, adenosine triphosphate.

In 1929, Yellapragada SubbaRow and Cyrus Fiske at Harvard, and independently Karl Lohmann in Germany, identified ATP in muscle extracts. SubbaRow had grown up in Bhimavaram and studied medicine in Madras. Identifying the molecule was one discovery; establishing its widespread role in energy transfer took further experiments and later work by many researchers.

The story behind this

The forgotten discoverer of the cell’s batteryBorn in Andhra Pradesh, he arrived in Boston almost penniless, helped identify ATP, later understood as a major cellular energy carrier, and created one of the first cancer chemotherapy drugs.
ATP (adenosine triphosphate)

A principal rechargeable energy carrier in cells. Enzymes couple ATP reactions to other chemical changes and cellular work. ATP is not the only energy carrier.

An ATP molecule contains adenine, a ribose sugar and three phosphate groups. After hydrolysis to ADP, adenosine diphosphate, two phosphates remain attached; the other product is inorganic phosphate, Pᵢ.

Follow one example: a motor protein binds ATP. Its reaction cycle includes ATP hydrolysis and changes in how the protein binds and changes shape. The linked cycle can produce movement. Hydrolysis in a separate beaker would not move that motor: the reactions and shape changes must be connected.

A different enzyme can transfer ATP’s terminal phosphate directly to another molecule. That produces a phosphorylated molecule, rather than releasing free phosphate in the same step. There is no single phosphate-transfer recipe used by every cellular machine.

Why can these reactions help? Under suitable cellular conditions, the overall ATP hydrolysis reaction lowers Gibbs free energy, the quantity used to judge the capacity of a chemical change to drive coupled work. Charge repulsion, the stability of the products and their interactions with water all contribute. Breaking a bond takes energy; the complete reaction can still release usable energy because it forms new interactions as well.

Think of ATP as a widely accepted ₹10 coin: useful for many transactions, but not the only currency. Cells regenerate ATP from ADP and phosphate through energy-coupled reactions. Respiration supplies such energy; chloroplasts also make ATP using light-supported processes.

How does a small pool support much larger daily turnover? Use illustrative adult-scale assumptions, not measurements of your body: a 50 g ATP pool and 40,000 g turned over per day.

40,000 ÷ 50 = 800 pool-equivalents per day.

1,440 minutes ÷ 800 = 1.8 minutes per pool-equivalent.

These calculations describe average turnover relative to an assumed pool. They do not say every molecule follows the same timetable. Actual pools and turnover vary with tissues, body size and activity.

Understand itATP

What is it?

A small molecule used as a rechargeable energy carrier in many cellular reactions.

Why is it called this?

Adenosine combines adenine and ribose; triphosphate means three phosphate groups. ADP has two attached phosphates.

What problem did it solve?

It helps connect energy-releasing reactions with transport, movement and chemical construction.

Why does it work?

Enzymes couple ATP reactions to other changes. The free-energy change of the whole coupled process determines whether it can proceed in the stated conditions.

How does it help?

A small, continually regenerated pool can support much larger turnover over time.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

ATP was identified in muscle in 1929. Later biochemical experiments established ATP-dependent reactions and their coupling to synthesis, transport and movement.

What it isn’t

A long-term fuel store, the only energy carrier, or a bond that gives out energy merely because it breaks.

Where does it stop working?

An ATP molecule alone does not make a complete working system. Suitable enzymes, reaction partners and conditions are required.

Your turn

Explain ATP to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“Snapping ATP’s end bond releases energy by itself.”

Bond breaking requires energy. Consider the full reaction, including the new interactions formed and the surrounding conditions. Also identify the coupling: an ATP reaction occurring separately cannot automatically drive another reaction elsewhere.

Check yourself

ATP is hydrolysed in a container beside an isolated motor protein. Must the motor move? Explain the missing connection.

Answer at the back of the book

1.4Seven processes in a living system

Once you understand what a living organism actually is—a cell-based machine that uses energy to maintain internal order and copy its genetic instructions—you no longer need to memorise a school textbook’s list of “seven characteristics of living things” as arbitrary rules. These processes describe living systems across their lives. They need not all be visible at once, and an individual can be alive without reproducing. A dry seed retains a capacity to resume development; it need not display rapid metabolism while dry.

In Cambridge IGCSE and British schools, the seven processes are remembered by the initials MRS GREN. Follow how these processes contribute to a living system:

Respiration (biological definition)

Cellular chemical reactions that break down nutrient molecules (such as glucose) and release energy for metabolism (recharging ATP). Never confuse it with breathing, which is just the muscular movement of air in and out of lungs.

Excretion vs. egestion

Excretion is the removal of waste products made by chemical reactions inside cells (such as $\text{CO}_2$ from respiration and urea from amino acid breakdown), plus excess water and salts. Egestion is passing out undigested food (such as plant cellulose fibre in faeces) that travelled through the gut tube without ever entering a body cell.

  1. Nutrition (getting raw materials and fuel): No machine can build new parts out of nothing or recharge ATP without an external energy source. Plants take in simple inorganic molecules ($\text{CO}_2$ gas from air, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and mineral ions from soil) and use sunlight to build their own organic food. Animals and fungi take in ready-made organic compounds by eating or absorbing other organisms.
  2. Respiration (unlocking fuel to recharge ATP): Stored nutrients can supply material for construction as well as chemical energy. Respiration transfers some of that energy into forms including ATP. Respiration is the set of chemical reactions inside cells that break down nutrient molecules (such as glucose) and release energy for metabolism. Active plant, animal, fungal and bacterial cells use nutrient reactions to supply energy. Extremely dry, inactive seeds remind us that rates can be greatly reduced during dormancy.
  3. Excretion (throwing out toxic chemical exhaust): Every chemical factory produces waste side-products that would poison the cell if allowed to build up. Aerobic respiration produces $\text{CO}_2$ (which turns blood acidic if not removed); breaking down excess amino acids in your liver produces toxic nitrogen waste (urea). Excretion is the removal from organisms of the waste products of metabolism, toxic materials, and substances in excess of requirements.
  4. Sensitivity (detecting clues in the outside world): A machine that cannot tell light from dark, hot from cold, or food from poison will quickly be destroyed. Sensitivity is the ability to detect or sense stimuli in the internal or external environment and to make appropriate responses.
  5. Movement (changing position to act on those clues): Movement is an action by an organism or part of an organism causing a change of position or place. Animals walk, swim or fly using muscles; plants move more slowly, growing their shoots towards light and opening or closing their leaf pores (stomata).
  6. Growth (building more ordered structure): Growth is a permanent increase in size and dry mass by an increase in cell number or cell size (or both). Notice the words permanent and dry mass: blowing up a balloon or soaking a sponge in water makes it bigger, but once you dry the sponge out, no new cellular matter was built!
  7. Reproduction (backing up the blueprint before the machine wears out): Every individual physical body eventually suffers too much damage or gets eaten. Reproduction is the processes that make more of the same kind of organism, copying the DNA instruction manual into a fresh generation.

Predict first

After you eat a bowl of sweetcorn or leafy greens, tough cellulose plant fibres pass all the way through your digestive tract without being broken down and leave your body in faeces. In biology, does passing faeces count as excretion?

  1. Yes, because faeces are waste leaving the body
  2. No—it is egestion, because those cellulose fibres never crossed into your body’s cells or took part in any metabolic chemical reaction inside a cell
  3. Yes, for animals, though not for plants

What happens

The second choice. Think of your digestive canal as a hollow tunnel running right through the middle of your body. A cellulose fibre that enters your mouth and leaves in faeces never crossed the gut wall into your bloodstream or entered a single cell’s metabolism. Passing undigested leftovers out of the gut tunnel is egestion. True excretion is getting rid of molecules that were produced by chemical reactions inside your cells (like $\text{CO}_2$ exhaled from your lungs, or urea filtered out of your blood into urine by your kidneys)—plus water and salts in excess.

Careful

“Animals breathe and respire, while plants only photosynthesise.”

Plants have no lungs, but their active cells carry out cellular respiration in both light and darkness. In a lit leaf, photosynthesis and respiration can occur together. Net gas exchange depends on their rates: bright light can produce net oxygen release; darkness removes the photosynthetic contribution. A dormant seed is a different state, with greatly restricted metabolic activity.

At school

For Cambridge IGCSE 0610 Topic 1.1: 1. If an exam question asks “Name the characteristic of living organisms shown when carbon dioxide leaves the lungs” or “when sweat/urine leaves the body”, the answer is excretion (never egestion). 2. If asked to define growth, always include “permanent increase in dry mass” (weighing an organism after all water has been removed, since temporary water intake is not growth).

Check yourself

A dry sponge dropped into a bucket of water swells to twice its size. A crystal of alum hung in a saturated alum solution slowly grows larger over a week. Using the biological definitions of growth and metabolism, explain why neither the sponge nor the alum crystal is carrying out biological growth.

Answer at the back of the book

1.5The outlaw at the border

Our working account of cellular life is this: living systems are made of one or more cells, use an internal metabolism with energy carriers such as ATP for maintenance and development, and inherit DNA instructions. The seven processes describe these systems across their lives.

And then a microscopic outlaw walks up to the border checkpoint and breaks our neat categories in half.

Virus

An infectious biological particle containing a DNA or RNA genome and a protein coat. Many familiar viruses are tens to hundreds of nanometres across, but sizes vary. Some have a lipid envelope. Viruses lack ribosomes and an independent cellular metabolism; replication requires a suitable host cell.

In 1892, the Russian botanist Dmitri Ivanovsky crushed up diseased tobacco leaves that were blotched with yellow-and-green spots (tobacco mosaic disease) and forced the sap through an ultra-fine porcelain filter whose pores were small enough to trap every known bacterium. To his astonishment, the crystal-clear liquid that dripped through the filter was still completely infectious! Six years later, the Dutch microbiologist Martinus Beijerinck repeated the test, showed that the invisible agent multiplied in living plant tissue, and named it a contagium vivum fluidum—a virus (from the Latin word for “slimy liquid” or “poison”).

When the electron microscope was invented in the 1930s, scientists finally saw what a virus looks like. Compare a bacterium and a virus in Figure 1.5:

Look at what a virus has, and what it lacks: - What it has: A short strip of genetic code (either DNA or RNA) locked inside a geometric protein coat (called a capsid, often shaped like a 20-sided icosahedron or a lunar lander), sometimes wrapped in a stolen patch of fatty membrane studded with spike proteins. - What it lacks: It has no cytoplasm, no ribosomes (no protein printers), no independent ATP-producing metabolism. A lipid envelope is not a complete cellular membrane system.

Outside a suitable host, a virus particle does not independently respire, grow or make proteins. Its molecules can still undergo chemical changes, so calling it chemically inert would go too far. Water and nutrients alone cannot supply the missing cellular machinery.

A virus depends on a host for replication, but it is more than software: its physical coat and, when present, envelope help deliver its genome. Different viruses enter in different ways; injection describes some bacteriophages, while other viruses use membrane fusion or uptake into the cell.

Inside a suitable cell, host ribosomes make viral proteins using RNA messages. Separate enzymes copy the viral genome; depending on the virus, these enzymes can be supplied by the host or encoded by the virus. New components assemble into particles, which may leave through cell rupture or budding. Ribosomes do not copy DNA or RNA genomes.

Predict first

A child comes down with a runny nose and fever caused by an influenza virus. Someone suggests taking an antibiotic (such as amoxicillin, which interferes with bacterial cell-wall construction; other antibiotics target bacterial ribosomes). Will the antibiotic cure the viral flu?

  1. Yes, because antibiotics kill all microscopic germs including viruses
  2. No, because a virus has no bacterial cell wall and no ribosomes of its own for the antibiotic to attack; unnecessary antibiotic use can select resistant bacteria
  3. Only if the virus has a fatty envelope

What happens

No. Antibiotics target specific bacterial machinery—such as bacterial cell-wall synthesis or bacterial ribosomes. Because a virus has no cell wall, no metabolism, and uses your own human ribosomes inside your cells to make its proteins, an antibiotic has nothing to attack in a virus. These antibiotics do not treat influenza. Unnecessary use can affect helpful bacteria and select resistant bacteria (Chapter 14).

Because viruses do not consist of cells and cannot carry out the MRS GREN processes on their own, Cambridge IGCSE and most biologists classify viruses as non-living—sitting right on the border between complex chemistry and cellular life. Cellular organisms are classified using shared features and evolutionary relationships. Two-part scientific names, developed systematically by Carl Linnaeus, identify species: for example Panthera pardus, the leopard. Later chapters return to ancestry and classification.

At school

In Cambridge IGCSE Biology (Topic 1.2 & 1.3), remember two exact exam rules: 1. Viruses are not in any of the Five Kingdoms (Prokaryote, Protoctist, Fungus, Plant, Animal). If an exam diagram shows a particle with only a protein coat and genetic material (DNA/RNA), identify it as a virus and state that it is non-living because it cannot reproduce or carry out metabolic processes outside a host cell. 2. In a two-part scientific name (binomial), the first word is the Genus (always written with a capital letter, e.g. Panthera) and the second word is the specific name (always written with a small letter, e.g. pardus), printed in italics (or underlined when handwritten). The two words together identify the species.

Check yourself

Compare three tiny objects: (1) a dry moong seed, (2) a rod-shaped bacterium (E. coli), and (3) a coronavirus particle. Which of the three contain ribosomes and can make their own ATP when given water and nutrients?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 1

The Viking Mars soil puzzle (1976)

NASA’s Viking landers investigated Martian soil in 1976. In the labelled-release experiment, adding nutrients containing radioactive carbon produced labelled gas. Heating a comparison sample strongly reduced the response. A later nutrient addition did not produce a renewed burst like the first.

Those observations raised a difficult question: metabolism or non-living soil chemistry? Heating can damage organisms, but it can also change chemical reactants. A second feeding is informative, but its result depends on the organisms and conditions assumed. It cannot alone settle every possible biological explanation.

The organic-chemical analyses were also difficult to interpret. Small chlorinated organic compounds were initially treated as contamination. Later experiments suggested that perchlorates, discovered on Mars by Phoenix in 2008, could destroy organics during heated analysis and produce such compounds. That interpretation does not establish life either. Viking provided no clear evidence of living microorganisms.

Which observations could fit both explanations? What further independent evidence would make a biological interpretation stronger?

Show the solution

Gas release and sensitivity to heating can occur in either biological or non-biological systems. Failure to respond to another feeding challenges a simple growth model, but does not identify the cause by itself. Seek independent evidence: reproducible activity under varied conditions, chemical analysis that accounts for reactive soil and instrument effects, and signs of a coordinated biological system. Organic molecules alone can also have non-biological origins. The lesson is to compare explanations and combine evidence, rather than turn one suggestive response into a verdict.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

We now know that every living thing on Earth—from a waking moong bean to a human detective—is built out of microscopic, ATP-powered compartments called cells. In Chapter 2, we will step inside that compartment in three dimensions, meet the ancient bacterial stowaways that power it, and solve a geometric puzzle: why can’t a single cell grow as big as a dog?
