Chapter 2

The nanocity under the microscope

The big questionWhy is your body built from trillions of tiny cells instead of one giant cell?

  1. 2.1Inside the walled city
  2. 2.2The stowaways that became power stations
  3. 2.3The geometry trap
  4. 2.4Specialists in the city

The moong bean in Chapter 1 kept its machinery and its instructions through the dry months. Add water, and its cells can resume the work of building a root. Now look more closely at the workers. What is inside one cell, and why does a growing root make more cells instead of simply swelling one cell larger and larger?

An often-used estimate puts an adult human body at about 30 trillion human cells. That is an estimate for a reference adult, not a count of you. The puzzle survives any change in the number: why divide a body into such small pieces? Start with something much easier to cut than a human body. An onion will do.

2.1Inside the walled city

Mumbai, an onion on the kitchen board

Peel a white onion bulb. Beside it, put a green leaf. Both came from plants. If every plant cell follows the same school drawing, both should be packed with green bodies. Yet the thin skin inside the onion is almost transparent. Where did its green parts go?

A drawing of “the plant cell” is a useful collection of features. It can tempt you into treating every real cell as a copy of that drawing.

Predict first

A white onion bulb cell has no developed green bodies for capturing light. What else must be missing?

  1. Its mitochondria, because plants use light instead of respiration
  2. Its cell membrane, because the wall does that job
  3. Neither: it can have mitochondria and a membrane without chloroplasts

What happens

The third choice. An ordinary white bulb cell has mitochondria and a cell membrane. It can use stored nutrients to supply ATP without capturing light itself.

How do we know? Two plant samples, different equipment Repeatable microscopy

Compare a thin onion bulb epidermis with a thin green leaf under a school microscope. Cell outlines appear in both. In suitable living leaf material, green bodies can be seen inside the outlines; the white bulb epidermis has no developed chloroplasts. That observation challenges a universal “all plant cells are green inside” rule.

It does not tell you everything in either cell. Ordinary light microscopy cannot resolve individual ribosomes or the two molecular layers of a cell membrane. Finer structural observations require other methods, including electron microscopy. A structure missing from your view may be too small or too transparent to see. Our labelled cutaway combines knowledge from several methods; it is not a photograph of what one school microscope reveals.

Start at the boundary. What keeps the inside separate, and what supports it?

Cell membrane

The thin boundary around a cell that controls movement of substances into and out of it. A plant’s cell wall lies outside this membrane.

The boundary that separates a cell’s internal mixture from its surroundings is a double layer of oily molecules called lipids, with proteins embedded in it. Small molecules cross in different ways; some pass through the lipid layer, while others use protein pathways. This boundary controls what enters and leaves: the cell membrane. In a plant, a supporting cellulose mesh lies outside it: the cell wall. A mesh that gives support and a boundary that controls passage do different jobs.

Inside is a crowded mixture of water, dissolved substances, large molecules and working structures. In a cell with a nucleus, the region inside the outer membrane but outside the nucleus is the cytoplasm. In a bacterium, which has no nucleus, that name covers the interior within its membrane. Our drawing leaves gaps so you can see the parts; those gaps do not mean the real cell is an almost-empty bag.

Follow the instructions. Where is information kept, and how is it used?

Most ordinary animal and plant cells keep most of their DNA behind another membrane boundary. This compartment is the nucleus. Cells with this arrangement are called eukaryotic. Bacteria have DNA too, but no membrane-enclosed nucleus; they are prokaryotic. In a typical bacterial diagram, the main DNA forms a circle in the cytoplasm. Smaller extra DNA rings, when present, are plasmids. Bacterial walls are usually made with peptidoglycan, a tough mesh of sugar chains linked by short protein-like chains. Plant cellulose is a different material.

All three cell types have tiny structures that join amino acids into proteins using a molecular message copied from DNA: ribosomes. That message is made of a molecule called RNA; we will follow the copying in Chapter 11.

Follow the energy supply. Which structures help supply ATP, and which capture light?

Typical plant and animal cells also contain mitochondria, where important stages of aerobic respiration supply ATP from the chemical energy in nutrients. Green leaf cells additionally contain chloroplasts, which use light energy to build carbohydrates. Many mature plant cells have a large vacuole containing cell sap, a watery solution of substances such as sugars and salts; its water helps press the cell contents against the supporting wall.

Read the plate from the outside in, then compare these selected specimens:

QuestionTypical animal cellGreen leaf cellTypical bacterium
Controlled boundary?Cell membraneMembrane inside a cellulose wallMembrane, usually inside a different wall
Instructions and protein making?Most DNA in nucleus; ribosomesMost DNA in nucleus; ribosomesDNA without a nucleus; ribosomes
ATP and light capture?Mitochondria; no chloroplastsMitochondria and chloroplastsATP-making machinery without either organelle; some bacteria capture light

The onion bulb gives us a fourth comparison: it retains plant boundaries and mitochondria without developed chloroplasts. The cards below revisit the equipment after the whole route; use them to explain the differences back in your own words.

Understand itNucleus and ribosomes

What is it?

The nucleus holds most DNA in a typical plant or animal cell. Ribosomes use RNA messages to join amino acids into proteins.

Why is it called this?

Nucleus comes from a Latin word for a kernel. Ribosome means a ribose-containing body: ribose is the sugar in RNA, which forms part of a ribosome.

What problem did it solve?

The distinction connects stored information with construction: DNA instructions can be copied into messages, then used to assemble particular proteins.

Why does it work?

RNA messages carry a sequence copied from DNA. At ribosomes, that sequence specifies the order of amino acids joined into a protein.

How does it help?

You can distinguish storing instructions from using a message to build something. A bacterium has ribosomes and DNA despite lacking an enclosed nucleus.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Microscopy and molecular experiments locate DNA and ribosomes and establish how RNA messages guide protein assembly.

What it isn’t

A cell nucleus is not the atomic nucleus from chemistry. A ribosome is a molecular assembly, not a tiny membrane-bounded room.

Where does it stop working?

Some specialised cells lose this equipment. A typical-cell inventory is not a list that every living cell must retain.

Your turn

Explain Nucleus and ribosomes to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Understand itMitochondria and chloroplasts

What is it?

Mitochondria carry out important stages of aerobic respiration that supply ATP. Chloroplasts use light energy to build carbohydrates.

Why is it called this?

Mitochondrion combines Greek words for thread and little granule. Chloroplast combines Greek roots meaning green and formed. These names describe appearance; they do not explain the chemistry.

What problem did it solve?

The distinction separates building carbohydrates with light from using chemical energy in nutrients to supply ATP for cellular work.

Why does it work?

Each contains membranes and protein machinery suited to particular reactions. The reactions transfer energy; neither structure creates it.

How does it help?

It explains why green leaf cells have both structures, while ordinary white onion bulb cells can keep working without developed chloroplasts.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Structural microscopy identifies the compartments; chemical experiments connect their machinery with light capture and respiration.

What it isn’t

“Power station” is a reminder of ATP supply, not an explanation by itself. Chloroplasts do not replace mitochondria in a green leaf cell.

Where does it stop working?

This is a typical-cell comparison. Bacteria perform their own metabolism without mitochondria or chloroplasts, and some specialised cells lose organelles.

Your turn

Explain Mitochondria and chloroplasts to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Understand itCell compartments

What is it?

A cell has a boundary and internal machinery. Some cells also separate particular jobs into membrane-bounded spaces.

Why is it called this?

A compartment is a separated space. Hooke used cell, meaning a small room, for the box-like spaces he saw in cork; those were remains of dead cells.

What problem did it solve?

Separating spaces allows different chemical conditions and reactions within one cell, while the outer membrane separates the cell from its surroundings.

Why does it work?

Membranes keep some substances apart and contain proteins that control passage and carry out reactions.

How does it help?

You can explain a cell’s equipment by the work it does, then compare real cells instead of copying one standard picture.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Microscopy reveals structures; other experiments establish their chemical contents and functions. One instrument does not reveal every part.

What it isn’t

A cell is neither a flat drawing nor a little city with people deciding what to do. Molecules interact through physical and chemical processes.

Where does it stop working?

Typical diagrams have exceptions. Mature human red blood cells, which we meet below, have lost their nucleus and mitochondria.

Your turn

Explain Cell compartments to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“Plant cells have chloroplasts instead of mitochondria.”

Ordinary green leaf cells have both. Chloroplasts build carbohydrates using light; mitochondria help supply ATP through respiration. Onion bulb and root cells can respire using nutrients without developed chloroplasts. Respiration continues in light and darkness.

A white peel and a green leaf

With an adult handling any knife, put a white onion peel beside a green leaf on a white plate. Look with your eyes or a hand lens. Record what you can see, and separately what would require a microscope. You can compare colour and texture; a phone photograph alone does not establish whether an individual cell contains a nucleus or mitochondria. If your school has slides, compare them with your teacher. Wash your hands and clear the plate afterwards.

At school

For IGCSE 0610 Topic 2.1, identify each structure and give its function in animal, plant and bacterial cells; bacteria have circular DNA in the cytoplasm and may have plasmids, rather than a nucleus. Topic 2.2 uses magnification = image size ÷ actual size, with both sizes in the same units.

Suppose a specimen is 50 µm long and its printed image is 40 mm long. These are example dimensions, not measurements of our schematic.

Actual size = 50 ÷ 1000 = 0.050 mm.

Magnification = 40 mm ÷ 0.050 mm = 800×.

A resized screen image has a different magnification. A correctly attached scale bar changes size with the image and remains useful. Enlarging an image alone cannot reveal details the microscope failed to resolve.

Open the 3D Cell Explorer to turn a cutaway and compare it with the plate. Keep asking which features belong to this specimen, and which have been enlarged for visibility.

The story behind this

The rooms in a piece of corkA piece of dead plant tissue supplied the name for the living units that build a body.

Check yourself

A cell has a wall, a membrane, ribosomes and DNA, but no membrane-enclosed nucleus. Is the wall enough to identify it as a plant cell? Explain.

Answer at the back of the book

2.2The stowaways that became power stations

Boston, 1967

You have just separated the nucleus from the rest of a cell in your mental picture. Now comes an awkward clue: some of the cell’s DNA is elsewhere. Mitochondria have their own inherited DNA. Chloroplasts do too.

Lynn Margulis, publishing as Lynn Sagan, brought evidence for a remarkable explanation together in a 1967 paper. Perhaps these structures descended from bacteria that once lived inside other cells. The idea had earlier advocates; she made a powerful case for taking it seriously again.

An internal working structure such as a mitochondrion or chloroplast is called an organelle: a “little organ”. Before accepting the ancestry idea, ask what evidence could distinguish an internal bacterial descendant from a compartment assembled entirely by its host.

Predict first

Which finding would give the stronger reason to investigate bacterial ancestry?

  1. A mitochondrion looks roughly oval, like some bacteria
  2. Mitochondria have their own DNA and bacterial-related protein-making machinery, and gene comparisons connect them to bacteria
  3. Mitochondria are too small to see clearly with unaided eyes

What happens

The second choice. Many unrelated things are oval or tiny. Several independent inherited similarities provide a much stronger test of ancestry.

How do we know? DNA outside the nucleus Ris and Plaut, 1962

Hans Ris and Walter Plaut investigated the chloroplast of the single-celled green alga Chlamydomonas. They combined electron microscopy with chemical tests for DNA. Particular regions stained as DNA, and fine fibres in those regions were sensitive to a DNA-breaking enzyme, DNase.

The comparison mattered: a thread-like appearance alone could mislead, while the chemical response tested what the material was. DNA was present inside a chloroplast, outside the nucleus. That result did not by itself establish the whole history of the organelle. It supplied a testable clue, alongside evidence gathered by other researchers. Later comparisons of inherited sequences helped establish which organisms were related to which. Margulis’s contribution was a synthesis of evidence and an evolutionary explanation, not one experiment that settled everything in 1967.

Consider a cell containing another organism. If the internal organism survives and divides, its descendants can pass into later host cells. If its chemical activity benefits the host, and the host supplies useful materials, the association can persist across generations. Changes that make the partners more dependent on each other can accumulate. No partner has to foresee the outcome or make an agreement.

Endosymbiosis

An association in which one organism lives inside another. The endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts explains their descent from internal bacterial partners.

This is the kind of history supported for mitochondria and chloroplasts: endosymbiosis. Their ancestors were bacteria. Across evolutionary time, many genes moved to the host’s nucleus or were lost. Present-day organelles rely on proteins and other supplies from the surrounding cell; you cannot simply release one and expect it to resume independent bacterial life.

The clues fit together. Each organelle is surrounded by two membranes. Each retains DNA and ribosomes related to bacterial machinery. New mitochondria and chloroplasts arise by growth and division of existing ones. Most tellingly, comparisons of genes connect mitochondria to bacterial ancestry and chloroplasts to cyanobacteria, a group that carries out photosynthesis.

Calling a mitochondrion a “power station” can help you remember its role after you understand the mechanism: reactions use chemical energy from nutrients to supply ATP for other work. It creates no energy. A chloroplast uses incoming light energy to build carbohydrates. An ordinary green plant cell carries descendants of both kinds of bacterial partner.

Understand itEndosymbiosis

What is it?

A lasting association with one organism inside another; in this case, bacterial partners became integrated organelles over evolutionary time.

Why is it called this?

Endo- means within; symbiosis means living together.

What problem did it solve?

It explains why some compartments in our cells have their own inherited machinery and particularly close bacterial relatives.

Why does it work?

Partners that persist and reproduce together can become dependent. Gene transfer and gene loss can make that dependence permanent.

How does it help?

It connects present cell structure to evolutionary history and generates predictions about DNA, ribosomes and division.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Structural observations, chemical tests and comparisons of inherited sequences support the same explanation.

What it isn’t

An intentional partnership, or a claim that every part of a cell began as a swallowed bacterium.

Where does it stop working?

It does not settle every detail of the first host or every step by which the association began.

Your turn

Explain Endosymbiosis to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“Margulis proved that mitochondria are ordinary bacteria living in us today.”

Their ancestry is bacterial. Their present dependence on host-cell machinery makes them integrated parts of the cell. The evidence accumulated through many researchers; the 1967 paper was a major contribution to that investigation.

At school

For 0610, give the present-day functions of mitochondria, chloroplasts and ribosomes precisely; “powerhouse” alone does not explain a function. This ancestry account explains why a cell can contain DNA outside its nucleus.

The story behind this

A cell with more than one ancestryThe clues inside mitochondria and chloroplasts connected cell structure with an ancient history of living together.

Check yourself

An unknown compartment has two membranes. Is that enough to conclude that it descended from a bacterium? Name two further tests.

Answer at the back of the book

2.3The geometry trap

Mumbai, cubes on the kitchen plate

Put a small potato cube beside a larger one. The larger cube has more outside surface. That seems helpful if its interior has to receive substances from the surrounding liquid. Perhaps a larger cell could feed itself more easily because its boundary is larger too.

There is a second quantity to count: how much interior that boundary serves. Keep shape and chemical demand per unit volume the same, and enlarge the cube. The outside and the inside do not grow at the same rate.

Predict first

A cube’s side doubles from 1 cm to 2 cm. What happens to its surface and volume?

  1. Both double
  2. Surface becomes four times as large; volume becomes eight times as large
  3. Surface becomes eight times as large; volume becomes four times as large

What happens

The second choice. Each face has two dimensions to double; the interior has three. The bigger cube has more surface in total but less surface for each cubic centimetre of interior.

How do we know? Count faces before trusting the picture A repeatable geometric test

A cube has six square faces. A 1 cm face has area 1 cm², so the cube has 6 cm² of surface around 1 cm³ of volume. Double the side: each face becomes 4 cm², giving 24 cm² around 8 cm³. Tenfold side gives 600 cm² around 1000 cm³.

You can check the middle case by cutting a 2 cm cube into eight 1 cm cubes. The total volume stays 8 cm³. If you separate the pieces so liquid reaches every face, the exposed area becomes 8 × 6 = 48 cm². Cutting has exposed new surface. This arithmetic is exact for ideal cubes; it makes no claim about how far a particular dye travels into potato tissue.

Surface-area-to-volume ratio

Surface area divided by volume. For the same shape, enlarging all lengths reduces the surface available per unit of interior.

Divide surface area by volume to ask how much boundary there is for each unit of interior. This is the surface-area-to-volume ratio, often written SA/V. A cube of side a has surface area 6a² and volume a³, so its ratio is 6/a. The ratio falls as the side grows.

Why should a cell care about that arithmetic? Its chemistry uses materials throughout its active interior. Substances entering through its outside must cross a limited boundary, then reach the places where reactions use them. If demand per unit volume stays similar, enlargement adds demand faster than exchange surface. The centre also lies farther from the outside. Small size helps with both constraints.

A thought experiment makes the difference visible. Choose a reached layer 2 mm deep around every face of a cube. In a 1 cm cube, that leaves a 0.6 cm core: 78.4% of the full volume lies in the reached layer. In a 10 cm cube, the same depth reaches only 11.5%. Those percentages follow from the geometry. We have not measured a dye speed, and real diffusion produces gradual concentration changes rather than a perfectly sharp coloured boundary.

There is no universal rule that every cell must fit one tiny size. A long, thin cell can keep its interior close to a surface. Folded boundaries provide extra area. Internal transport can carry materials, and a large storage compartment can leave only a thin active layer. Geometry sets a constraint; structure changes how the constraint applies.

A large body still has a second supply problem. Its internal cells do not all touch outside air or food. Many small cells shorten routes within each cell, but transport systems must also bring supplies close to them and carry wastes away. In animals, circulation helps do that; in a plant, conducting tissues connect roots and leaves with other parts. Dividing a body into cells and supplying those cells are two connected jobs.

Understand itSurface-area-to-volume ratio

What is it?

A comparison of the area across which exchange can occur with the volume that may depend on that exchange.

Why is it called this?

The name states the calculation: surface area divided by volume.

What problem did it solve?

It explains why making a cell larger can make exchange harder even while its total surface increases.

Why does it work?

For similarly shaped objects, area grows with the square of length while volume grows with the cube.

How does it help?

It connects small cells, thin extensions and folded exchange surfaces with the same geometry.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Count areas and volumes, then test exchange while controlling other factors such as material, temperature and time.

What it isn’t

A rule that every large cell dies, or a measurement of a particular substance’s diffusion rate.

Where does it stop working?

Ratio alone cannot predict exchange when permeability, chemical demand, shape or internal transport differs.

Your turn

Explain Surface-area-to-volume ratio to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“The large cube has more surface, so it must exchange substances more easily.”

It has more surface in total, but less per unit of volume. Compare both quantities. A dyed surface also does not show that every living cell inside the potato has received the same amount of a substance.

Investigation 2.3: Keep the material, change the shape

Use one clean piece of soft roti dough. First shape a compact lump; then flatten the same piece into a thin disc, without adding or removing dough. Before flattening, predict what happens to the shortest route from the centre to a surface. Compare that route with your eyes or a ruler. The disc’s centre is much closer to its nearest surface. The amount of material has stayed approximately the same while the shape has changed.

This is a geometry model: dough does not test a living cell membrane. Keep it separate from food being served, and wash your hands before and after. The cube arithmetic and this shape comparison are the main investigation; the optional staining activity below asks a less predictable question about real tissue.

Optional exploration: How far does the colour go?

An adult must cut the potato and make every later centre cut. Use raw potato cubes with sides about 0.5 cm, 1 cm and 2 cm, three small cups, a ruler, and cool beetroot juice or water with food colouring. Put each cube in enough of the same liquid to cover it fully. Keep the cups together, record the starting time, and predict which cube will have the largest fraction visibly coloured.

Inspect after 15 minutes. Rinse and blot the outside briefly; have the adult cut each cube through its centre. Record any visible penetration depth and untouched centre. If there is no clear boundary, write that down: do not invent a depth. You can compare another set after a longer recorded time. Dye binding, tissue permeability and damaged cut cells can make the result patchy or faint; this activity may not produce a neat coloured layer.

Use the live model to explore a chosen or measured depth, keeping its geometric assumption separate from your observations. Never eat the used pieces. Clear them away the same day, and wash hands and surfaces. No heating or microbial growing is involved.

At school

For 0610, relate efficient exchange to a large surface area and a short diffusion distance, and distinguish total area from area relative to volume; Topic 3.1 also asks how surface area and distance affect diffusion. Give units when calculating: cm² ÷ cm³ gives cm⁻¹.

Eight separate 1 cm cubes have the same total volume as one 2 cm cube. Which arrangement has more exposed surface when all faces touch the surrounding liquid, and by what factor?

Answer at the back of the book

2.4Specialists in the city

Mumbai, a breath on a dusty afternoon

Air entering your breathing passages carries tiny particles. A sticky layer traps many of them. Under a microscope, the surface beneath that layer is busy: rows of tiny hairs beat and move the mucus towards your throat.

Now compare one of those cells with a red blood cell or a root hair cell. A single standard “cell” outline would hide the feature that explains each job. We have reached the next reason a body contains many cells: different arrangements of the shared machinery support different work.

Predict first

Two root cells contain similar amounts of active material and have equally permeable membranes. Which feature gives the stronger reason to predict faster absorption under the same surrounding conditions?

  1. A long, thin extension that increases exposed contact area and keeps routes short
  2. A compact sphere because reducing its surface always speeds absorption
  3. The same volume guarantees the same absorption rate, whatever the shape

What happens

The extension increases exposed contact area while keeping routes short. Equal volume does not guarantee equal absorption: shape changes the exchange surface and distances even when the amount of active material stays similar.

How do we know? Follow the moving layer Microscopy and comparison

In living airway tissue, microscopy shows hairs beating along the cell surface while the mucus above them moves. Compare the moving surface with the flexible discs seen in a blood sample and the extensions seen on young roots. Different structures recur in different places, associated with different activities.

A still image helps identify shape; watching living material supplies evidence of movement. Neither observation alone explains every molecular step. The model improves when we connect structure with a physical job: beating hairs exert forces on the surrounding layer; a thin disc shortens the distance across it; an extension adds contact surface. These are repeatable observations and comparisons, not a fictional experiment performed by one historical discoverer. Use prepared school material or documented microscopy; do not collect blood or culture airway samples at home.

The beating hairs are cilia, and the cells carrying them are ciliated epithelial cells. Their coordinated, ATP-driven movements shift mucus in the trachea and bronchi. The mucus traps particles; the cilia move the layer.

A mature human red blood cell is a flexible disc with a dip on both broad faces. Its thin shape gives oxygen a short route across the cell, and haemoglobin inside binds oxygen for transport. It has lost its nucleus and mitochondria. It still obtains ATP through reactions that do not require mitochondria. “Every animal cell has a nucleus” was only a typical-cell shortcut.

A root hair cell extends part of its surface into the spaces around soil particles, increasing contact for absorption of water and mineral ions. A palisade mesophyll cell in a leaf contains many chloroplasts. Its position and column-like arrangement help expose photosynthetic machinery to light. It also has mitochondria. A neurone has long, narrow processes and branches that connect it with other cells; electrical impulses travel along its membrane. Length does not require the whole cell to become a thick sphere.

Reproductive cells specialise too. A sperm cell has a tail whose movement propels it through fluid. An egg cell has a much larger cytoplasm containing materials for early development. Both carry hereditary information. We will investigate how that information combines later in the book.

Specialised cell

A cell whose structure suits a particular function, such as moving mucus, absorbing materials or transporting oxygen.

New cells are produced by division of existing cells. As a root grows, it makes more cells; those cells can then develop different structures. Cells with particular structures and functions are specialised cells. They arise as cells develop different patterns of activity and structure; an individual cell does not decide which equipment to grow.

Cells working together in a shared function form a tissue. Different tissues working together form an organ; several organs can cooperate in an organ system, within the whole organism. Follow a palisade cell into palisade mesophyll tissue, then into the leaf, the shoot system and the bean plant. The leaf also contains other tissues, including protective and transport tissues. A tissue need not contain only identical cells.

Understand itSpecialised cells and organisation

What is it?

Cells have structures suited to particular functions. Their coordinated work builds tissues, organs and organ systems within an organism.

Why is it called this?

Specialised means suited to a particular kind of work. Organ comes from a word for an instrument or tool.

What problem did it solve?

One cell shape cannot perform every job equally well. Different structures support exchange, transport, movement and communication.

Why does it work?

Physical features change performance: extensions add area, thin regions shorten distances and beating hairs move a fluid layer.

How does it help?

You can infer a possible job from structure and test it against observations, rather than learning disconnected cell pictures.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Microscopy reveals structures and activities; experiments test the relationship between a changed structure and its performance.

What it isn’t

A claim that each cell chooses its role, or that an organ contains only one kind of tissue.

Where does it stop working?

An outline alone cannot identify every cell. Chemical composition and activity matter too.

Your turn

Explain Specialised cells and organisation to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“A bigger animal is made by making all its cells bigger.”

Larger bodies generally contain more cells. Their different cell types also have different shapes and sizes. A long neurone is compatible with the geometry argument because it remains thin; a mature human red blood cell is compatible with cell theory despite having lost its nucleus.

Return to the dough comparison in Investigation 2.3. Flattening shortened the route from the centre to the nearest surface without changing the amount of material. A red blood cell’s thin regions give oxygen a short exchange distance. Its real performance also depends on its membrane and haemoglobin; the dough models only the geometry.

At school

For 0610 Topic 2.1, connect each specialised cell to its function, including sperm and egg cells for reproduction; use cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism with an example at every level. Cambridge commonly spells the nerve cell neurone.

Check yourself

A student writes “palisade cell → leaf → palisade tissue → plant”. Repair the order, add the missing level, and explain why a leaf is an organ.

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 2

The pearl in the coastal mud

In 1997, researchers collected sediment from the continental shelf off Namibia. The bacterium described in 1999, Thiomargarita namibiensis, formed pale beads. Some cells reached 750 µm across, large enough to see without a microscope.

Three clues sit in the file: it really is a bacterium; a huge nitrate-storing vacuole occupies much of its interior; most active cytoplasm forms a thin layer around that store. Does this overturn the geometry argument? Explain which distance and which volume matter.

Show the solution

It changes how the argument applies. Most of the large cell’s volume is storage, so it is misleading to treat all of it as equally active cytoplasm. The thin active layer keeps much of the working machinery close to an exchange surface. Area, active volume, transport and chemical demand still matter. This coastal-sediment bacterium is a counterexample to “all bacteria are tiny”, not a suspension of geometry.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

A boundary creates a new puzzle. A cell must keep its internal chemistry separate while continually exchanging materials. How can anything cross without the cell simply mixing into the world outside? Next, we follow the random movements of molecules—and ask how Mumbai’s mangroves survive with their roots in salty water.

Where this chapter comes from

3

Chapter 3

The Crowded Train & The Salty Sea

The big questionMangroves stand in salty tidal water that makes many garden plants wilt. How can their roots take up water from it?

  1. 3.1Blind bounces, not wishes
  2. 3.2Water potential and the selective gate
  3. 3.3Balloons inside boxes
  4. 3.4Pushing uphill: roots and the salty sea

Chapter 2 gave our microscopic city a boundary. Now there is a problem at every doorway. Oxygen must enter, waste must leave, and water must stay within useful limits. A membrane that blocked everything would make a very secure, very short-lived cell.

Walk along Carter Road and look towards the mangroves from the public path. Their roots occupy mud reached by salty tides. Put an ordinary garden plant in similarly salty conditions and it may lose water, even with wet soil around it. The mangrove has no exemption from physics. Its survival depends on the same rules that can make a potato strip go limp in a kitchen cup. To understand those roots, begin with a crowded train.

3.1Blind bounces, not wishes

Mumbai, a crowded local train doorway

At a station, people pass through a train doorway in both directions. Counting only the people getting off gives you a poor account of how the carriage population changes. You must subtract those getting on. That difference is the net change.

Keep the two-way counting. Leave people’s decisions behind. A molecule has no destination in mind, and it cannot inspect the other side of a membrane for an empty seat.

Predict first

Two equal-sized chambers contain the same gas at the same temperature. One begins with more molecules than the other. An opening connects them. Which account best predicts the change after the opening is made?

  1. Crossings occur only from the more crowded chamber until concentrations match
  2. Crossings occur both ways, with more expected from the more concentrated side
  3. Equal temperature means the expected numbers crossing each way must already be equal

What happens

The second account follows from random motion. More molecules near one side of the opening give more opportunities to cross from that side. Individual molecules need no instruction about the other chamber.

How do we know? A spreading colour, then a stricter test Repeatable observation

Place a drop of food colouring in water and its colour spreads. This establishes something observable: the coloured material changes its distribution. It does not, by itself, establish how. A falling drop, small temperature differences and accidental stirring can move whole parcels of water too.

Our chamber model asks a more limited question. If all particles follow the same blind movement rule, with no preference for the emptier side, can their distribution spread out? Count crossings in both directions. Starting with unequal concentrations usually gives a net transfer towards the less concentrated side; starting equally still gives crossings. This is a test of what the rule predicts, not a substitute for observing real molecules. The distinction matters: a convincing animation is evidence about its own instructions before it is evidence about nature.

Gas molecules continually move and collide. A small dissolved molecule also changes direction through encounters with the surrounding liquid. Thermal motion does not stop when the distribution looks even. In The Invisible World, you met this restless molecular motion; here we count one of its consequences.

Take an invented model with 80 particles on the left and 20 on the right, in equal volumes. Suppose each has the same one-in-ten chance of crossing during an interval. We expect about eight crossings rightward and two leftward. That gives a net six rightward. These are averages for our chosen rule, not a prediction that exactly six real molecules cross a cell each second.

Diffusion

The net movement of particles down their concentration gradient as a result of random movement. Individual particles can move in either direction.

The amount of a substance in a given volume is its concentration. Its net spreading from higher to lower concentration, through random motion, is diffusion. The change in concentration across a distance is a concentration gradient. More particles in a larger volume need not mean a higher concentration; that is why the two chamber volumes matter.

At 50 particles on each side, our rule predicts about five crossings each way. The expected net change is zero. A small sample can still fluctuate: 49 and 51 is no surprise. This moving balance is dynamic equilibrium. “No net movement” describes the difference between two flows, not the behaviour of each molecule.

A respiring cell can keep using oxygen, maintaining a lower oxygen concentration inside than outside. Oxygen then has a net inward diffusion. Carbon dioxide made inside can have its own outward gradient at the same time. Each substance has its own account; the membrane does not send “everything” one way.

For a quantitative connection to physics: At about 27 °C, the characteristic thermal energy scale called kᵦT is about 4.14 × 10⁻²¹ J. Here T is temperature in kelvin, and kᵦ is the constant that converts temperature into this energy scale. It is a scale for comparison, not a fixed energy carried by every molecule.

A steeper gradient and a larger exchange area increase net transfer, other conditions being equal. A shorter path helps too: a particle’s wandering includes many steps that undo earlier progress. Higher temperature generally speeds diffusion because molecular motion is faster. The cell spends no ATP to instruct these crossings. Their energy comes from molecular motion.

Understand itDiffusion

What is it?

Net spreading down a concentration gradient, produced by particles moving randomly in both directions.

Why is it called this?

The word comes from a Latin root meaning to spread or pour out. The name describes the result; random movement explains it.

What problem did it solve?

It explains how a substance can spread without a cell directing each particle or paying ATP for each crossing.

Why does it work?

With more particles in an equal volume on one side, more have opportunities to cross from that side. Opposing flows usually differ until concentrations become similar.

How does it help?

It explains oxygen uptake, carbon dioxide loss and why a short exchange distance matters.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Spreading observations and molecular evidence support the account. A random-walk model lets us test whether blind motion alone can produce net spreading.

What it isn’t

A decision to find space, or a rule that every particle travels downhill at every instant.

Where does it stop working?

Bulk flow can also transport material. A membrane that excludes a substance prevents that crossing even if a concentration gradient exists.

Your turn

Explain Diffusion to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“Once it is evenly spread, the molecules have finished moving.”

They keep moving. Near equilibrium, crossings in opposite directions balance on average. Closing the opening stops transfer between chambers; it does not switch off motion within each chamber.

A drop with no spoon

Use food colouring and a clear glass of cool tap water on a stable tray. Let the water settle, add one small drop gently, and watch without stirring. Sketch the coloured region at the start and after a few minutes. Keep the glass away from food and drinking cups afterwards.

If a coloured plume falls or swirls, record it. That is a clue that whole water parcels are moving, so you cannot use this glass to measure a pure diffusion rate. Compare your observation with the model’s isolated random movement rule. Empty the glass, rinse it and wipe spills; do not taste the coloured water.

At school

For 0610 Topic 3.1, include net movement, higher to lower concentration, and random movement in your explanation; the energy comes from the particles’ kinetic energy. The four named rate factors are surface area, temperature, concentration gradient and distance.

Check yourself

An equal-volume model starts with 80 particles left and 20 right. You count 17 rightward crossings and 11 leftward crossings. How many particles are now on each side, and has movement been one-way?

Answer at the back of the book

3.2Water potential and the selective gate

Baltimore, a water-channel experiment published in 1992

Two frog egg cells sit in very dilute water. They look much alike at first. One soon swells much faster than the other. The important difference is a protein placed in its membrane.

The surprise concerns the boundary. A cell is surrounded by water, and filled with water. Why should changing a protein alter how fast water crosses?

Predict first

Researchers arrange for some frog egg cells to make a suspected water-channel protein. Control eggs do not receive the instructions for that protein. What result would support the channel idea?

  1. The two groups always swell at exactly the same rate
  2. Eggs making the protein take up water much faster in dilute surroundings
  3. Only salt can enter eggs making the protein

What happens

The second result supports a water pathway. The control comparison matters: swelling by itself would not identify which protein changed water permeability.

How do we know? The protein that changed the boundary 1992 publication

Gregory Preston, Peter Agre and their colleagues tested a protein originally found in red blood cells. They arranged for frog egg cells to make it, then compared those eggs with controls in dilute water. The eggs making the protein took up water and swelled much more rapidly. Controls changed little over the comparison period.

The experiment connected a particular protein with increased water permeability. It did not mean control membranes were absolutely waterproof. Nor did it show that the protein spent ATP pumping water. Water already had a direction of net transfer under those conditions; the protein provided a faster route. The team called this kind of protein an aquaporin, a water pore. Agre’s account dates the first test to 1991; the research paper appeared in 1992.

The story behind this

The unknown protein and the swelling eggsA protein found during other work became a testable explanation for rapid water passage across membranes.

A membrane’s oily middle makes passage much easier for some substances than others. Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross readily. Charged salt ions interact strongly with surrounding water; entering the oily layer is energetically unfavourable. Sucrose also crosses that layer poorly. This is more than a kitchen sieve sorting by size. Electrical charge and chemical interactions matter.

Water can cross the lipid layer, and many cells have faster water-selective protein channels: aquaporins. A typical water-specific aquaporin provides a route for water while excluding sucrose and salt ions. Other proteins can provide routes for particular ions or sugars. “Blocked here” never means “blocked by every possible cell membrane”.

Partially permeable

Allowing some substances to pass through while restricting others. A membrane’s permeability depends on both its lipid layer and the proteins present.

The boundary is partially permeable: it permits some substances to cross more readily than others.

First, keep the pressures equal. Picture a small compartment holding sugar solution. Its membrane floor passes water but retains sugar; outside is more dilute water. Water molecules cross both ways. Dissolved substances change water’s chemical environment, so at the same pressure the opposing transfers do not balance: there is net entry from the more dilute side. Sugar need not cross at all. The net passage of water across a partially permeable membrane is osmosis.

Next, let pressure build. Give the compartment a movable lid. Entry raises the lid. If the lid meets resistance, pressure rises inside and opposes further net entry. With enough opposing pressure, the two transfers balance. Sugar is still more concentrated inside, and individual water molecules still cross. A plant’s supporting wall will let a cell build pressure in a related way.

Now keep both effects in one account. We use a quantity called water potential to predict net water movement. Dissolved substances lower it; pushing on water raises it. Net water transfer goes from higher total water potential to lower total water potential. Pure water at the reference pressure is assigned zero. Below zero, −0.30 is higher than −0.80, just as −3 is higher than −8 on a number line.

Start with a chosen outside value of −0.30 MPa and an inside solute contribution of −0.80 MPa, with no added pressure inside. Which side is higher? The outside, so net entry is favoured. MPa means megapascals, a pressure unit used for water potential. Add +0.50 MPa of pressure inside and its total becomes −0.30 MPa: the two sides now match. We have changed the pressure account without making the solute concentrations equal.

Water potential

A measure used to predict net water movement, affected by dissolved substances and pressure. Water moves overall from higher to lower water potential.

Osmosis

Net movement of water molecules from higher to lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.

At equal pressure, dilute-to-concentrated is a useful shortcut when the solute cannot cross. With unequal pressures, compare the total water potentials. “Concentrated solution” means more dissolved substance per volume, not higher water potential.

Use the live model in that same order: compare the solute contributions first, then add inside pressure. Predict the direction before moving a control. At equal total potentials, look for two-way exchange rather than a frozen boundary.

Understand itOsmosis and water potential

What is it?

Osmosis is net water passage through a partially permeable membrane from higher to lower water potential. Water potential includes the effects of solute and pressure.

Why is it called this?

Osmosis comes from a Greek word connected with pushing or impulse. It is a historical name, not an explanation that salt pulls deliberately on water.

What problem did it solve?

It explains water movement across boundaries that water can cross more readily than particular dissolved substances.

Why does it work?

Dissolved substances change water’s chemical environment. Pressure also affects transfer, so unequal opposing flows can balance even with unequal solutes.

How does it help?

It predicts whether a cell gains water, loses it or has no sustained net water change.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Membrane experiments measure water transfer. Adding a water-channel protein increases permeability; opposing pressure can balance net entry.

What it isn’t

Sugar or salt moving across the membrane. An aquaporin is a pathway, not an ATP-driven water pump.

Where does it stop working?

The dilute-to-concentrated shortcut assumes comparable pressures and a solute that cannot readily cross. Different pressures or permeant solutes require a fuller account.

Your turn

Explain Osmosis and water potential to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“Salt sucks water through any barrier.”

A gradient cannot make an impermeable barrier pass water. Where passage is possible, net movement depends on water potential, including pressure. Salt ions may remain on their own side throughout.

At school

In 0610 Extended Topic 3.2, connect water molecules, higher to lower water potential, and a partially permeable membrane. Use dilute-to-concentrated as the equal-pressure example; avoid the ambiguous phrase “concentration of solution”.

Check yourself

A supported cell has a solute contribution of −0.80 MPa. Outside water potential stays at −0.30 MPa. Predict net movement first with no added pressure inside, then with +0.50 MPa inside. In the second case, must every water molecule stop crossing?

Answer at the back of the book

3.3Balloons inside boxes

Mumbai, two cups and a raw potato

A raw potato strip can become firmer in plain water and limper in salty water. The water outside is visible; the changing water inside its cells is hidden. A potato gives you a way to feel a consequence of a microscopic boundary.

Before cutting anything, compare two kinds of boundary. An animal cell has a cell membrane. A plant cell also has a supporting wall outside that membrane. The difference changes what happens after water enters.

Predict first

An animal cell and a plant cell are placed in very dilute surroundings. Water can enter both. Which outcome is most plausible?

  1. Both must burst because water enters both
  2. The plant wall can support rising pressure, while an animal cell may swell and burst
  3. The plant wall completely blocks water, leaving the cell dry

What happens

The second outcome. The wall allows pressure to build as water enters. That pressure raises internal water potential and can balance further net entry. A red blood cell lacks that supporting wall.

How do we know? The outline that stays, and the contents that retreat Repeatable microscopy

At school, compare a suitable plant epidermis under a microscope before and after adding a sufficiently concentrated salt solution. Watch the outer cell outlines and the membrane-bound contents separately. With enough water loss, the contents contract away from the wall; the outer wall remains largely in place. Replacing the salt solution with water can reverse the change if the cells have not been badly damaged.

That comparison identifies which structure changed. A vague instruction to “look for shrunken cells” would miss the important distinction between wall and contents. A potato becoming limp supports a water-loss interpretation at tissue scale, but a ruler cannot show membrane separation. The microscope and the kitchen strip answer related questions at different scales.

In dilute surroundings, a human red blood cell gains water. Its membrane accommodates some swelling, but excessive swelling can rupture it. In a concentrated solution of solute that does not readily enter, the cell loses water and shrivels. Neither event requires the solute to rush into the cell first.

Turgid

Firm with water and turgor pressure. Turgor is the pressure of the cell contents against the supporting wall.

A plant cell’s vacuole can take up water and enlarge. The contents press outwards against the wall; the wall resists further expansion. Internal pressure rises and opposes further net entry. A cell held firm by this pressure is turgid, and the pressure is turgor pressure. Soft stems and leaves gain support from many such pressurised cells together. Think of a filled balloon inside a supporting box, while remembering that a real wall is a mesh and a real membrane is a molecular layer.

Flaccid

Having little turgor pressure, so the cell is less firm.

Plasmolysis

Separation of the membrane-bound contents from the plant cell wall after sufficient water loss by osmosis.

As water leaves, the vacuole becomes smaller and turgor falls. A cell with little turgor is flaccid. After sufficient loss, the membrane-bound contents pull away from the wall: plasmolysis. This names a visible separation, not every instance of wilting. A limp strip alone does not prove that every cell inside it has plasmolysed.

The intact wall is not the selective gate responsible for this water exchange. The cell membrane is. Water entering a plant cell also crosses the vacuole’s membrane on its way into the vacuole. Our simple envelope drawing omits that extra molecular boundary so the pressure comparison remains readable.

Understand itTurgor and plasmolysis

What is it?

Turgor is pressure supported by the wall. Plasmolysis is the separation of membrane-bound contents from that wall after substantial water loss.

Why is it called this?

Turgid means swollen. Plasmolysis combines word-parts for formed substance and loosening; here the visible clue is the contents drawing away from the wall.

What problem did it solve?

It connects water movement inside individual cells with the firmness or wilting of a whole leaf or potato strip.

Why does it work?

Water entry expands the contents against a resisting wall and raises pressure. Water loss reduces pressure and can shrink the contents away from the wall.

How does it help?

It explains why plants can stand firm without a skeleton and why the same dilute water has different effects on plant cells and red blood cells.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Microscopy distinguishes the outer wall from the retreating contents; tissue experiments compare firmness and dimensions before and after immersion.

What it isn’t

A wall sucking up water, or the rigid wall shrinking by the same amount as the vacuole.

Where does it stop working?

Severe damage may prevent recovery. Whole tissues include cut cells and several cell types, so their measured changes are not an exact picture of one cell.

Your turn

Explain Turgor and plasmolysis to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“The salty cup makes the potato limp because salt enters and bursts its cells.”

The initial explanation is net water loss from cells to lower-water-potential surroundings. Loss of turgor makes tissue less firm. Salt permeability and damage can matter during longer exposure, but they do not turn this into the dilute-water bursting of an animal cell.

Two cups, six strips, one fair comparison

An adult should cut the potato and handle the knife. Use one raw potato to make six similar strips, about 60 mm long and 5 mm across. Prepare one cup with 100 mL of tap water. For the other, dissolve 5 g of table salt and add water to a final volume of 100 mL. This chosen 5% mass/volume solution is not a recipe for seawater. Without a suitable scale, a level teaspoon is an approximate alternative; label the concentration “approximate”.

Measure and label each strip. Put three in each cup, fully immersed, at the same room temperature and for the same time. Keep cups covered loosely against spills and dust. Predict changes in length and firmness. After 30 minutes, remove the strips, blot each gently in the same way, and measure again without squeezing. If the difference is unclear, note that and compare after a longer immersion, up to an hour. Never replace an awkward result with the expected one.

Record initial length, final length and firmness for each strip; compare the three-strip averages and their spread. Calculate percentage length change as 100 × (final − initial) ÷ initial. A ruler with millimetre marks may miss a small change. A reliable mass measurement, if a sufficiently precise scale is available, gives another comparison; consistent blotting matters. A kitchen scale that reads only whole grams is too coarse for small changes in these strips. You can transfer the salty strips to fresh water to test possible recovery, without promising it.

Different potatoes, damaged cut surfaces and measurement uncertainty affect results. Do not eat the used potato or taste the liquids. Dispose of them the same day, wash hands and clean the cups and board.

At school

For 0610 Topic 3.2, explain the water-potential direction and use turgid, turgor pressure, flaccid, or plasmolysis for the observed state. Reserve plasmolysis for contents separating from the wall; your kitchen strip tests tissue changes rather than showing that separation directly.

Check yourself

A plant cell’s membrane-bound contents have visibly pulled away from an intact wall. Which way has net water movement occurred, and what would you need to know before predicting recovery?

Answer at the back of the book

3.4Pushing uphill: roots and the salty sea

Aarhus, crab nerve membranes, 1957

A membrane can provide a route for an ion. That leaves another puzzle. How can cells maintain more of an ion on the side where it is already concentrated? If electrical effects do not oppose it, passive spreading through an open route would tend to undo the concentration difference.

Jens Christian Skou investigated an enzyme in crab nerve membranes that broke down ATP. Its activity depended on the ions present. The link between chemical reactions and an uneven distribution of ions was becoming something experimenters could test.

Predict first

A root hair cell contains more nitrate ions per volume than the surrounding soil solution. Which explanation could sustain further nitrate uptake against that concentration gradient?

  1. A nitrate pathway alone guarantees further accumulation, regardless of electrical conditions
  2. Increasing membrane area alone can sustain uptake against an unfavourable combined gradient
  3. A transporter couples nitrate entry to an energy source, such as another ion gradient

What happens

The third explanation supplies the missing account. A root can use ATP to establish another gradient, then couple nitrate entry to movement down that gradient. Concentration is part of the story for ions; electrical forces matter too.

How do we know? ATP chemistry in the membrane Skou's 1957 paper

Skou studied preparations of crab nerve membranes. He measured ATP breakdown while changing the ions in the mixture. Sodium and potassium affected the enzyme’s activity. These chemical responses helped identify machinery involved in maintaining unequal ion distributions across a living membrane.

This was a clue linking ATP-consuming chemistry with ion transport, rather than a film of every individual pumping step. Later work established the sodium–potassium pump’s transport mechanism. The experiment did not identify a nitrate pump in a root, and those two machines should not be confused. What carries across to the root problem is the principle: a membrane protein can couple a chemical energy transfer to transport that passive spreading alone would not maintain.

The story behind this

An ATP reaction at the membraneChanging the ions around a nerve-membrane enzyme helped connect ATP chemistry with the maintenance of ion gradients.
Active transport

Energy-coupled movement across a membrane against a concentration gradient, or, for ions, against the combined concentration and electrical gradient. ATP may power transport directly or establish a gradient that powers another transport step.

When ATP breakdown is coupled to changes in a carrier protein’s shape, the protein can move ions against an unfavourable gradient. Such energy-coupled movement is active transport. A protein path alone is not enough to identify it: passive channels and carriers exist too. For a charged ion, the distinguishing question is whether energy is used to maintain transport against its combined concentration and electrical gradient.

Follow a root hair’s relay in three frames.

  1. Build the gradient. One membrane protein uses ATP to export hydrogen ions, H⁺. The resulting difference in proton concentration and electrical charge stores energy.
  2. Use the gradient. Protons return down that combined gradient through a second protein. Their return is coupled to nitrate entry, even when nitrate is already more concentrated inside. This second protein is a cotransporter. Respiration supplies ATP to maintain the first step.
  3. Account for water separately. Changing dissolved-substance distributions can change water potential. Water can then enter passively through available routes when its total water potential is lower inside. The nitrate transporter is not an ATP-powered water pump.

The electricity qualification matters. An ion carries charge, so electrical attraction or repulsion contributes alongside concentration. We call their combined effect an electrochemical gradient. The school concentration-gradient description gives a useful starting account; the proton relay shows how a real root can achieve it without inventing a motor that burns exactly one ATP for every nitrate.

Now return to the mangroves. Grey mangroves, Avicennia marina, occur along Maharashtra’s coast. Their roots exclude much of the salt from entering the water-conducting tissues. “Much” matters: the exclusion is not perfect. Nor is it enough on its own. Water still has to enter from salty soil with a low water potential.

Mangroves maintain a still lower water potential in the absorbing tissues and along the uptake pathway. Dissolved substances contribute: ions can be kept in vacuoles, while other dissolved compounds help the cytoplasm function under these conditions. Evaporation from leaves also contributes to tension in the water-conducting system; we will follow that pull in Chapter 5. Grey mangroves can secrete some salt through glands on their leaves. Other mangroves use different combinations of salt-handling features.

The answer to Carter Road’s puzzle is therefore a coordinated account. Restrict salt entry, manage the salt that enters, and maintain conditions in which water moves down its water-potential gradient into the plant. Energy helps establish and maintain the living machinery and dissolved-substance distributions. Water itself still enters by passive movement along its gradient. Its adaptations maintain the conditions for ordinary osmosis.

Understand itActive transport

What is it?

Energy-coupled membrane transport against a concentration gradient, or for ions against the combined concentration and electrical gradient.

Why is it called this?

Active distinguishes transport coupled to the cell’s energy supply from passive movement down a gradient. It does not imply conscious effort.

What problem did it solve?

It explains how a root can keep taking up a scarce mineral ion when the cell already contains more of it per volume than the soil solution.

Why does it work?

ATP breakdown can be coupled to a protein’s transport cycle. A gradient built by one pump can also supply energy to a second transporter.

How does it help?

It connects mineral uptake, ion balance and the continuous ATP supply needed by living cells.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Membrane experiments link ATP-consuming proteins and particular ions. Transport studies distinguish energy-coupled accumulation from passive equilibration.

What it isn’t

Every passage through a protein, or a water pump that forces osmosis uphill. Aquaporins can carry water passively.

Where does it stop working?

A sustained energy shortage prevents gradients being maintained indefinitely. Stored gradients can persist for a while, so loss of ATP need not stop every crossing instantly.

Your turn

Explain Active transport to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“Roots actively suck in water because the plant needs a drink.”

Name the transported substance and its route. Mineral-ion uptake can depend on energy-coupled transport; net water uptake follows water potential. A mangrove’s salt barriers alone cannot explain intake unless its water-potential account also works.

At school

For 0610 Topic 3.3, connect movement from lower to higher concentration, against a concentration gradient, carrier proteins, and energy from respiration. Root hair uptake of mineral ions is the key example; the proton relay explains how that energy can be supplied indirectly.

Does a root cell stop requiring respiration because the leaves can capture sunlight?

Answer at the back of the book

Check yourself

A mangrove excludes much salt at its roots. A second plant excludes the same amount, but its absorbing tissues have a higher water potential than the soil water. Will equal salt exclusion guarantee equal water uptake?

Case file 3

Surrounded by water, losing water

A sailor has run out of fresh water. Seawater surrounds the boat. The sailor argues that a drink must help: it contains far more water than salt.

Clue one: dissolved substances can change the distribution of water between body fluids and cells. Clue two: absorbed excess salt must be removed, and the kidneys use water to excrete it. Clue three: humans do not have a mangrove’s salt-handling system.

Why can drinking seawater make the sailor more dehydrated, despite the water swallowed?

Show the solution

The salt load matters along with the water intake. Human kidneys require water to remove that excess salt; dealing with seawater can cause a net loss of body water. Raised salt concentration in body fluids also favours water leaving cells. Osmosis explains those cell-level shifts, while salt excretion explains why the whole-body water account can worsen. Seawater is not safe drinking water. This is a reasoning case, never a drinking experiment.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

We can now follow molecules through a membrane, and we have seen proteins acting as channels, carriers and pumps. But how can a folded protein distinguish one molecule from another? In Chapter 4, a molecular shape will become the next piece of evidence.

This chapter draws on Biology 2e by OpenStax. Access for free at https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/1-introduction. Changes were made to the original material.
