Chapter 11

The Twisted Ladder & The Protein Printers

The big questionHow does a two-nanometre twisted ladder of just four chemical letters store the blueprints for thousands of folded protein machines, and why does changing one letter in Child Y alter red blood cells while changing one letter in Child X leaves the protein completely unchanged?

  1. 11.1The hidden instruction book: chromosomes, DNA and genes
  2. 11.2The twisted ladder: Photo 51, Chargaff’s ratios and the double helix
  3. 11.3Cracking the triplet cipher and printing the protein: from mRNA to the ribosome
  4. 11.4One letter changed: beta-globin, silent triplets and why sequence controls shape

In Volume III you watched a living human body hold the line against heat, starvation, dehydration and microbial invasion. Every single step in that defence depended on a specific protein folded into an exact three-dimensional shape: amylases and proteases hydrolysing food in your gut (Chapter 7), haemoglobin ferrying oxygen inside red blood cells (Chapter 8), voltage-gated sodium channels and postsynaptic neurotransmitter receptors passing electrical signals across 20 nm synapses (Chapter 9), and insulin, glucagon, aquaporins, sodium–glucose carrier proteins and antibodies guarding your internal environment (Chapter 10).

Think back to what G. N. Ramachandran proved in Madras in Chapter 4: a protein folds into its working three-dimensional shape—whether an enzyme active site, a membrane channel or an antibody binding tip—because of the exact linear sequence of the twenty kinds of amino acids linked along its polypeptide chain. And think back to what Obaid Siddiqi discovered in Drosophila fruit flies at Caltech and TIFR Colaba in Chapter 9: a single change in one gene (para) altered one voltage-gated sodium channel protein so that the fly’s nerve axons stopped firing at 29 °C.

Those discoveries point to the central question of Volume IV (The Master Code & The Four-Billion-Year Case File): Where does a cell keep the master instruction book for building thousands of different proteins, what is that instruction book made of, and how do tiny ribosomes in the cytoplasm read a four-letter chemical script to print the right protein on demand?

11.1The hidden instruction book: chromosomes, DNA and genes

A pathology bench in London, 1928, a biochemical laboratory in New York, 1944, and a Mumbai kitchen counter

Look inside the nucleus of a plant or animal cell under a microscope (Chapter 2). When the cell is about to divide, the grainy tangle inside the nucleus condenses into dark, thread-like structures called chromosomes (from Greek chroma, “colour”, and soma, “body”, because nineteenth-century microscopists noticed how strongly they soaked up coloured aniline dyes). Chemical analysis of isolated cell nuclei soon showed that chromosomes contain two main classes of giant molecules: proteins (built from 20 different amino acids) and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA, built from just 4 different nucleotide building blocks).

For more than forty years, almost every biologist in the world bet on the wrong molecule. Because proteins are built from a rich twenty-letter alphabet of amino acids that fold into countless shapes, while DNA uses only a four-letter alphabet, most researchers assumed that chromosomal proteins must carry the cell’s hereditary instructions (genes), while DNA was merely a dull wooden frame holding the proteins in place.

How do you test which molecule in a chromosome actually carries the genes? You cannot guess from how complicated a molecule looks on paper; you have to isolate the hereditary signal in a test tube, destroy one candidate molecule at a time, and see which destruction erases the instructions.

In 1928 in London, the medical officer Frederick Griffith was studying two strains of the pneumonia bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae:

  • A Smooth (S) strain, whose cells build a smooth, glistening polysaccharide capsule around themselves that shields them from the host’s phagocytes (Chapter 10), causing fatal pneumonia in mice.
  • A Rough (R) strain, whose cells lack the gene for building the protective capsule, form rough-edged colonies on agar, and are harmlessly cleared by a mouse’s immune system.

Griffith found that injecting heat-killed Smooth (S) bacteria alone did not harm mice, and injecting live Rough (R) bacteria alone did not harm mice. Yet when he injected a mixture of heat-killed S bacteria together with live R bacteria, the mice developed severe pneumonia—and their blood teamed with living Smooth (S) bacteria whose descendants kept making smooth capsules generation after generation. Some heat-stable chemical molecule—which Griffith called the transforming principle—had passed from the dead S cells into the living R cells and handed them the working hereditary instruction for building a capsule. :::

Predict first

In 1944 at the Rockefeller Institute in New York, Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty broke open heat-killed Smooth (S) bacteria, removed the lipids and polysaccharide coats, and divided the active cell-free transforming extract into three test tubes before adding live Rough (R) bacteria:

  1. Tube 1 was treated with protease enzymes (trypsin and chymotrypsin, Chapter 7), which digest proteins.
  2. Tube 2 was treated with ribonuclease (RNase), an enzyme that digests RNA.
  3. Tube 3 was treated with deoxyribonuclease (DNase), an enzyme that digests DNA. If DNA—and not protein or RNA—is the molecule that carries genes, which tubes will still transform harmless Rough (R) bacteria into capsulated Smooth (S) bacteria, and which tube will fail?
  4. Tube 1 (protease-treated) will fail to transform R bacteria, while Tubes 2 and 3 will still produce live S bacteria
  5. Tubes 1 and 2 will still transform R bacteria into live Smooth (S) bacteria because destroying protein or RNA leaves the DNA intact, whereas Tube 3 (DNase-treated) will produce only Rough (R) bacteria because destroying DNA destroys the gene
  6. All three tubes will fail because genes require protein, RNA and DNA to stay glued together at all times

What happens

The second choice. Because enzymes have complementary active sites that are strictly specific to their substrates (Chapter 4), proteases destroy only proteins, RNase destroys only RNA, and DNase destroys only DNA. When Avery, MacLeod and McCarty destroyed all the protein in Tube 1 or all the RNA in Tube 2, the extract transformed Rough (R) cells into Smooth (S) cells just as strongly as the untreated control. Only when DNase chopped up the DNA in Tube 3 did hereditary transformation vanish completely.

How do we know? New York, 1944, and Cold Spring Harbor, 1952: Avery–MacLeod–McCarty and Hershey–Chase Biochemical & isotopic proof

In their landmark February 1944 paper in the Journal of Experimental Medicine, Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty combined three independent lines of evidence on the purified transforming substance from Streptococcus pneumoniae:

  1. Enzymatic elimination: Crystalline trypsin, chymotrypsin (proteases) and ribonuclease (RNase) had zero effect on transforming activity, whereas trace amounts of deoxyribonuclease (DNase) permanently abolished transformation.
  2. Elemental stoichiometry: Pure proteins contain nitrogen (N) and sulfur (S) but almost no phosphorus (P), whereas DNA contains phosphorus in every nucleotide of its backbone and no sulfur. The purified transforming substance had a nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio (N : P ≈ 1.67) matching pure sodium deoxyribonucleate (DNA).
  3. Eight years later (1952), Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase confirmed the result using bacteriophage T2—a virus made of a protein coat enclosing a DNA core (Chapter 1). They grew one batch of phages with radioactive sulfur (³⁵S, which labels protein coats because the amino acids cysteine and methionine contain sulfur, while DNA contains zero sulfur) and a second batch with radioactive phosphorus (³²P, which labels DNA, while phage protein contains zero phosphorus). After allowing the phages to infect E. coli bacteria and shearing off the empty virus coats in a kitchen blender, roughly 80 percent of the ³⁵S protein stayed outside in the liquid, whereas the ³²P DNA entered the bacterial cells and directed the assembly of new phages.

Trace the exact scale hierarchy in the middle panel of Figure 11.1 from largest to smallest so you never muddle where these structures sit in a eukaryotic cell (0893 9Bs.01, 9Bs.02; 0610 17.1 Core 1–2):

Chromosome, DNA, and gene
  • Chromosome: a thread-like structure located in the nucleus of a cell, made of DNA, which carries genetic information in the form of genes.
  • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid): the giant double-stranded polymer molecule that chromosomes and genes are made of.
  • Gene: a length of DNA that codes for a protein (and therefore helps to determine a characteristic of an organism).
  1. Cell (~10–50 µm across): a living plant, animal or fungal cell bounded by a cell membrane.
  2. Nucleus (~5–10 µm diameter): the membrane-bound compartment inside a eukaryotic cell that houses the cell’s hereditary archive. (Remember from Chapter 2 that prokaryotic bacterial cells have no nucleus; their main circular DNA molecule and tiny circular plasmids float in the cytoplasm.)
  3. Chromosome: a long, coiled thread-like structure found inside the nucleus and made of DNA wrapped around packaging proteins. Each chromosome is a single, unbroken, extraordinarily long DNA molecule containing hundreds or thousands of genes arranged in a line like recipes in a multi-volume encyclopaedia.
  4. Gene: a specific length (segment) of DNA at a particular position on a chromosome that codes for a specific protein—and by coding for that protein (alongside other genes and the organism’s environment), helps to determine the characteristics of the organism.
  5. DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid, 2.0 nm diameter): the chemical polymer molecule itself, whose sequence of chemical bases along each gene spells out the genetic code.

Why is it important to say at Lower Secondary level (0893 9Bs.02) that genes help to determine an organism’s characteristics rather than acting alone in a vacuum? A gene supplies the DNA code for building a specific protein—for instance, an enzyme that synthesises chlorophyll in a young mango leaf, or growth proteins in human bones. Whether the plant actually turns deep green also depends on environmental supplies of light and magnesium ions (Mg²⁺, Chapter 5), and how tall a child grows depends on dozens of genes interacting with childhood nutrition and health (Chapter 7). Some characteristics (such as your ABO blood group or the sequence of your beta-globin protein) are set directly by your genes, while most whole-body traits emerge from genes and environment working together.

Understand itChromosomes, DNA, and genes inside the nucleus

What is it?

The three-level filing system of heredity inside a eukaryotic cell: the nucleus holds thread-like chromosomes, each chromosome is made of a long coiled molecule of DNA, and each gene is a specific length of that DNA that codes for one protein.

Why is it called this?

Chromosome means “coloured body” (from how strongly chromosomal threads take up microscope dyes); gene comes from Greek genos (“birth / origin”), coined by Wilhelm Johannsen in 1909 for the unit of heredity.

What problem did it solve?

A single human cell nucleus is only ~6 µm across, yet it must store roughly 2 metres of DNA carrying around 20,000 protein-coding recipes without tangling or losing a single recipe. Coiling long DNA molecules into chromosomes keeps the library organised inside the nucleus.

Why does it work?

Each chromosome is one continuous DNA double helix divided into thousands of distinct genes along its length; when the cell needs a particular enzyme, hormone or membrane channel, it looks up just that gene’s segment of DNA.

How does it help?

Keeping the hierarchy straight (Nucleus → Chromosome → Gene → DNA base sequence) prevents one of the most common biology exam confusions—mixing up which structure is made of which, or which one is larger.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944) proved that DNase (which destroys DNA) erases gene function while proteases and RNase do not; Hershey and Chase (1952) proved that phage ³²P-labelled DNA enters cells to direct new virus production.

What it isn’t

A gene is not larger than a chromosome (a single chromosome carries hundreds or thousands of genes), and a gene does not “turn into” a protein—it is a permanent DNA instruction segment that codes for a protein.

Where does it stop working?

Red blood cells in mammals eject their nucleus as they mature to pack in more haemoglobin (Chapter 2), so mature red blood cells contain zero chromosomes and zero genes—they must print all their haemoglobin proteins while they are still young nucleated bone-marrow cells.

Your turn

Explain Chromosomes, DNA, and genes inside the nucleus to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“DNA is made of chromosomes, and each chromosome is inside a gene.”

Reverse that hierarchy completely. Think of a multi-volume recipe encyclopaedia locked inside a library reading room:

  • The library room = the cell nucleus.
  • Each bound volume = one chromosome (made of one continuous, tightly coiled DNA thread).
  • One recipe printed on a few pages of that volume = one gene (a specific length of DNA that codes for one protein).
  • The paper and ink letters themselves = the DNA molecule and its bases.

Therefore, from largest to smallest: Cell → Nucleus → Chromosome → Gene → DNA nucleotide bases. Chromosomes are made of DNA, and each chromosome contains many genes along its length.

Spooling white threads of DNA from a mashed banana

Disclosure: This is an optional kitchen-chemistry demonstration based on standard school and outreach nucleic-acid precipitation protocols (not a laboratory trial performed during the authoring of this chapter). If you try it at home, work with an adult and use chilled rubbing alcohol (70–91% isopropyl alcohol or surgical spirit) strictly as an external reagent in a glass—never taste or swallow rubbing alcohol, keep it away from stove flames, and wash your hands afterwards.

  1. Place half a ripe banana in a resealable plastic bag with 100 mL (about half a teacup) of warm water and mash it thoroughly with your fingers for two minutes until it forms a smooth porridge (Step 1 in Figure 11.1: mechanical mashing separates clumped cells and breaks open cellulose cell walls).
  2. In a clear glass cup, gently stir together 10 mL (two teaspoons) of liquid dishwashing detergent and 3 g (half a teaspoon) of table salt (NaCl) in 50 mL of water without whipping up foam. Pour this lysis mixture into the mashed banana bag, rock gently for five minutes, and filter the liquid through a fine tea strainer or coffee filter into a narrow glass (Step 2: detergent dissolves the fatty lipid bilayers of both the cell membrane and the nuclear membrane, releasing DNA into solution; Step 3: positively charged sodium ions Na⁺ from the salt shield the negatively charged phosphate groups along the DNA backbones so the strands can come together instead of repelling each other).
  3. Tilt the narrow glass and slowly pour an equal volume of ice-cold rubbing alcohol (chilled in the freezer for 30 minutes) down the inside wall of the glass so it floats as a clear top layer above the cloudy banana filtrate (Step 4: DNA is soluble in salty water but insoluble in cold alcohol).
  4. Watch the boundary between the two layers for two minutes: millions of microscopic DNA molecules precipitate out of solution together as cloudy white, mucus-like threads rising into the cold alcohol layer, which you can spool around a wooden toothpick. Remember what you are looking at: a single DNA double helix is only 2.0 nm wide—far too thin to see with the naked eye or a school light microscope—so the white thread on your toothpick is millions of DNA strands clumped side by side like fibres twisted into cotton yarn.

At school

Cambridge Lower Secondary Science (0893) requires you to describe how chromosomes are found in the nucleus of a cell and are made of DNA (9Bs.01), and how genes are located on chromosomes and help to determine the characteristics of an organism (9Bs.02). Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610, Topic 17.1 Core 1–2) requires you to state that chromosomes are made of DNA, which contains genetic information in the form of genes, and to define a gene precisely as a length of DNA that codes for a protein.

Check yourself

Arrange the following five biological structures in order of size from largest to smallest, and explain how Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty (1944) proved which chemical molecule in a chromosome carries hereditary instructions: gene, eukaryotic cell, DNA base pair, chromosome, nucleus.

Answer at the back of the book

11.2The twisted ladder: Photo 51, Chargaff’s ratios and the double helix

Columbia University, New York, 1950, King’s College London, May 1952, and the Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, April 1953

Once Avery’s team proved that genes are made of DNA, a fierce race began to solve a physical puzzle: how are the atoms inside a DNA molecule arranged in three-dimensional space, and how can a molecule built from just four kinds of bases store thousands of different protein recipes?

Start with what chemists already knew about the building blocks of DNA. DNA is a long biological polymer (macromolecule, Chapter 4) assembled from repeating monomer units called nucleotides. Each DNA nucleotide consists of three parts joined together:

  1. A phosphate group (which gives DNA its acidic nature and negative electrical charge),
  2. A five-carbon sugar called deoxyribose (which joins with alternating phosphate groups to form the strong outer sugar–phosphate backbone of each strand), and
  3. One of four nitrogen-containing organic bases projecting inward from the sugar: - Adenine (A) — a larger, two-ring base (a purine), - Guanine (G) — a larger, two-ring base (also a purine), - Thymine (T) — a smaller, one-ring base (a pyrimidine), or - Cytosine (C) — a smaller, one-ring base (also a pyrimidine).

Look closely at the three experimental clues that converged between 1950 and 1953 to reveal how two DNA strands lock together (0610 4.1 Core & Supplement; 17.1 Core 3):

  • Clue 1 · Erwin Chargaff’s base-equivalence rules (New York, 1950): Using paper chromatography and ultraviolet light, Erwin Chargaff measured the exact percentages of A, T, G, and C in DNA extracted from humans, cattle, salmon, maize, yeast, and bacteria. Across every species, he found that the percentage of adenine always equalled thymine (%A ≈ %T) and the percentage of guanine always equalled cytosine (%G ≈ %C). For example, in human thymus DNA, Chargaff measured 30.9% A and 29.4% T, alongside 19.9% G and 19.8% C. In the GC-rich bacterium Sarcina lutea, %A was only 13.4% and %T was 13.1%, while %G was 37.1% and %C was 36.4%—yet %A still matched %T and %G still matched %C.
  • Clue 2 · Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling’s Photo 51 (London, May 1952): At King’s College London, the physical chemist Rosalind Franklin and her graduate student Raymond Gosling shone a narrow beam of X-rays through a single microscopic fibre of calf-thymus DNA held at 92 percent relative humidity (the hydrated B-form that DNA takes inside living cells). After a 62-hour exposure, their film—Photo 51—revealed a sharp X-shaped cross of dark spots. In X-ray crystallography, an X-shaped diffraction pattern is the unmistakable signature of a helix (a spiral coil). From the spacing of the horizontal layer lines and the dark arcs at the very top and bottom of Photo 51, Rosalind Franklin measured the exact geometry of the B-DNA helix:
  • One complete helical turn (360°) repeats every 3.4 nm (34 Å) along the fibre axis.
  • The vertical step from one stacked base to the next is 0.34 nm (3.4 Å). Dividing 3.4 nm by 0.34 nm proves there are exactly 10 base pairs per complete turn of the helix (each base pair rotated by 36° relative to its neighbour).
  • The cylinder has a uniform diameter of 2.0 nm (20 Å), with the water-loving sugar–phosphate backbones on the outside and the bases stacked flat like steps on the inside.

  • Clue 3 · James Watson and Francis Crick’s complementary base-pairing model (Cambridge, April 1953): At the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, Francis Crick and James Watson combined Franklin’s B-DNA X-ray dimensions and antiparallel chain symmetry with Jerry Donohue’s keto base chemistry and Erwin Chargaff’s ratios. They realised why the double helix has a completely uniform 2.0 nm diameter from end to end:

    • If you try to pair two large two-ring purines (A with G, or A with A), the rung is too wide (> 2.0 nm) and forces a bulge in the sugar–phosphate backbone.
    • If you try to pair two small one-ring pyrimidines (T with C, or T with T), the rung is too narrow (< 2.0 nm) and the bases cannot reach across the cylinder to form hydrogen bonds.
    • Only when a two-ring purine pairs with a one-ring pyrimidine does the rung span exactly 2.0 nm—and the hydrogen-bond positions on the rings allow only two specific partnerships: Adenine (A) always pairs with Thymine (T) via two hydrogen bonds (A=T), and Cytosine (C) always pairs with Guanine (G) via three hydrogen bonds (C≡G). :::

Predict first

Suppose a biochemist analyses a double-stranded DNA molecule from a newly discovered deep-sea fish and finds that 22% of all the bases in the DNA are cytosine (C). Using complementary base pairing and Chargaff’s rules, what are the percentages of guanine (G), adenine (A), and thymine (T) in that DNA molecule?

  1. 22% G, 22% A, and 34% T, because C, G and A are always equal
  2. 28% G, 25% A, and 25% T, because C and G always add up to 50%
  3. 22% G, 28% A, and 28% T, because C always pairs with G (so %G = %C = 22%, totalling 44%), and the remaining 56% of bases must be split equally between A and T pairs (%A = %T = 28%)

What happens

The third choice. Work through the two-step arithmetic:

  1. Because every cytosine (C) on one strand is paired across the rung with a guanine (G) on the opposite strand (C≡G), %G must equal %C = 22%. Together, C + G account for 22% + 22% = 44% of all bases.
  2. That leaves 100% − 44% = 56% of the bases for A and T. Because every adenine (A) pairs with a thymine (T) (A=T), %A must equal %T = 56% ÷ 2 = 28%. Check the total: 22% C + 22% G + 28% A + 28% T = 100%.

How do we know? London and Cambridge, 25 April 1953: Photo 51 and the double-helix papers in Nature Crystallographic & chemical proof

In the 25 April 1953 issue of Nature, three back-to-back papers laid out the structure of DNA: James Watson and Francis Crick’s model paper (“Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid”), Maurice Wilkins, Alec Stokes, and Herbert Wilson’s fibre diffraction paper, and Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling’s paper (“Molecular Configuration in Sodium Thymonucleate”), which published Photo 51 and proved that the phosphate groups lie on the outside of a hydrated 2.0 nm B-form helix with 3.4 nm turns and 0.34 nm vertical spacing between stacked bases.

Notice the two biological problems that complementary base pairing (A=T and C≡G) solved immediately:

  1. Unrestricted information storage along one strand: The chemical geometry of the double helix places zero restriction on the order of bases (A, T, C, G) running lengthwise along a single strand—a gene can spell G–T–G–C–A–C–C–T–G... or any other sequence of thousands of letters.
  2. Automatic complementarity between the two strands: Once the sequence of bases along Strand 1 is fixed, the sequence of bases along Strand 2 is automatically determined (A opposite T, T opposite A, C opposite G, G opposite C). As Watson and Crick noted in a famous one-sentence understatement near the end of their paper, this complementary pairing immediately suggests how the genetic material can be copied before a cell divides (which you will trace in Chapter 12).

You can also inspect and rotate a full three-dimensional molecular model of the B-DNA double helix—and test how its base triplets specify the first seven amino acids of human beta-globin—in the front-matter 3D workbench: Open The Master Code 3D Explorer.

The story behind this

A humid X-ray camera in London and a synthetic gene bench from Raipur to MadisonHow humidified X-ray diffraction at King’s College London, paper chromatography in New York, and chemically synthesised repeating RNA messages built by a village clerk’s son from Punjab revealed the double helix and cracked all sixty-four triplets of the genetic code.

Summarise the four essential structural features of a DNA molecule that you need for Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610 4.1):

DNA double helix and complementary base pairing
  • Double helix: the three-dimensional structure of DNA, consisting of two strands coiled together around a common axis, with sugar–phosphate backbones on the outside and paired bases forming cross-links on the inside.
  • Complementary base pairing: the invariant rule by which DNA bases form cross-links between the two strands: A (adenine) always pairs with T (thymine), and C (cytosine) always pairs with G (guanine).
  1. Two strands coiled together to form a double helix: imagine a flexible rope ladder whose two side rails are twisted around a central axis into a spiral staircase (2.0 nm wide, completing one full turn every 3.4 nm or 10 base pairs). The two sugar–phosphate strands run in opposite directions (antiparallel, one running 5' → 3' and its partner running 3' → 5').
  2. Each strand contains chemicals called bases: projecting inward from the sugar–phosphate backbone of each strand is a linear sequence of four bases—adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), and guanine (G).
  3. Cross-links (bonds) between the strands are formed by pairs of bases: the two strands are held together across the middle of the helix by hydrogen bonds between paired bases (forming the rungs of the twisted ladder).
  4. The bases always pair up in the same complementary way (A with T, and C with G): adenine (A) always pairs with thymine (T) (2 hydrogen bonds), and cytosine (C) always pairs with guanine (G) (3 hydrogen bonds).

Understand itThe DNA double helix and complementary base pairing

What is it?

A two-nanometre-wide twisted ladder (double helix) made of two sugar–phosphate strands coiled together, linked across the middle by pairs of chemical bases that obey a strict partnership rule: A always pairs with T (A=T), and C always pairs with G (C≡G).

Why is it called this?

Helix means a three-dimensional spiral curve (like a corkscrew or spiral staircase); double helix because two polynucleotide strands wind around the same axis; complementary (with an e, from “complement”, meaning matching counterpart) because each base’s shape and hydrogen-bonding groups fit only its specific partner.

What problem did it solve?

A genetic archive must satisfy two demands that seem to pull in opposite directions: its outer geometry must be completely regular so it can pack neatly into chromosomes inside a 6 µm nucleus, yet its inner letter sequence must be completely free to spell out any protein recipe. Putting the sugar–phosphate backbones on the outside (2.0 nm apart) and pairing a two-ring purine with a one-ring pyrimidine on the inside (A=T, C≡G) satisfies both demands at once.

Why does it work?

Every A=T rung and every C≡G rung has the exact same 2.0 nm width, so any sequence of bases can run along one strand without bulging or pinching the helix, while weak individual hydrogen bonds (2 per A=T, 3 per C≡G) add up over millions of rungs to hold the two strands firmly together at 37 °C yet still allow enzymes to unzip a single gene when needed.

How does it help?

If you know the sequence of bases on one strand of a DNA double helix (for example, 5'-G–T–G–C–A–C–C–T–G-3'), you can write down the exact complementary sequence on the opposite strand (3'-C–A–C–G–T–G–G–A–C-5') and calculate the percentages of all four bases from just one base percentage.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Erwin Chargaff (1950) proved chemically that %A = %T and %G = %C across all double-stranded cellular DNA; Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling’s Photo 51 (1952) proved the B-DNA helix has a 3.4 nm pitch and 0.34 nm base step (10 base pairs per turn).

What it isn’t

A never pairs with C or G in normal DNA, and the genetic information does not lie in the sugar–phosphate backbone (which is identical in every gene and every organism)—the genetic information lies in the sequence (order) of bases along the length of a strand.

Where does it stop working?

A few tiny single-stranded DNA viruses (such as bacteriophage φX174) carry only one strand of DNA inside their protein coat instead of a double helix; in those single-stranded viral genomes, %A does not have to equal %T until the virus synthesises its complementary second strand inside a host cell.

Your turn

Explain The DNA double helix and complementary base pairing to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“Different organisms have different proteins because their DNA has different sugar–phosphate backbones or pairs A with G instead of A with T.”

Neither is true. From a banana tree to an E. coli bacterium to your own neurones, every DNA double helix uses the exact same deoxyribose sugar–phosphate backbone and the exact same complementary base-pairing rule (A with T, C with G). What makes a human insulin gene different from a human beta-globin gene—or a human different from a banana—is the sequence (order) of bases (A, T, C, G) running lengthwise along the DNA strands of each gene (0610 17.1 Core 3).

At school

Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610, Topic 4.1) requires every candidate to describe the structure of a DNA molecule as: (a) two strands coiled together to form a double helix, (b) each strand contains chemicals called bases, (c) cross-links between the strands are formed by pairs of bases, and (d) the bases always pair up in the same way: A with T, and C with G. Note that while knowing the full names adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine deepens your biochemical understanding, the 0610 syllabus notes that Core exam questions do not require you to recall the full names from memory as long as you use the letters A, T, C, and G accurately.

Check yourself

A short segment along one strand of a DNA double helix has the base sequence A – T – G – G – T – G – C – A – C.

  1. Write down the complementary base sequence along the opposite DNA strand.
  2. State how many hydrogen bonds link these 9 base pairs together across the double helix, and explain why Rosalind Franklin’s Photo 51 showed a vertical spacing of 0.34 nm and a turn repeat of 3.4 nm.

Answer at the back of the book

11.3Cracking the triplet cipher and printing the protein: from mRNA to the ribosome

The Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, 1961, Bethesda, Maryland, May 1961, and Madison, Wisconsin, 1964–1968

Solving the double helix in 1953 revealed how the master instruction book is bound, but it immediately exposed two new puzzles:

  • The coding puzzle: DNA has an alphabet of only four bases (A, T, C, G), whereas proteins are built from twenty different amino acids (Chapter 4). How can a four-letter alphabet spell out twenty different amino-acid names?
  • The location puzzle: In every eukaryotic plant, animal and fungal cell, the chromosomes and their genes stay locked inside the nucleus (11.1), whereas the ribosomes—the tiny molecular machines that actually link amino acids together into proteins (Chapter 2)—sit outside the nucleus in the cytoplasm (and on the rough endoplasmic reticulum). If the DNA gene never leaves the nucleus, how does the instruction reach the ribosome?

Take the coding puzzle first. Imagine trying to write a code for 20 different amino acids using an alphabet of 4 letters:

  • If each code word is 1 base long (a singlet code), there are only 4¹ = 4 possible words (A, T, C, G)—leaving 16 amino acids with no code at all.
  • If each code word is 2 bases long (a doublet code), there are 4² = 4 × 4 = 16 possible two-letter words (AA, AT, AC, AG, and so on)—still 4 short of the 20 amino acids.
  • If each code word is 3 bases long (a triplet or codon), there are 4³ = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 possible three-letter words—more than enough to specify all 20 amino acids plus “stop” punctuation marks at the end of a gene. :::

Predict first

Because 4³ = 64 three-letter triplets are available to code for only 20 amino acids (plus 3 stop signals), what must be true about the relationship between triplets (codons) and amino acids?

  1. 44 of the 64 triplets are unused blanks that pause the ribosome, while each of the 20 amino acids has only 1 triplet
  2. Each single triplet codes for 3 different amino acids at random, so the same gene makes many different proteins
  3. Most amino acids are coded for by more than one triplet (for example, 6 different triplets code for leucine), while every individual triplet specifies one unambiguous meaning (either one specific amino acid or STOP)

What happens

The third choice. Biologists call this property of the genetic code degeneracy (or redundancy):

  • Unambiguous in the forward direction (codon → amino acid): Every one of the 61 sense codons specifies one and only one amino acid (for instance, GAG always specifies glutamic acid, never valine or leucine).
  • Degenerate / redundant in the reverse direction (amino acid → codons): Because 61 sense codons share 20 amino acids, most amino acids have 2, 3, 4, or 6 synonymous codons (usually differing at the third base of the triplet). As you will see in Section 11.4 and the end-of-chapter case, this degeneracy shields living cells against many single-base mutations.

How do we know? Cambridge & Bethesda (1961) and Madison (1964–1968): Crick & Brenner, Nirenberg, and Har Gobind Khorana Genetic & synthetic biochemical proof

Three classic experiments proved that the genetic code is a non-overlapping triplet code and deciphered all 64 codons:

  1. Crick, Brenner, Barnett, and Watts-Tobin (1961) — the +1 / +2 / +3 frameshift proof: Using chemical mutagens that insert (+) or delete (−) single bases in the rII gene of bacteriophage T4, Francis Crick and Sydney Brenner showed that a ribosome reads a gene from a fixed starting point in non-overlapping groups of three bases. If you represent a triplet message with three-letter words—say, CAT · CAT · CAT · CAT · CAT—inserting one extra letter (+1, X) shifts every triplet boundary after that point (CAX · TCA · TCA · TCA...), scrambling every downstream amino acid and destroying the protein. Inserting two letters (+2) (CAX · YTC · ATC · ATC...) leaves the downstream frame scrambled. Only when they combined three single-base insertions (+3) (or three deletions, −3) did the triplets after the third change snap back into their original reading frame (CAX · YZT · CAT · CAT...), restoring a working phage protein.
  2. Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei (May 1961) — cracking the first codon with poly-U: At the National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei added a synthetic RNA chain composed entirely of uracil bases (UUUUUUUUUUUU..., poly-U) to a cell-free E. coli ribosome extract containing amino acids and energy (ATP). The ribosomes assembled a polypeptide chain made purely of phenylalanine (Phe–Phe–Phe...), proving that the RNA triplet UUU codes for phenylalanine (Phe).
  3. Har Gobind Khorana (1964–1968) — synthetic repeating copolymers crack the full 64-codon dictionary: At the University of Wisconsin–Madison, Har Gobind Khorana (born in Raipur, Punjab and trained at Punjab University in Lahore) solved the hardest part of the cipher: determining the exact order of letters inside mixed triplets. By chemically synthesising short DNA templates of known repeating sequence and copying them with polymerases into long repeating mRNA chains, Khorana fed ribosomes messages whose triplets alternated in a mathematically known way: - Repeating dinucleotide (UC)ₙ = UCUCUCUCUCUC... is read in triplets as alternating UCU | CUC | UCU | CUC. Ribosomes printed strictly alternating serine–leucine–serine–leucine (Ser–Leu–Ser–Leu), proving UCU = Ser and CUC = Leu. - Repeating dinucleotide (UG)ₙ = UGUGUGUGUGUG... (UGU | GUG) yielded alternating cysteine–valine (Cys–Val–Cys–Val); (AG)ₙ (AGA | GAG) yielded alternating arginine–glutamic acid (Arg–Glu–Arg–Glu); (AC)ₙ (ACA | CAC) yielded alternating threonine–histidine (Thr–His–Thr–His). - Synthetic templates containing UAA, UAG, and UGA proved that these three triplets code for no amino acid at all—they are the three stop (nonsense) codons that signal the ribosome to release the finished polypeptide chain, matching Obaid Siddiqi’s genetic discovery of nonsense codons (Chapter 9).

Now solve the location puzzle: how does a gene sitting inside the nucleus direct a ribosome sitting out in the cytoplasm to assemble a specific protein?

Think of the DNA chromosomes in the nucleus as a priceless, irreplaceable master reference encyclopaedia kept inside a locked archive room. If the cell dragged an entire chromosome out into the busy cytoplasm every time a ribosome needed to print a few molecules of amylase or insulin, cytoplasmic enzymes and reactive chemicals would quickly nick and damage the master DNA. Instead, the cell keeps the master gene safely inside the nucleus, makes a short, disposable working copy of just that one gene in the form of messenger RNA (mRNA), and sends the mRNA copy out through a microscopic doorway (nuclear pore) in the nuclear membrane to feed through the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.

Trace the exact six-step protein synthesis pathway required by Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610 17.1 Supplement 5) in Figure 11.4:

Messenger RNA (mRNA) and ribosomes in protein synthesis
  • Messenger RNA (mRNA): a single-stranded nucleic acid molecule that is made in the nucleus as a copy of one gene (using bases A, U, C, G) and moves to the cytoplasm, where it passes through ribosomes to direct protein synthesis.
  • Ribosome: the cytoplasmic organelle through which mRNA passes; the ribosome reads the sequence of bases in the mRNA three bases (one codon) at a time and assembles amino acids into protein molecules in the exact order specified by the mRNA.
  1. The gene coding for the protein remains in the nucleus: When a cell needs to make a specific protein (such as human beta-globin or insulin), enzymes inside the nucleus locate that single gene on its chromosome and temporarily unzip the hydrogen bonds between the two DNA strands across just that gene. The master DNA gene itself never leaves the nucleus.
  2. Messenger RNA (mRNA) is a copy of a gene: Inside the nucleus, the enzyme RNA polymerase moves along the unzipped DNA template strand and links free RNA nucleotides into a single-stranded messenger RNA (mRNA) molecule whose base sequence is a complementary copy of the template strand (and therefore matches the coding strand of the gene, except that RNA uses the base uracil (U) in place of thymine (T)). For example, where the coding strand of the human beta-globin gene reads G–T–G · C–A–C · C–T–G · A–C–T · C–C–T · G–A–G · G–A–G (and the template strand reads C–A–C · G–T–G · G–A–C · T–G–A · G–G–A · C–T–C · C–T–C), the transcribed mRNA copy reads G–U–G · C–A–C · C–U–G · A–C–U · C–C–U · G–A–G · G–A–G. Making this mRNA copy from a DNA gene in the nucleus is called transcription.
  3. mRNA molecules are made in the nucleus and move to the cytoplasm: Once the mRNA copy of the gene is complete, it detaches from the DNA (which zips right back up into its protected double helix) and moves out of the nucleus through a nuclear pore into the cytoplasm.
  4. The mRNA passes through ribosomes: In the cytoplasm (or on the rough endoplasmic reticulum), a ribosome clamps onto the start of the mRNA strand (AUG) and the mRNA passes through the ribosome like a punched tape, three bases (one triplet codon) at a time.
  5. The ribosome assembles amino acids into protein molecules: As each three-base mRNA codon sits inside the ribosome’s reading slot, small adapter molecules in the cytoplasm called transfer RNA (tRNA)—each carrying one specific amino acid at one end and a complementary three-base anticodon loop at the other—match up with the mRNA codon. The ribosome links each incoming amino acid to the growing chain by forming a peptide bond, assembling the amino acids one by one into a long polypeptide (protein) molecule. Reading the mRNA codon sequence at the ribosome to build a polypeptide chain is called translation.
  6. The specific sequence of amino acids is determined by the sequence of bases in the mRNA: Because each three-base codon on the mRNA specifies one exact amino acid (GUG → Valine, CAC → Histidine, CUG → Leucine, ACU → Threonine, CCU → Proline, GAG → Glutamic acid), the sequence of bases in the DNA gene determines the sequence of bases in the mRNA, which in turn determines the specific sequence of amino acids in the protein. When the ribosome reaches a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA), it releases the completed polypeptide chain.

Why does controlling the sequence of amino acids allow DNA to control everything a living cell does (0610 17.1 Supplement 4)?

Follow the causal chain in Figure 11.5 back to G. N. Ramachandran’s discovery in Chapter 4 (story p-ramachandran): as soon as a ribosome links amino acids into a polypeptide chain, the sizes, electrical charges, and water-loving (hydrophilic) or water-repelling (hydrophobic) side chains of those amino acids force the backbone angles (φ, ψ) to fold into a unique three-dimensional shape held together by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and disulfide bridges. That three-dimensional shape determines the working pocket or channel of every protein machine in the cell:

  1. Enzymes (biological catalysts, Chapter 4): DNA codes for intracellular and extracellular enzymes such as amylase, pepsin, catalase, and DNA/RNA polymerases. The amino-acid sequence folds the enzyme’s 3D active site so it is complementary to its specific substrate. By controlling which enzymes a cell builds, DNA controls every metabolic chemical reaction in the cell.
  2. Membrane carriers and channel proteins (Chapters 2, 3, 9, and 10): DNA codes for the carrier proteins that perform active transport and facilitated diffusion across cell membranes—such as the Na⁺–glucose cotransporters in your small intestine and kidney nephrons, Peter Agre’s aquaporins (p-agre), and Obaid Siddiqi’s voltage-gated sodium channels (siddiqi-para-channels). If a gene changes the amino-acid sequence of a membrane carrier, the cell can no longer pump or gate that ion or molecule properly.
  3. Receptors for neurotransmitters and hormones (Chapters 9 and 10): DNA codes for the receptor proteins embedded in postsynaptic neurone membranes (which bind neurotransmitters diffusing across a synaptic gap to trigger the next impulse) and in target-organ membranes (such as liver insulin and glucagon receptors). The 3D binding cleft of each receptor must be complementary to its chemical messenger.
  4. Antibodies and structural/transport proteins (Chapters 8 and 10): DNA codes for antibodies secreted by lymphocytes (whose variable tips fold into a 3D shape complementary to one specific pathogen antigen), oxygen-carrying haemoglobin in red blood cells, and structural fibres like collagen and keratin.

Before leaving Section 11.3, inspect Figure 11.6 to lock in the six structural and functional contrasts between DNA and messenger RNA (mRNA):

Feature DNA (Deoxyribonucleic acid) Messenger RNA (mRNA)
1. Number of strands Two strands coiled together in a double helix One single-stranded polynucleotide chain
2. Organic bases Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G) Adenine (A), Uracil (U), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G) (U replaces T)
3. Five-carbon sugar Deoxyribose sugar Ribose sugar
4. Location in cell Remains inside the nucleus (in chromosomes) Made in the nucleus, then moves to the cytoplasm and passes through ribosomes
5. Length & scope Very long molecule carrying thousands of genes Much shorter molecule: a working copy of one single gene
6. Lifespan & role Permanent master archive kept for the life of the cell Temporary working transcript broken down after printing proteins

Understand itTranscription (mRNA copy in nucleus) and translation (protein assembly at the ribosome)

What is it?

The two-stage pipeline by which a eukaryotic cell builds a protein from a gene: first making a single-stranded mRNA copy of the gene inside the nucleus, and then running that mRNA through a ribosome in the cytoplasm to link amino acids into a protein in the exact order specified by the mRNA bases.

Why is it called this?

Transcription means copying a message within the same language (4-letter nucleotide script in DNA copied into 4-letter nucleotide script in mRNA); translation means converting a message into a completely different language (4-letter nucleotide codons translated into the 20-letter amino-acid alphabet of proteins).

What problem did it solve?

It allows a cell to print thousands of copies of a needed protein (like insulin after a mango meal or antibodies during an infection) using dozens of cytoplasmic ribosomes simultaneously, without ever taking the master DNA chromosome out of the protective nucleus.

Why does it work?

Complementary base pairing ensures that the mRNA made in the nucleus faithfully preserves the gene’s base sequence (U replacing T), and complementary codon–anticodon pairing inside the ribosome ensures that each three-base mRNA triplet inserts the exact right amino acid.

How does it help?

It explains how every protein machine you met in Chapters 4–10—enzymes, membrane carriers, receptors for neurotransmitters, and antibodies—is built from the cell’s DNA archive.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Radioactive pulse-chase experiments in the 1950s and 1960s (using radioactive uridine to label newly made RNA) showed that RNA is synthesised first inside the nucleus and then migrates into the cytoplasm to associate with ribosomes, where radioactive amino acids are incorporated into growing polypeptide chains.

What it isn’t

The DNA gene does not travel to the ribosome, and mRNA is not converted chemically into amino acids—mRNA is the instruction tape that passes through the ribosome while free amino acids from the cytoplasm are linked together by peptide bonds.

Where does it stop working?

If a toxin (such as α-amanitin from the death-cap mushroom Amanita phalloides) blocks RNA polymerase in the nucleus, the cell cannot transcribe new mRNA copies of its genes, and protein synthesis grinds to a halt even though the DNA genes and cytoplasmic ribosomes are still intact.

Your turn

Explain Transcription (mRNA copy in nucleus) and translation (protein assembly at the ribosome) to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“To make a protein, the gene leaves the nucleus and goes to the ribosome, where the ribosome turns the mRNA bases into amino acids.”

Correct both parts—examiners penalise both phrasing slips heavily on Cambridge IGCSE 0610 17.1:

  1. The gene never leaves the nucleus: State clearly that the gene coding for the protein remains in the nucleus, and that a messenger RNA (mRNA) copy of the gene is made in the nucleus and moves to the cytoplasm.
  2. Bases are not turned into amino acids: Nucleotides (A, U, C, G) and amino acids are completely different chemical monomers. As mRNA passes through a ribosome, the ribosome reads the sequence of bases in the mRNA and assembles free amino acids into a protein molecule in the corresponding order.

At school

Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610, Topic 17.1 Core 3 & Supplement 4–5) requires you to:

  • Core (17.1.3): Explain that the sequence of bases in a gene is the genetic code for putting together amino acids in the correct order to make a specific protein (note that Core exam papers do not test the detailed mechanism of triplet anticodons or nucleotide monomer chemistry, which belong to Supplement/enrichment).
  • Supplement (17.1.4): Explain that DNA controls cell function by controlling the production of proteins, including enzymes, membrane carriers, and receptors for neurotransmitters.
  • Supplement (17.1.5): Explain how a protein is made using the six-point spine: (1) the gene coding for the protein remains in the nucleus, (2) messenger RNA (mRNA) is a copy of a gene, (3) mRNA molecules are made in the nucleus and move to the cytoplasm, (4) the mRNA passes through ribosomes, (5) the ribosome assembles amino acids into protein molecules, and (6) the specific sequence of amino acids is determined by the sequence of bases in the mRNA.

  1. Write down the base sequence of the mRNA molecule transcribed from this segment, and state where in the cell this mRNA is made and where it moves next.
  2. Using the genetic code (GUG = Val, CAC = His, CUG = Leu, ACU = Thr), write down the four-amino-acid sequence assembled when this mRNA passes through a ribosome, and explain how DNA controls the function of a synapse (Chapter 9) and active transport (Chapter 3).

Answer at the back of the book

11.4One letter changed: beta-globin, silent triplets and why sequence controls shape

The Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, 1956–1957, and a haematology laboratory in Mumbai

Now put the entire causal spine of Chapter 11—DNA base sequence → mRNA codon sequence → amino-acid sequence → 3D folded protein shape → cellular function—to a quantitative test on a single human protein you already know from Chapter 8: haemoglobin.

Each red blood cell in your bloodstream is packed with roughly 280 million molecules of adult haemoglobin (HbA). Each haemoglobin molecule is a four-subunit protein tetramer made of two alpha-globin (α) polypeptide chains (141 amino acids each) and two beta-globin (β) polypeptide chains (146 amino acids each, coded for by 146 × 3 = 438 sense bases in the HBB gene on human chromosome 11), with each subunit cradling an iron-containing haem group (Fe²⁺) that reversibly binds oxygen (O₂).

In sickle-cell anaemia, a person’s red blood cells produce an altered version of haemoglobin called sickle-cell haemoglobin (HbS). When HbS carries oxygen in the lungs and arteries, it stays dissolved. But when HbS releases its oxygen in respiring capillaries where oxygen concentration is low, the deoxygenated HbS molecules stick to one another head-to-tail, zipping up into long, rigid insoluble rods that stretch the flexible biconcave red blood cell into a stiff crescent (sickle) shape that can jam narrow capillaries and cause painful tissue oxygen starvation.

In 1949, Linus Pauling, Harvey Itano, S. J. Singer, and Ibert Wells showed that HbS moves more slowly toward the positive electrode than normal HbA during electrophoresis, proving that HbS carries a different electrical charge. But out of 146 amino acids in each beta-globin chain, how many amino acids are different between normal HbA and sickle-cell HbS?

In 1956 and 1957 at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, the biochemist Vernon Ingram answered that question by inventing peptide fingerprinting. He used the protease trypsin (Chapter 7) to snip both normal HbA and sickle-cell HbS beta-globin chains into 26 short peptide pieces, separated the 26 spots on filter paper using electric current in one direction and chromatography solvent in the other, and sequenced the single peptide spot (#4) that shifted position. :::

Predict first

When Vernon Ingram sequenced the 146 amino acids of the normal beta-globin chain (HbA) and the 146 amino acids of the sickle-cell beta-globin chain (HbS), how many of the 146 amino acids had changed, and what happened to the electrical charge and water solubility of that spot?

  1. 42 out of the 146 amino acids were scrambled because a single-base insertion near the start shifted the entire reading frame
  2. The chain was cut in half at residue 73 by a premature stop codon, leaving a 72-amino-acid fragment
  3. Only 1 amino acid out of 146 changed—at position 6 (Codon 6), where a single base substitution (DNA GAG → GTG, mRNA GAG → GUG) replaced negatively charged, hydrophilic glutamic acid (Glu⁶) with neutral, hydrophobic valine (Val⁶)

What happens

The third choice. Out of 438 coding bases (146 triplets) in the mature beta-globin gene, 437 bases are completely unchanged. At Codon 6, the middle base of the triplet changes from A to T on the coding DNA strand (GAG → GTG, or CTC → CAC on the template strand), which changes the sixth mRNA codon from GAG to GUG. Instead of inserting glutamic acid (Glu⁶)—whose side chain carries a negative electrical charge (−COO⁻) and loves water (hydrophilic)—the ribosome inserts valine (Val⁶), whose hydrocarbon side chain carries zero charge and repels water (hydrophobic).

How do we know? Cambridge, 1956–1957: Vernon Ingram’s peptide fingerprint of beta-globin Codon 6 Molecular sequence proof

In his 1956 and 1957 Nature papers, Vernon Ingram proved for the first time in the history of biology that a human hereditary condition results from changing a single amino acid in a protein molecule:

  • Normal adult beta-globin (HbA, Codons 1–7):
  • Coding DNA: 5'- G T G · C A C · C T G · A C T · C C T · G A G · G A G -3'
  • mRNA codons: 5'- G U G · C A C · C U G · A C U · C C U · G A G · G A G -3'
  • Amino acids 1–7: Val¹ – His² – Leu³ – Thr⁴ – Pro⁵ – Glu⁶ – Glu⁷
  • At position 6, glutamic acid (Glu⁶) sits on the outside of the folded beta-globin subunit; its negatively charged, hydrophilic side chain interacts smoothly with surrounding water molecules in the red blood cell cytoplasm so HbA tetramers remain separate and soluble.
  • Sickle-cell beta-globin (HbS, Codons 1–7):
  • Coding DNA: 5'- G T G · C A C · C T G · A C T · C C T · G T G · G A G -3' (single base change at Codon 6: GAG → GTG)
  • mRNA codons: 5'- G U G · C A C · C U G · A C U · C C U · G U G · G A G -3' (mRNA Codon 6: GAG → GUG)
  • Amino acids 1–7: Val¹ – His² – Leu³ – Thr⁴ – Pro⁵ – Val⁶ – Glu⁷ (Residue 6: Glu⁶ → Val⁶)
  • At position 6, valine (Val⁶) puts an oily, non-polar hydrophobic patch on the outer surface of the beta-globin subunit. When HbS releases oxygen in tissue capillaries, that sticky hydrophobic Val⁶ patch locks into a complementary hydrophobic pocket on a neighbouring HbS tetramer, zipping millions of HbS molecules into stiff polymers.

Now ask a subtler question that tests whether you truly understand how the 64-codon triplet dictionary works. Does every single-base substitution in the coding sequence of a gene alter the protein?

Compare the three possible molecular outcomes of substituting a single base inside a protein-coding gene, shown side by side in Figure 11.8:

  1. Outcome A · Silent (synonymous) substitution — zero change in the amino-acid sequence or 3D protein: Look at Codon 3 of the normal human beta-globin gene (GTG · CAC · CTG · ACT · CCT · GAG · GAG), where the coding DNA triplet CTG is transcribed into the mRNA codon CUG, coding for the third amino acid, leucine (Leu³). Suppose a single-base substitution changes the third base of Codon 3 from G to T on the coding DNA strand (CTG → CTT), so the mRNA codon changes from CUG to CUU. When the ribosome reads CUU, which amino acid does it insert? Because the 64-codon genetic code is degenerate, six different mRNA codons (UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, CUG) all code for leucine (Leu). The ribosome still inserts leucine (Leu³) at position 3, the 146-amino-acid sequence (Val¹–His²–Leu³–Thr⁴–Pro⁵–Glu⁶–Glu⁷...) is 100 percent identical to normal beta-globin, the 3D Ramachandran folding is completely unchanged, and the red blood cell carries 100 percent normal, soluble HbA.
  2. Outcome B · Missense substitution — one amino acid replaced by a different amino acid: When a single-base substitution changes a codon into a codon that specifies a different amino acid—as in beta-globin Codon 6 (GAG → GTG, mRNA GAG → GUG, Glu⁶ → Val⁶)—the ribosome prints a full-length polypeptide chain with one altered amino acid. If the new amino acid has a very different charge, size, or hydropathy (like hydrophobic valine replacing hydrophilic glutamic acid, or if the change sits right inside an enzyme’s active site or a voltage-gated ion channel), the 3D surface or folding of the protein changes.
  3. Outcome C · Nonsense (stop) substitution — premature chain termination: When a single-base substitution turns an amino-acid-coding triplet into one of the three stop codons (UAA, UAG, or UGA)—for example, changing beta-globin Codon 39 from coding DNA CAG (mRNA CAG, which codes for glutamine, Gln³⁹) to TAG (mRNA UAG, an amber stop codon)—the ribosome halts translation at residue 38 and releases a short, incomplete polypeptide fragment missing more than 70 percent of its amino acids. That truncated fragment cannot fold into a working globin subunit (causing severe beta-thalassaemia), just as Obaid Siddiqi’s nonsense mutations halted phage and bacterial protein synthesis in Chapter 9.

Understand itWhy one base change can be silent, missense, or nonsense

What is it?

The three different ways a single-base substitution in a DNA gene can affect the protein printed by a ribosome: silent (same amino acid, unchanged protein), missense (one amino acid swapped for another), or nonsense (an amino-acid codon turned into a premature STOP codon).

Why is it called this?

Silent (or synonymous) because the new triplet is a synonym for the exact same amino acid, leaving no trace in the finished protein; missense because one triplet now sends a different amino-acid meaning; nonsense (coined by Brenner, Crick and Siddiqi’s generation) because a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) specifies no amino acid at all.

What problem did it solve?

It explains why sequencing healthy people’s DNA reveals thousands of harmless single-letter spelling differences that never cause disease (silent changes buffered by the 64-codon degenerate dictionary), whereas a single missense change at Beta-Globin Codon 6 (GAG → GTG) or a single nonsense change at Codon 39 (CAG → TAG) has dramatic clinical effects.

Why does it work?

A ribosome does not inspect the DNA directly; it reads three-base mRNA codons using the 64-codon table. If the mutated mRNA codon maps to the same amino acid (CUG → CUU = Leu), the polypeptide chain has the exact same side chains and folds into the exact same 3D shape. If it maps to a different amino acid (GAG → GUG, Glu → Val) or to STOP (CAG → UAG), the polypeptide’s side-chain chemistry or length changes.

How does it help?

Whenever you are given a DNA or mRNA base change in a genetics problem, you can trace DNA → mRNA codon → amino acid → 3D shape step by step instead of assuming that every DNA mutation breaks a protein.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Vernon Ingram’s (1956–1957) peptide fingerprinting proved the Glu⁶ → Val⁶ missense change in HbS, while Marshall Nirenberg and Har Gobind Khorana’s 64-codon table explained why third-base changes such as CUG → CUU leave the amino acid unchanged.

What it isn’t

A silent mutation does not mean “the cell repaired the DNA back to the original letter”—the DNA base change (CTG → CTT) and mRNA change (CUG → CUU) are real and permanent, but both codons specify the same amino acid (Leu).

Where does it stop working?

Unlike a single-base substitution (which changes only 1 codon), a single-base insertion (+1) or deletion (−1) inside a coding sequence is almost never silent because it shifts the three-base reading frame for every codon downstream (Section 11.3).

Your turn

Explain Why one base change can be silent, missense, or nonsense to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“Every mutation in a gene’s DNA base sequence changes the amino-acid sequence and alters the 3D shape of the protein.”

Not every single-base substitution changes the amino-acid sequence. Because 64 triplets (4³) code for only 20 amino acids (plus 3 stop signals), most amino acids are specified by several synonymous codons (for example, CUU, CUC, CUA, and CUG all code for leucine). If a single-base substitution changes one codon into another codon for the same amino acid (a silent / synonymous change), the amino-acid sequence is completely unchanged, so the polypeptide folds into the exact same 3D shape and works normally.

At school

Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610, Topics 4.1 & 17.1, connecting to 17.4) expects you to connect the sequence of bases in a gene (A, T, C, G) to the sequence of bases in mRNA (A, U, C, G), the sequence of amino acids in a protein, and the 3D shape and function of that protein (such as an enzyme active site, a membrane carrier, a neurotransmitter receptor, an antibody, or haemoglobin). Notice how Chapter 11 keeps our focus strictly at the molecular sequence-to-protein level (DNA → mRNA → amino acid → 3D protein); how alternative versions of a gene (alleles) are inherited from parents to children belongs to Chapter 13, and how natural selection acts on variation in malaria zones belongs to Chapter 14.

Check yourself

Compare what happens to the mRNA codon, the amino-acid sequence, and the 3D folded beta-globin protein when:

  1. A single-base substitution changes beta-globin Codon 3 on the coding DNA strand from CTG to CTT (given that both CUG and CUU code for leucine, Leu).
  2. A single-base substitution changes beta-globin Codon 6 on the coding DNA strand from GAG to GTG (given that GAG codes for hydrophilic glutamic acid, Glu, and GUG codes for hydrophobic valine, Val).

Case file 11

Two children, two single-base changes, one unchanged protein

This is a fictional molecular-diagnostics reasoning case uniting Section 11.2 (complementary base pairing), Section 11.3 (transcription of mRNA and translation at the ribosome), and Section 11.4 (the degenerate 64-codon genetic code and beta-globin folding), not medical advice about any individual patient.

A paediatric haematology laboratory in Mumbai sequences the first seven codons (Codons 1 to 7, 21 bases) of the beta-globin (HBB) gene from a healthy reference standard and from two twelve-year-old patients, Child X and Child Y. Remarkably, both Child X and Child Y have exactly 1 base out of the 21 bases changed compared with the standard reference sequence:

Sample Coding DNA strand (5' → 3', Codons 1–7) Location of single-base change Red blood cell & haemoglobin test result
Reference (HbA) GTG · CAC · CTG · ACT · CCT · GAG · GAG None (0 bases changed) Normal soluble HbA; flexible biconcave red blood cells
Child X GTG · CAC · CTT · ACT · CCT · GAG · GAG Codon 3: CTG → CTT (1 base changed: G → T) 100% normal soluble HbA; flexible biconcave red blood cells
Child Y GTG · CAC · CTG · ACT · CCT · GTG · GAG Codon 6: GAG → GTG (1 base changed: A → T) Sticky HbS fibres at low O₂; sickled red blood cells

A relevant excerpt of the standard mRNA genetic code dictionary is provided alongside the sequencing report:

  • GUG, GUU, GUC, GUA = Valine (Val) (neutral, hydrophobic side chain)
  • CAC, CAU = Histidine (His)
  • CUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, UUA, UUG = Leucine (Leu) (hydrophobic interior residue)
  • ACU, ACC, ACA, ACG = Threonine (Thr)
  • CCU, CCC, CCA, CCG = Proline (Pro)
  • GAG, GAA = Glutamic acid (Glu) (negatively charged, hydrophilic surface residue)

A classmate looks at the table and says: “The laboratory must have mixed up Child X’s blood sample. Child X has a one-letter DNA mutation (G → T) in the beta-globin gene just like Child Y (A → T), so Child X’s ribosomes must also be printing a mutated, abnormally folded beta-globin protein.”

Use the molecular mechanisms of Sections 11.2, 11.3, and 11.4 to prove why the laboratory did not mix up the samples:

  1. For both Child X and Child Y, write down (a) the complementary template DNA strand (3' → 5') inside the nucleus and (b) the mRNA codon sequence (5' → 3') that moves through a nuclear pore to pass through the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
  2. Translate both mRNA sequences into their seven-amino-acid chains (Residues 1–7) using the codon table, and explain why Child X’s single-base DNA mutation produces zero change in the amino-acid sequence or 3D protein shape, whereas Child Y’s single-base DNA mutation alters the 3D surface behavior of haemoglobin.
  3. Suppose a third patient, Child Z, had a single base deleted (−1) from Codon 3 (so Codon 3 lost its G and became CT, instead of G being substituted by T). Would Child Z’s mutation also be silent like Child X’s? Explain why or why not using Francis Crick and Sydney Brenner’s (1961) discovery.
Show the solution

  1. Template DNA strands (3' → 5') in the nucleus and transcribed mRNA codons (5' → 3') in the cytoplasm: Using DNA complementary pairing (A ↔ T, C ↔ G) for the template strand, and RNA transcription (U replacing T of the coding strand) for the mRNA copy that moves from the nucleus to the cytoplasmic ribosomes: - Child X:

    • Template DNA (3' → 5'): 3'- CAC · GTG · GAA · TGA · GGA · CTC · CTC -5' (Codon 3 template changed from GAC to GAA)
    • Transcribed mRNA (5' → 3'): 5'- GUG · CAC · CUU · ACU · CCU · GAG · GAG -3' (mRNA Codon 3 changed from CUG to CUU)
    • Child Y:
    • Template DNA (3' → 5'): 3'- CAC · GTG · GAC · TGA · GGA · CAC · CTC -5' (Codon 6 template changed from CTC to CAC)
    • Transcribed mRNA (5' → 3'): 5'- GUG · CAC · CUG · ACU · CCU · GUG · GAG -3' (mRNA Codon 6 changed from GAG to GUG)

  2. Translation at the ribosome and why Child X is silent while Child Y is missense: - Child X polypeptide (Residues 1–7): Reading GUG · CAC · CUU · ACU · CCU · GAG · GAG at the ribosome gives Val¹ – His² – Leu³ – Thr⁴ – Pro⁵ – Glu⁶ – Glu⁷. Because the 64-codon genetic code is degenerate, both CUG (Reference) and CUU (Child X) code for the exact same amino acid: Leucine (Leu³), and Codon 6 is still GAG (hydrophilic Glu⁶). Because the linear sequence of all 146 amino acids in Child X’s beta-globin is 100% identical to the Reference chain, G. N. Ramachandran’s steric and side-chain folding rules fold Child X’s polypeptide into the exact same 3D shape (HbA) (silent / synonymous substitution). - Child Y polypeptide (Residues 1–7): Reading GUG · CAC · CUG · ACU · CCU · GUG · GAG at the ribosome gives Val¹ – His² – Leu³ – Thr⁴ – Pro⁵ – Val⁶ – Glu⁷. At Codon 6, changing GAG to GUG is a missense substitution that replaces negatively charged, water-loving glutamic acid (Glu⁶) with neutral, water-repelling valine (Val⁶). That exposed hydrophobic Val⁶ patch causes deoxygenated HbS molecules to stick together into rigid fibres that distort red blood cells into sickles.

  3. Why a single-base deletion (−1) at Codon 3 in Child Z would NOT be silent (Crick & Brenner 1961 frameshift): Deleting the G at the end of Codon 3 leaves only 2 bases (CT), so the ribosome—which reads mRNA in non-overlapping triplets without commas—pulls the first base of Codon 4 into Codon 3 and shifts the reading frame of every single triplet downstream (GTG · CAC · CTA · CTC · CTG · AGG · AG... → mRNA GUG · CAC · CUA · CUC · CUG · AGG...). Instead of Val–His–Leu–Thr–Pro–Glu–Glu, Child Z’s ribosome prints Val–His–Leu–Leu–Leu–Arg..., scrambling every amino acid from position 4 to the end of the gene and destroying the 3D beta-globin protein (frameshift mutation).

What this chapter can’t explain yet

You now know how a living cell stores its protein recipes as sequences of A, T, C, and G bases inside chromosomes in the nucleus, and how mRNA and ribosomes read that four-letter triplet cipher to print folded enzymes, membrane carriers, receptors, antibodies, and haemoglobin. That solved puzzle immediately opens three huge questions across the life of an organism:

  1. You began your life as a single fertilised egg cell (zygote) containing just one nuclear archive of 46 chromosomes. How did that single cell unzip and copy two metres of DNA with near-perfect accuracy again and again so that all 37 trillion cells in your body today carry a complete copy of the library (DNA replication and mitosis)?
  2. If a beta cell in your pancreas, a cone cell in your retina, and a motor neurone in your spinal cord all inherited the exact same set of genes, why does only the pancreas beta cell print insulin while the retina cell prints light-detecting opsins (stem cells, specialisation, and why only the genes needed by a specific cell are expressed)?
  3. When parents produce sperm and egg cells (gametes), how do reproductive organs halve the chromosome number from diploid (46) to haploid (23)—and shuffle parental chromosomes—so that fertilisation restores 46 chromosomes instead of doubling the genome to 92 (46 + 46) in the next generation (meiosis)?

Volume IV continues in Chapter 12: Copying the Blueprint: Mitosis, Stem Cells & Meiosis.
