Chapter 13

“The Monk’s Spreadsheet: Mendel, Alleles & Inheritance”

The big questionHow do two copies of every gene on homologous chromosomes interact to build your traits, why do Mendel’s crosses, ABO blood groups, and X-linked traits obey exact mathematical ratios, and how can geneticists solve a Mumbai maternity-ward bracelet swap from a single drop of blood?

  1. 13.1The monk in the pea patch: why traits don’t blend, and how genes come in alleles
  2. 13.2The Punnett ledger: monohybrid crosses, test crosses, and family pedigrees
  3. 13.3When neither allele yields: codominance and the ABO blood group puzzle
  4. 13.4The twenty-third pair: XX, XY, and sex-linked inheritance

Picture two real-world medical puzzles unfolding on the same rainy afternoon at a teaching hospital in Parel, Mumbai.

Upstairs in the maternity ward, two healthy baby boys were born during a brief generator switchover before their ankle identity bands were clipped on. Baby 1 has Blood Group O; Baby 2 has Blood Group A. The ward register lists the two sets of parents: Couple 1 (the Desais) are a Group AB mother and a Group O father, while Couple 2 (the Kulkarnis) are a Group A mother and a Group B father. Without waiting days for a full DNA sequence, the on-call geneticist looks at those four blood-group letters, sketches two small four-box grids on a notepad, and assigns each baby to his biological parents in less than sixty seconds.

Downstairs in the paediatric clinic, a second couple—both of whom have completely normal trichromatic colour vision and normal blood clotting—are astonished to learn that their six-year-old son has red–green colour vision deficiency, while their eight-year-old daughter sees every red and green traffic light on Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar Road without difficulty. How can a trait that neither parent shows appear in their son? And why did the boy’s maternal grandfather have the exact same condition, even though the boy’s mother has normal colour vision?

In Chapter 12 you saw how Walther Flemming traced chromosome threads through mitosis (12.2), and how meiosis (12.4) halves the chromosome count in reproductive organs from diploid (2n = 46, or 23 homologous pairs) to haploid (n = 23 single chromosomes) in sperm and egg cells so fertilisation restores 2n = 46 in every new zygote. That chromosome dance gives us the master key to Chapter 13:

  1. Two copies of every gene (13.1): Because every diploid body cell carries two sets of homologous chromosomes—one maternal homologue inherited from your mother’s ovum and one paternal homologue inherited from your father’s sperm—you carry two copies (alleles) of every autosomal gene. What happens when those two copies carry slightly different DNA base sequences (Chapter 11), and why did an Augustinian friar in Brno prove in 1866 that alleles behave like discrete, unblending packets rather than mixed paint?
  2. The 2 × 2 Punnett ledger and family pedigrees (13.2): How does meiotic segregation (2n → n) combine with random fertilisation (n + n → 2n) to generate the famous 3 : 1, 1 : 2 : 1, and 1 : 1 ratios of monohybrid crosses, diagnostic test crosses, and clinical pedigree charts?
  3. Multiple alleles and codominance (13.3): What happens when neither allele masks the other—as in the Iᴬ, Iᴮ, and Iᴼ alleles of the human ABO blood group gene on Chromosome 9?
  4. Sex chromosomes (XX vs XY) and sex-linked inheritance (13.4): How does the twenty-third chromosome pair lock human births to a 1 : 1 sex ratio, and why do recessive alleles located on the X chromosome—such as red–green colour vision deficiency and haemophilia—strike males far more often than females?

13.1The monk in the pea patch: why traits don’t blend, and how genes come in alleles

St Thomas’s Abbey, Brno (Moravia), 1856–1866

Walk into the walled kitchen garden of St Thomas’s Abbey in Brno in the spring of 1856, and you would find a thirty-four-year-old Augustinian friar named Johann Gregor Mendel kneeling beside rows of climbing garden peas (Pisum sativum) with a pair of jeweller’s forceps, a camel-hair paintbrush, and a ruled ledger book.

Before Johann Gregor Mendel began his eight-year pea investigation, almost every naturalist in Europe—including Charles Darwin—assumed that heredity worked by blending inheritance. According to the blending view, the hereditary material of the mother and the father mixed irreversibly inside the offspring like a pot of red paint stirred into a pot of white paint to make pink paint. Once mixed, red and white could never be separated again.

Trained in experimental physics and combinatorial probability at the University of Vienna, Johann Gregor Mendel saw a fatal flaw in the paint-pot story—and realised why garden peas were the ideal organism to test it:

  • Strict pollination control: A pea flower’s reproductive organs (pollen-making anthers and ovule-holding carpel) are sealed inside a boat-shaped keel petal, so pea plants naturally self-pollinate. By snipping off a flower bud’s immature anthers with forceps (emasculation) before its pollen ripened and dusting the stigma with pollen from a chosen partner plant, Johann Gregor Mendel could control the exact parentage of every seed.
  • Sharp, either-or characters: After two years (1854–1856) of testing thirty-four pea varieties to confirm which lines bred true (producing identical offspring generation after generation when self-pollinated), he selected seven distinct, non-overlapping characters—such as round versus wrinkled seeds, yellow versus green seed cotyledons, purple versus white flowers, and tall (1.8–2.1 m) versus dwarf (0.3–0.45 m) stems.
  • Large sample sizes: A single pea cross yields dozens of dry seeds that can be counted like beads in a tray, allowing thousands of independent fertilisations to be scored in a few seasons.

Predict first

Suppose Johann Gregor Mendel crosses a pure-breeding round-seeded pea plant with a pure-breeding wrinkled-seeded pea plant to produce first-generation (F₁) hybrid seeds, and then allows those F₁ plants to self-pollinate to produce second-generation (F₂) seeds. If the paint-pot blending hypothesis were true, what should the F₁ and F₂ seeds look like—and what did Johann Gregor Mendel actually observe?

  1. Blending predicts 100% round F₁ seeds and 75% round : 25% wrinkled F₂ seeds; Mendel observed 100% half-wrinkled F₁ and F₂ seeds
  2. Blending predicts semi-wrinkled intermediate F₁ seeds that stay semi-wrinkled forever in F₂; Mendel observed 100% round F₁ seeds, and in F₂ the wrinkled trait returned completely unblemished in roughly 25% of the seeds (a 3 : 1 ratio of round to wrinkled)
  3. Blending predicts 50% round and 50% wrinkled seeds in both F₁ and F₂; Mendel observed 100% wrinkled seeds in F₁

What happens

The second choice. If maternal and paternal instructions blended like paint, crossing round with wrinkled would produce intermediate, mildly dimpled F₁ seeds, and self-pollinating those F₁ plants could never recover a purely wrinkled seed. Instead, Johann Gregor Mendel observed that 100% of the F₁ seeds were completely smooth and round. Even more strikingly, when those round F₁ plants self-pollinated to form F₂ seeds, roughly one quarter (25.3%) of the F₂ seeds were completely wrinkled, indistinguishable from the original wrinkled grandparent. The wrinkled instruction had lain hidden inside the F₁ plants for an entire generation without being diluted or contaminated by a single molecule.

How do we know? Brno, Moravia, 1856–1866: Johann Gregor Mendel’s 19,959-outcome F₂ ledger and F₃ progeny verification Quantitative breeding proof

In his 1866 monograph Versuche über Pflanzen-Hybriden (Experiments on Plant Hybrids), Johann Gregor Mendel reported the exact counts from his 35 m × 7 m abbey plot across all seven pea characters:

  1. Uniformity in the F₁ generation: Regardless of whether the round-seeded parent supplied the ovule (egg) or the pollen (sperm)—a reciprocal cross—100% of the F₁ hybrid offspring displayed only one of the two parental traits (e.g. round seeds, yellow cotyledons, purple flowers, tall stems). Johann Gregor Mendel named the trait that appeared in 100% of F₁ hybrids dominant, and the trait that vanished in F₁ recessive (from the Latin recedere, “to step back”).
  2. The 3 : 1 split across 19,959 F₂ outcomes: When the F₁ hybrids self-pollinated, the recessive trait reappeared across all seven characters in a constant 3 : 1 ratio (75% dominant : 25% recessive):
    • Seed shape (7,324 seeds): 5,474 round to 1,850 wrinkled = 2.96 : 1 (74.74% : 25.26%).
    • Seed cotyledon colour (8,023 seeds): 6,022 yellow to 2,001 green = 3.01 : 1 (75.06% : 24.94%).
    • Flower / seed-coat colour (929 plants): 705 purple to 224 white = 3.15 : 1 (75.89% : 24.11%).
    • Ripe pod shape (1,181 plants): 882 inflated to 299 constricted = 2.95 : 1.
    • Unripe pod colour (580 plants): 428 green to 152 yellow = 2.82 : 1.
    • Flower position (858 plants): 651 axial to 207 terminal = 3.14 : 1.
    • Stem length (1,064 plants): 787 tall (1.8–2.1 m) to 277 dwarf (0.3–0.45 m) = 2.84 : 1.
    • Combined ledger total (19,959 outcomes): 14,949 dominant (74.90%) to 5,010 recessive (25.10%) = 2.98 : 1.
  3. The F₃ progeny test proving the hidden 1 : 2 : 1 ratio: Johann Gregor Mendel did not stop at F₂. He planted 565 round F₂ seeds and let each grown plant self-pollinate to form F₃ seeds. If all round F₂ seeds were genetically identical, all 565 should behave alike. Instead, 193 plants (34.2%) bred true (producing only round seeds), while 372 plants (65.8%) segregated 3 : 1 again just like F₁ hybrids—a 1 : 1.93 ratio (1 : 2 theoretical). Combined with the 25% pure wrinkled F₂ seeds, this proved that the 3 : 1 visible ratio is actually a 1 : 2 : 1 genetic ratio (¼ pure dominant : ½ hybrid : ¼ pure recessive).

Genes, loci, and alleles on homologous chromosomes

Why did Johann Gregor Mendel’s pea traits come in pairs (RR, Rr, rr) inside every parent plant, separate to single copies (R or r) inside pollen and ovules, and rejoin in pairs at fertilisation? Because Johann Gregor Mendel was tracking the behaviour of homologous chromosomes forty years before William Bateson coined the word genetics—and nearly a century before Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray diffraction and Har Gobind Khorana’s synthetic codons revealed that hereditary instructions are written in DNA base triplets (Chapter 11).

Let us lock in the exact Cambridge definitions that connect Chapter 11 (DNA and proteins) and Chapter 12 (meiosis and chromosomes) to Chapter 13:

  • Inheritance is the transmission of genetic information from generation to generation (0610 17.4.1 Core).
  • A gene is a length of DNA that codes for a protein (0610 17.1.2 Core). Every gene sits at a fixed physical address—called its locus (plural loci)—along a specific chromosome.
  • An allele is an alternative form of a gene (0610 17.1.3 Core). All alleles of the same gene occupy the exact same locus on homologous chromosomes and govern the same feature, but they differ slightly in their DNA base sequence (A, T, C, G).
  • Because a diploid (2n) cell contains two sets of homologous chromosomes—one maternal homologue and one paternal homologue in each pair—every diploid cell carries two allele copies for each autosomal gene (one on each homologue). During meiosis (2n → n), homologous chromosomes separate into different haploid (n) gametes, so each gamete carries only one allele of each gene.

When we compare the two alleles at a single locus inside a diploid organism, three combinations are possible:

Term Definition (0610 17.4) Pea Example
Homozygous Having two identical alleles of a particular gene (RR or rr). Two identical homozygous individuals that breed together will be pure-breeding (0610 17.4.6–17.4.7). RR (homozygous dominant, pure round) or rr (homozygous recessive, pure wrinkled)
Heterozygous Having two different alleles of a particular gene (Rr). A heterozygous individual is not pure-breeding (0610 17.4.8–17.4.9). Rr (F₁ hybrid; round seed phenotype, but passes r to 50% of its gametes)
Genotype vs Phenotype Genotype is the genetic make-up of an organism in terms of the alleles present (RR, Rr, rr); phenotype is the observable features of an organism (0610 17.4.4–17.4.5). Genotypes RR and Rr both produce the round seed phenotype; rr produces wrinkled

Why is one allele dominant and the other recessive? The enzyme bridge

Students often picture a dominant allele as a “bully” that physically attacks or deletes the recessive allele on the partner chromosome. Look back at Chapter 4 (enzymes as folded 3D protein catalysts, whose polypeptide conformation was mapped by G. N. Ramachandran) and Chapter 11 (how DNA base sequences are transcribed into mRNA and translated by ribosomes into enzymes). The two homologous chromosomes in a nucleus do not fight each other at all; both sit quietly in chromatin and are transcribed independently.

Here is the real molecular reason why R (round) is dominant and r (wrinkled) is recessive—discovered when Cathie Martin, Alison Smith, and Madan Bhattacharyya sequenced Johann Gregor Mendel’s seed-shape gene in 1990:

  1. The dominant allele (R) codes for a functional enzyme: On pea Chromosome 5, the R allele is an intact DNA sequence coding for starch-branching enzyme isoform I (SBEI). Inside a developing pea seed, SBEI catalyses the branching of linear starch chains (amylose) into compact, insoluble amylopectin starch grains.
  2. The recessive allele (r) codes for a non-functional enzyme: In wrinkled peas, the r allele contains an 800-base-pair (0.8 kb) transposon DNA insertion right inside the coding sequence. Ribosomes translating r mRNA print a truncated polypeptide whose active site cannot fold or catalyse starch branching (0% SBEI activity).
  3. Why rr seeds wrinkle (osmosis from Chapter 3): In a homozygous recessive (rr) seed with zero functional SBEI (0% enzyme dose), unbranched sugars (sucrose and fructose) pile up in the cytoplasm. Those dissolved sugars lower the seed’s water potential, drawing extra water into the young seed by osmosis and swelling it up. Later, as the ripe pod dries out in the sun, the swollen rr seed loses that extra water and its stretched seed coat collapses into deep wrinkles.
  4. Why Rr heterozygotes are completely round (haplosufficiency): In a heterozygous (Rr) seed, the r allele produces no working enzyme, but the single R allele on the homologous chromosome still transcribes normal mRNA and builds a 50% dose of active SBEI enzyme. Because enzymes are reusable biological catalysts (Chapter 4), a 50% enzyme dose is more than enough to convert the seed’s sugar into branched amylopectin starch. Consequently, Rr seeds have the exact same round phenotype as RR (100% enzyme dose) seeds.

The exact same molecular rule explains Johann Gregor Mendel’s other pea traits: in flower colour (B vs b), B codes for a working transcription factor that switches on purple anthocyanin pigment synthesis, whereas b carries a single-base splice mutation (G → A) that produces no pigment (white petals); in stem height (T vs t), T codes for active gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase enzyme that builds growth hormone GA₁ for tall internodes (1.8–2.1 m), whereas t carries an amino-acid substitution (Ala²²⁹ → Thr²²⁹) in the active site that cuts hormone synthesis by over 90%, leaving tt plants dwarf (0.3–0.45 m).

  • A dominant allele is an allele that is expressed if it is present in the genotype (whether in one copy Rr or two copies RR; 0610 17.4.2 Core).
  • A recessive allele is an allele that is only expressed when there is no dominant allele of the gene present in the genotype (only in the homozygous recessive state rr; 0610 17.4.3 Core).

Letter choice in genetic diagrams: Always use the uppercase letter of the dominant trait for the dominant allele (e.g. R for round, B for purple/blue-violet, T for tall) and the matching lowercase letter for the recessive allele (r for wrinkled, b for white, t for dwarf)—never two different letters like R for round and W for wrinkled. Where uppercase and lowercase look similar in handwriting (C/c, S/s, W/w, P/p), write curved or serifed uppercase letters or choose letters with unmistakable shapes (A/a, B/b, D/d, R/r, T/t).

Understand it

What is the difference between a gene and an allele?

A gene is a specific length of DNA at a fixed chromosome address (locus) that codes for a protein (such as the starch-branching enzyme gene in peas or the beta-globin gene in humans). An allele is one of the alternative versions of that gene (such as the functional R allele versus the non-functional r allele), differing slightly in its DNA base sequence.

Why does a diploid organism have two alleles for each gene, while a gamete has only one?

A diploid (2n) organism inherited two complete sets of homologous chromosomes—one set from its mother’s egg and one set from its father’s sperm—so it has two copies of every chromosome and two alleles for every autosomal gene. When the organism makes gametes (sperm or egg cells, or pollen and ovules) by meiosis (2n → n), homologous chromosome pairs separate so each haploid gamete receives only one chromosome from each pair and therefore only one allele per gene.

Why is a heterozygous Rr pea seed just as round as a homozygous RR pea seed?

Because the R allele codes for a working starch-branching enzyme (SBEI). Even though the r allele in an Rr seed makes no working enzyme, the single R copy makes a 50% dose of reusable enzyme catalyst, which is plenty to convert linear sugars into branched starch and keep the seed smooth and round.

What does it mean to say that two homozygous individuals are pure-breeding, whereas a heterozygous individual is not?

A homozygous individual (RR or rr) carries two identical alleles, so 100% of its gametes carry that same allele; crossing two identical homozygotes (RR × RR or rr × rr) produces offspring that are 100% identical to the parents generation after generation (pure-breeding). A heterozygous individual (Rr) produces 50% R gametes and 50% r gametes, so self-crossing (Rr × Rr) splits the offspring into round (RR, Rr) and wrinkled (rr) seeds (not pure-breeding).

Can two organisms have the exact same phenotype but different genotypes?

Yes. In simple dominance, a homozygous dominant pea (RR) and a heterozygous pea (Rr) have different genotypes (RR versus Rr), but both have the exact same phenotype (round seed) because a single R allele is expressed whenever it is present.

Go deeper how did johann gregor mendel prove that the round seeds in his f₂ generation were actually a 1 : 2 mixture of two different genotypes (rr and rr), why did carl nägeli’s suggestion to test hawkweed (hieracium) fail to reproduce mendel’s 3 : 1 ratios, and how does e. k. janaki ammal’s cytogenetics work (chapter 12) explain why, if a recessive allele (r) is not expressed in the phenotype of an rr f₁ hybrid, why doesn’t it weaken or disappear over ten generations of heterozygotes
How did Johann Gregor Mendel prove that the round seeds in his F₂ generation were actually a 1 : 2 mixture of two different genotypes (RR and Rr)?

He planted 565 round F₂ seeds and let each grown plant self-pollinate to produce F₃ seeds. One third (193 plants) bred true and produced only round seeds (proving their F₂ genotype was RR), whereas two thirds (372 plants) segregated in a 3 : 1 ratio of round to wrinkled seeds (proving their F₂ genotype was heterozygous Rr).

Why did Carl Nägeli’s suggestion to test hawkweed (Hieracium) fail to reproduce Mendel’s 3 : 1 ratios, and how does E. K. Janaki Ammal’s cytogenetics work (Chapter 12) explain why?

Mendel’s 3 : 1 ratio requires sexual reproduction—specifically meiosis separating alleles into haploid gametes followed by fertilisation fusing pollen and ovule nuclei. Hawkweed (Hieracium) frequently forms seeds asexually without meiosis or fertilisation (apomixis), producing maternal clones just like the mitotic sugarcane stem cuttings studied by E. K. Janaki Ammal.

If a recessive allele (r) is not expressed in the phenotype of an Rr F₁ hybrid, why doesn’t it weaken or disappear over ten generations of heterozygotes?

Because an allele is a covalent sequence of DNA nucleotides (A, T, C, G) on a chromosome. Even when the r allele makes a non-functional protein, semi-conservative DNA replication copies the r chromosome base-for-base before every cell division with the same one-in-a-billion proofreading accuracy as the R chromosome, passing it intact into 50% of the gametes during meiosis.

Your turn

Explain to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

Two frequent traps to avoid when using dominant and recessive:

  1. “Dominant” does NOT mean “more common in the population” or “stronger/healthier”: Dominance only describes which allele is expressed inside a heterozygote (Aa). Whether an allele is common or rare in a population depends on natural selection and history (Chapter 14), not on whether it is dominant. For example, in humans, having six fingers or toes (polydactyly) and Huntington’s disease are caused by dominant alleles, yet both are very rare in the population (over 99.9% of people are homozygous recessive aa with five fingers per hand). Conversely, Blood Group O (IᴼIᴼ) is recessive, yet it is the single most common blood group in many human populations.
  2. Never write “a dominant gene” or “a recessive gene”: Everyone has the same genes (the seed-shape gene, the flower-colour gene, the beta-globin gene). Always write “a dominant allele” or “a recessive allele”.

At school

Cambridge Lower Secondary Science (0893) and Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610, Topic 17.4 Core) require word-accurate definitions of these nine terms:

  • Inheritance (17.4.1): The transmission of genetic information from generation to generation.
  • Gene (17.1.2) vs Allele (17.1.3): A gene is a length of DNA that codes for a protein; an allele is an alternative form of a gene.
  • Dominant allele (17.4.2): An allele that is expressed if it is present in the genotype.
  • Recessive allele (17.4.3): An allele that is only expressed when there is no dominant allele of the gene present in the genotype.
  • Genotype (17.4.4) vs Phenotype (17.4.5): Genotype is the genetic make-up of an organism in terms of the alleles present; phenotype is the observable features of an organism.
  • Homozygous (17.4.6–17.4.7) vs Heterozygous (17.4.8–17.4.9): Homozygous means having two identical alleles of a particular gene (two identical homozygous individuals that breed together will be pure-breeding); heterozygous means having two different alleles of a particular gene (a heterozygous individual is not pure-breeding).

Check yourself

  1. Define (a) allele, (b) genotype, (c) phenotype, (d) homozygous, and (e) heterozygous, and state which of (d) or (e) is pure-breeding.
  2. In pea plants, the allele for tall stems (T) is dominant to the allele for dwarf stems (t), where T codes for functional gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase enzyme and t codes for an inactive enzyme. State the genotype, zygosity, relative enzyme dose (100%, 50%, or 0%), and stem-length phenotype of (a) a pure-breeding tall plant, (b) a pure-breeding dwarf plant, and (c) an F₁ hybrid produced by crossing (a) and (b).

Answer at the back of the book

13.2The Punnett ledger: monohybrid crosses, test crosses, and family pedigrees

University of Cambridge, 1900–1905, and Tata Memorial Centre, Parel, Mumbai, 1950s

When Johann Gregor Mendel’s 1866 paper was rediscovered in the spring of 1900, Cambridge biologist William Bateson read it on the train to London to address the Royal Horticultural Society and realised that biology had found its atomic theory. Over the next five years in Cambridge, William Bateson coined the terms genetics, allele, homozygote, and heterozygote, while his collaborator Reginald Punnett introduced a simple visual matrix—the 2 × 2 Punnett square—that turns meiotic chromosome segregation and random fertilisation into a foolproof accounting grid.

Every monohybrid cross (a genetic cross tracking one gene locus with two alleles) follows the same six-line genetic diagram protocol:

  1. Parental phenotypes: Write the observable feature of each parent (e.g. Purple flower × Purple flower).
  2. Parental genotypes (2n): Write two allele letters for each diploid parent (e.g. Bb × Bb).
  3. Gametes (n): Because meiosis halves the chromosome number (2n → n) by separating homologous chromosomes, each haploid gamete receives only one allele letter. Always draw a circle around each gamete allele—or write (B) and (b)—to show it is a separate haploid cell (50% B and 50% b from a Bb parent).
  4. 2 × 2 Punnett square: Place the two maternal gametes along the left side and the two paternal gametes along the top. Fill each of the 4 interior boxes by combining one maternal gamete (n) + one paternal gamete (n) → one diploid zygote (2n), writing the uppercase allele first (Bb, never bB). Each box represents an independent 1/4 (25% or 0.25) probability.
  5. Offspring genotypes and phenotypes: Read the 4 boxes (1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb) and translate each genotype into its observable phenotype (3 Purple : 1 White).
  6. Expected ratios / probabilities: Express both the genotype ratio (1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb, or 25% : 50% : 25%) and the phenotype ratio (3 dominant : 1 recessive, or 75% : 25%) in simplest whole numbers.

The diagnostic test cross: unmasking a hidden recessive allele

Look closely at the 3 : 1 outcome of Bb × Bb. The white-flowered offspring (25%) have an unmistakable genotype: because white is recessive, every white-flowered pea plant must be homozygous recessive (bb).

What about a purple-flowered pea plant (B_)? By sight alone, you cannot tell whether its genotype is homozygous dominant (BB) or heterozygous (Bb), because both genotypes make enough anthocyanin enzyme to colour the petals deep purple. How can a plant breeder or geneticist discover which genotype a dominant-phenotype individual carries?

Predict first

A plant breeder in Pune has a prize purple-flowered pea plant (B_) and wants to know whether it is pure-breeding (BB) or a heterozygous carrier (Bb) of the white-flower allele. Which partner should she cross the mystery purple plant with to get a clear, unambiguous answer in a single generation—and what offspring ratios distinguish BB from Bb?

  1. Cross the mystery plant with a homozygous dominant purple plant (BB); if it is Bb, 25% of the offspring will have white flowers
  2. Cross the mystery plant with a homozygous recessive white-flowered tester plant (bb, a test cross); if the mystery plant is BB, 100% of the offspring will be purple (Bb), whereas if the mystery plant is Bb, the offspring will split in a 1 : 1 ratio (50% purple Bb : 50% white bb)
  3. Cross the mystery plant with a known heterozygote (Bb); only a 3 : 1 ratio can reveal a hidden allele

What happens

The second choice. Crossing with BB (the first choice) is useless because BB gives a dominant B allele to every single gamete, making 100% of the offspring purple regardless of whether the mystery plant is BB or Bb. By crossing the mystery plant (B_) with a homozygous recessive tester (bb)—a procedure Johann Gregor Mendel invented and called a test cross—every tester gamete contributes only the recessive allele (b). Therefore the offspring phenotypes directly display the gametes of the mystery parent:

  • If the mystery parent is homozygous dominant (BB × bb): All gametes from the mystery parent are (B), so 100% of the offspring are heterozygous (Bb) and purple-flowered (0% white).
  • If the mystery parent is heterozygous (Bb × bb): Half of its gametes are (B) and half are (b), producing 50% purple (Bb) and 50% white (bb) offspring—an exact 1 : 1 ratio. Even a single white-flowered (bb) offspring proves beyond doubt that the purple parent carried a hidden b allele.

How do we know? Brno, 1866 & Cambridge, 1905: Mendel’s test-cross verifications and Reginald Punnett’s gamete matrix Experimental & algebraic proof

In his 1866 paper, Johann Gregor Mendel used test crosses (Rr × rr and Yy × yy) to verify that F₁ hybrids produce dominant and recessive gametes in an exact 1 : 1 (50% : 50%) ratio in both ovules and pollen:

  1. Reciprocal test-cross counts: Crossing F₁ hybrid plants (Rr Yy) with pure recessive plants (rr yy)—first using the hybrid as the female seed parent and then as the male pollen parent—yielded equal numbers of dominant and recessive traits (1 : 1 at each locus), proving that female meiosis and male meiosis segregate alleles with identical 50% : 50% fairness.
  2. Summary of the four fundamental monohybrid crosses: Every single-gene cross in Reginald Punnett’s 2 × 2 matrix reduces to one of four canonical patterns:
Parental Cross Offspring Genotypes Offspring Phenotypes
1. AA × aa (Pure dom × Pure rec) 100% Aa (all heterozygous) 100% dominant : 0% recessive
2. Aa × Aa (Heterozygote × Heterozygote) 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa (25% : 50% : 25%) 3 dominant : 1 recessive (75% : 25%)
3. Aa × aa (Heterozygote test cross) 1 Aa : 1 aa (50% : 50%) 1 dominant : 1 recessive (50% : 50%)
4. AA × Aa (Homozygous dom × Heterozygote) 1 AA : 1 Aa (50% : 50%) 100% dominant (50% carriers)

The story behind this

Twenty-eight thousand pea plants in Brno, a white-eyed fly in New York, and blood-group pedigrees in MumbaiHow an Augustinian friar trained in physics counted 19,959 pea outcomes in Brno, how Cambridge geneticists invented the Punnett square, how mealworm beetles and a single white-eyed fruit fly tied genes to chromosomes, and how L. D. Sanghvi mapped blood groups and carrier pedigrees in Mumbai.

Reading family trees: the two ironclad pedigree detective rules

With pea plants or fruit flies, geneticists can perform controlled test crosses and count hundreds of offspring. With human families, we cannot design experimental crosses, and most families have only a few children. Instead, human geneticists—like L. D. Sanghvi at the Tata Memorial Centre in Mumbai—trace inheritance across three or four generations using a pedigree diagram (0610 17.4.11 Core):

  • Squares (□ / ■) represent males; circles (○ / ●) represent females.
  • Unshaded symbols (□, ○) represent unaffected individuals; shaded symbols (■, ●) represent affected individuals showing the trait or condition.
  • A horizontal marriage/mating line connects two parents; a vertical line drops to a horizontal sibling bracket listing their children in birth order from left to right across numbered generations (I, II, III).
  • An unaffected individual who carries one hidden copy of a recessive allele (Aa) is called a heterozygous carrier.

Whenever you are handed an unfamiliar pedigree chart in a clinic or an examination, look immediately for a parent–child triad where the child’s phenotype differs from both parents. Two ironclad deductive rules solve any autosomal pedigree:

  1. Pedigree Detective Rule 1 (Unaffected × Unaffected → Affected child proves RECESSIVE):
    • Suppose two unaffected parents (I-1 and I-2, unshaded) have an affected child (II-2, shaded).
    • Deduction: The condition must be caused by a recessive allele (a), the affected child must be homozygous recessive (aa), and both unaffected parents must be heterozygous carriers (Aa).
    • Why? The affected child (aa) had to inherit one a allele from each parent. Because both parents are unaffected, each parent must also have a dominant normal allele (A) masking a. If the condition were dominant, an affected child (A_) would have had to inherit A from at least one parent, making that parent affected too. Thus only a recessive trait can “skip” a generation via unaffected carriers.
  2. Pedigree Detective Rule 2 (Affected × Affected → Unaffected child proves DOMINANT):
    • Suppose two affected parents (I-1 and I-2, shaded) have an unaffected child (II-2, unshaded).
    • Deduction: The condition must be caused by a dominant allele (A), the unaffected child must be homozygous recessive (aa), and both affected parents must be heterozygous (Aa).
    • Why? If the condition were recessive, two affected parents would both be aa × aa and could pass only a alleles, making 100% of their children affected (aa). Having even one unaffected child (aa) proves both affected parents carried a hidden recessive normal allele (a).

Try it at home

The Two-Coin & Two-Dal Mendel Ledger (Mumbai Kitchen Investigation)

Educational adaptation disclosure: This safe household probability model is a non-trialled educational adaptation designed to demonstrate how independent gamete segregation (50% : 50%) generates 1 : 2 : 1 genotype ratios, 3 : 1 phenotype ratios, 1 : 1 test crosses, and convergence from small (N = 16) to larger (N = 64) samples. It uses only dry kitchen items or coins (0 chemicals, 0 heat, 0 biological fluids).

What you need: Two identical Indian coins (₹1, ₹2, or ₹5, where Heads = dominant allele R and Tails = recessive allele r)—or two small bowls each holding 20 pale kabuli chana (chickpeas = R) and 20 dark kala chana (black gram = r) mixed thoroughly—plus a notebook and pen.

Part A — Simulating a monohybrid Rr × Rr cross (N = 16 vs N = 64):

  1. Small-family run (16 fertilisations): Toss both coins together (or draw one bean blindfolded from Bowl 1 and one from Bowl 2, returning the beans and remixing after each draw) 16 times. Coin 1 is the maternal ovule (R or r); Coin 2 is the paternal pollen grain (R or r). Tally each outcome in four columns: RR (Heads–Heads, Round), Rr (Heads–Tails or Tails–Heads, Round), rr (Tails–Tails, Wrinkled), and Total Round (RR + Rr) vs Wrinkled (rr).
  2. Check the small-sample bounce: With only 16 trials, your theoretical expectation is 4 RR : 8 Rr : 4 rr (12 Round : 4 Wrinkled = 3 : 1), but random luck often gives 10 : 6 (1.67 : 1) or 14 : 2 (7 : 1). That is why a single pea pod or a human family of four children rarely shows an exact 3 : 1 split.
  3. Full 64-trial convergence run: Continue tossing for 48 more trials to reach N = 64 total fertilisations (expecting 16 RR : 32 Rr : 16 rr, or 48 Round : 16 Wrinkled). Notice how the combined RR + Rr percentage moves much closer to 75% (3 : 1) and why Rr (Heads–Tails + Tails–Heads) occurs twice as often (50%) as RR (25%) or rr (25%).

Part B — Simulating a 1 : 1 diagnostic test cross (Rr × rr):

  1. Lay Coin 2 flat on the table showing Tails (r) permanently—this is your homozygous recessive tester (rr), which can only ever supply (r) gametes.
  2. Toss only Coin 1 (Rr parent) 32 times. Every Heads gives Rr (Round); every Tails gives rr (Wrinkled). Verify that the outcome converges on 50% Rr : 50% rr (1 : 1).

Why does Aa occur twice in Aa × Aa? When you toss two coins, there is only one way to get AA (Maternal A + Paternal A) and only one way to get aa (Maternal a + Paternal a), but there are two distinct ways to get Aa: either Maternal A + Paternal a, or Maternal a + Paternal A. That two-way symmetry is why the middle term of (0.5 A + 0.5 a)² = 0.25 AA + 0.50 Aa + 0.25 aa is always 2 (1 : 2 : 1).

Understand it

Why do we draw only ONE allele letter inside each gamete circle in a genetic diagram?

Because gametes (sperm and egg cells, or pollen and ovules) are haploid (n) cells produced by meiosis (2n → n). During Meiosis I, the two homologous chromosomes carrying the parent’s two alleles separate into different daughter cells, so each gamete receives only one chromosome and therefore only one allele of the gene.

Why do we write a 1 : 2 : 1 genotype ratio as a 3 : 1 phenotype ratio when A is dominant over a?

In Aa × Aa, 1/4 (25%) of the offspring are homozygous dominant (AA) and 2/4 (50%) are heterozygous (Aa). Because A is dominant, both AA and Aa express the exact same dominant phenotype (25% + 50% = 75%, or 3/4), leaving 1/4 (25%) homozygous recessive (aa) with the recessive phenotype (3 : 1).

How does a test cross tell you whether a tall pea plant (T_) is TT or Tt?

You cross the tall plant (T_) with a dwarf plant that is homozygous recessive (tt). Since the tt tester passes only t gametes, if the tall parent is TT all offspring receive T and are 100% tall (Tt); if the tall parent is Tt, half the offspring receive t from both parents and are dwarf (tt), giving a 1 : 1 ratio of tall to dwarf.

In a family pedigree, how can you tell immediately that a genetic condition is recessive?

Look for two unaffected parents (□ and ○) who have an affected child (■ or ●). Because the condition was hidden in both parents and appeared in their child (aa), the allele must be recessive and both parents must be heterozygous carriers (Aa).

If two carrier parents (Aa × Aa) already have three children—two unaffected and one affected (aa)—what is the probability that their fourth child will be affected?

Still exactly 25% (1 in 4, or 0.25). Chromosomes and gametes have no memory of earlier pregnancies; every new fertilisation is an independent 2 × 2 Punnett event with the same 1/4 chance of aa.

Go deeper suppose two unaffected carrier parents (aa × aa) have a daughter who is already born and known to be unaffected. what is the probability that she is a heterozygous carrier (aa), and why is the answer 2/3 rather than 1/2, in a pedigree where two affected parents have an unaffected daughter, could the condition be recessive? explain why or why not., why did johann gregor mendel count 7,324 seeds to get 2.96 : 1, whereas a single pea pod of 8 seeds might show 5 round : 3 wrinkled (1.67 : 1)
Suppose two unaffected carrier parents (Aa × Aa) have a daughter who is already born and known to be unaffected. What is the probability that she is a heterozygous carrier (Aa), and why is the answer 2/3 rather than 1/2?

Before birth, the four equally likely Punnett boxes are 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa (25% each). Once the daughter is born and observed to be unaffected, the aa box is ruled out (0%). Out of the three remaining equally likely boxes (1 AA and 2 Aa), two boxes are Aa, so her probability of being a carrier is 2/3 (66.7%).

In a pedigree where two affected parents have an unaffected daughter, could the condition be recessive? Explain why or why not.

No. If the condition were recessive, both affected parents would have to be homozygous recessive (aa × aa). Since neither parent would possess a normal A allele, 100% of their gametes would be (a) and 100% of their children would be affected (aa). Having an unaffected child (aa) proves the condition is dominant and both parents are heterozygous (Aa).

Why did Johann Gregor Mendel count 7,324 seeds to get 2.96 : 1, whereas a single pea pod of 8 seeds might show 5 round : 3 wrinkled (1.67 : 1)?

Each fertilisation is an independent random sampling event with a 75% chance of round and 25% chance of wrinkled. In a small sample of 8 seeds, random chance causes large percentage swings (sampling error); by the law of large numbers, averaging across thousands of independent fertilisations (7,324 seeds) cancels out random fluctuations and converges on the theoretical 3.00 : 1 expectation.

Explain to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

Watch out for three classic Punnett and pedigree mistakes:

  1. Gametes carry 1 allele, never 2: In a monohybrid cross of Bb × Bb, the gametes are (B) and (b)—never (BB) or (Bb). Putting two letters of the same gene into one gamete means meiosis failed to separate homologous chromosomes.
  2. Probabilities do not “use up” squares across siblings: A 1 in 4 (25%) chance of an aa child in Aa × Aa does not mean that if the first child is aa, the next three children are guaranteed to be unaffected. Every pregnancy draws fresh gametes from the 2 × 2 grid with the same 25% probability.
  3. Always write ratios in simplest whole numbers: Write 3 : 1 (not 75% : 25% or 12 : 4 when a ratio is asked for) and 1 : 1 (not 2 : 2), and always label which phenotype belongs to which number (e.g. 3 round : 1 wrinkled).

At school

Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610, Topic 17.4 Core & Supplement) tests three core diagram skills here:

  • Monohybrid Punnett squares (17.4.10 & 17.4.12 Core): Construct and interpret genetic diagrams, including Punnett squares, to predict the results of monohybrid crosses and calculate phenotypic ratios (1 : 1 and 3 : 1) and probabilities (100%, 75%, 50%, 25%, 0%).
  • Pedigree diagrams (17.4.11 Core): Use and interpret pedigree diagrams for the inheritance of a given characteristic (Rule 1: Unaffected × Unaffected → Affected = recessive; Rule 2: Affected × Affected → Unaffected = dominant).
  • Test crosses (17.4.13–17.4.14 Supplement): Identify an unknown dominant genotype (AA vs Aa) by crossing with a homozygous recessive individual (aa) and interpreting the resulting 100% dominant versus 1 : 1 offspring ratio.

Check yourself

  1. In humans, cystic fibrosis (and beta-thalassaemia) is caused by an autosomal recessive allele (f), while the normal allele is dominant (F). Two unaffected parents (Ff × Ff) are expecting a child. Construct the six-line genetic diagram (parental phenotypes, parental genotypes, gametes, 2 × 2 Punnett square, offspring genotypes/phenotypes, and ratios) and state the percentage probability that the child will (a) have the condition, (b) be an unaffected heterozygous carrier, and (c) be unaffected overall.
  2. A farmer in Nashik buys a black-coated ram. In this sheep breed, black coat (B) is dominant to white coat (b). Explain how the farmer can use a test cross to determine whether the ram is pure-breeding (BB) or heterozygous (Bb).

Answer at the back of the book

13.3When neither allele yields: codominance and the ABO blood group puzzle

Institute of Pathological Anatomy, Vienna, 1900–1901, and Indian Cancer Research Centre, Parel, Mumbai, 1950s

In Johann Gregor Mendel’s seven pea characters, one allele was always completely dominant over the other: a heterozygous Rr seed looked identical to an RR seed. Soon after 1900, however, geneticists discovered traits where neither allele masks the other inside a heterozygote.

In 1900–1901 in Vienna, physician Karl Landsteiner solved the mystery of why blood transfusions between some people succeeded while others caused fatal clumping (agglutination) of red blood cells. As you learned in Chapter 8 (8.4) and Chapter 10 (10.4), the cell membranes of human red blood cells carry carbohydrate identity tags (antigens), while blood plasma carries Y-shaped antibodies against whichever foreign ABO antigens the person lacks. In 1924, mathematician Felix Bernstein proved that all four human blood groups—Group A, Group B, Group AB, and Group O—are controlled by a single gene locus on Chromosome 9 that exists in three allelic forms (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, and Iᴼ), and in the 1950s L. D. Sanghvi mapped the frequencies and family pedigrees of those alleles across Mumbai and western India.

Multiple alleles and codominance at the Chromosome 9 ABO locus

When a single gene locus has three or more alternative alleles circulating in a population (such as Iᴬ, Iᴮ, and Iᴼ, where I stands for isoagglutinogen, Landsteiner’s term for a blood-group antigen), geneticists call it a multiple-allele system. Remember the diploid chromosome rule from Section 13.1: even though three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, Iᴼ) exist in the human population, any individual person has only two copies of Chromosome 9 (2n), so each person inherits at most two ABO alleles (and each haploid gamete carries only one).

In 1990, Fumi-ichiro Yamamoto and colleagues sequenced the ABO gene on Chromosome 9 (9q34.2) and revealed the exact enzyme chemistry of the three alleles:

  1. Allele Iᴬ (codes for active enzyme GTA): Instructs ribosomes to build α-1,3-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase (GTA), an enzyme that attaches the sugar N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) onto the precursor H-antigen oligosaccharide stalks on red blood cell membranes, creating Antigen A.
  2. Allele Iᴮ (codes for active enzyme GTB): Differs from Iᴬ at just four amino-acid positions (codons 176, 235, 266, 268). Those four substitutions reshape the enzyme’s active site (Chapter 4) so it binds and attaches a different sugar—D-galactose (D-Gal)—onto H-antigen stalks, creating Antigen B.
  3. Allele Iᴼ (loss-of-function frameshift ΔG261): Carries a single-base deletion (G deleted at nucleotide 261) that shifts the mRNA triplet reading frame (Chapter 11) and hits an early stop codon, producing a truncated protein with zero transferase activity (0%). The H-antigen stalks remain unmodified (neither Antigen A nor Antigen B is added).

Now ask: what happens when a child inherits Iᴬ on one Chromosome 9 and Iᴮ on the partner Chromosome 9 (IᴬIᴮ)? Neither enzyme blocks the other. Inside the developing red blood cell precursor in the bone marrow, both GTA and GTB enzymes work simultaneously, attaching Antigen A (GalNAc) to some membrane stalks and Antigen B (D-Gal) to neighbouring stalks on the exact same red blood cell.

  • Codominance is a pattern of inheritance in which both alleles in a heterozygous organism are expressed independently and simultaneously in the phenotype (0610 17.4.15 Supplement).
  • Because both Iᴬ and Iᴮ are expressed side-by-side without blending, Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant with each other (IᴬIᴮ = Blood Group AB).
  • At the same time, both Iᴬ and Iᴮ are completely dominant over the recessive Iᴼ allele: a single active copy of Iᴬ in IᴬIᴼ attaches enough Antigen A to give Blood Group A (identical in routine blood typing to IᴬIᴬ), and a single active copy of Iᴮ in IᴮIᴼ attaches enough Antigen B to give Blood Group B (identical to IᴮIᴮ). Only IᴼIᴼ (zero active enzyme copies) produces Blood Group O.
Blood Group (Phenotype) Possible Genotypes (2n) Red Blood Cell Surface Antigens & Plasma Antibodies
Group A IᴬIᴬ (homozygous) or IᴬIᴼ (heterozygous) Antigen A on RBCs; Anti-B antibodies in plasma
Group B IᴮIᴮ (homozygous) or IᴮIᴼ (heterozygous) Antigen B on RBCs; Anti-A antibodies in plasma
Group AB IᴬIᴮ (codominant heterozygote) Both Antigen A and Antigen B on RBCs; no Anti-A or Anti-B
Group O IᴼIᴼ (homozygous recessive) Neither Antigen A nor B (unmodified H-stalk); both Anti-A and Anti-B

Predict first

Suppose a mother with Blood Group A whose father was Group O marries a father with Blood Group B whose mother was Group O. What are the exact genotypes of the two parents, and which ABO blood groups can appear among their children?

  1. The parents are IᴬIᴬ and IᴮIᴮ; 100% of their children will have Blood Group AB (IᴬIᴮ)
  2. Because each parent inherited an Iᴼ allele from a Group O (IᴼIᴼ) grandparent, the mother is IᴬIᴼ and the father is IᴮIᴼ; their children have an equal 25% (1 in 4) chance of each of the four blood groups—Group AB (IᴬIᴮ), Group A (IᴬIᴼ), Group B (IᴮIᴼ), and Group O (IᴼIᴼ) (a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio)
  3. Their children can only be Group A (50%) or Group B (50%), because Group O and Group AB cannot appear in the same family

What happens

The second choice. A Group O grandparent has the genotype IᴼIᴼ and can pass only an (Iᴼ) gamete to every child. Therefore the Group A mother must be heterozygous IᴬIᴼ (producing 50% (Iᴬ) and 50% (Iᴼ) ova), and the Group B father must be heterozygous IᴮIᴼ (producing 50% (Iᴮ) and 50% (Iᴼ) sperm). Combining those gametes in a 2 × 2 Punnett square yields:

  • (Iᴬ) + (Iᴮ) → IᴬIᴮ = Group AB (25%)
  • (Iᴬ) + (Iᴼ) → IᴬIᴼ = Group A (25%)
  • (Iᴼ) + (Iᴮ) → IᴮIᴼ = Group B (25%)
  • (Iᴼ) + (Iᴼ) → IᴼIᴼ = Group O (25%)

Four siblings in the same family can legally and biologically have all four human ABO blood groups (1 AB : 1 A : 1 B : 1 O).

How do we know? Vienna, 1901, Göttingen, 1924 & Seattle, 1990: Landsteiner’s agglutination groups, Bernstein’s 3-allele model, and Yamamoto’s ABO sequence Serological & molecular proof

Three milestones established the ABO system as biology’s benchmark for multiple alleles and codominance:

  1. Karl Landsteiner (1901): Mixing washed red blood cells from laboratory colleagues with separated blood serum proved that humans fall into discrete agglutination groups (A, B, O, and AB added by Decastello and Sturli in 1902).
  2. Felix Bernstein (1924): Analysing family blood-group pedigrees across thousands of parents and children proved that A, B, and O are not inherited at two separate gene loci (A/a and B/b), which would allow a Group AB (AABB) × Group O (aabb) couple to have Group AB (AaBb) or Group O (aabb) children in later generations. Instead, because IᴬIᴮ × IᴼIᴼ parents produce exclusively Group A (IᴬIᴼ, 50%) and Group B (IᴮIᴼ, 50%) children—never Group AB (0%) and never Group O (0%)—all three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, Iᴼ) must occupy the exact same locus on a single chromosome pair.
  3. Fumi-ichiro Yamamoto et al. (1990, Nature 345: 229–233): Cloning the cDNA of the Iᴬ, Iᴮ, and Iᴼ alleles on Chromosome 9 confirmed the four amino-acid substitutions between GTA (Iᴬ) and GTB (Iᴮ) and the ΔG261 single-base deletion in Iᴼ.

Why codominance gives a 1 : 2 : 1 phenotype ratio instead of 3 : 1

What happens when two codominant heterozygotes breed together—such as two Group AB parents (IᴬIᴮ × IᴬIᴮ), or two roan cattle (CᴿCᵂ × CᴿCᵂ) where Cᴿ codes for red hairs and Cᵂ codes for white hairs so the heterozygote CᴿCᵂ grows both pure red hairs and pure white hairs side-by-side in a roan coat?

Trace the 2 × 2 Punnett grid for IᴬIᴮ × IᴬIᴮ:

  • Parental phenotypes: Group AB mother × Group AB father
  • Parental genotypes: IᴬIᴮ × IᴬIᴮ
  • Gametes: (Iᴬ) and (Iᴮ) × (Iᴬ) and (Iᴮ)
  • Offspring genotypes (1 : 2 : 1): 25% IᴬIᴬ : 50% IᴬIᴮ : 25% IᴮIᴮ
  • Offspring phenotypes (1 : 2 : 1): 25% Group A (1) : 50% Group AB (2) : 25% Group B (1) (0% Group O).

Notice the key difference from Johann Gregor Mendel’s 3 : 1 pea crosses: in simple dominance (Rr × Rr), the RR (25%) and Rr (50%) boxes collapse into a single phenotype (75% round, 3 : 1). In codominance (IᴬIᴮ × IᴬIᴮ or CᴿCᵂ × CᴿCᵂ), the heterozygote (IᴬIᴮ or CᴿCᵂ) has its own distinct third phenotype where both alleles are visibly expressed, so the phenotype ratio is 1 : 2 : 1—matching the 1 : 2 : 1 genotype ratio directly. (Recall from Chapter 11 that at the molecular protein level, sickle-cell trait HbᴬHbˢ also shows codominance: red blood cells contain both normal HbA and sickle HbS haemoglobin molecules.)

Superscript notation for codominance (0610 17.4.15): Because uppercase-versus-lowercase (R vs r) implies that one allele is dominant over the other, Cambridge 0610 uses a common base letter for the gene with uppercase superscripts for codominant alleles—such as Iᴬ and Iᴮ for ABO blood groups (with Iᴼ for the recessive allele at the same locus), Cᴿ and Cᵂ for coat/petal colour, Fᴮ and Fᵂ for black-and-white speckled feathers in Andalusian/erminette chickens, and Hbᴬ and Hbˢ for beta-globin alleles.

Understand it

What is codominance?

Codominance is a pattern of inheritance in which both alleles in a heterozygous organism are expressed simultaneously and independently in the phenotype, so neither allele masks the other (for example, IᴬIᴮ produces both Antigen A and Antigen B on red blood cells, giving Blood Group AB).

Why does each human inherit only two ABO alleles even though three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, Iᴼ) exist in the population?

Because the ABO gene sits at a single locus on Chromosome 9, and every diploid (2n) human inherits only two copies of Chromosome 9—one from their mother’s ovum (n) and one from their father’s sperm (n).

Why is Blood Group AB an example of codominance, whereas Blood Group A (IᴬIᴼ) is an example of simple dominance?

In IᴬIᴮ (Group AB), both Iᴬ and Iᴮ code for active sugar-transferring enzymes (GTA and GTB), so both Antigen A and Antigen B are built side-by-side on the red blood cell membrane (codominance). In IᴬIᴼ (Group A), Iᴼ codes for a non-functional enzyme while the single Iᴬ copy builds enough Antigen A to give full Group A blood, so Iᴬ is dominant over recessive Iᴼ.

Why can’t a parent with Blood Group AB (IᴬIᴮ) ever have a biological child with Blood Group O (IᴼIᴼ) in standard Mendelian inheritance?

A child with Blood Group O (IᴼIᴼ) must inherit one Iᴼ allele from their mother and one Iᴼ allele from their father. Because a Group AB parent has the genotype IᴬIᴮ, their gametes carry either (Iᴬ) or (Iᴮ)—they do not possess an Iᴼ allele to pass on.

Why does crossing two codominant heterozygotes (IᴬIᴮ × IᴬIᴮ or CᴿCᵂ × CᴿCᵂ) give a 1 : 2 : 1 phenotype ratio instead of 3 : 1?

In 3 : 1 simple dominance, the homozygous dominant (25%) and heterozygous (50%) genotypes look identical and merge into 75%. In codominance, the heterozygote (IᴬIᴮ or CᴿCᵂ, 50%) expresses both alleles and looks distinct from both homozygotes (IᴬIᴬ 25% and IᴮIᴮ 25%), so all three genotypes are visibly distinguishable in a 1 : 2 : 1 phenotype ratio.

Go deeper why isn’t codominance a return to the nineteenth-century paint-pot blending hypothesis, can two parents who both have blood group a ever have a child with blood group o? show the punnett logic., if a mother is group b and her baby is group o (iᴼiᴼ), what is the mother’s exact genotype, and which blood groups can be ruled out for the biological father
Why isn’t codominance a return to the nineteenth-century paint-pot blending hypothesis?

Two reasons: (1) At the cellular and molecular level, the two alleles in a codominant heterozygote do not blend into a lukewarm compromise molecule—in IᴬIᴮ cells, discrete Antigen A (GalNAc) molecules and discrete Antigen B (D-Gal) molecules sit side-by-side on the membrane, and in roan cattle (CᴿCᵂ), individual hairs are either 100% red or 100% white. (2) When two IᴬIᴮ parents have children, pure Group A (IᴬIᴬ, 25%) and pure Group B (IᴮIᴮ, 25%) segregate out unblemished in the very next generation.

Can two parents who both have Blood Group A ever have a child with Blood Group O? Show the Punnett logic.

Yes, if both Group A parents are heterozygous (IᴬIᴼ × IᴬIᴼ). Each parent produces 50% (Iᴬ) gametes and 50% (Iᴼ) gametes. Their 2 × 2 Punnett grid yields 25% IᴬIᴬ (Group A), 50% IᴬIᴼ (Group A), and 25% IᴼIᴼ (Group O)—a 3 Group A : 1 Group O ratio.

If a mother is Group B and her baby is Group O (IᴼIᴼ), what is the mother’s exact genotype, and which blood groups can be ruled out for the biological father?

Because the baby is IᴼIᴼ, the baby inherited one Iᴼ allele from the mother and one Iᴼ allele from the father. Therefore the Group B mother must be heterozygous IᴮIᴼ. The biological father must also carry at least one Iᴼ allele (IᴬIᴼ, IᴮIᴼ, or IᴼIᴼ), which rules out Blood Group AB (IᴬIᴮ) (as well as homozygous IᴬIᴬ and IᴮIᴮ).

Your turn

Explain to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

Three high-frequency notation and conceptual rules for codominance and ABO blood groups:

  1. Keep the base letter I on all three ABO alleles: Always write Iᴬ, Iᴮ, and Iᴼ—never mix Iᴬ and Iᴮ with a bare lowercase o or i in Cambridge 0610 exams (17.4.17).
  2. Never write IᴬIᴮIᴼ for one person: Three alleles exist in the human population, not inside one diploid cell. Every person’s genotype has exactly two alleles (e.g. IᴬIᴼ, IᴮIᴼ, IᴬIᴮ, IᴼIᴼ), and every gamete has exactly one ((Iᴬ), (Iᴮ), or (Iᴼ)).
  3. Group O is recessive (IᴼIᴼ), not codominant: Only Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant (IᴬIᴮ = Group AB). The Iᴼ allele is recessive to both Iᴬ (IᴬIᴼ = Group A) and Iᴮ (IᴮIᴼ = Group B).

At school

Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610, Topic 17.4 Supplement) specifies:

  • Codominance (17.4.15): Describe codominance as a situation in which both alleles in heterozygous organisms contribute to the phenotype.
  • ABO blood groups (17.4.17): Explain the inheritance of ABO blood groups: phenotypes are A, B, AB and O blood groups and alleles are Iᴬ, Iᴮ and Iᴼ.
  • Codominant Punnett squares (17.4.18): Construct and interpret genetic diagrams to predict the results of monohybrid crosses involving codominance and calculate phenotypic ratios (1 : 2 : 1, 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, 1 : 1) and probabilities.

Check yourself

  2. A woman with Blood Group AB (IᴬIᴮ) marries a man with Blood Group O (IᴼIᴼ). Construct the six-line genetic diagram (including gametes and a 2 × 2 Punnett square) and state the percentage probability that their child will have (a) Group A, (b) Group B, (c) Group AB, and (d) Group O.

Answer at the back of the book

13.4The twenty-third pair: XX, XY, and sex-linked inheritance

Bryn Mawr College, Pennsylvania, 1905, and the Fly Room, Columbia University, New York, 1910

In Sections 13.1 to 13.3, every gene we tracked—pea seed shape (R/r), stem height (T/t), and human ABO blood group on Chromosome 9 (Iᴬ/Iᴮ/Iᴼ)—behaved identically in males and females. That is because 22 of the 23 homologous chromosome pairs in a human diploid cell (2n = 46) are autosomes (Chromosomes 1 to 22), which are present in two matched copies of equal length and equal gene content in both sexes.

What about the twenty-third pair—the sex chromosomes first linked to sex determination by Nettie Stevens in 1905?

  1. Human females are XX (44 autosomes + XX = 46): In a female diploid cell, Pair 23 consists of two large, homologous X chromosomes. When a woman’s ovaries produce haploid egg cells (ova, n = 23) by meiosis, every single ovum receives 22 autosomes plus one X chromosome (100% X ova).
  2. Human males are XY (44 autosomes + XY = 46): In a male diploid cell, Pair 23 consists of one large X chromosome and one much smaller Y chromosome. When a man’s testes produce haploid sperm cells (n = 23) by meiosis, the X and Y chromosomes separate into different cells: exactly 50% of sperm carry an X chromosome (22 + X) and 50% of sperm carry a Y chromosome (22 + Y).

Place whole X and Y chromosomes into a 2 × 2 Punnett square (XX × XY):

  • Maternal gametes (ova): (X) and (X)
  • Paternal gametes (sperm): (X) and (Y)
  • Zygotes (2 × 2): Two boxes are XX (50% female) and two boxes are XY (50% male)—an exact, unchanging 1 : 1 sex ratio at every fertilisation (0893 8Bp.01/9Bp.01, 0610 17.1 & 17.4).

Notice two immediate consequences of this chromosome geometry:

  • Sperm chromosome sets the zygote’s genetic sex: Because every ovum supplies an X, whether the zygote is XX (female) or XY (male) depends on whether an X-bearing sperm or a Y-bearing sperm fertilises the ovum.
  • Who gives which sex chromosome to sons versus daughters: A mother passes one of her two X chromosomes to every child (both daughters and sons). A father passes his single X chromosome to 100% of his daughters (XX) and his Y chromosome to 100% of his sons (XY)—a father never passes an X chromosome to a son (0%).

Why X-linked recessive traits strike males far more often than females

Look closely at the physical size difference in Figure 13.7 between the X chromosome and the Y chromosome:

  • The human X chromosome is a long rod of roughly 156 million base pairs (~156 Mb) carrying ~850–900 protein-coding genes—most of which have nothing to do with sex determination at all, but instead build everyday body proteins such as red-sensitive and green-sensitive retinal cone opsin photopigments (Chapter 9, Section 9.4) and blood-clotting enzyme Factors VIII and IX (Chapter 8, Section 8.4, and Chapter 10, Section 10.4).
  • The human Y chromosome is a short rod of roughly 57 million base pairs (~57 Mb) carrying fewer than 100 protein-coding genes (most notably the SRY gene that triggers testis development in an embryo). Crucially, the short Y chromosome lacks the non-homologous portion of the X chromosome and therefore carries zero alleles for red–green colour vision or clotting Factor VIII/IX.

That structural asymmetry between X and Y creates a distinct pattern of inheritance discovered by Thomas Hunt Morgan in his 1910 fruit-fly crosses:

  • A sex-linked characteristic is a characteristic in which the gene responsible is located on a sex chromosome and that this makes it more common in one sex than in the other (0610 17.4.16 Supplement).
  • Because the allele sits on the X chromosome and not on the Y chromosome, we write the allele as a superscript on X only (e.g. Xᴮ for normal colour vision and Xᵇ for red–green colour vision deficiency; or Xᴴ for normal blood clotting factor and Xʰ for haemophilia, where soluble plasma fibrinogen cannot be rapidly converted into an insoluble fibrin mesh to seal wounds). The Y chromosome is always written bare (Y)—never with a superscript (Yᵇ is wrong because Y lacks that gene locus).

Compare the five possible genotypes for an X-linked recessive condition such as red–green colour vision deficiency (Xᴮ = normal opsin, Xᵇ = altered opsin) or haemophilia (Xᴴ = normal clotting factor, Xʰ = non-functional clotting factor):

Sex & Genotype Phenotype & Clinical Status Why (X vs Y Gene Dosage)
Female XᴮXᴮ (or XᴴXᴴ) Normal female (homozygous dominant) Two functional copies on her two X chromosomes
Female XᴮXᵇ (or XᴴXʰ) Normal carrier female (heterozygous) One Xᴮ copy makes enough functional cone opsin (or clotting factor) to mask Xᵇ
Female XᵇXᵇ (or XʰXʰ) Affected female (homozygous recessive; rare) Requires inheriting a recessive Xᵇ allele from both her mother and her affected father
Male XᴮY (or XᴴY) Normal male (hemizygous dominant) His single X chromosome carries the functional Xᴮ allele
Male XᵇY (or XʰY) Affected male (hemizygous recessive; much more common) His single X carries Xᵇ, and his short Y chromosome has no second locus to mask it

Notice the two-part clinical rule that follows from this table:

  1. Why males cannot be unaffected carriers of an X-linked recessive allele: A carrier is an individual who has a recessive allele masked by a dominant allele on a second homologous chromosome (XᴮXᵇ). Because an XY male has only one X chromosome (he is hemizygous), any recessive allele (Xᵇ or Xʰ) on his single X chromosome is immediately expressed in his phenotype.
  2. Why X-linked recessive conditions are much more common in males than in females: A male needs to inherit only one recessive allele (XᵇY, from his mother, probability = q) to show the condition, whereas a female must inherit two recessive alleles (XᵇXᵇ, one from her mother and one from an affected father, probability = q²). In India and worldwide, roughly 6%–8% of males (q ≈ 0.08) have red–green colour vision deficiency, whereas only 0.4%–0.6% of females (q² ≈ 0.0064) are affected—more than ten times rarer in females.

Predict first

Contrast two X-linked family crosses for red–green colour vision (Xᴮ = normal colour vision, Xᵇ = red–green colour vision deficiency):

  1. Cross A: An unaffected carrier mother (XᴮXᵇ) and a normal-vision father (XᴮY).
  2. Cross B: A homozygous normal-vision mother (XᴮXᴮ) and a colour-blind father (XᵇY). In which cross can a son inherit red–green colour vision deficiency (XᵇY), and why do 0% of the sons in Cross B inherit their father’s colour vision deficiency?
  3. In Cross B, 50% of sons are colour-blind because the father is affected (XᵇY); in Cross A, 0% of sons are colour-blind because both parents have normal vision
  4. In Cross A (XᴮXᵇ × XᴮY), 50% of sons are affected (XᵇY) (25% of all children) because sons inherit their single X chromosome from their carrier mother; in Cross B (XᴮXᴮ × XᵇY), 0% of sons are affected (100% XᴮY) because a father always passes his Y chromosome to his sons and passes his Xᵇ chromosome exclusively to his daughters (100% XᴮXᵇ carriers)
  5. In both Cross A and Cross B, 25% of daughters and 25% of sons are colour-blind

What happens

The second choice. Trace the sex chromosomes in each cross:

  • In Cross A (XᴮXᵇ × XᴮY): Maternal ova are (Xᴮ) and (Xᵇ); paternal sperm are (Xᴮ) and (Y).
    • Daughters (XX): 50% XᴮXᴮ (normal) and 50% XᴮXᵇ (unaffected carrier) → 0% of daughters are affected.
    • Sons (XY): 50% XᴮY (normal) and 50% XᵇY (colour-blind) → 50% of sons are affected (which equals 25% of all children).
  • In Cross B (XᴮXᴮ × XᵇY): Maternal ova are all (Xᴮ); paternal sperm are (Xᵇ) and (Y).
    • Sons (XY): Every son receives his father’s (Y) sperm and his mother’s (Xᴮ) ovum → 100% XᴮY normal sons (0% affected sons). There is zero father-to-son transmission of an X-linked gene.
    • Daughters (XX): Every daughter receives her father’s (Xᵇ) sperm and her mother’s (Xᴮ) ovum → 100% XᴮXᵇ unaffected carrier daughters (who can then pass Xᵇ to 50% of their own sons in the next generation, explaining the famous “grandfather-to-carrier-mother-to-grandson” pedigree pattern).

How do we know? Bryn Mawr, 1905 & Columbia University, 1910: Nettie Stevens’s mealworm XY karyotypes and Thomas Hunt Morgan’s white-eyed Drosophila Cytogenetic & breeding proof

Two classic experiments anchored sex determination and sex linkage to physical chromosomes:

  1. Nettie Stevens (1905, Studies in Spermatogenesis): Comparing stained metaphase chromosomes in the yellow mealworm beetle (Tenebrio molitor), Nettie Stevens showed that somatic female cells contain 20 large chromosomes (XX) and produce uniform 10-chromosome eggs, whereas somatic male cells contain 19 large chromosomes plus 1 diminutive chromosome (XY) and produce two equal classes of sperm (50% X and 50% Y), proving that sex is inherited as a 1 : 1 Mendelian chromosome cross at fertilisation.
  2. Thomas Hunt Morgan (1910, Science 32: 120–122): Crossing a spontaneous white-eyed male fruit fly (XʷY) with pure red-eyed females (X⁺X⁺) produced 1,237 red-eyed F₁ offspring (X⁺Xʷ females and X⁺Y males). Interbreeding those F₁ flies yielded 3,470 red-eyed and 782 white-eyed F₂ flies—and 100% of the white-eyed F₂ flies were male (XʷY). When Thomas Hunt Morgan then crossed a carrier female (X⁺Xʷ) with a white-eyed male (XʷY), 50% of the daughters (XʷXʷ) and 50% of the sons (XʷY) had white eyes, proving that the eye-colour gene resides physically on the X chromosome.

How can a female ever be affected by an X-linked recessive condition (XᵇXᵇ or XʰXʰ)? A female has two X chromosomes (XX), one inherited from her mother and one inherited from her father. For a daughter to be homozygous recessive (XᵇXᵇ), two conditions must hold simultaneously: (1) her father must be affected (XᵇY) so his X-sperm gives her an Xᵇ, and (2) her mother must be either a carrier (XᴮXᵇ) or affected (XᵇXᵇ) so her ovum also gives her an Xᵇ. In the cross XᴮXᵇ × XᵇY, 50% of daughters are carriers (XᴮXᵇ) and 50% of daughters are affected (XᵇXᵇ).

Understand it

What are the sex chromosomes in a human female and in a human male, and why is the probability of a boy or a girl always 50% (1 : 1)?

A human female has XX sex chromosomes and produces 100% (X) egg cells; a human male has XY sex chromosomes and produces 50% (X) sperm and 50% (Y) sperm. At fertilisation, an (X) egg has an equal 50% chance of fusing with an (X) sperm (XX, girl) or a (Y) sperm (XY, boy), giving a 1 : 1 ratio.

What is a sex-linked characteristic?

A sex-linked characteristic is a feature controlled by a gene located on a sex chromosome (usually on the non-homologous region of the large X chromosome, with no corresponding locus on the shorter Y chromosome), making the characteristic more common in one sex than in the other.

Why can’t a male (XY) be an unaffected carrier of red–green colour blindness (Xᵇ) or haemophilia (Xʰ)?

Because a male has only one X chromosome (XY) and the short Y chromosome does not carry the colour-vision or blood-clotting gene. If his single X chromosome carries the recessive allele (XᵇY or XʰY), there is no second X chromosome with a dominant allele to mask it, so he shows the condition.

Why can’t a father with haemophilia (XʰY) or red–green colour blindness (XᵇY) pass the condition directly to his son?

Because a father always gives his son his Y chromosome (which makes the child XY male), never his X chromosome. The son’s single X chromosome always comes from his mother’s ovum.

Why is it critical to check whether an X-linked question asks for the probability “among sons” versus “among all children”?

In XᴮXᵇ × XᴮY, the 2 × 2 Punnett grid has 4 boxes total (2 daughters and 2 sons), and only 1 box (XᵇY) is affected. If the question asks for the probability among all children, the denominator is 4 (1/4 = 25%). If the question asks for the probability that a son is affected (among sons only), the denominator is the 2 male boxes (1/2 = 50%).

Go deeper a boy has haemophilia (xʰy), yet both his mother and his father have completely normal blood clotting. state the exact genotypes of the boy, his father, and his mother, and explain how the boy inherited xʰ., if a colour-blind man (xᵇy) and a homozygous normal-vision woman (xᴮxᴮ) have children, none of their sons or daughters are colour-blind—yet their daughter later has a colour-blind son with a normal-vision husband (xᴮy). trace the xᵇ allele across all three generations., why do defects in the x-linked xᴴ/xʰ gene cause prolonged bleeding in chapter 10’s blood clotting pathway, whereas defects in the x-linked xᴮ/xᵇ gene alter colour vision in chapter 9’s retina
A boy has haemophilia (XʰY), yet both his mother and his father have completely normal blood clotting. State the exact genotypes of the boy, his father, and his mother, and explain how the boy inherited Xʰ.
  • Boy’s genotype: XʰY (affected male).
  • Father’s genotype: XᴴY (normal male; if he had Xʰ, he would have haemophilia himself, and he gave the boy his Y chromosome anyway).
  • Mother’s genotype: XᴴXʰ (unaffected heterozygous carrier female). Her Xᴴ allele produces enough clotting Factor VIII/IX for her own blood to clot normally, while meiosis placed her hidden Xʰ allele into the ovum (50% chance) that formed her son.
If a colour-blind man (XᵇY) and a homozygous normal-vision woman (XᴮXᴮ) have children, none of their sons or daughters are colour-blind—yet their daughter later has a colour-blind son with a normal-vision husband (XᴮY). Trace the Xᵇ allele across all three generations.
  1. Generation I (XᴮXᴮ × XᵇY): The affected grandfather (XᵇY) passes his (Xᵇ) sperm to 100% of his daughters, making his daughter an unaffected carrier (XᴮXᵇ) in Generation II.
  2. Generation II → III (XᴮXᵇ × XᴮY): When that carrier daughter (XᴮXᵇ) has children with a normal-vision father (XᴮY), she passes (Xᵇ) to 50% of her ova, giving each of her sons (Generation III) a 50% chance of inheriting XᵇY and being colour-blind like his maternal grandfather.
Why do defects in the X-linked Xᴴ/Xʰ gene cause prolonged bleeding in Chapter 10’s blood clotting pathway, whereas defects in the X-linked Xᴮ/Xᵇ gene alter colour vision in Chapter 9’s retina?

Different loci on the X chromosome code for completely different proteins via selective gene expression (12.3): liver cells express the F8/F9 locus (Xᴴ) to secrete plasma clotting enzymes that catalyse soluble fibrinogen → insoluble fibrin mesh at wounds (10.4), whereas foveal cone photoreceptors (9.4) express the red/green opsin locus (Xᴮ) to detect red and green wavelengths of light.

Your turn

Explain to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

Three essential exam rules for sex-linked genetic diagrams (0610 17.4.19–17.4.20):

  1. Always write the X and Y chromosomes in genotypes and gametes: For sex-linked traits, never write bare letters like Bb or Hh as if the gene were autosomal. Always write XᴮXᵇ, XᴮY, XᵇY (or XᴴXʰ, XᴴY, XʰY), and write gametes as (Xᴮ), (Xᵇ), and (Y).
  2. Never attach an X-linked superscript to Y: Write XᴮY and XᵇY—never XᴮYᵇ or XYᵇ. The Y chromosome lacks the non-homologous X-linked locus.
  3. Check the denominator (“of all children” vs “of sons” vs “of daughters”): Always write both numbers clearly in your answer (e.g. “25% of all children, which is 50% of the sons”), so your answer is unambiguous under any mark scheme.

  • Sex-linked characteristic (0610 17.4.16): Describe a sex-linked characteristic as a characteristic in which the gene responsible is located on a sex chromosome and that this makes it more common in one sex than in the other.
  • Red–green colour blindness (17.4.19) & sex-linked Punnett squares (17.4.20): Describe red–green colour blindness as an example of sex linkage, and construct/interpret genetic diagrams using X/Y superscripts (Xᴮ, Xᵇ, Y or Xᴴ, Xʰ, Y) to predict phenotypes, carrier status, ratios, and probabilities.

  1. Define a sex-linked characteristic (0610 17.4.16) and explain why X-linked recessive conditions such as red–green colour blindness (Xᵇ) and haemophilia (Xʰ) are much more common in males (XY) than in females (XX).

Construct a six-line genetic diagram (including gametes and a 2 × 2 Punnett square) and state (a) the probability that a son has haemophilia, (b) the probability that a daughter is a carrier, and (c) the probability that any child born to the couple has haemophilia.
