(1) Selective agent: in natural selection the environment selects, whereas in selective breeding humans select; (2) Trait favoured: natural selection favours features that increase survival and reproduction in the wild, whereas selective breeding favours features useful or attractive to humans (which may lower wild fitness); (3) Speed: selective breeding usually changes traits faster over fewer generations; (4) Genetic diversity: selective breeding reduces genetic diversity much more sharply, increasing the risk of inbreeding depression.

Explain why selective breeding over many generations can lead to inbreeding depression and susceptibility to disease epidemics.

Repeatedly breeding closely related individuals with the desired phenotype narrows the gene pool (reduces genetic diversity) and increases homozygosity, so hidden harmful recessive alleles (aa) are much more likely to come together in offspring (causing genetic defects and lower vigour). Because all individuals become genetically similar, if a new pathogen arrives to which one individual is susceptible, the entire population lacks resistance alleles and can be devastated.

How did E. K. Janaki Ammal use wild Indian sugarcane (Saccharum spontaneum) in Coimbatore, and why are wild relatives vital for crop breeding?

E. K. Janaki Ammal crossed sweet tropical sugarcane (S. officinarum) with hardy wild Indian S. spontaneum and selected polyploid hybrids over generations, combining high sucrose yield (16.4%) with frost and disease resistance. Wild relatives maintain a wide reservoir of genetic diversity and resistance alleles that have been lost from inbred domesticated monocultures.

Explain how comparing DNA base sequences and amino acid sequences (such as Cytochrome c) helps biologists classify organisms and determine evolutionary relationships.

Because DNA mutations accumulate over evolutionary time, species that share a more recent common ancestor have more similar DNA base sequences and fewer amino acid differences in their proteins, whereas species that diverged longer ago have accumulated more sequence differences. This provides a quantitative molecular clock that avoids mistakes caused by superficial morphological similarity (convergent evolution).

Go deeper why can classifying organisms by visible morphology alone sometimes mislead biologists (as with sharks and dolphins, or bacteria and archaea), what was birbal sahni’s pentoxyleae discovery in the jurassic rajmahal hills of bihar, and why are such fossils important for evolutionary biology, why do two species with 0 amino acid differences in cytochrome c (such as humans and chimpanzees) still show ~1.2% differences in their coding dna base sequences
Why can classifying organisms by visible morphology alone sometimes mislead biologists (as with sharks and dolphins, or Bacteria and Archaea)?

Because convergent evolution under similar environmental selection pressures can mould distantly related lineages into similar outer shapes (such as streamlined bodies and dorsal fins in sharks and dolphins), while microscopic organisms (such as Bacteria and Archaea) may look like simple rods or spheres under a microscope despite having diverged billions of years ago in their 16S rRNA and DNA sequences.

What was Birbal Sahni’s Pentoxyleae discovery in the Jurassic Rajmahal Hills of Bihar, and why are such fossils important for evolutionary biology?

In 1948, Birbal Sahni discovered Pentoxyleae, an extinct Jurassic gymnosperm order whose petrified stems, leaves, and cones combined anatomical traits of ancient seed-ferns, cycads, and conifers—providing direct transitional fossil evidence of how major plant groups diverged over geological time.

Why do two species with 0 amino acid differences in Cytochrome c (such as humans and chimpanzees) still show ~1.2% differences in their coding DNA base sequences?

Because the genetic code is degenerate: silent base substitutions in the third position of DNA triplets (such as GAA → GAG) change the DNA base sequence without changing the amino acid incorporated into the Cytochrome c protein, so DNA base sequences record even finer recent evolutionary divergence than amino acid sequences.

Your turn

Explain to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

  • Misconception: “Selective breeding is the same thing as genetic engineering.” Correction: Selective breeding crosses whole organisms of the same (or closely related) species over many generations and selects offspring without directly editing DNA molecules. Genetic engineering (which we will study in Chapter 15) transfers or edits a specific gene directly at the molecular level (often between unrelated species, such as inserting the human insulin gene into a bacterial plasmid) in a single laboratory generation.
  • Misconception: “Humans evolved from chimpanzees, so chimpanzees are our ancestors.” Correction: No living species evolved from another modern living species. Humans and chimpanzees are evolutionary cousins that diverged from a shared common ancestor roughly 6.5 million years ago.
  • Misconception: “Selective breeding creates new alleles to make cows give more milk.” Correction: Human breeders cannot cause new alleles to appear; selective breeding selects and combines pre-existing alleles (and rare spontaneous mutations) across generations.

At school

How school exams phrase 14.4 (Cambridge 0610 Topics 18.3 & 1.2):

  • Selective Breeding (18.3.2 Core): Always include all five points in order: (1) selection by humans of individuals with desirable features; (2) crossing these individuals to produce the next generation; (3) selection of offspring showing the desirable features; (4) repetition over many generations (plus naming the specific desirable feature in the question).
  • Natural vs Artificial Selection (18.3.5 Supplement): Outline the differences between natural and artificial selection (selective agent, traits selected, effect on wild survival fitness, rate, and genetic diversity).
  • Sequence Classification (1.2.5 & 1.2.6 Supplement): State that sequences of bases in DNA and of amino acids in proteins are used as a more accurate means of classification, and explain that organisms which share a more recent ancestor (are more closely related) have base sequences in DNA that are more similar than those that share only a distant ancestor.

Check yourself

  1. Designing a selective breeding programme for drought-tolerant millet: An agricultural institute in Rajasthan wants to breed a variety of pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum) that produces heavy grain heads under low-rainfall conditions (<250 mm yr⁻¹). Describe step by step how the scientists should carry out this selective breeding programme.
  2. Interpreting a DNA sequence alignment table: Biologists sequence a 200-base segment of a respiratory gene in a newly discovered forest mammal (Species X) and compare the percentage of identical DNA bases against four known mammals: Species P (96.5%), Species Q (82.0%), Species R (91.0%), and Species S (78.5%). State which species (P, Q, R, or S) is most closely related to Species X and which is most distantly related, and explain your reasoning using evolutionary principles.

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 14

Why the sickle-cell allele stays common in malaria belts

We are now ready to solve the chapter’s central mystery—and tie together the entire four-chapter arc of Volume IV (Chapters 11, 12, 13, and 14).

In a public-health genetics seminar at KEM Hospital in Mumbai, Kym compares two districts from the surveys of Anthony Allison (1954) and L. D. Sanghvi: District H, a cool, high-altitude mountain valley (2,400 m) where Anopheles mosquitoes and Plasmodium falciparum malaria are completely absent (carrier frequency HbᴬHbˢ = 0.8%, q ≈ 0.004), and District M, a warm, humid lowland forest belt where P. falciparum malaria has been holoendemic for centuries (carrier frequency HbᴬHbˢ = 26.6%, q ≈ 0.158).

Genotype (Chr 11) Anaemia & P. falciparum Malaria Effects Relative Fitness (w)
HbᴬHbᴬ (Normal) 100% HbA biconcave discs; no anaemia, but high malaria susceptibility (45.7% parasite rate) w ≈ 0.85 (selected against by malaria)
HbᴬHbˢ (Carrier) ~60% HbA + ~40% HbS; no severe anaemia and 60–80% protected against severe malaria (27.9% rate) w = 1.00 (HIGHEST fitness)
HbˢHbˢ (Sickle) 100% HbS polymerises at low O₂ into rigid crescents; severe sickle-cell anaemia w ≈ 0.20 (selected against by anaemia)

Use all four sections of Chapter 14 (together with Chapters 11–13) to answer three synthesis questions:

  1. Molecular origin and non-directed mutation (14.1 & Ch 11): Explain how the Hbˢ allele originally arose on Chromosome 11, and evaluate the claim that “living in a malarial forest caused people’s beta-globin genes to mutate into Hbˢ for protection.”
  2. Punnett inheritance and opposing selection pressures (14.2–14.3 & Ch 13): Construct the 2 × 2 Punnett square outcome when two heterozygous carriers (HbᴬHbˢ × HbᴬHbˢ) have children. Then explain why the Hbˢ allele is driven down to <0.5% in malaria-free District H, whereas it stays high (q ≈ 15.8%, 26.6% carriers) in malarial District M.
  3. Heterozygote advantage and eradication prediction (14.3–14.4): Suppose a public-health campaign completely eradicates Anopheles mosquitoes and Plasmodium falciparum malaria from District M over the next 20 generations while everything else stays constant. Predict and explain what will happen to the frequency of the Hbˢ allele in District M over those 20 generations.
Show the solution
  1. Molecular origin (14.1 & Ch 11): The Hbˢ allele arose by a spontaneous, random gene mutation—specifically a single base substitution (CCT GAG GAG → CCT GTG GAG, transcribed as GUG in mRNA) at codon 6 of the beta-globin (HBB) gene on Chromosome 11, substituting hydrophobic valine (Val⁶) for hydrophilic glutamic acid (Glu⁶). The claim that malaria caused the mutation is false: environments and pathogens never direct DNA mutations. The GAG → GTG glitch occurred randomly at low baseline rates (~10⁻⁹ per base pair) in both malarial and non-malarial populations; malaria acted only afterward as an environmental selection pressure.
  2. Punnett inheritance & balancing selection (14.2–14.3 & Ch 13):
    • Cross (HbᴬHbˢ × HbᴬHbˢ): Gametes (Hbᴬ) and (Hbˢ) combine in a 2 × 2 grid to yield 25% HbᴬHbᴬ : 50% HbᴬHbˢ : 25% HbˢHbˢ (1 : 2 : 1 genotype ratio).
    • In malaria-free District H: There is no malaria mortality, so HbᴬHbᴬ and HbᴬHbˢ individuals have equal high fitness (w = 1.00), while HbˢHbˢ individuals suffer severe sickle-cell anaemia (w ≈ 0.20) and often die before reproducing. Every early death of an HbˢHbˢ individual removes two Hbˢ alleles from the population without any compensating advantage, driving Hbˢ frequency down toward zero (q ≈ 0.004).
    • In malarial District M: Two opposing selection pressures operate simultaneously. Homozygous normal (HbᴬHbᴬ) children suffer high mortality from severe P. falciparum malaria (w ≈ 0.85), and homozygous sickle (HbˢHbˢ) children suffer high mortality from sickle-cell anaemia (w ≈ 0.20). Heterozygous carriers (HbᴬHbˢ) have the highest fitness (w = 1.00, heterozygote advantage) because ~60% HbA prevents severe anaemia while infected cells sickle prematurely and are cleared by the spleen (60–80% protection against severe malaria). Because HbᴬHbˢ survivors reproduce most successfully and pass Hbˢ to 50% of their gametes, the allele is maintained at a stable equilibrium (balancing selection, q ≈ 15.8%).
  3. Prediction after malaria eradication (14.3–14.4): Once Plasmodium falciparum malaria is eradicated from District M, the selective advantage of HbᴬHbˢ carriers over HbᴬHbᴬ individuals disappears (HbᴬHbᴬ and HbᴬHbˢ now have equal survival fitness w = 1.00), while natural selection against HbˢHbˢ (due to sickle-cell anaemia) continues to remove Hbˢ alleles every generation. Consequently, the frequency of the Hbˢ allele (q) and the percentage of HbᴬHbˢ carriers will steadily decrease over the next 20 generations toward the low baseline seen in District H.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

Over the past four chapters, we have traced the master code of life from a single DNA base pair (Chapter 11) through cell division (Chapter 12), family inheritance (Chapter 13), and four billion years of natural selection (Chapter 14).

Now, in our final chapter of The Living World, we zoom all the way out to the living planet and all the way forward to the modern biotechnology lab:

  1. How does solar energy flow from producers to consumers and decomposers through food chains, food webs, and pyramids of numbers, biomass, and energy—and why is roughly 90% of energy lost at every trophic step?
  2. How do carbon, water, and nitrogen cycle endlessly between the atmosphere, soil bacteria, plants, and animals, and what happens when human deforestation, greenhouse gases, and eutrophication disrupt those cycles across the Western Ghats and the Sundarbans?
  3. How do modern biotechnologists and genetic engineers use fermenters, restriction enzymes, DNA ligase, and the very bacterial plasmids we met in Chapter 2 and Chapter 14 to insert the human insulin gene into bacteria and manufacture life-saving medicines?

Volume IV concludes in Chapter 15: Web of Life & Code Rewritable: Ecology, Nutrient Cycles & Biotechnology.

The big questionWhy can an entire monsoon forest of thousands of caterpillars, birds, and leopards feed only four or five links high before energy runs out—while the carbon, water, and nitrogen atoms inside their bodies cycle forever, and their universal DNA code can be spliced into bacteria to brew human insulin?

  3. 15.3Footprints on the web: farming, deforestation, eutrophication and conservation

At the close of Chapter 14, we stood at the edge of two worlds: the four-billion-year filter of natural selection (Charles Robert Darwin, Alfred Russel Wallace, Salvador Luria, and Birbal Sahni) shaping wild populations across forests, creeks, and hospital wards, and the new human power to steer evolution deliberately. Every organism we have met since Chapter 0—from the dry chickpea seed waking on a monsoon window-ledge to the spotted deer, mangroves, and dividing bacteria of Mumbai—lives inside a shared planetary household.

In this final chapter of The Living World, we follow the two master rules that govern that household (Cambridge 0893 Stages 7–9 and Cambridge 0610 Topics 19, 20 & 21): energy flows one way from the Sun to heat, matter cycles endlessly through air, water, soil, and cells, and the universal DNA code that natural selection wrote across four billion years can now be spliced into bacterial plasmids and edited letter by letter.

15.1Sunlit chains & the ten-percent tax: food webs, ecological pyramids and population growth

Sanjay Gandhi National Park (SGNP), Borivali & Oval Maidan, Mumbai

It is early October in Sanjay Gandhi National Park (SGNP) in Borivali, at the northern edge of Mumbai, just after the monsoon rains have triggered the once-in-eight-years mass flowering of the Karvi shrub (Strobilanthes callosa). Purple-blue blossoms carpet the basalt hillsides below the Kanheri Caves. Honeybees and carpenter bees hum from corolla to corolla; caterpillars chew the tender green leaves; a praying mantis waits motionless on a stem; a rufous treepie and a spotted owlet watch from a teak branch; and in the dappled shade below, a herd of spotted deer (Axis axis) grazes while an Indian leopard (Panthera pardus fusca) rests on a warm boulder overhead. Beneath their hooves, white threads of bracket fungi and billions of soil bacteria quietly digest fallen petals, shed antlers, and deer droppings back into dark forest humus. Across town at Oval Maidan, a single centuries-old banyan tree (Ficus benghalensis) spreads its aerial prop roots like a miniature forest of its own, feeding thousands of fig wasps, caterpillars, and fruit bats from one massive woody trunk.

Every living interaction on that Borivali hillside belongs to an ecosystem—a distinct unit containing all the interacting organisms in a given area (the community) together with their non-living physical and chemical environment (sunlight, basalt rock, rainwater, soil mineral ions, and air). Within an ecosystem, the specific place where an organism lives is its habitat (such as the damp leaf-litter floor for a bracket fungus or the canopy twigs for a fig wasp), a group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time is a population (such as all the spotted deer in SGNP), and all the populations of different species living and interacting in that ecosystem form the community.

To trace how an ecosystem stays alive, we must distinguish two quantities that never behave the same way: energy and matter. The Sun is the principal source of energy input to biological systems. In Chapter 5 (5.1–5.3), after Jan Baptista van Helmont weighed his willow tree and Jan Ingenhousz watched sunlit leaves bubble oxygen, we saw how chlorophyll inside green plants, algae, and photosynthetic bacteria traps light energy from the Sun and transfers it into chemical energy stored in the covalent bonds of glucose (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂). When animals eat plants, or predators eat prey, that stored chemical energy is passed from one organism to the next. At every step, organisms oxidise glucose in aerobic respiration (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O, Chapter 6 6.2) to power muscle contraction, active transport, nerve impulses, and protein synthesis, transferring energy to the surroundings as thermal energy (heat). Once energy has radiated into the air as low-grade heat, no plant or chloroplast can ever trap it again. Energy therefore flows through ecosystems in one direction only (non-cyclical: Sun → producers → consumers and decomposers → dissipated heat). By contrast, the chemical elements and mineral ions (carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, magnesium) are recycled over and over within the ecosystem (cyclical).

Food chains, food webs, and the exact meaning of the arrow

A food chain is a diagram showing the transfer of energy from one organism to the next, beginning with a producer:

Karvi shrub (Producer) → Spotted deer (Primary consumer) → Indian leopard (Secondary consumer)

Look closely at the arrows (→). In ecology and in every Cambridge examination, an arrow in a food chain or food web points in the direction of energy transfer—from the organism being eaten into the body of the organism that eats it (Grass → Deer, never Deer → Grass). Because most animals eat more than one kind of food and are eaten by more than one predator, real ecosystems are woven into a food web—a network of interconnected food chains. Every organism in a food chain or food web occupies a specific feeding position called a trophic level (from the Greek trophē, meaning nourishment):

Trophic Level & Role Syllabus Definition (0610 19.2) SGNP & Mumbai Examples
Level 1: Producer An organism that makes its own organic nutrients, usually using energy from sunlight, through photosynthesis. Karvi shrubs, grasses, Ficus benghalensis (banyan tree), creek phytoplankton.
Level 2: Primary consumer An organism that gets its energy by feeding on producers; classified by diet as a herbivore (an animal that gets its energy by eating plants). Spotted deer, caterpillars, fig wasps, fruit bats, zooplankton.
Level 3: Secondary consumer An organism that gets its energy by feeding on primary consumers; may be a carnivore (an animal that gets its energy by eating other animals) or an omnivore (eating both plants and animals). Praying mantids, tree frogs, rufous treepies, barn owls, Indian leopards (when eating deer).
Level 4: Tertiary consumer / Quaternary consumer Predators that feed on secondary consumers (Level 4) or tertiary consumers (Level 5, apex predators). Crested serpent eagles eating tree frogs or rat snakes; Indian pythons.
Decomposer An organism (principally saprotrophic fungi and bacteria) that gets its energy from dead or waste organic material (faeces, urea, dead leaves, carcasses). Bracket fungi, soil mould, putrefying bacteria in forest humus and creek mud.

Predict first

Walk across Oval Maidan in south Mumbai and count the organisms in this four-step food chain: 1 giant banyan tree → 8,000 fruit bats and caterpillars → 350 praying mantids and tree frogs → 6 crested serpent eagles. Compare the shapes of the pyramid of numbers, the pyramid of biomass (dry mass g m⁻²), and the pyramid of energy (kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹) for this banyan food chain.

  1. All three pyramids are inverted at the base because there is only 1 banyan tree
  2. The pyramid of numbers is inverted at the base (1 tree < 8,000 primary consumers), whereas both the pyramid of biomass (4,500 kg → 120 kg → 12 kg → 1.2 kg dry mass) and the pyramid of energy (45,000 → 4,500 → 450 → 45 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹) are strictly upright
  3. The pyramid of energy is inverted because eagles fly faster and burn more energy than trees

What happens

The second choice. If you plot the number of individuals, the bottom bar (Level 1: 1 banyan tree) is tiny while the second bar (Level 2: 8,000 bats and caterpillars) is huge—producing an inverted pyramid of numbers at the base because counting individuals treats one 4,500 kg tree and one 0.5 g caterpillar as equal counts (1 = 1).

If you instead weigh the dry mass of living material at each level (pyramid of biomass), the single banyan tree (4,500 kg dry wood, roots, and leaves) vastly outweighs all 8,000 primary consumers (120 kg), which outweigh the 350 secondary consumers (12 kg) and the 6 eagles (1.2 kg)—restoring an upright pyramid. And if you plot the energy flowing through each trophic level per year (pyramid of energy, in kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹), the diagram is always upright without exception (45,000 → 4,500 → 450 → 45 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹), because roughly 90% of energy is lost at every transfer and a consumer level can never receive more energy than its food source captured.

How do we know? Oxford, 1927 & Cedar Creek Bog, Minnesota, 1942: Elton’s pyramids and Lindeman’s ten-percent energy budget Thermodynamic ecological proof

In 1927, the English ecologist Charles Elton introduced the “pyramid of numbers” after observing Arctic and woodland food webs where abundant small herbivores supported progressively fewer larger predators. Fifteen years later, in 1942, the twenty-six-year-old American ecologist Raymond Lindeman (working with Eleanor Hall at Cedar Creek Bog in Minnesota) published the first complete thermodynamic energy budget of an ecosystem. By measuring the chemical energy stored and respired across producers, herbivores, and carnivores over an entire year, Lindeman proved that only about 10% of the energy entering one trophic level is transferred into new biomass at the next trophic level. The remaining ~90% is lost between levels—establishing why ecological pyramids of energy can never invert and why food chains are strictly limited in length.

Comparing pyramids of numbers, biomass, and energy

Ecologists use three different ecological pyramids to quantify trophic levels (Level 1 always at the bottom bar, stepping upward to Level 2, Level 3, and Level 4):

  1. Pyramid of numbers: Bar width shows the number of individual organisms at each trophic level in a fixed area. Advantage: Fast and non-destructive to count in the field. Disadvantage: Ignores organism size (1 banyan tree counts the same as 1 aphid), so the pyramid is inverted or spindle-shaped whenever a single large producer supports thousands of small herbivores (Tree → Caterpillars → Songbirds), or when hundreds of fleas or protozoan parasites feed on a single bird or mammal (L4 > L3).
  2. Pyramid of biomass: Bar width shows the dry mass of living material (g m⁻² or kg ha⁻¹) present at each trophic level at a single moment in time (standing crop). Organisms are dried in an oven at ~80 °C until constant mass so that variable water content (which contains zero chemical energy) does not distort the measurement. Advantage: Overcomes the size distortion of pyramids of numbers; on land, pyramids of biomass are almost always upright because producer dry mass exceeds consumer dry mass. Disadvantage: Destructive (requires killing and oven-drying samples) and measures only a single snapshot in time, not the rate of production.
  3. Pyramid of energy: Bar width shows the rate of energy flow (kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹) passing through each trophic level over a full year. Advantage: Always upright (pyramid-shaped) without exception in every terrestrial and aquatic ecosystem, because the Second Law of Thermodynamics guarantees that less chemical energy is available to each successive trophic level. Disadvantage: Difficult and time-consuming to measure calorific values and respiration rates of every species across twelve months.

The ten-percent rule, short food chains, and human diet efficiency

Why does roughly 90% of the energy vanish between one trophic level and the next, leaving only ~10% to become new biomass available to the next consumer? Four biological processes account for the loss (0610 19.2):

  1. Aerobic respiration and heat loss (~50–60% of ingested energy): Every living organism oxidises glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O) to generate ATP (discovered by Yellapragada SubbaRow) for muscle movement, foraging, heartbeats, active transport across membranes, and maintaining body temperature (especially warm-blooded endotherms such as mammals and birds, Chapter 10 10.3). All of this energy eventually escapes to the environment as thermal energy (heat).
  2. Uneaten parts: Consumers rarely eat the entire organism below them—woody tree trunks, deep roots, thorns, tough bark, hoofs, bones, scales, and feathers are left behind, and some individuals die of disease or old age without being eaten. Their chemical energy passes to decomposers, not to the next consumer level.
  3. Indigestible egested waste (faeces): Much of what an animal swallows cannot be hydrolysed by its digestive enzymes—especially plant cellulose cell walls, lignin, insect chitin exoskeletons, hair, and bone. This undigested material is egested as faeces (Chapter 7 7.1), carrying chemical energy to soil decomposers.
  4. Excreted metabolic waste (urea and urine): Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver and excreted by the kidneys as urea in urine (Chapter 8 8.5), along with lost heat and sweat.

This ~90% tax at every step explains two major patterns in biology:

  • Why food chains rarely have more than 4 or 5 trophic levels: Suppose 10,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ of chemical energy is fixed by Karvi shrubs (Level 1). Primary consumers (Level 2, deer) build 1,000 kJ of biomass; secondary consumers (Level 3, leopards) build 100 kJ; tertiary consumers (Level 4) build 10 kJ; and a hypothetical 5th level receives only 1 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. By the 4th or 5th level, so little usable energy remains per square kilometre that a higher predator would spend more energy hunting over a vast territory than it could ever recover from its prey, making a breeding population impossible to sustain.
  • Why supplying humans with crop plants is far more energy-efficient than feeding crops to livestock: When humans eat crop plants directly (rice, wheat, chickpeas, vegetables), the food chain has only two trophic levels (1 transfer step):

Crop plants (10,000 kJ) → Humans (1,000 kJ assimilated, 10%)

When humans grow arable crops (maize, soya, grain), feed those crops to livestock (cattle, pigs, poultry), and then eat the meat, milk, or eggs, the food chain has three trophic levels (2 transfer steps):

Crop plants (10,000 kJ) → Livestock (1,000 kJ) → Humans (100 kJ assimilated, 1%)

Because the livestock lose ~90% of the crop’s chemical energy in their own respiration, body heat, egested faeces, and excreted urine, eating crop plants directly delivers roughly ten times more food energy per hectare of farmland (and supports far more people on the same land area) than routing crops through livestock.

Populations and the four-phase sigmoid growth curve

How fast can any population grow inside its ecosystem? The rate of growth of a population depends on four main environmental factors (0610 19.4): food supply, competition (for food, space, water, light, or mates), predation, and disease.

When a small number of microorganisms (such as yeast cells in a flask of sugar broth or bacteria in a batch culture) or colonising organisms enter a closed environment with finite resources, the population size plotted against time traces a characteristic S-shaped curve called a sigmoid growth curve with four distinct phases (Figure 15.2):

  1. Lag phase (birth rate low, N very small): Population size increases very slowly at first because there are very few reproducing individuals present and cells are adjusting to the new environment (synthesising enzymes to digest the available substrate, absorbing water, and preparing to divide).
  2. Exponential phase (or log phase, birth rate ≫ death rate): Food/nutrients and space are abundant, toxic waste concentration is negligible, and no environmental limiting factors restrict growth. Every cell or organism divides at its maximum physiological rate (1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32...), so the curve rises steeply.
  3. Stationary phase (birth rate = death rate around carrying capacity K): One or more limiting factors take effect—food/substrate begins to run low, space becomes crowded, intraspecific competition intensifies, predators or infectious diseases spread rapidly through the dense population, or toxic metabolic waste products accumulate. The birth rate falls and the death rate rises until birth rate equals death rate, and the population size plateaus around the maximum number of individuals the environment can support, called its carrying capacity (K).
  4. Death phase (death rate > birth rate): In a closed container where no fresh nutrients are added and wastes are not removed, the food supply is exhausted and toxic metabolic wastes (such as ethanol in yeast or organic acids in bacteria) reach lethal levels, so the death rate exceeds the birth rate and the population crashes.

Why human population growth looks like an extended exponential curve. Over the past 250 years, the global human population has surged from under 1 billion to over 8 billion, tracing a steep exponential (J-shaped) curve without yet entering a global stationary phase. Humans raised our effective carrying capacity and sharply lowered infant and adult death rates through agricultural machinery and chemical fertilisers (increasing food supply), clean piped water, oral rehydration therapy (Dilip Mahalanabis), and sewage sanitation, vaccination and antibiotics (controlling infectious disease, Chapters 10 and 14), and shelter from predators.

Understand it

What is the principal source of energy input to biological systems, and in what form is energy eventually lost from food chains to the environment?

The Sun is the principal source of energy input (trapped as light energy by chlorophyll during photosynthesis and converted into chemical energy in organic molecules); energy is eventually transferred to the environment as thermal energy (heat) released during respiration.

In the food chain Phytoplankton → Krill → Penguin → Leopard seal, what do the arrows (→) represent, which organism is the secondary consumer, and which trophic level does the leopard seal occupy?

The arrows (→) represent the direction of energy transfer from one organism to the next. The penguin is the secondary consumer (Level 3), and the leopard seal occupies the fourth trophic level (Level 4, tertiary consumer).

State four reasons why only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred into new biomass at the next trophic level.

(1) Energy is lost as heat during aerobic respiration (for movement, active transport, and body temperature); (2) some parts of organisms are not eaten (roots, woody stems, bones, fur); (3) indigestible material (such as cellulose) is egested in faeces; and (4) metabolic waste (urea) is excreted in urine.

Explain why a pyramid of numbers for a food chain starting with a single banyan or oak tree is inverted at the base, whereas its pyramid of biomass and pyramid of energy are upright.

A pyramid of numbers counts individual organisms regardless of size, so 1 giant tree supporting 8,000 caterpillars gives a tiny bottom bar (1 < 8,000). A pyramid of biomass measures total dry mass (4,500 kg tree > 120 kg insects), and a pyramid of energy measures annual energy flow (kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹), which is always upright because ~90% of energy is lost at each trophic step.

Name the four phases of a sigmoid population growth curve in order, and state the relationship between birth rate and death rate during the stationary phase.

(1) Lag phase, (2) Exponential (log) phase, (3) Stationary phase, and (4) Death phase. During the stationary phase, the birth rate equals the death rate (B = D) as environmental limiting factors stabilise the population around carrying capacity K.

Go deeper a farmer harvests 50,000 kj of chemical energy in maize grain from a field. using the 10% trophic transfer rule, calculate how much energy reaches human tissues if (a) humans eat the maize directly, and (b) the maize is fed to cattle and humans eat the beef. explain why eating crop plants directly supports a larger human population per hectare., explain why terrestrial and marine food chains very rarely have more than four or five trophic levels., a student inoculates 100 yeast cells into a sealed flask of sterile glucose broth at 30 °c and counts the living cells every 2 hours for 48 hours. explain the biological causes of the change in gradient between the exponential (log) phase, the stationary phase, and the death phase.
A farmer harvests 50,000 kJ of chemical energy in maize grain from a field. Using the 10% trophic transfer rule, calculate how much energy reaches human tissues if (a) humans eat the maize directly, and (b) the maize is fed to cattle and humans eat the beef. Explain why eating crop plants directly supports a larger human population per hectare.

(a) Direct crop diet (1 transfer step): 10% of 50,000 kJ = 5,000 kJ. (b) Livestock beef diet (2 transfer steps): cattle retain 10% (5,000 kJ) and humans assimilate 10% of that = 500 kJ. Eating crop plants directly eliminates the intermediate livestock trophic level, avoiding the 90% energy loss in cattle respiration, heat, faeces, and urine, and therefore delivers 10× more food energy per hectare.

Explain why terrestrial and marine food chains very rarely have more than four or five trophic levels.

Because roughly 90% of energy is lost at every trophic transfer, by the fourth or fifth trophic level only 0.1% to 0.01% of the original producer energy remains—too little energy per unit area to support a viable breeding population of a higher predator.

A student inoculates 100 yeast cells into a sealed flask of sterile glucose broth at 30 °C and counts the living cells every 2 hours for 48 hours. Explain the biological causes of the change in gradient between the exponential (log) phase, the stationary phase, and the death phase.

In the exponential phase, glucose and space are abundant with no limiting factors, so division rate ≫ death rate. In the stationary phase, glucose becomes scarce and ethanol waste builds up (limiting factors), slowing division until division rate = death rate. In the death phase, glucose is exhausted and toxic ethanol kills cells (death rate > division rate).

Your turn

Explain to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

  • Never draw food chain arrows pointing from predator to prey: Writing Leopard → Deer → Grass to mean “the leopard eats the deer” is the single commonest ecological mistake. Arrows (→) always point in the direction of energy flow (Grass → Deer → Leopard).
  • Energy is NEVER recycled: Do not write that “decomposers recycle energy back to plants.” Decomposers respire dead organic matter and release its remaining energy as heat, which escapes to the atmosphere. Decomposers recycle mineral ions and carbon/nitrogen atoms, never energy.
  • Pyramids of biomass vs pyramids of energy: A pyramid of biomass shows the dry mass of organisms at each trophic level at a single moment (g m⁻²). A pyramid of energy shows the annual rate of energy flow (kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹) and never inverts under any circumstances.

At school

How school exams phrase 15.1 (Cambridge 0610 Topics 19.1, 19.2 & 19.4):

  • Core definitions (19.2 & 19.4): Memorise the exact wording for food chain, food web, producer, consumer (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary), herbivore, carnivore, decomposer, trophic level, population, community, and ecosystem.
  • Energy efficiency questions (19.2 Supplement): When asked why energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient (or why eating plants is more efficient than eating livestock), always name at least three specific losses: heat lost in respiration, energy in egested faeces (indigestible cellulose/bone), energy in excreted urine (urea), and uneaten body parts passing to decomposers.
  • Sigmoid curve questions (19.4 Supplement): Always link each phase to both the relative rates of birth and death (B ≫ D in exponential, B = D in stationary, D > B in death) and the specific limiting factors (food supply, space, competition, predation, disease, toxic waste accumulation).

Check yourself

  1. SGNP trophic energy calculation: In Sanjay Gandhi National Park, Karvi shrubs trap 20,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ of solar energy into net plant biomass. Assuming a 10% energy transfer efficiency at each step, calculate how much energy (kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹) is incorporated into the biomass of secondary consumers (such as Indian leopards feeding on spotted deer), and state four pathways by which the other 90% is lost at each transfer.
  2. Evaluating pyramid types: Explain one advantage of using a pyramid of biomass rather than a pyramid of numbers, and one advantage of using a pyramid of energy rather than a pyramid of biomass.

15.2Atoms on loan: the water, carbon and nitrogen cycles

Marine Drive Monsoon Promenade & Dadar Kitchen Sink, Mumbai

Stand on the promenade at Marine Drive as the June southwest monsoon rolls in off the Arabian Sea. Warm ocean water that evaporated under the May sun has cooled high in the sky into towering cumulonimbus clouds. Within minutes, sheets of rain drum onto the basalt ridges of Malabar Hill and Borivali; some flows down storm drains and the Mithi River back to the sea, while some soaks into the soil where banyan and mango roots drink it up by osmosis and send it skyward through xylem vessels to evaporate out of leaf stomata as water vapour. Now step into a kitchen in Dadar where Kym is helping wash a fresh bundle of methi (fenugreek, Trigonella foenum-graecum) pulled soil-and-all from a suburban farm. Clinging to the pale branching roots are dozens of tiny, rounded root nodules the size of mustard seeds. Slice one open with a fingernail and its inside gleams pinkish-red—coloured by an oxygen-binding protein called leghaemoglobin, cousin to the haemoglobin in Kym’s own red blood cells, shielding millions of Rhizobium bacteria as they crack atmospheric nitrogen gas (N₂) into the amino acids that will build Kym’s enzymes and DNA.

Because Earth is virtually a closed system for matter, every carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen atom inside your body has been borrowed from the atmosphere, oceans, and soil—and will be returned to them. Three interlocking biogeochemical loops keep the biosphere stocked with raw materials (0610 19.3): the water cycle, the carbon cycle, and the nitrogen cycle.

The water cycle and the carbon cycle

The water cycle is powered by solar thermal energy and gravity (Figure 15.3A):

  • Evaporation: Heat from the Sun warms liquid water in oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp soil, giving water molecules enough kinetic energy to escape into the air as invisible water vapour.
  • Transpiration: Plant roots absorb liquid water from the soil by osmosis (Chapter 3 3.2) and pull it up xylem vessels; inside leaves, water evaporates from the wet cell walls of spongy mesophyll cells and diffuses out through open stomata as water vapour (Chapter 5 5.5). Over a tropical rainforest like the Western Ghats, transpiration returns more than half of all rainfall directly back to the atmosphere.
  • Condensation: Warm moist air rises, expands, and cools high in the troposphere; water vapour condenses around microscopic dust and salt nuclei into tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals, forming clouds.
  • Precipitation: When cloud droplets coalesce and grow too heavy to remain suspended, water falls back to Earth as rain, snow, sleet, or hail, returning to rivers and seas via surface runoff and groundwater percolation.

The carbon cycle revolves around atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂, ~0.04% of air, or ~426 ppm) and five core processes (Figure 15.3B):

  1. Photosynthesis (the single biological entry doorway): Green plants, algae, and photosynthetic bacteria absorb CO₂ from the air (or dissolved HCO₃⁻/CO₂ in water) and use light energy trapped by chlorophyll to fix carbon atoms into glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆), starch, cellulose, lipids, and proteins (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂).
  2. Feeding (and assimilation): Animals eat plants (or other animals), digest their polymers with carbohydrases, proteases, and lipases (Chapter 7 7.3), and assimilate the carbon compounds into animal tissues.
  3. Respiration: Producers, consumers, and decomposers all carry out aerobic respiration (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O) twenty-four hours a day, oxidising organic carbon compounds to release ATP energy and returning CO₂ gas to the atmosphere.
  4. Decomposition: When plants and animals die, or shed leaves, faeces, and urea, decomposers (saprotrophic fungi and bacteria) secrete extracellular enzymes onto the dead organic matter, absorb the soluble products, and respire them, releasing CO₂ back to the air.
  5. Fossilisation and combustion: When dead plants, peat bog mosses, or marine plankton are buried under mud and sediment in anaerobic, acidic, or high-pressure conditions where decomposers cannot break them down completely, geological heat and pressure over millions of years transform their carbon into fossil fuels (coal, crude oil, and natural gas) or carbonate rocks (limestone). When humans burn fossil fuels or wood in power stations, vehicles, factories, and forest fires (combustion), stored carbon reacts with oxygen to release CO₂ rapidly back into the atmosphere:

Fossil fuel / Hydrocarbon + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O

The nitrogen cycle: four bacterial guilds and the N≡N triple bond

Why do plants need nitrogen at all? As we saw in Chapter 5 (5.3) and Chapter 11 (11.2–11.3), carbohydrate molecules made in photosynthesis (C₆H₁₂O₆) contain only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. To build amino acids, proteins (enzymes, cell membrane carriers, rubisco, antibodies), DNA, RNA, and ATP, plants and animals must add nitrogen (N).

At first glance, nitrogen looks abundant: 78% of Earth’s atmosphere is nitrogen gas (N₂). Yet a plant starving in nitrogen-poor soil will turn yellow and stunted even though its leaves are bathed in 78% N₂ air. Why? Because the two nitrogen atoms in an N₂ molecule are locked together by an extraordinarily strong triple covalent bond (N≡N) that neither plant chloroplasts nor animal enzymes can split. No plant and no animal can fix N₂ gas from the air. Instead, non-leguminous plants must absorb soluble nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) (and some ammonium ions, NH₄⁺) dissolved in soil water through their root hair cells by active transport (Chapter 3 3.4).

The entire biosphere depends on four specialized guilds of soil bacteria—plus lightning and industrial chemistry—to keep nitrogen moving through the nitrogen cycle (0610 19.3, Figure 15.4):

Nitrogen Cycle Stage Chemical Transformation Organisms / Agents & Environmental Conditions
1. Nitrogen fixation N₂ (gas) → NH₃ / NH₄⁺ or NO₃⁻ (a) Nitrogen-fixing bacteria: Mutualistic Rhizobium inside root nodules of leguminous plants (peas, beans, clover, chickpeas/chana, lentils/toor dal, fenugreek/methi) and free-living soil Azotobacter reduce N₂ → NH₄⁺ using the enzyme nitrogenase.
(b) Lightning: High-voltage electrical discharge provides activation energy to react N₂ + O₂ → nitrogen oxides, which dissolve in rainwater to enter soil directly as nitrate ions (NO₃⁻).
(c) Industrial Haber process: Reacts N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ at 450 °C and 200 atm over an iron catalyst to make ammonium nitrate fertilisers.
2. Absorption, Assimilation, Feeding & Deamination NO₃⁻ → Amino acids → Proteins → Urea Plant root hair cells absorb NO₃⁻ from soil water by active transport (using ATP from aerobic root respiration) and combine it with carbohydrates to synthesize amino acids and plant proteins. Animals eat plants, digest proteins with proteases (pepsin, trypsin), and assimilate amino acids into animal proteins. Excess amino acids undergo deamination in the liver (Chapter 8 8.5), converting the amino group into urea, which is excreted in urine.
3. Decomposition (Ammonification) Dead proteins, faeces & urea → NH₄⁺ Decomposers (putrefying bacteria and saprotrophic fungi) secrete extracellular proteases and urease onto dead plants, carcasses, egested faeces, and excreted urea, releasing ammonium ions (NH₄⁺) into the soil.
4. Nitrification NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻ Chemoautotrophic aerobic nitrifying bacteria in well-aerated soil oxidise ammonium ions in two steps: first ammonium ions to nitrite ions (NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻, e.g. Nitrosomonas), and second nitrite ions to nitrate ions (NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻, e.g. Nitrobacter). Requires dissolved oxygen (O₂) in soil air spaces.
5. Denitrification NO₃⁻ → N₂ (gas) Anaerobic denitrifying bacteria (e.g. Pseudomonas) thriving in waterlogged, compacted, unploughed soils lacking O₂ use nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) in place of oxygen for respiration, reducing NO₃⁻ back into inert N₂ gas that escapes into the air and reduces soil fertility.

Predict first

During the July monsoon deluge in coastal Maharashtra, a farmer’s low-lying tomato field becomes completely waterlogged for two weeks because its drainage ditch is blocked. Even though the farmer added ammonium fertiliser before the rains, the tomato plants turn pale yellow with stunted growth (nitrogen deficiency). Which combination of soil and root processes explains why waterlogging starves the plants of nitrate?

  1. Waterlogging washes nitrogen gas (N₂) out of the leaves through the stomata
  2. Waterlogged soil lacks oxygen (O₂), which (1) stimulates anaerobic denitrifying bacteria to convert soil NO₃⁻ → N₂ gas, (2) stops aerobic nitrifying bacteria from oxidising NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻, and (3) starves root hair cells of O₂ needed for aerobic respiration to make ATP for active transport of NO₃⁻
  3. Excess water converts Rhizobium bacteria inside tomato roots into viruses

What happens

The second choice. Waterlogging fills all the air spaces between soil particles with water, driving out oxygen (O₂) and creating anaerobic soil conditions:

  1. Denitrification surges (NO₃⁻ → N₂): Anaerobic denitrifying bacteria multiply in the oxygen-starved mud and convert existing soil nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) into N₂ gas, which bubbles out into the atmosphere and is lost.
  2. Nitrification stops (NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻ halts): Aerobic nitrifying bacteria require oxygen to oxidise the ammonium fertiliser (NH₄⁺) into nitrite (NO₂⁻) and nitrate (NO₃⁻), so new nitrate production halts.
  3. Root hair active transport fails: Tomato root hair cells absorb NO₃⁻ against a concentration gradient by active transport, which requires ATP from aerobic respiration (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O). Without soil O₂, root cells cannot make enough ATP to pump nitrate ions in. (This is why farmers plough and drain fields to keep soil aerated.)

How do we know? Delft, 1888, Zurich, 1890 & Mauna Loa, 1958: Beijerinck, Winogradsky, and Keeling’s biogeochemical proofs Microbiological & atmospheric proof

In 1888, the Dutch microbiologist Martinus Beijerinck isolated the rod-shaped bacterium Rhizobium leguminosarum from the root nodules of pea and bean plants and proved that sterile soil lacking these bacteria could not trigger nodule formation or nitrogen fixation. Between 1887 and 1891, the Russian microbiologist Sergei Winogradsky designed mineral media completely free of organic carbon and isolated the two obligate chemoautotrophic bacterial guilds that run soil nitrification: Nitrosomonas (which gains energy by oxidising NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻) and Nitrobacter (which oxidises NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻). Seven decades later, in 1958, Charles David Keeling began continuous infrared measurements of atmospheric CO₂ at Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii, providing direct chemical proof that human fossil-fuel combustion and deforestation were disrupting the global carbon cycle.

The story behind this

lindeman-chain-boyer-doudna-biosphere-biotech

Try it at home

Inspecting legume root nodules at the kitchen sink (Mumbai Kitchen Investigation)

Educational adaptation disclosure: This safe household observation has been reviewed for safety and feasibility (using only market-fresh culinary herbs/legumes, tap water, a hand lens, and standard soap-and-water handwashing), though it has not been classroom-trialled for this edition.

Next time your family brings home a fresh, soil-dusted bunch of fenugreek (methi), groundnuts (shengdana), or green chickpea (hara chana) plants from the market, rinse the roots gently in a bowl of water instead of cutting them straight off:

  1. Locate the root nodules: Look through a hand lens (×10) at the branching lateral roots. You will spot small, rounded root nodules (1–3 mm across) growing like tiny beads along the root surface.
  2. Observe the leghaemoglobin pigment: Press one nodule gently between two fingernails or the back of a spoon on a sheet of white paper (wash hands thoroughly with soap and water afterwards). Healthy, actively fixing nodules reveal a pink or reddish-brown interior—the colour of leghaemoglobin, an iron-containing oxygen-binding protein made by the legume host to keep free O₂ away from the bacterial nitrogenase enzyme while delivering just enough oxygen for Rhizobium respiration.
  3. Connect to crop rotation: This mutualistic partnership is why Indian farmers have rotated cereal crops (such as wheat, jowar, or rice, which deplete soil NO₃⁻) with leguminous pulses (tur, moong, chana, groundnut) for thousands of years: when the legume roots decompose after harvest, their fixed nitrogen is ammonified and nitrified into fresh NO₃⁻ for the next cereal crop.

How the nitrogen cycle connects Chapters 3, 5, 7, 8, and 11. Every stage of the nitrogen cycle uses physiological mechanisms you mastered earlier in The Living World:

  • Chapter 3 (3.4 Active Transport) & Chapter 5 (5.3 Mineral Requirements): Root hair cells pump NO₃⁻ across their partially permeable membranes using protein carriers and ATP so leaves can join nitrogen to glucose skeletons to build amino acids and proteins.
  • Chapter 7 (7.3 Chemical Digestion): Animals hydrolyse plant proteins into amino acids using pepsin in the stomach and trypsin in the duodenum before absorbing them through intestinal villi into the hepatic portal vein.
  • Chapter 8 (8.5 Excretion & Deamination): The mammalian liver removes the nitrogen-containing amino group (-NH₂) from excess amino acids (deamination), converting ammonia (NH₃) into urea for kidney excretion—the exact urea that soil decomposers turn back into NH₄⁺.

Understand it

Name the four main processes of the water cycle and explain the exact role of plant stomata in transpiration.

(1) Evaporation, (2) Transpiration, (3) Condensation, and (4) Precipitation. During transpiration, liquid water evaporates from the moist cell walls of spongy mesophyll cells inside the leaf, and the resulting water vapour diffuses out through open stomatal pores down a water potential gradient.

Which single biological process removes carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the atmosphere, and which three processes return CO₂ to the atmosphere?

Photosynthesis is the single biological process that removes CO₂ from the atmosphere. (1) Aerobic respiration (by plants, animals, and decomposers), (2) microbial decomposition, and (3) combustion (burning fossil fuels and wood) return CO₂ to the atmosphere.

Why are green plants unable to use atmospheric nitrogen gas (N₂) directly even though N₂ makes up 78% of the air, and in what ionic form do non-leguminous plants absorb nitrogen from the soil?

The two nitrogen atoms in N₂ are joined by a very strong, unreactive triple covalent bond (N≡N) that plant enzymes cannot break. Non-leguminous plants absorb nitrogen dissolved in soil water as nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) (and some ammonium ions, NH₄⁺) through root hair cells by active transport.

Distinguish clearly between nitrogen fixation, nitrification, and denitrification by stating the starting substance, the end product, and the type of bacteria involved in each.

Nitrogen fixation converts nitrogen gas (N₂) → ammonium (NH₄⁺) / amino acids via nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium in legume root nodules and free-living soil Azotobacter, plus lightning). Nitrification converts ammonium ions (NH₄⁺) → nitrite ions (NO₂⁻) → nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) via aerobic nitrifying bacteria in well-aerated soil. Denitrification converts nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) → nitrogen gas (N₂) via anaerobic denitrifying bacteria in waterlogged soil.

How does deamination in the mammalian liver (Chapter 8) connect animal nutrition to the soil nitrogen cycle?

Excess dietary amino acids are deaminated in the liver to form ammonia (NH₃) and then urea, which is excreted in urine; soil decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down excreted urea into ammonium ions (NH₄⁺), returning nitrogen to the soil for nitrification.

Go deeper explain why farmers (a) include leguminous crops such as clover, beans, or chickpeas in a crop rotation, and (b) plough and drain heavy clay fields before sowing seeds., in the mauna loa keeling curve (figure 15.3), atmospheric co₂ concentration shows both a regular annual sawtooth wave and a continuous upward trend from 315 ppm in 1958 to over 425 ppm today. explain the biological and human causes of both features., trace the complete pathway of a single nitrogen atom from a protein molecule inside a dead autumn leaf on the floor of sanjay gandhi national park until it becomes part of an enzyme molecule inside a living spotted deer. name every ion and every bacterial group involved.
Explain why farmers (a) include leguminous crops such as clover, beans, or chickpeas in a crop rotation, and (b) plough and drain heavy clay fields before sowing seeds.

(a) Leguminous plants have root nodules containing mutualistic nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria that convert atmospheric N₂ into ammonium and amino acids; when the legume roots decompose, decomposers and nitrifying bacteria convert this organic nitrogen into soil nitrate ions (NO₃⁻), restoring fertility without synthetic fertiliser. (b) Ploughing and drainage introduce oxygen (O₂) into soil air spaces, which promotes aerobic nitrification (NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻), inhibits anaerobic denitrification (NO₃⁻ → N₂), and enables aerobic respiration in root hair cells for active transport of NO₃⁻.

In the Mauna Loa Keeling curve (Figure 15.3), atmospheric CO₂ concentration shows both a regular annual sawtooth wave and a continuous upward trend from 315 ppm in 1958 to over 425 ppm today. Explain the biological and human causes of both features.

The annual sawtooth wave is caused by seasonal changes in Northern Hemisphere land forests: in spring and summer, photosynthesis exceeds respiration, drawing CO₂ down; in autumn and winter, deciduous leaves fall and respiration and decomposition exceed photosynthesis, raising CO₂. The long-term upward climb is caused by human combustion of fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) and deforestation.

Trace the complete pathway of a single nitrogen atom from a protein molecule inside a dead autumn leaf on the floor of Sanjay Gandhi National Park until it becomes part of an enzyme molecule inside a living spotted deer. Name every ion and every bacterial group involved.

(1) Decomposers (putrefying bacteria and fungi) digest the dead leaf protein into amino acids and deaminate them into ammonium ions (NH₄⁺) (ammonification); (2) aerobic nitrifying bacteria in aerated soil oxidise NH₄⁺ → nitrite ions (NO₂⁻) → nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) (nitrification); (3) Karvi shrub root hair cells absorb NO₃⁻ by active transport and combine it with photosynthetic carbohydrates to synthesize amino acids and plant proteins; (4) the spotted deer eats the shrub, digests the plant protein to amino acids using proteases (pepsin/trypsin), absorbs them in the ileum, and translates them on ribosomes into a deer enzyme.

Your turn

Explain to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

  • Plants do NOT absorb N₂ through their stomata: Never write that “plants take in nitrogen from the air through their leaves.” Only nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium in root nodules and free-living soil Azotobacter) and lightning can fix N₂ gas. Plants absorb nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) (or NH₄⁺) from soil water through root hair cells.
  • Do not confuse the three -fication terms:
  • Nitrogen fixation: N₂ (gas) → NH₄⁺ / amino acids (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, lightning).
  • Nitrification: NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ (nitrite) → NO₃⁻ (nitrate) (aerobic nitrifying bacteria in aerated soil).
  • Denitrification: NO₃⁻ → N₂ (gas) (anaerobic denitrifying bacteria in waterlogged soil; harmful to crop yield).
  • Plants respire 24 hours a day: In carbon cycle questions, remember that plants carry out aerobic respiration continuously day and night (releasing CO₂), while carrying out photosynthesis only in the light.

At school

How school exams phrase 15.2 (Cambridge 0610 Topic 19.3):

  • Water & Carbon Cycles (Core 19.3.1–19.3.2): Describe the water cycle in terms of evaporation, transpiration, condensation, and precipitation, and the carbon cycle in terms of photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition, formation of fossil fuels, and combustion.
  • Extended Nitrogen Cycle (19.3.3–19.3.4 Supplement): Cambridge Extended papers expect you to name nitrite (NO₂⁻) as the intermediate ion between ammonium (NH₄⁺) and nitrate (NO₃⁻) during nitrification, and to state the specific roles of microorganisms in decomposition, nitrification, nitrogen fixation, and denitrification alongside plant uptake of NO₃⁻, protein synthesis, feeding/digestion, and liver deamination.

Check yourself

  1. Comparing aerated legume soil vs waterlogged soil: A soil scientist analyses two adjacent agricultural plots in Maharashtra: Plot A is well-drained, ploughed, and planted with chickpea (Cicer arietinum, a legume); Plot B is compacted, waterlogged, and unploughed. Compare the rates of nitrogen fixation, nitrification, and denitrification in Plot A versus Plot B, and state which plot will have a higher soil nitrate (NO₃⁻) concentration.
  2. Identifying bacterial guilds: Name the specific type of bacteria that carries out each reaction: (a) N₂ → NH₄⁺ inside pea root nodules; (b) NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻ in aerated soil; (c) NO₃⁻ → N₂ in waterlogged mud.
