15.3Footprints on the web: farming, deforestation, eutrophication and conservation

Powai Lake Outfall, Carter Road Mangroves & Thane Creek Flamingo Sanctuary, Mumbai

Take a morning walk along the eastern shore of Powai Lake in central Mumbai where an urban storm-water drain empties nutrient-rich runoff into a sheltered cove. The water surface is choked with a thick emerald-green mat of floating algae and water hyacinth. Beneath that green blanket, the water is dark, murky, and foul-smelling; no submerged pondweed survives on the lake bed, and several silver tilapia fish float belly-up near the reeds, their gill covers flared in water that has been stripped of dissolved oxygen. An hour later, ride the train west to Carter Road in Bandra at low tide, where tangled shopping bags and polystyrene cups snag on the pencil-like breathing roots (pneumatophores) of Avicennia marina mangroves. Yet just across the harbour in the Thane Creek Flamingo Sanctuary, protected mudflats and treated wetland buffers host tens of thousands of lesser and greater flamingos—living proof of what happens when an ecosystem is monitored, legally protected, and managed sustainably.

How did a single species of bipedal primate come to reshape every nutrient cycle on Earth? Modern agriculture and industry have solved the problem of feeding over eight billion humans, but those same methods place intense pressure on habitats, water bodies, the atmosphere, and wild species (0610 Topic 20).

Modern food production, monocultures, and intensive livestock

During the twentieth century—and especially across India during the Green Revolution—food production per hectare multiplied through five technologies (0610 20.1):

  1. Agricultural machinery (tractors, seed drills, combine harvesters), allowing farmers to cultivate and harvest much larger land areas rapidly and efficiently.
  2. Chemical fertilisers (N-P-K compounds supplying nitrate NO₃⁻, phosphate PO₄³⁻, and potassium K⁺ ions), replenishing limiting soil minerals so crops grow faster and synthesize more protein and chlorophyll.
  3. Insecticides, killing insect pests that eat crop leaves/fruits or act as vectors of plant viruses, thereby increasing crop yield and quality.
  4. Herbicides, killing competing weeds so the crop receives a larger share of sunlight, soil water, and mineral ions.
  5. Selective breeding (Chapter 14 14.4), breeding high-yielding, disease-resistant crop varieties and high-producing livestock.

However, two modern farming systems carry severe ecological trade-offs:

Farming System Agricultural Advantages Ecological Disadvantages & Risks (0610 20.1)
Large-scale monoculture (growing a single genetically uniform crop species across vast fields year after year) Uniform plant height and ripening time allow efficient mechanised sowing, spraying, and harvesting; tailored fertiliser and herbicide schedules maximize single-crop yield. 1. Loss of biodiversity: Replaces diverse wild habitats and food webs with one plant species.
2. Pest and pathogen explosions: An unbroken sea of genetically identical hosts allows specialist insect pests or fungal diseases to multiply exponentially, requiring heavy insecticide spraying (which also kills beneficial pollinators like bees, kills natural pest predators, and selects for insecticide-resistant pests).
3. Soil mineral depletion: Every plant withdraws the exact same mineral ions from the same root depth, forcing heavy fertiliser use.
Intensive livestock production (keeping large numbers of cattle, pigs, or poultry indoors in high-density temperature-controlled pens) Maximises energy efficiency and growth rate by restricting movement and keeping surroundings warm (so animals lose less energy in aerobic respiration and heat, 15.1), producing cheaper meat, milk, and eggs on less land. 1. Rapid disease spread: Crowded conditions allow viral and bacterial infections to sweep rapidly from animal to animal.
2. Overuse of antibiotics: Routine prophylactic feeding of antibiotics selects strongly for antibiotic-resistant bacteria (MRSA, Salmonella, Chapter 14 14.3) that can infect humans.
3. Pollution & ethical welfare: Concentrated urine and faeces (slurry) pollute waterways (eutrophication), ruminant cattle release methane (CH₄), and crowding causes animal stress and welfare concerns.

Habitat destruction and the four effects of deforestation

Around the world, natural habitats are destroyed when humans clear land for crops and livestock grazing, housing and road infrastructure, extraction of timber and paper pulp, open-cast mining and quarrying, and polluting marine and freshwater environments (0610 20.2). Because species in a food web are interdependent, removing even a single producer, pollinator, or predator species can trigger a trophic cascade across the entire community.

The most widespread form of habitat destruction is deforestation—the clearing of forests on a massive scale. In the Cambridge syllabus (0610 20.2), you must be able to explain the undesirable effects of deforestation across four interconnected domains (Figure 15.6A):

  1. Reduction of biodiversity and extinction: Tropical rainforests (such as the Western Ghats and Silent Valley studied by E. K. Janaki Ammal, Salim Ali, and Madhav Gadgil) contain over half of Earth’s terrestrial species in layered canopy, epiphyte, understorey, and forest-floor microhabitats. Felling trees destroys food sources, nesting sites, and shelter, fragmenting populations until species become endangered or extinct (no living individuals remain).
  2. Severe soil erosion and leaching: In an intact forest, the leafy canopy breaks the mechanical force of heavy monsoon raindrops, while a dense network of tree roots binds soil particles together. Once trees are felled, heavy rain hammers bare ground and washes away the nutrient-rich topsoil (soil erosion) while dissolved nitrate and magnesium ions wash deep out of reach (leaching), leaving barren rock or laterite hardpan where forests cannot easily regrow.
  3. Flooding and disruption of the water cycle: Without tree canopies intercepting rain, spongy humus absorbing water, and transpiration returning water vapour to the sky (15.2), rainwater rushes straight down bare hillsides as surface runoff. Simultaneously, eroded topsoil washes into rivers and silts up riverbeds, reducing channel capacity so rivers burst their banks and cause destructive floods downstream (while reduced transpiration makes regional climates drier).
  4. Increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂): Living forests are major carbon sinks that remove CO₂ from the air via photosynthesis. When forests are cut down, less CO₂ is removed by photosynthesis, and when felled timber and forest undergrowth are burned (combustion) or left to rot via microbial decomposition (respiration), vast stores of carbon are oxidised back into atmospheric CO₂, intensifying global warming.

Pollution: the seven-step eutrophication cascade, plastics, and the enhanced greenhouse effect

What killed the fish in that stagnant cove of Powai Lake? When farmers apply excess nitrate (NO₃⁻) and phosphate (PO₄³⁻) chemical fertilisers to fields before heavy rain, the soluble ions leach through soil into rivers and lakes. Exactly the same thing happens when untreated sewage (rich in organic matter, ammonium, and phosphates) or livestock slurry drains into water. The resulting ecological collapse is called eutrophication, and it unfolds in a strict seven-step causal sequence (0610 20.3, Figure 15.5A):

  1. Increased availability of nitrate (NO₃⁻) and other mineral ions: Leached chemical fertilisers or untreated sewage enter the lake, river, or estuary, steeply raising mineral ion concentrations.
  2. Rapid growth of algae and surface water plants (algal bloom): Because mineral ions were previously the limiting factor for producer growth, unicellular green algae and floating plants multiply rapidly across the water surface.
  3. Algal bloom blocks sunlight from reaching submerged aquatic plants: The thick green carpet at the surface absorbs and reflects light, so rooted aquatic plants deeper in the water column cannot photosynthesise.
  4. Death of submerged aquatic plants (and short-lived surface algae): Starved of light, the submerged plants die and sink to the bottom as dead organic detritus (joined by dying surface algae once nutrients are exhausted).
  5. Rapid multiplication of aerobic decomposer bacteria: Saprotrophic bacteria in the water and sediment feed on the huge pile of dead organic matter (and any raw sewage solids) and reproduce exponentially.
  6. Depletion of dissolved oxygen (O₂) via bacterial aerobic respiration: As the vast population of decomposer bacteria carries out aerobic respiration (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O), it consumes dissolved O₂ from the water far faster than diffusion from the air can replace it (creating a spike in biochemical oxygen demand, BOD, and a sharp oxygen sag).
  7. Death of aerobic aquatic organisms (fish, crabs, insect larvae): Without sufficient dissolved oxygen for their own aerobic respiration, fish and aquatic invertebrates suffocate and die, collapsing the aquatic food web and leaving only anaerobic bacteria thriving in the foul mud.

Predict first

A student writes in an exam: “When nitrate fertiliser washes into a river, the nitrates poison the fish and the algae on top use up all the oxygen during the day, so the fish die.” Identify the scientific errors in this statement and select the true mechanism that removes dissolved oxygen from the water.

  1. The student is right: nitrate ions are a direct neurotoxin to fish gills
  2. Nitrate ions do not poison fish, and living surface algae actually release O₂ by photosynthesis during daylight; instead, the surface algal bloom blocks sunlight to submerged plants below, causing them to die, and aerobic decomposer bacteria multiplying on the dead organic matter consume the dissolved O₂ via aerobic respiration
  3. Fish die because the algae eat all the fish eggs at night

What happens

The second choice. Let us correct both errors:

  1. Error 1: Nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) at agricultural runoff concentrations do not directly poison fish; they act as plant mineral nutrients that trigger a surface algal bloom.
  2. Error 2: Living surface algae actually produce oxygen by photosynthesis during daylight (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂); they do not strip the water of oxygen during the day.
  3. True mechanism: The surface algal bloom blocks sunlight to submerged aquatic plants below, causing those plants (and later the algae) to die. Aerobic decomposer bacteria then multiply rapidly on the dead organic matter and carry out aerobic respiration, which consumes the dissolved O₂ in the water and causes fish to suffocate.

How do we know? USA, 1962 & Silent Valley, Kerala, 1973–1983: Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring and the Silent Valley rainforest campaign Ecotoxicological & conservation proof

In 1962, the marine biologist Rachel Carson published Silent Spring, compiling chemical and field evidence that persistent synthetic insecticides such as DDT are not broken down by soil or water decomposers; instead, they undergo bioaccumulation within tissues and biomagnification up food chains (water → plankton → small fish → large fish → ospreys and bald eagles), interfering with calcium deposition in bird oviducts so apex predators laid thin-shelled eggs that crushed during incubation. In India during the 1970s and early 1980s, when a proposed hydroelectric dam threatened to flood 830 hectares of pristine tropical evergreen rainforest in Silent Valley, Kerala, cytogeneticist E. K. Janaki Ammal, ornithologist Salim Ali, and ecologist Madhav Gadgil documented the valley’s endemic lion-tailed macaques, rare orchids, wild crop relatives, and watershed stability, persuading the Government of India to cancel the dam and declare Silent Valley a National Park in 1983.

Alongside eutrophication, two global pollution streams threaten terrestrial, marine, and atmospheric systems (0610 20.3 and 0893 8Be.02):

  • Non-biodegradable plastics and bioaccumulation: Natural polymers like starch, cellulose, and proteins are hydrolysed by bacterial and fungal enzymes. Most synthetic plastics (polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, nylon) have carbon-carbon backbones that decomposer enzymes cannot recognise or cleave, making them non-biodegradable. In terrestrial and marine ecosystems (such as Mumbai’s creeks and beaches), discarded plastics cause three major harms: (1) Ingestion and starvation (sea turtles mistake floating plastic bags for jellyfish, and seabirds, whales, and fish swallow indigestible plastic that fills their stomachs); (2) Entanglement and suffocation (discarded ghost fishing nets and plastic rings trap marine mammals, turtles, and birds); and (3) Microplastics, bioaccumulation, and biomagnification (plastic fragments < 5 mm absorb persistent fat-soluble toxins that build up inside organisms via bioaccumulation and magnify up food chains via biomagnification to reach lethal concentrations in apex predators).
  • Greenhouse gases (CO₂ and CH₄) and the enhanced greenhouse effect: Short-wave radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth’s surface, which re-emits longer-wave infrared (thermal) radiation. Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb part of this infrared radiation and re-radiate it back toward the surface. Human activities are rapidly raising the concentrations of two primary greenhouse gases (0610 20.3, Figure 15.5B): carbon dioxide (CO₂), released by combustion of fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and deforestation; and methane (CH₄), released by anaerobic methanogenic microorganisms in the digestive rumen of cattle and other livestock, in waterlogged anaerobic rice paddy fields, and in decomposing organic waste buried in anaerobic landfill sites. The resulting enhanced greenhouse effect drives climate change: global warming, melting polar ice caps and glaciers, thermal expansion of seawater and sea-level rise, extreme weather, and habitat shifts.

Conservation: sustainable resources, forestry, fisheries, seed banks, and assisted reproduction

A sustainable resource is one that is produced as rapidly as it is removed from the environment so that it does not run out (0610 20.4). Whereas fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and metallic ores are non-renewable, biological resources such as forests (timber) and fish stocks can be maintained sustainably if managed with scientific rules (Figure 15.6B):

Resource or Target Management & Conservation Methods (0610 20.4) Why Each Method Works Biologically
Sustainable forestry (conserving forests while harvesting timber) 1. Selective logging: Felling only mature trees of selected species rather than clear-felling.
2. Coppicing: Cutting tree stems near ground level and allowing new shoots to regrow from the living stump.
3. Reforestation (replanting): Planting at least one sapling for every tree felled.
4. Education, legal quotas & protected reserves.		 Preserves canopy structure, soil root binding, and wildlife habitats; ensures young trees grow to replace harvested biomass at the same rate it is removed.
Sustainable fisheries (conserving wild fish stocks) 1. Legal catch quotas: Limiting the total mass and species of fish each boat may land.
2. Minimum net mesh size: Using larger diamond or square mesh holes (and escape panels).
3. Closed seasons & marine no-take zones: Banning fishing in spawning grounds during breeding months.
4. Education, licensing & monitoring.		 Prevents overfishing; larger mesh holes allow juvenile (immature) fish to escape, grow to adulthood, and reproduce at least once to replenish the population.
Conserving endangered species (preventing extinction) 1. Monitoring & protecting species and habitats: National parks (SGNP, Silent Valley), anti-poaching laws, CITES bans on ivory/fur trade.
2. Education of local communities.
3. Captive breeding programmes in zoos.
4. Seed banks (storing dried seeds at -20 °C).
5. Assisted reproduction: Artificial insemination (AI) and in vitro fertilisation (IVF).		 Protects wild food webs; studbooks, AI, and IVF allow gametes to be exchanged between zoos globally without perilous animal transport, preventing inbreeding depression.

Why do species become endangered or extinct in the first place? Six major pressures drive species toward extinction (0610 20.4): climate change, habitat destruction, hunting and poaching, overharvesting, pollution, and introduced (invasive) species (which outcompete native species for food/space, predate them, or introduce novel diseases).

Crucially, once a population shrinks to a very small size (a genetic bottleneck), it faces a severe genetic danger even if hunting stops: loss of genetic variation (0610 20.4, linking Chapters 13 and 14). In a tiny population, closely related individuals are forced to mate with one another (inbreeding). Inbreeding reduces heterozygosity and steeply increases the proportion of offspring that are homozygous for harmful recessive alleles (inbreeding depression, lowering fertility and survival). Furthermore, without a wide pool of different alleles, the population lacks the genetic variation needed for natural selection to adapt if a new pathogen or climate shift arrives. This is why seed banks collect seeds from thousands of wild plants across different habitats (preserving allele diversity in a tiny space at -20 °C) and why zoo captive breeding programmes use DNA profiles, artificial insemination (AI), and in vitro fertilisation (IVF) to pair unrelated mates across continents before reintroducing offspring into restored wild habitats.

Connecting eutrophication and inbreeding to earlier chapters. Notice how Section 15.3 builds directly on cell physiology and genetics:

  • Eutrophication (20.3) combines plant mineral nutrition (NO₃⁻ from Chapter 5), light as a limiting factor of photosynthesis (Chapter 5), and aerobic cellular respiration (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O from Chapter 6).
  • Small population risks (20.4) apply Mendelian recessive inheritance (aa homozygotes from Gregor Mendel and L. D. Sanghvi in Chapter 13) and evolutionary selection pressure (Chapter 14).

Understand it

State two advantages and two ecological disadvantages of growing crops as a large-scale monoculture.

Advantages: (1) Uniform crop height and ripening allow efficient mechanised planting and harvesting; (2) targeted fertiliser and herbicide application increases single-crop yield. Disadvantages: (1) Drastic loss of biodiversity and wildlife habitats; (2) rapid spread of specialist insect pests and plant diseases across genetically identical plants (requiring heavy insecticide spraying) and depletion of specific soil mineral ions.

State four undesirable effects of deforestation on the environment.

(1) Loss of biodiversity and species extinction due to habitat destruction; (2) severe soil erosion and mineral leaching because tree roots no longer bind topsoil and canopy no longer breaks rainfall impact; (3) increased surface runoff, river siltation, and flooding (alongside reduced transpiration); and (4) increased atmospheric CO₂ due to loss of photosynthetic uptake and combustion/decomposition of felled timber.

Place the seven steps of eutrophication in exact causal order, starting with leached nitrate ions entering a lake and ending with the death of fish.

(1) Excess nitrate (NO₃⁻) and mineral ions leach into the water; (2) rapid growth of surface algae (algal bloom); (3) the algal bloom blocks sunlight from reaching submerged aquatic plants; (4) submerged plants (and surface algae) die; (5) aerobic decomposer bacteria multiply rapidly on the dead organic matter; (6) the bacteria carry out aerobic respiration, consuming dissolved oxygen (O₂); (7) fish and aerobic aquatic invertebrates suffocate and die from lack of dissolved O₂.

Name two major greenhouse gases enhanced by human activities, and state two specific human sources for each gas.

(1) Carbon dioxide (CO₂): released by combustion of fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and deforestation / burning forests. (2) Methane (CH₄): released by cattle and other ruminant livestock digestion, anaerobic rice paddy fields, and decomposing organic waste in landfill sites.

Define a sustainable resource and state three regulations used to conserve wild fish stocks.

A sustainable resource is one that is produced as rapidly as it is removed from the environment so that it does not run out. Fish stocks are conserved by: (1) legal catch quotas, (2) minimum net mesh size regulations (allowing juvenile fish to escape and grow to breeding age), and (3) closed seasons and protected marine no-take zones during spawning.

Go deeper explain why a population of an endangered mammal that drops to only 30 surviving individuals remains at high risk of extinction even after its habitat is legally protected, and explain how captive breeding using artificial insemination (ai) and ivf helps overcome this genetic problem., explain why conserving wild plant species in a seed bank is often easier and cheaper than conserving endangered animal species in zoos, and explain why periodic germination tests are required., compare how (a) untreated sewage and (b) non-biodegradable plastics harm aquatic animals in an estuary such as thane creek.
Explain why a population of an endangered mammal that drops to only 30 surviving individuals remains at high risk of extinction even after its habitat is legally protected, and explain how captive breeding using artificial insemination (AI) and IVF helps overcome this genetic problem.

A tiny population suffers a severe loss of genetic variation (genetic bottleneck) and forced inbreeding between close relatives, which increases homozygosity for harmful recessive alleles (inbreeding depression, causing low fertility and genetic defects) and leaves the population unable to adapt by natural selection if a new disease or environmental change occurs. AI and IVF allow zoos in different countries to exchange frozen sperm, ova, or embryos paired using DNA studbooks to maximise genetic diversity without stressing or transporting wild animals.

Explain why conserving wild plant species in a seed bank is often easier and cheaper than conserving endangered animal species in zoos, and explain why periodic germination tests are required.

Millions of dormant seeds occupy very little space, require minimal maintenance when dried and frozen at -20 °C, do not suffer captivity stress, and represent wide allele diversity from many wild populations. Periodic germination tests (and growing out fresh seed lots) are needed to verify viability before stored embryos lose the ability to germinate.

Compare how (a) untreated sewage and (b) non-biodegradable plastics harm aquatic animals in an estuary such as Thane Creek.

Untreated sewage provides organic matter and mineral ions (NH₄⁺, NO₃⁻, PO₄³⁻) that fuel aerobic decomposer bacteria and algal blooms (eutrophication), whose aerobic respiration strips dissolved O₂ from the water so fish suffocate. Non-biodegradable plastics cannot be broken down by decomposer enzymes; they persist for decades, causing starvation when ingested (blocking digestive tracts), drowning/suffocation by entanglement, and bioaccumulation of toxic microplastics up food chains.

Your turn

Explain to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

  • Eutrophication exam precision (0610 20.3): Never skip the middle links of the chain. You must state explicitly that: (1) nitrates/mineral ions cause rapid growth of algae (algal bloom), (2) the surface algae block light to submerged plants below, (3) plants die, (4) decomposer bacteria increase in number on the dead organic matter, and (5) the bacteria carry out aerobic respiration, which uses up dissolved oxygen (O₂) so fish suffocate.
  • Greenhouse effect vs ozone hole (0610 20.3): Do not confuse the enhanced greenhouse effect (CO₂ and CH₄ trapping outgoing long-wave infrared heat radiation, causing global warming) with ozone depletion (CFCs thinning stratospheric ozone O₃, which filters ultraviolet light). They are completely different physical processes.

At school

How school exams phrase 15.3 (Cambridge 0610 Topic 20):

  • Deforestation (20.2.3 Core): Always cover all four syllabus dimensions: extinction / loss of biodiversity, soil erosion, flooding, and increase of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
  • Eutrophication (20.3.4 Supplement): Examiners award 5–6 marks for the exact causal sequence: increased availability of nitrate and other ions → increased growth of producers → increased decomposition after death of producers → increased aerobic respiration by decomposers → reduction in dissolved oxygen → death of organisms requiring dissolved oxygen in water.
  • Conservation & Sustainability (20.4 Core & Supplement): Give specific, actionable methods—for forests: selective logging, coppicing, replanting/reforestation, quotas, education, protected reserves; for fish stocks: catch quotas, minimum net mesh size (so young fish escape and breed), closed breeding seasons, protected marine areas, monitoring.

Check yourself

  1. Restoring a collapsed coastal fishery: A commercial fishing fleet uses fine-mesh bottom trawl nets year-round in a coastal bay. Within five years, the annual fish catch drops by 80%. Explain why the fine-mesh nets caused the population crash, and describe three specific legal regulations that would restore the fishery as a sustainable resource.
  2. Tracing downstream river pollution: Raw sewage is discharged into a slow-flowing river at Point X. Explain why the concentration of dissolved oxygen (O₂) drops sharply 2 km downstream of Point X and then gradually recovers 15 km further downstream.

Answer at the back of the book

15.4Living factories & rewritable code: fermenters, plasmids, recombinant insulin and CRISPR

Irani Bakery at Dhobi Talao, Mumbai & Hindustan Antibiotics Fermenter Hall, Pimpri

It is five o’clock in the morning at a century-old Irani bakery near Dhobi Talao in south Mumbai. Inside the warm proofing trough, a baker punches down a pillowy mound of brun-pav bread dough that has doubled in volume overnight. Millions of microscopic yeast cells (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) have been respiring anaerobically through the flour sugars, blowing tiny bubbles of carbon dioxide (CO₂) into the stretchy gluten network; when the trays slide into the wood-fired brick oven at 220 °C, the trapped gas expands into a crisp, airy crumb while every trace of ethanol evaporates up the chimney. Two hours away along the Mumbai–Pune expressway at Pimpri, three-storey stainless-steel industrial fermenters gleam inside the halls of Hindustan Antibiotics—descendants of the vessels launched in 1954 with the help of biochemist Yellapragada SubbaRow—where sterile air bubbles through spargers, motorised paddles churn nutrient broth, and cold-water jackets carry away kilowatts of microbial heat. And inside a cool refrigerator at a clinic in Parel sits a glass vial of recombinant human insulin—synthesised not by a pig’s pancreas, but by Escherichia coli bacteria carrying a human gene stitched into their circular plasmids.

Long before humans knew what DNA or enzymes looked like—and long before Louis Pasteur proved in the 1850s that living microorganisms drive fermentation—bakers and brewers were using microbes to transform food. Today, biotechnology uses microorganisms (bacteria, yeast, and filamentous fungi) and their purified enzymes on an industrial scale, while genetic modification (genetic engineering) rewrites the DNA of cells directly (0610 Topic 21).

Why bacteria and fungi are ideal for biotechnology and genetic modification

Why do biotechnologists choose bacteria (and unicellular fungi like yeast) over multicellular plants or animals as living factories? Four biological features make bacteria uniquely suited (0610 21.1):

  1. Rapid reproduction rate: Under optimum conditions (37 °C, abundant nutrients), bacteria divide by binary fission every 20 minutes, growing from a single cell into billions of protein-synthesising cells within a few hours.
  2. Ability to make complex molecules: Despite their simple prokaryotic structure (Chapter 2 2.2), bacteria possess 70S ribosomes and metabolic pathways capable of synthesising complex polypeptides, enzymes, vitamins, and antibiotics—and because the genetic code is universal (deciphered by Har Gobind Khorana and colleagues after Rosalind Franklin, Watson, and Crick revealed the DNA helix, Chapter 11 11.3), a bacterium reads a human gene using the exact same triplet codons as a human cell.
  3. Few ethical concerns: Manipulating, culturing, and harvesting bacteria or fungi in vats raises no animal-welfare or pain concerns compared with experimenting on vertebrates.
  4. Presence of plasmids: Alongside their main circular chromosome, bacteria carry plasmids—small, circular, double-stranded loops of DNA (Chapter 2 2.2) that are easy to extract from cells, cut open, splice foreign genes into, and transfer from one bacterium to another as genetic vectors.

Everyday biotechnology: yeast, pectinase, biological washing powders, and immobilised lactase

Four classic microbial and enzyme processes appear throughout industry and daily life (0610 21.2, Figure 15.7A):

Biotechnology Application Organism or Enzyme & Reaction How It Works & Why It Is Useful (0610 21.2)
1. Yeast in biofuel & bread-making Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) carrying out anaerobic respiration:
Glucose → Ethanol + Carbon dioxide
C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂		 • Bread-making: Amylase in flour hydrolyses starch to maltose/glucose; yeast respires producing CO₂ gas bubbles that get trapped in elastic gluten proteins, making dough rise. Oven baking (>200 °C) expands the gas, kills the yeast, and evaporates all the ethanol.
• Biofuels: Yeast ferments sugars from maize starch (digested by amylase) or sugarcane in anaerobic tanks; the ethanol is distilled for renewable bioethanol fuel.
2. Fruit juice extraction Pectinase (an extracellular fungal enzyme) Plant cell walls are cemented together by an insoluble polysaccharide called pectin. Adding pectinase to crushed apples or citrus fruits breaks down insoluble pectin into soluble sugars, which (a) increases the total volume (yield) of juice released from cells and (b) clarifies cloudy juice into a clear liquid by dissolving suspended pectin particles.
3. Biological washing powders Bacterial proteases, lipases, and amylases Stubborn clothing stains are often insoluble biological polymers: proteases hydrolyse protein stains (blood, egg, gravy, grass chlorophyll-protein) into soluble amino acids; lipases hydrolyse lipid/fat stains (butter, cooking oil, collar grease) into soluble fatty acids and glycerol; amylases hydrolyse starch stains into soluble sugars. They clean effectively at low temperatures (30–40 °C), saving electricity and protecting delicate fabrics (whereas boiling water >60 °C denatures the enzymes, Chapter 4 4.3).
4. Lactose-free milk Lactase (often immobilised in sodium alginate beads) Many adults stop making intestinal lactase (lactase non-persistence), so undigested milk lactose (a disaccharide) is fermented by colon bacteria, causing cramps and diarrhoea. Passing milk through a column of immobilised lactase hydrolyses lactose → glucose + galactose (two soluble, easily absorbed monosaccharides), producing lactose-free milk while keeping the enzyme beads reusable and out of the milk.

Inside an industrial fermenter: six controlled variables

When Ernst Chain and Howard Florey scaled up penicillin production from Alexander Fleming’s mould (Penicillium chrysogenum) in the 1940s—and when Hindustan Antibiotics built its deep-tank plant at Pimpri in 1954—they used giant stainless-steel vessels called fermenters. Today, industrial fermenters produce penicillin (from the fungus Penicillium), mycoprotein (high-protein vegetarian food from the fungus Fusarium venenatum), industrial enzymes, and human insulin (from genetically modified E. coli).

To keep billions of microorganisms growing at their maximum rate, an industrial fermenter continuously monitors and controls six conditions (0610 21.2, Figure 15.7B):

  1. Aseptic precautions (high-pressure steam sterilization): Before inoculation, the entire stainless-steel vessel and all pipes are sterilized with high-pressure steam, and incoming air is passed through fine sterile filters. Reason: Kills foreign contaminant bacteria and fungi so they cannot compete with the culture microorganism for nutrients/oxygen or contaminate the medical/food product with toxic waste.
  2. Nutrients (carbon and nitrogen inlets): Measured supplies of glucose, starch, or molasses (providing a carbon source and energy for respiration) plus ammonia (NH₃), ammonium ions (NH₄⁺), or nitrate ions (providing a nitrogen source for amino acid and protein synthesis) and mineral salts are fed in through sterile pipes.
  3. Optimum temperature (temperature probe + cold-water cooling jacket): As trillions of bacteria or fungal hyphae respire rapidly inside a giant tank, they release huge amounts of thermal energy (heat). Cold water circulating through an outer water-cooled jacket absorbs and carries away this excess heat to maintain the exact optimum temperature (~26–28 °C for Penicillium, 37 °C for E. coli). Reason: If temperature rises too high (>45 °C), the microorganisms’ enzymes denature and the culture dies; if temperature falls too low, kinetic energy drops and enzyme-catalysed reactions become too slow.
  4. Optimum pH (pH probe + acid/alkali inlets): Dissolving CO₂ and metabolic acids shift the broth pH. Electronic pH probes trigger automatic addition of dilute acid or alkali (buffers) to hold pH steady at the optimum (e.g. pH 6.5–7.0). Reason: Extreme pH breaks ionic bonds in enzyme active sites, causing denaturation (Chapter 4 4.3).
  5. Oxygenation (sterile air sparger): For aerobic microorganisms (Penicillium, Fusarium, aerobic E. coli), sterile compressed air or oxygen is bubbled through a perforated ring (sparger) at the bottom of the tank. Reason: Supplies dissolved oxygen (O₂) required for aerobic respiration to generate ATP for rapid growth and protein synthesis.
  6. Agitation (motor-driven stirring paddles / impellers): Rotating paddles mix the liquid culture continuously. Reason: Prevents microorganisms from settling to the bottom, keeps every cell in uniform contact with nutrients and dissolved oxygen, and ensures an even temperature and pH throughout the entire tank.

Genetic modification: the five-step recombinant human insulin pipeline

In Chapter 10 (10.4 and the companion story of Frederick Banting, Charles Best, and Dilip Mahalanabis), we saw how diabetic patients whose pancreatic β-cells cannot secrete insulin were saved by insulin extracted from the pancreases of slaughtered pigs and cattle. Yet animal insulin had serious drawbacks: it differed by one to three amino acids from human insulin (causing allergic immune reactions in some patients), supply was tied to slaughterhouse numbers, and religious or ethical diets objected to porcine or bovine products.

Genetic modification (or genetic engineering) is changing the genetic material of an organism by removing, changing, or inserting individual genes (0610 21.3). Following the 1973 discovery of recombinant plasmids by Herbert Boyer and Stanley Cohen, scientists engineered E. coli bacteria to manufacture pure human insulin via a precise five-step molecular pipeline (0610 21.3, Figure 15.8A):

  1. Isolate and cut the human insulin gene using a restriction enzyme: The human insulin gene is isolated from a human cell and cut out of human chromosomal DNA using a specific restriction enzyme (restriction endonuclease, molecular scissors such as EcoRI). The restriction enzyme recognises a specific base sequence and makes a staggered cut across the double-stranded DNA, leaving short, exposed single-stranded overhangs of unpaired bases called sticky ends (e.g. -AATT-).
  2. Cut a bacterial plasmid vector with the EXACT SAME restriction enzyme: Circular plasmids are extracted from bacteria and cut open using the same restriction enzyme. Because the exact same restriction enzyme is used, the cut ends of the open plasmid carry complementary sticky ends (-TTAA-) that match the sticky ends on the human insulin gene.
  3. Join the human gene and plasmid using DNA ligase to form a recombinant plasmid: The cut human insulin gene fragments and the cut open plasmids are mixed together. Their complementary sticky ends pair up by complementary base pairing (A hydrogen-bonds with T, C with G), and the enzyme DNA ligase (“molecular glue”) forms covalent bonds along the sugar-phosphate backbone to seal them into a single circular molecule of recombinant DNA (recombinant plasmid).
  4. Insert the recombinant plasmid into host bacteria (transformation): The recombinant plasmids are mixed with host E. coli bacteria (treated with calcium ions and a brief heat or electric shock) so that the bacteria take up the recombinant plasmids into their cytoplasm.
  5. Clone the transformed bacteria in an industrial fermenter and express the gene: The genetically modified bacteria are cultured inside an industrial fermenter under optimum aseptic conditions (37 °C, pH 7.0, glucose/amino acid nutrients, sterile O₂, stirring). Every 20 minutes, the bacteria divide by binary fission, copying (cloning) the recombinant plasmid into every daughter cell and transcribing and translating the human gene into pure human insulin protein, which is extracted, purified, and bottled for patients.

Predict first

Suppose a molecular biologist accidentally cuts the human DNA containing the insulin gene with restriction enzyme EcoRI (which leaves sticky ends -AATT-), but cuts the bacterial plasmid vector with a different restriction enzyme, BamHI (which leaves sticky ends -GATC-), before adding DNA ligase. What will happen in Step 3, and how much human insulin will the bacteria produce?

  1. DNA ligase will force any two DNA ends together regardless of base sequence, so normal human insulin is produced
  2. Because two different restriction enzymes were used, the sticky ends (-AATT- vs -GATC-) are not complementary and cannot base-pair (A–T, C–G); zero recombinant plasmids form and 0 mg of human insulin is produced
  3. The bacteria will make pig insulin instead of human insulin

What happens

The second choice. Because two different restriction enzymes were used, the sticky ends on the human insulin gene (-AATT-) and the sticky ends on the bacterial plasmid (-GATC-) are not complementary (A only pairs with T, and C only pairs with G). Without complementary base pairing between sticky ends, the human gene cannot anneal into the open plasmid, so DNA ligase cannot seal them together into a recombinant plasmid. Using the same restriction enzyme on both the human DNA and the plasmid is essential.

How do we know? San Francisco & Stanford, 1973–1978 & Berkeley/Umeå, 2012: Boyer & Cohen’s recombinant plasmids and Doudna & Charpentier’s CRISPR-Cas9 Molecular genetic proof

In 1973, Herbert Boyer and Stanley Cohen demonstrated that cutting two different DNA molecules with the same restriction endonuclease (EcoRI), annealing their complementary sticky ends, and sealing the backbone with DNA ligase produces a functional recombinant plasmid that replicates inside transformed E. coli cells. By 1978, Boyer’s team expressed the human insulin gene in E. coli, leading to the first licensed recombinant human medicine (Humulin, 1982). In 2012, Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier proved that the bacterial immune nuclease CRISPR-Cas9 can be programmed with a synthetic 20-nucleotide guide RNA (gRNA) to cut any target DNA sequence next to a PAM motif, enabling precise single-locus genome editing.

Genetically modified (GM) crops, selective breeding vs GM, and CRISPR-Cas9

Genetic modification is also used to engineer crop plants with novel traits (0610 21.3, Figure 15.8B):

GM Crop Modification How It Works & Agricultural Advantages Disadvantages, Risks & Concerns (0610 21.3)
1. Insect-resistant crops (e.g. Bt cotton in Maharashtra & Bt maize) Inserted cry gene from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis causes the plant to make a crystal protein toxic specifically to bollworm and stem-borer caterpillars that chew the crop. Advantages: Higher crop yield, less crop damage, and far fewer broad-spectrum chemical insecticide sprays (protecting bees and farmworkers). Selection for resistant pests: Constant exposure to Bt toxin selects for rare mutant caterpillars resistant to Bt (natural selection, Chapter 14 14.3), requiring farmers to plant non-Bt “refuge” rows. Potential effects on non-target insects.
2. Herbicide-resistant crops (e.g. glyphosate-resistant soya beans & maize) Inserted bacterial gene makes the crop resistant to a specific broad-spectrum herbicide. Advantages: Farmers can spray the field after crop emergence to kill competing weeds with a single application without harming the crop, raising yield and reducing mechanical ploughing. Gene transfer to wild relatives (“superweeds”): Wind or insect pollen from the GM crop could cross-pollinate closely related wild weed species, transferring the herbicide-resistance gene into wild weeds. Loss of field-margin weeds reduces food for wild insects and birds.
3. Nutritionally enhanced crops (e.g. Golden Rice) Inserted genes from maize/daffodil and a soil bacterium enable rice endosperm to synthesize beta-carotene, which the human body converts into Vitamin A (Chapter 7 7.1). Advantages: Prevents childhood Vitamin A deficiency and night blindness in regions where polished white rice is the staple diet. Economic and seed concerns: Patented GM seeds can be expensive for smallholder farmers if new seed must be purchased each season; consumer scepticism about GM labelling and long-term ecological monitoring.

How does genetic modification (Chapter 15) compare with selective breeding (artificial selection, studied in Chapter 14 14.4 with E. K. Janaki Ammal’s sugarcane and Gir cattle)?

  1. Source of genes: Selective breeding can only select alleles already present within the same species (or closely related cross-fertile species); genetic modification can transfer a gene from any species across kingdoms (such as a human gene into E. coli or a bacterial gene into cotton).
  2. Precision: Selective breeding mates whole organisms, shuffling thousands of alleles together during meiosis (Chapter 12 12.3 and Chapter 13 13.2) and often dragging along unwanted linked alleles (inbreeding depression); genetic modification isolates and inserts one single target gene without altering the rest of the genome.
  3. Timescale: Selective breeding requires many generations (years or decades) of selecting and breeding offspring; genetic modification produces a transformed cell line in a single laboratory generation.

Why a bacterial ribosome can translate a human gene. Remember from Chapter 2 (2.2) and Chapter 11 (11.3) that although E. coli has 70S ribosomes and no nucleus, the triplet genetic code is universal across almost all living organisms on Earth: the mRNA codon AUG codes for methionine, GAG codes for glutamic acid, and UGU codes for cysteine whether the ribosome sits inside a Borivali bacterium, a banyan leaf, or a human pancreatic β-cell.

Finally, in 2012, Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier transformed genetic engineering by adapting a natural bacterial antiviral defence system called CRISPR-Cas9 (Figure 15.8B). Instead of inserting a foreign plasmid vector at random, scientists synthesize a 20-nucleotide guide RNA (gRNA) whose base sequence matches a chosen address in a cell’s own DNA next to a short marker (PAM). The guide RNA leads the Cas9 endonuclease enzyme directly to that chromosomal locus to make a precise cut—allowing doctors and plant breeders to correct a single mutated letter (such as repairing the sickle-cell HbS allele we traced from Gregor Mendel and L. D. Sanghvi in Chapter 13 to balancing selection in Chapter 14, or editing stem cells first shown to carry the full genome by Matthew Meselson and John Gurdon in Chapter 12).

Understand it

State four reasons why bacteria are useful in biotechnology and genetic modification.

(1) Rapid reproduction rate (dividing every ~20 minutes by binary fission); (2) ability to synthesize complex molecules using the universal genetic code; (3) few ethical concerns over their manipulation and culture; and (4) presence of circular plasmids that are easy to extract, modify, and transfer as vectors.

Write the word and balanced chemical equations for anaerobic respiration in yeast, and explain why baked bread contains zero alcohol even though yeast produces ethanol in dough.

Word equation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide. Balanced symbol equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. During bread-making, CO₂ gas bubbles get trapped in elastic gluten and make the dough rise, while the high temperature of baking in the oven (>200 °C, well above ethanol’s boiling point of 78 °C) evaporates all the ethanol (and kills the yeast).

State the role of (a) pectinase in fruit juice production, (b) proteases and lipases in biological washing powders, and (c) immobilised lactase in producing lactose-free milk.

(a) Pectinase hydrolyses insoluble pectin gluing plant cell walls together, increasing juice volume (yield) and clarifying cloudy juice. (b) Proteases and lipases hydrolyse insoluble protein stains (blood, egg) into soluble amino acids and lipid stains (grease, butter) into soluble fatty acids and glycerol at low washing temperatures (30–40 °C). (c) Immobilised lactase (in alginate beads) hydrolyses milk lactose into soluble glucose and galactose, producing enzyme-free milk safe for lactose-intolerant people while allowing the beads to be reused continuously.

Name six conditions that are monitored and controlled inside an industrial fermenter, and explain why the vessel is surrounded by a water-cooled jacket.

(1) Aseptic steam sterilization, (2) nutrients (glucose carbon source + ammonia/nitrate nitrogen source), (3) optimum temperature, (4) optimum pH (via pH probes and acid/alkali addition), (5) oxygenation (via a sterile air sparger), and (6) agitation (via motorised stirring paddles). The water-cooled jacket removes the intense heat released by microbial respiration so the temperature stays at the optimum (e.g. 28 °C or 37 °C) and does not denature the microorganisms’ enzymes.

List the five steps used to engineer bacteria to produce human insulin, naming the specific enzyme used to cut DNA (leaving sticky ends) and the specific enzyme used to join DNA molecules together.

(1) Cut the human insulin gene from human DNA using a restriction enzyme, leaving sticky ends; (2) cut a bacterial plasmid vector open using the same restriction enzyme, leaving complementary sticky ends; (3) mix the gene and plasmid with DNA ligase to join their sticky ends into a recombinant plasmid; (4) insert the recombinant plasmid into host bacteria; (5) culture the transformed bacteria in an industrial fermenter so they divide rapidly and express the gene to synthesize human insulin.

Go deeper explain why both the human dna containing the insulin gene and the bacterial plasmid vector must be cut with the exact same restriction enzyme., state two advantages and two potential disadvantages of growing genetically modified (gm) crops such as bt cotton or herbicide-resistant soya beans., state three differences between selective breeding (chapter 14) and genetic modification (chapter 15).
Explain why both the human DNA containing the insulin gene and the bacterial plasmid vector must be cut with the exact same restriction enzyme.

Cutting both DNA molecules with the same restriction enzyme produces complementary sticky ends (exposed unpaired bases that match by A–T and C–G complementary base pairing), allowing the human gene to anneal into the open plasmid before DNA ligase seals the sugar-phosphate backbone.

State two advantages and two potential disadvantages of growing genetically modified (GM) crops such as Bt cotton or herbicide-resistant soya beans.

Advantages: (1) Higher crop yields and reduced crop loss to pests or weeds; (2) reduced spraying of broad-spectrum chemical insecticides (Bt crops, protecting non-target pollinators) or prevention of nutritional deficiency (Golden Rice supplying provitamin A). Disadvantages: (1) Risk of gene transfer via pollen to wild relatives (creating herbicide-resistant “superweeds”) or natural selection for Bt-resistant insect pests; (2) higher cost of patented GM seeds for smallholder farmers and reduced weed biodiversity in field margins.

State three differences between selective breeding (Chapter 14) and genetic modification (Chapter 15).

(1) Gene source: Selective breeding uses only alleles within the same (or closely related) species, whereas GM can transfer genes between completely different species/kingdoms; (2) Precision: Selective breeding shuffles thousands of alleles across whole genomes (risking linked undesirable alleles), whereas GM transfers a single isolated target gene; (3) Timescale: Selective breeding takes many generations, whereas GM produces a modified line in one generation.

Your turn

Explain to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

  • Restriction enzymes vs DNA ligase (0610 21.3): Never swap their jobs. Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific base sequences to produce sticky ends. DNA ligase joins two DNA fragments together by sealing bonds along the sugar-phosphate backbone after complementary sticky ends have base-paired, forming recombinant DNA.
  • Plasmids vs bacterial chromosomes (0610 21.1 & 21.3): The vector used to carry the human insulin gene into bacteria is a circular plasmid, not the main bacterial chromosome and not a ribosome.
  • Bread-making vs Bioethanol (0610 21.2): In bread-making, it is CO₂ gas that makes the dough rise (while ethanol evaporates during baking). In biofuel production, it is the ethanol that is collected and distilled as fuel.

At school

How school exams phrase 15.4 (Cambridge 0610 Topic 21):

  • Why bacteria are useful (21.1.1–21.1.2 Core & Supplement): State: (1) rapid reproduction rate, (2) ability to make complex molecules, (3) few ethical concerns over their manipulation and growth, and (4) the presence of plasmids.
  • Human insulin 5-step exam checklist (21.3.3 Supplement): Whenever an Extended paper asks how human insulin is produced by genetic modification (5–6 marks), write these five points in order: (1) cut human DNA to isolate the human insulin gene using a restriction enzyme, forming sticky ends; (2) cut a bacterial plasmid DNA with the same restriction enzyme, forming complementary sticky ends; (3) use DNA ligase to join the human insulin gene and plasmid DNA to form a recombinant plasmid; (4) insert the recombinant plasmid into bacteria; (5) grow the bacteria in a fermenter to replicate the plasmid and synthesize human insulin.

Check yourself

  1. Cooling-jacket failure in an antibiotic fermenter: Inside an industrial fermenter producing penicillin from the fungus Penicillium, the cold water supply to the outer cooling jacket accidentally shuts off for three hours while the nutrient and oxygen supplies continue. Predict and explain what will happen to the temperature inside the fermenter and to the rate of penicillin production.
  2. Washing powder enzyme temperature: A parent washes a blood-stained cotton shirt in biological washing powder using boiling water at 90 °C instead of warm water at 35 °C, and finds the blood stain is still stuck to the fabric. Explain why the stain was removed at 35 °C but not at 90 °C.

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 15

The Mumbai watershed & the Pimpri vial: closing the four-billion-year case file

On the final Saturday of the school year, Kym and her biology class carry out a two-part capstone investigation that ties together every scale of The Living World—from molecules and cells to organs, inheritance, evolution, and the biosphere (Figure 15.9).

Part 1 — Three-Station Ecological Audit Across Mumbai: The class compares water and soil samples from three stations along a single monsoon watershed:

Watershed Station Nitrate [NO₃⁻], Algal Cover & DO Biological Community & Ecological State
Station 1: SGNP Forest Headwaters (Borivali slope) Soil rich in NO₃⁻; stream [NO₃⁻] = 1.1 mg L⁻¹; 5% algal cover; 92% light; low BOD = 1.3 mg L⁻¹; High DO = 8.2 mg L⁻¹ Wild legumes with pink Rhizobium root nodules, submerged pondweed, mayfly nymphs, frogs, fish
Station 2: Powai / Mithi Outfall Plume (sewage + runoff) Stream [NO₃⁻] = 24.0 mg L⁻¹; 95% surface algal bloom; 8% light; High BOD = 16.4 mg L⁻¹; Hypoxic DO = 1.4 mg L⁻¹ Submerged plants dead on bed; dense aerobic decomposer bacteria; dead tilapia fish
Station 3: Thane Creek Mangrove Sanctuary (treated buffer) Stream [NO₃⁻] = 3.2 mg L⁻¹; 18% algal cover; moderate BOD = 2.8 mg L⁻¹; Restored DO = 6.8 mg L⁻¹ Avicennia marina mangroves, fiddler crabs, mudskippers, flamingos

Part 2 — From the Watershed to the Recombinant Insulin Vial: Back in the school laboratory, Kym’s teacher places a 10 mL vial of recombinant human insulin (100 IU mL⁻¹, manufactured in stainless-steel fermenters at Pimpri/Biocon) beside a germinating chickpea (chana) seed—the very same kind of seed Kym placed on wet cotton wool on her monsoon window-ledge in Chapter 0.

Use all four sections of Chapter 15 (and the Five Big Ideas across The Living World) to answer three capstone questions:

  1. Trophic energy & population limits (15.1): At Station 1, forest producers fix 30,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ of solar energy into net plant biomass. Calculate how much energy (kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹) reaches tertiary consumers (Level 4) at 10% transfer efficiency per step, explain why no 6th-level predator exists in the park, and state why energy cannot be recycled by decomposers.
  2. Nitrogen cycle & eutrophication (15.2–15.3): Explain how wild legumes and soil bacteria keep the aerated forest soil at Station 1 fertile without chemical fertiliser, and trace the exact seven-step mechanism that caused dissolved oxygen at Station 2 to crash from 8.2 mg L⁻¹ to 1.4 mg L⁻¹.
  3. Recombinant biotechnology (15.4 & Chapters 10–11): Describe the five-step process used to engineer E. coli bacteria to manufacture the human insulin inside the clinic vial, and explain why a prokaryotic bacterium can translate a human gene into the exact same amino acid sequence as a human pancreatic β-cell.
Show the solution
  1. Trophic energy & one-way flow (15.1):
    • Calculation: Level 1 (Producers) = 30,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ → Level 2 (Primary consumers) = 3,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ → Level 3 (Secondary consumers) = 300 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ → Level 4 (Tertiary consumers) = 30 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹.
    • Why no 6th level exists: Because ~90% of energy is lost at each step (via aerobic respiration/heat, indigestible egested faeces, excreted urea, and uneaten parts), a 5th level would receive only 3 kJ and a 6th level only 0.3 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹—far below the minimum energy required to sustain a viable breeding predator population.
    • Why energy is never recycled: Decomposers oxidise dead organic matter by respiration and release its remaining chemical energy as thermal energy (heat) to the atmosphere, which chloroplasts cannot trap; decomposers recycle mineral ions and carbon/nitrogen atoms, never energy.
  2. Nitrogen cycle at Station 1 & Eutrophication at Station 2 (15.2–15.3):
    • Station 1 fertility: Mutualistic nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria inside the pink root nodules of wild legumes (together with free-living soil Azotobacter and monsoon lightning) convert atmospheric N₂ → NH₄⁺ / amino acids. When leaves and roots fall, decomposers break proteins down into NH₄⁺ (ammonification), and because the hillside soil is well-drained and aerated with O₂, aerobic nitrifying bacteria oxidise NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻ (nitrification) for root hair active transport.
    • Station 2 eutrophication (7 steps): (1) Leached NO₃⁻ fertiliser and sewage (24.0 mg L⁻¹) enter the water; (2) they stimulate a dense surface algal bloom (95% cover); (3) the surface bloom blocks sunlight (8% transmission) to submerged aquatic plants below; (4) submerged plants die and sink as organic detritus; (5) aerobic decomposer bacteria multiply rapidly on the dead organic matter; (6) the bacteria carry out aerobic respiration (BOD = 16.4 mg L⁻¹), stripping dissolved O₂ down to 1.4 mg L⁻¹; (7) tilapia fish suffocate and die from lack of O₂.
  3. Recombinant human insulin & the universal code (15.4 & Chapters 10–11):
    • Five-step pipeline: (1) Isolate and cut the human insulin gene from human DNA using a restriction enzyme, leaving sticky ends; (2) cut a circular bacterial plasmid vector using the exact same restriction enzyme, creating complementary sticky ends; (3) mix the gene and plasmid with DNA ligase to seal the sugar-phosphate backbone and form a recombinant plasmid; (4) insert the recombinant plasmid into host E. coli bacteria; (5) culture the transformed bacteria in a steam-sterilized, water-jacket-cooled industrial fermenter (37 °C, pH 7.0, nutrients, sterile O₂, stirring paddles) so they divide every 20 minutes by binary fission and express pure human insulin.
    • Why bacteria translate human mRNA accurately: Because all living organisms share the universal triplet genetic code (Chapter 11): the bacterial 70S ribosomes and tRNAs read the exact same mRNA codons (AUG, GAG, UGU, etc.) as human 80S ribosomes, assembling the identical 51-amino-acid human insulin polypeptide that regulates blood glucose homeostasis (Chapter 10).

What this chapter can’t explain yet

Pick up that germinating chickpea seed one last time and look at how far you have travelled since Chapter 0:

  1. Life is built of compartments (Chapters 1–3, 15): You stepped inside the cell wall and partially permeable cell membrane of plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, and viruses (Chapters 1–2), watched water cross membranes by osmosis and root hairs pump nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) by active transport (Chapter 3), and scaled all the way up to bacterial plasmids and planetary ecosystems (Chapter 15).
  2. Life is Chemistry on a budget (Chapters 4–8, 15): You saw how enzymes lower activation energy through complementary active sites (Chapter 4), how photosynthesis traps sunlight into glucose (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, Chapter 5) and respiration releases ATP (Chapter 6), how the human digestive, circulatory, respiratory, and excretory systems supply reactants and clear urea (Chapters 7–8), and how energy flows one way (the 10% trophic rule) while carbon, water, and nitrogen atoms recycle endlessly (Chapter 15).
  3. Form fits job at every scale (Chapters 5–9, 14–15): From hollow lignified xylem vessels, one-cell-thick alveoli, and microvilli (Chapters 5–8) to myelinated motor neurones (Chapter 9), sunken xerophyte stomata (Chapter 14), pink leghaemoglobin-filled legume root nodules, and complementary sticky ends (Chapter 15), biological architecture is shaped to match physical laws.
  4. Insides stay steady while outsides wild-swing (Chapters 9–10, 15): You traced how negative feedback loops hold human body temperature at 37 °C, blood glucose steady via insulin and glucagon, and blood water potential steady via ADH (Chapters 9–10), how limiting factors balance birth and death rates around an ecosystem’s carrying capacity (K), and how cooling jackets and pH probes maintain homeostasis inside an industrial fermenter (Chapter 15).
  5. Code copies, mutates, and gets filtered (Chapters 11–15): You read the DNA double helix and universal triplet code (Chapter 11), watched chromosomes divide by mitosis and meiosis (Chapter 12), solved Mendelian ratios and sex linkage (Chapter 13), followed four billion years of mutation and natural selection (Chapter 14), and saw how recombinant plasmids and CRISPR-Cas9 allow human hands to edit that same universal code (Chapter 15).

The dry seed on Kym’s window-ledge, the Rhizobium bacterium in its root nodule, the spotted deer on the Borivali hillside, and the thinking brain reading this sentence are all variations on one unbroken four-billion-year theme—written in four DNA letters, powered by sunlight, and entrusted to our care.

PA

Peter Agre

The unknown protein and the swelling eggs

1949Physician and researcher whose team identified a water-channel protein

Baltimore, a water-channel paper published in 1992

A red blood cell has a boundary that keeps many dissolved substances apart. Water nevertheless passes across it rapidly. Knowing the boundary’s name does not explain the passage. A membrane is a structure, and a structure can contain several different routes.

Peter Agre’s route into that problem began with a protein that his group had not set out to discover. While studying red blood cell membrane proteins, they found a component whose function was unclear. Its presence was a fact. Calling it a protein was another fact. Neither told them what it did.

A useful scientific question has to connect an observation with a comparison that might go differently. Does this component merely accompany water-permeable membranes, or does it help make them permeable? Removing or adding the suspected component could distinguish those possibilities.

Agre’s account credits a conversation with the physiologist John Parker in 1991. Parker suggested that the mysterious protein might be a water channel. That suggestion did not settle its function. It supplied a hypothesis that could be tested. There was an important change in the question: from “What is this?” to “What difference would its presence make?”

Gregory Preston, working with Agre and their collaborator William Guggino, used frog egg cells. These cells were useful because their normal water permeability was relatively low. The team arranged for some eggs to produce the suspected protein. Control eggs did not receive the instructions for making it. The two groups could then face the same dilute surroundings.

The eggs making the protein swelled much faster. The controls changed little during the comparison. Agre dates the first experiment to October 1991; Preston and colleagues’ paper appeared in Science in 1992. Keeping those dates separate avoids turning the year on a paper into an invented date for everything that led to it.

What did the comparison establish? Adding the protein greatly increased the membrane’s water permeability. The result connected a molecular component with a physical function. It went beyond observing that some natural cells happened to gain water faster than others, because those cells might differ in many ways. Here the suspected component was deliberately changed.

There are limits to the conclusion. Low permeability is not zero permeability. A control egg that changes little over a short comparison has not been shown to have an absolutely waterproof membrane. And faster water movement is not evidence for an ATP-driven water pump. The dilute surroundings already favour net water entry; the protein provides a route through the boundary.

The name aquaporin means water pore. It is a useful reminder of the route, provided you keep the mechanism beside the name. A typical water-specific aquaporin allows water passage while excluding ions. Other membrane proteins can have other selectivities. A cell membrane is therefore a collection of chemically different pathways, not one coarse net that admits every sufficiently small object.

Chapter 3 uses this experiment for two purposes. First, it gives the membrane’s “partial permeability” an actual molecular component. Second, it shows what a control does. Both sets of eggs encounter dilute water, but only one makes the added protein. The difference in response becomes evidence about that protein’s role.

On the chapter’s pressure balance, the channel cannot choose a direction. Water potential determines the net transfer; the pathway affects how readily it can happen. A convincing explanation needs both the route and the conditions on its two sides.

SA

Salim Ali

The ten-year-old boy and the yellow-throated sparrow

1896 to 1987Ornithologist and ecologist born in Bombay; pioneered systematic bird surveys across India and led the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS)

Khetwadi & Apollo Street, Bombay, 1906

In 1906, a ten-year-old orphan named Salim Moizuddin Abdul Ali, growing up in a big family house in Khetwadi in central Bombay, shot a sparrow with his toy airgun. When he picked it up, he noticed something odd: although it looked like an ordinary house sparrow, it had a bright yellow patch on its throat.

His uncle, Amiruddin Tyabji, wrote a note of introduction and walked young Salim over to the rooms of the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), where the honorary secretary, W. S. Millard, took the boy gently by the shoulder, identified the bird as a Yellow-throated Sparrow (Gymnoris xanthocollis), and opened cabinet after cabinet of Indian bird skins, teaching him how to observe, measure and record birds in the field without shooting them.

Thirty years later, watching Baya Weavers (Ploceus philippinus) weaving their hanging gourd-shaped nests on palm trees near Kihim across Mumbai harbour, Salim Ali carried out one of the world’s first quantitative studies of tropical bird behaviour: numbering nests and banding individual birds to prove that the male weaves the nest frame and only when a female inspects and approves the engineering does he finish the egg chamber and move on to weave another! His ten-volume Handbook of the Birds of India and Pakistan and The Book of Indian Birds remain the foundation of Indian ecology.

EA

E. K. Janaki Ammal

The woman who sweetened India’s sugarcane

1897 to 1984Indian cytogeneticist and botanist; bred high-yield polyploid sugarcane varieties in Coimbatore and co-authored the Chromosome Atlas of Cultivated Plants

Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, 1934

In the 1920s, India—the ancestral home of sugarcane—was ironically importing refined white sugar from Java because native Indian canes were hardy against drought and frost but thin and low in sucrose, whereas tropical Javanese canes (Saccharum officinarum) were sweet and thick-stemmed but died in northern Indian winters.

Edavalath Kakkat Janaki Ammal, born in Thalassery in Kerala in 1897, turned down an arranged marriage to study botany at Queen Mary’s College and Presidency College in Madras, then sailed to the University of Michigan on a Barbour Scholarship, becoming one of the first Indian women to earn a doctorate in botany in the United States (1931).

Joining the Imperial Sugarcane Breeding Station in Coimbatore, she peering through her microscope at the chromosomes inside dividing sugarcane cells (Chapter 12). By crossing tropical sweet canes with wild Indian grasses (Saccharum spontaneum) and even bamboo and maize—and selecting polyploid hybrids that carried multiple sets of chromosomes—she helped create the famed Co (Coimbatore) sugarcane varieties that combined high sugar yield with rugged Indian disease and cold resistance. During World War II in London (working through nightly air raids at the John Innes Horticultural Institution and later at Kew Gardens), she co-authored the landmark Chromosome Atlas of Cultivated Plants (1945) before returning to India at Jawaharlal Nehru’s invitation to reorganise the Botanical Survey of India and fight to save Kerala’s Silent Valley rainforest.

JB

Jagadish Chandra Bose

The crescograph and the electrical pulse of plants

1858 to 1937Physicist and plant physiologist in Calcutta; pioneer of millimetre radio waves and discoverer of rapid electrical signalling in plants

Presidency College, Calcutta, 1901

If you have read Book 2 (The Moving World, Chapter 13), you already met Jagadish Chandra Bose ringing a bell and firing a pistol across the Presidency College hall in Calcutta in 1895 using invisible $5\text{ mm}$ electromagnetic waves. Yet around 1900, Bose noticed something strange: his delicate metal wave-detectors (“coherers”) grew sluggish after repeated stimulation and recovered after a rest—almost like a tired muscle!

Curious whether living plant tissues and animal nerves shared the same physical laws of electrical response, Bose built the crescograph: a clockwork lever system using two smoked-glass plates and fine magnetic mirrors that magnified the tiny elongation of a growing plant tip by $10,000\times$, allowing him to measure growth over a few seconds instead of days. Using fine galvanometers on Mimosa pudica (chui-mui, the touch-me-not plant) and Desmodium gyrans (the telegraph plant), Bose showed that plants transmit measurable electrical action potentials along their vascular bundles when pinched or heated, and that these signals slow down under cold or chloroform vapour and stop permanently when poisoned. Today, plant neurobiologists studying glutamate and calcium waves in wounded leaves trace their field directly to Bose’s Calcutta bench.

JH

Jan Baptista van Helmont

The doctor who weighed a pot of dirt for five years

1580 to 1644Flemish physician and chemist who coined the word gas and reported a five-year willow-weighing experiment

An experiment published after its author’s death, 1648

A tree’s roots disappear into soil. It is tempting to picture that soil being eaten and rebuilt as trunk and branches. A balance offers a test: compare the tree’s gain with the soil’s loss. Jan Baptista van Helmont reported doing just that over five years.

His account describes 200 pounds of oven-dried earth in an earthen pot and a willow shoot weighing 5 pounds. He supplied rainwater or distilled water. A perforated tin-plated iron lid was intended to keep airborne dust from mixing with the soil. It did not seal the plant away from air. These are the reported historical quantities; their exact conversion into modern kilograms is uncertain.

After five years, he reported a tree weighing 169 pounds and about 3 ounces. The soil, dried again, had lost about 2 ounces. On those reported figures, a large tree gain accompanied a small soil loss. The comparison challenged the idea that the whole gain was simply soil transferred into the tree.

But the ledger had gaps. He had not recorded the masses of fallen leaves or all the water supplied. Gases entering and leaving were unmeasured. The soil was dried before weighing; the tree was not established to be dry at either weighing. The unrecorded water content prevents treating the whole gain as new dry wood.

Van Helmont concluded that the new wood, bark and roots came from water alone. Water really does contribute material, but that conclusion left out another source. Modern evidence shows that carbon dioxide supplies the carbon in plant carbohydrates. Soil still supplies essential mineral nutrients, and roots obtain water as well as anchoring the plant. A small mineral contribution can be indispensable without accounting for most of the plant’s dry organic material.

Van Helmont also investigated gases and introduced the word gas. His gas sylvestre was later identified as carbon dioxide. Recognising a gas in one investigation did not by itself establish its role in building plant material. That connection required further evidence, rather than a cleverer reading of the willow’s final weight.

The publication date is another entry to keep straight. Van Helmont died in 1644. His son, Franciscus Mercurius, issued the collection Ortus medicinae in 1648. That is when the account appeared, not the year the five-year experiment began. The sources used here do not establish its exact starting and finishing dates.

Carry the unfinished ledger into Chapter 5. A balance can show that an explanation is missing something without identifying every missing input. The next investigators must ask what leaves exchange with air, when light matters and how to follow particular atoms into plant material.

RH

Robert Hooke

The rooms in a piece of cork

1635 to 1703Microscopist whose cork observations gave cells their name

London, 1665

Cut cork thin enough and light passes through it. Under Robert Hooke’s microscope, that ordinary material showed a pattern of little compartments. In Micrographia, published in 1665, he described them as cells: small rooms.

There is a useful trap in the story. Cork was not a window into a complete, busy living cell. Hooke was looking at dead tissue, where the surrounding walls remained. The spaces and walls supplied the name before scientists understood the machinery that living cells contain.

A modern school drawing puts a nucleus, mitochondria and other labelled structures inside a boundary. It combines findings made through many methods over many years. You could not have read that inventory from Hooke’s cork alone.

The same caution belongs beside your own microscope. First record what you can see. Then distinguish it from what other observations allow you to infer. A pale region may contain structures that your instrument cannot resolve. An empty-looking compartment may once have been alive. Better evidence comes from comparing preparations and using methods suited to the question.

The name cell survived because the pattern was memorable. The explanation grew far beyond the pattern. When you call an onion’s little compartments “cells”, keep both parts of the history: the visible rooms that supplied the word, and the later work that revealed what living cells do.

JI

Jan Ingenhousz

The condition hidden inside “plants improve air”

1730 to 1799Dutch physician and natural philosopher who investigated light, green tissues and plant gas exchange

London, a book published in 1779

A result can be real and its first explanation incomplete. That is the difficulty behind one of the most familiar stories in plant science. A plant changes the air around it. Another investigator tries a related experiment and obtains a different result. Should the first result be discarded, or has an important condition been left out of the sentence describing it?

Jan Ingenhousz was a Dutch physician and natural philosopher, born in Breda in 1730. His 1779 book, published in London, placed conditions at the centre of the plant-and-air question. Its title referred to plants affecting air differently in sunshine, shade and night. Those distinctions are more useful than a tidy slogan saying that plants always improve air.

Joseph Priestley had already reported mint altering air in which a candle had burned out. His account included a valuable comparison: portions of altered air kept in the same exposure, one with a plant and one without. Later, a candle could burn in the plant-treated air while the comparison portion still would not support it. That separated a plant’s effect from simply leaving the air standing. It did not identify every condition needed for the effect, or show where the atoms of the gas came from.

Ingenhousz made gas collection a way to follow the process. In his book’s account, leaves were placed in a transparent vessel filled with water and inverted over water. Bubbles could collect at the top. The visible gas offered something to compare as exposure changed. Light and shade, different tissues and different plant materials could now become separate questions rather than being buried together inside “a plant”.

There is an instructive detail in the original text: the bubbles were not all the same. Ingenhousz described differences in their forms on different leaves. That observation still matters to a pupil counting bubbles today. A count of events is not automatically a measurement of gas volume. If one bubble contains more gas than another, the number of bubbles alone does not tell you the total amount collected.

His experiments linked the favourable gas effect with light and green tissues. These comparisons narrowed the explanation. They did not reveal chloroplast membranes, electron carriers or the origin of every oxygen atom. A new question remained: did the collected oxygen come from the water, the carbon dioxide or some other material in the leaf? Comparing light and shade could not decide between those sources.

The distinction between a condition and a cause is useful here. Finding that light matters does not mean light supplies the atoms. Finding that green tissues matter does not mean the green pigment turns into food. Later evidence must connect the observations to a mechanism. Chapter 5 supplies that connection through chlorophyll, water oxidation and carbon incorporation, while keeping the older experiments visible as the steps that posed sharper questions.

There is also a limit to the language of good and bad air. It records what historical tests could show under particular circumstances. It is not a modern guarantee that any closed vessel containing a plant is safe for an animal, or that more plant material always maintains a favourable gas balance. Plant respiration, decomposition, light and finite resources all matter. Historical apparatus involving flames, reactive gases or confined animals is evidence to read about, not a home demonstration to repeat.

Ingenhousz died in 1799. His lasting place in this chapter is not that he supplied a finished equation for a leaf. He helped make a vague claim conditional and testable. When an investigation seems to contradict another, ask which variables were matched, which changed and what the instrument actually measured. Carry that question into the limiting-factor explorer in Chapter 5: selecting a condition is only preparation; the comparison still has to be run.
