AL

Antonie van Leeuwenhoek

The cloth merchant who found an invisible kingdom

1632 to 1723Cloth merchant and self-taught microscopist in Delft; first human to see bacteria, protozoa, red blood cells and sperm cells

Delft, the Netherlands, September 1674

Antonie van Leeuwenhoek never learned Latin, the language every European scholar in the seventeenth century used to write books. He was the son of a basket-maker in Delft, apprenticed at sixteen to a linen draper in Amsterdam, and returned home to run a cloth shop and serve as chamberlain to the sheriffs of Delft.

What Leeuwenhoek had was patience, steady hands, and an obsession with seeing smaller than anyone had ever seen. Cloth merchants used small magnifying glasses to count the warp and weft threads in linen. In 1665, Robert Hooke’s book Micrographia had become the talk of Europe for its dramatic engravings of flea legs, fly eyes and cork “cells”. Hooke used a compound microscope—two lenses in a tube—which magnified about $30\times$ to $50\times$. When Hooke tried to push two lenses to higher power, every edge blurred into rainbow fringes.

Leeuwenhoek realised that a single, tiny spherical lens of very short focal length could magnify five to九 times more sharply than two large lenses, provided you didn’t mind holding the metal plate right up against your eyelashes. He heated thin soda-lime glass rods in a flame, pulled them into threads, and melted the thread tip into a tiny glass bead barely $1.5\text{ mm}$ across—or ground and polished tiny biconvex lenses by hand. Between two brass or silver plates the size of a matchbox, he mounted the lens in a pinhole and attached a pointed brass screw to position a glass capillary tube or a speck of wax less than a millimetre behind the bead.

In 1673, the Delft physician Reinier de Graaf wrote to the Royal Society in London that a local shopkeeper had built instruments far surpassing anything then known. Leeuwenhoek began sending long, conversational letters in Dutch to London—more than 300 letters over the next fifty years.

In September 1674, crossing the lake of Berkelse Mere, he scooped up a vial of summer water clouded with green streaks. Through his lens he saw spiral green ribbons and tiny creatures darting and spinning through the water. When London scholars doubted that thousands of living creatures could swim in a single drop of water, Robert Hooke himself followed Leeuwenhoek’s instructions, infused peppercorns in water, and confirmed every word before the Royal Society in November 1677.

In September 1683, Leeuwenhoek scraped white matter from between his own teeth—even though, as he proudly told the Royal Society, he rubbed his teeth every morning with salt—mixed it with clean rainwater, and discovered rods, spheres and corkscrews: the first sight of bacteria. He kept grinding lenses and writing letters until he was ninety years old, even dictating letters from his deathbed to describe the exact structure of the diaphragm whose spasms were killing him.

LM

Lynn Margulis

A cell with more than one ancestry

1938 to 2011Biologist who brought evidence for the bacterial ancestry of organelles into an evolutionary synthesis

Boston, 1967

A mitochondrion is part of a cell. It also has inherited DNA of its own. That combination is a question, not an explanation. Why would one compartment retain its own genetic machinery?

In 1967, Lynn Margulis published On the origin of mitosing cells under her name at the time, Lynn Sagan. She developed an older proposal: important parts of complex cells descended from organisms that had lived inside other organisms.

The proposal connected observations that might otherwise have stayed in separate files. Mitochondria and chloroplasts had bacterial similarities. They divided from existing organelles. Evidence placed DNA outside the nucleus. Ris and Plaut’s 1962 work on a green alga’s chloroplast was one such piece: microscopy and chemical tests supported the presence of DNA there.

A theory had to do more than collect intriguing outlines. It had to explain inheritance and generate further tests. Comparisons of genes later provided particularly strong evidence for bacterial ancestry. Chloroplasts connect with cyanobacteria, while mitochondria connect with another bacterial lineage.

The history did not end with tiny independent bacteria trapped inside us. Gene transfer and gene loss helped integrate the partners. The organelles we have now depend on their host cells. Their bacterial ancestry explains their unusual machinery; their dependence explains why they are parts of a larger cellular system.

Margulis did not invent every part of the idea, and one paper did not prove the whole account at once. Her contribution shows how an explanation can gather strength: make a connection, state what it predicts, and compare those predictions with independent evidence. Some details of her broader proposals have not been accepted. The bacterial origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts rests on the evidence that has survived testing.

LP

Louis Pasteur

The chemist who bent a glass neck and saved millions

1822 to 1895French chemist and microbiologist; disproved spontaneous generation with swan-neck flasks, proved the germ theory of fermentation and disease, and developed vaccines for anthrax and rabies

Paris, 1859

Louis Pasteur was trained not as a doctor, but as a chemist and crystallographer. At twenty-five he noticed that crystals of tartaric acid made by living wine yeast were all “left-handed” in how they twisted polarised light, whereas tartaric acid made in a chemical factory was an equal mix of left- and right-handed crystals. That clue convinced him that microscopic living cells carry out specific chemical reactions that non-living solutions do not.

When French wine and beer makers asked him why vats sometimes turned sour into vinegar or lactic acid instead of alcohol, Pasteur looked through his microscope and saw that healthy vats contained budding round yeast cells, whereas sour vats were overrun by tiny rod-shaped bacteria. Heating the wine gently to $55\text{–}60^\circ\text{C}$ for a few minutes killed the spoilage bacteria without ruining the flavour—the process the world still calls pasteurisation.

To silence critics who claimed those bacteria arose spontaneously out of the liquid, Pasteur designed his famous swan-neck flasks in 1859. The long S-shaped glass neck stayed completely open to room air, yet gravity trapped dust and bacterial spores in the low bend of the tube. Several of Pasteur’s original sealed and swan-neck flasks still sit at the Institut Pasteur in Paris today, crystal clear more than 160 years later.

GR

G. N. Ramachandran

The drawing that atoms had to fit

1922 to 2001Physicist whose collaborators developed collagen models and maps of possible protein-backbone arrangements

Madras, protein structure work, 1954–1963

A molecular model can look persuasive and still be wrong. A line on paper can cross another line without complaint. Atoms in a proposed structure cannot simply occupy the same space. How do you turn that difference into a test that another researcher can use?

Gopalasamudram Narayana Ramachandran approached biological structures with a physicist’s training. Born in Ernakulam in 1922, he worked with C. V. Raman at the Indian Institute of Science and later studied at Cambridge. In 1952 he became head of physics at the University of Madras. The city is now called Chennai. Here a physics department became an important centre for investigating the molecules of life.

The material at the heart of one problem was collagen. It helps support tissues such as skin and tendons. Calling it a protein did not specify how its long chains were arranged. Nor could an attractive drawing settle that arrangement. A model had to agree with evidence from X-ray diffraction and with what was known about chemical structures.

Ramachandran and Gopinath Kartha proposed a triple-helical structure in a paper published in Nature in August 1954. Three chains, rather than a single chain folded alone, were central to their proposal. In 1955, their revised model coiled the chains around a common axis, rather than keeping the individual helix axes parallel. Further refinements included contributions from other research groups. The familiar short statement that “Ramachandran solved collagen in 1954” compresses a developing investigation into one person’s finished answer. Keeping Kartha and the later work visible gives a truer account.

One difficulty opened a broader question. A protein contains repeated backbone groups joined through carbon atoms. How freely can neighbouring groups turn? If every turn were an independent choice, a model-maker could propose a huge variety of arrangements. Chemical geometry removes many of them before the rest of a protein is even considered.

A peptide group is relatively planar. Important rotations are possible around neighbouring backbone bonds, but a rotation moves several atoms together. Turning one part can bring its atoms uncomfortably close to another part. The local arrangement must therefore be examined as a pair of turns, with the attached groups included, rather than as isolated hinges with nothing around them.

In their 1963 paper, Ramachandran, C. Ramakrishnan and V. Sasisekharan described a way to represent those turns and calculate which combinations avoided short contacts. Known small-molecule and peptide structures supplied information about dimensions and plausible nonbonded distances. The researchers considered more than one set of limiting distances, so the boundary between acceptable and crowded was tied to stated assumptions rather than drawn by taste.

The calculation produced regions of possible arrangements and regions ruled out by crowding. Known peptide and polypeptide structures could then be compared with the permitted regions. That connection was useful in both directions: the dimensions constrained a proposed structure, and structural observations tested how well the constraints described actual molecules.

The modern map bears Ramachandran’s name, but the original paper carries all three authors’ names. It also gives the University of Madras affiliation and a submission date in December 1962. Its publication year, 1963, marks when the paper appeared, not an invented afternoon on which all the calculations happened.

There is a powerful limit to this achievement. Local turns that avoid clashes do not determine a unique full protein fold. Distant parts of a chain can still meet, attract, repel or crowd one another. Water and other surroundings also matter. A map of possible turns helps rule out bad proposals; it does not provide every missing coordinate of the right one.

That is the historical question worth carrying back to Chapter 4. When a model looks convincing, ask what would make it impossible. The active site in the next section must satisfy spatial restrictions and chemical interactions together. A neat pocket drawn around a substrate is only a beginning.

FR

Francesco Redi

Six jars of meat in the Florentine heat

1626 to 1697Physician to the Medici court in Florence and pioneer of controlled biological experiments

Florence, summer 1668

Francesco Redi was chief physician to the Grand Dukes of Tuscany, Ferdinand II and Cosimo III de’ Medici, in the city where Galileo had lived a generation earlier. When courtiers argued about whether scorpion venom kills only when injected or also when swallowed, or whether viper fangs poison through their teeth or through yellow bile in their gums, Redi never quoted ancient Greek books—he ran side-by-side tests.

In 1668 he published Esperienze intorno alla generazione degl’insetti (Experiments on the Generation of Insects). Having read William Harvey’s suggestion that insects grow from seeds or eggs too small to notice, Redi placed dead snakes, fish, eels and veal into sets of wide-mouthed flasks—first leaving half open and sealing half with paper and string, and then covering a third set with fine velo di Napoli (Naples veil) so air could circulate freely while flies were kept out. Watching flies lay eggs on top of the gauze—and tracking the maggots from the open jars through their hard pupal cases until adult flies emerged—Redi gave biology its first modern controlled experiment.

JS

Jens Christian Skou

An ATP reaction at the membrane

1918 to 2018Researcher who identified an ion-transporting ATPase in nerve membranes

Aarhus, a crab nerve membrane study, 1957

A living nerve cell contains different concentrations of sodium and potassium from the fluid around it. A membrane can slow the leakage that would erase those differences. Slowing leakage, however, leaves an accounting problem. If ions continue to leak, what maintains the distribution?

The answer requires more than calling the membrane a boundary. A boundary can contain both passive routes and machinery coupled to a chemical energy supply. Distinguishing those functions was a problem for experiments.

Jens Christian Skou investigated enzymes in nerve membranes from crabs. Working with membrane preparations allowed him to ask a chemical question: which conditions changed the rate at which ATP was broken down? ATP breakdown could be measured, even when a whole living cell’s behaviour was much harder to disentangle.

His 1957 paper connected the activity of a membrane enzyme with the ions in the mixture. Sodium and potassium affected that activity. This made the enzyme a candidate for involvement in active ion transport. Its reaction was associated with the same kinds of ions whose distributions living nerve cells maintained.

The word candidate matters in following the evidence. Detecting ATP breakdown in a membrane preparation did not display a complete pumping cycle. A broken-cell chemical assay was not a miniature film of an intact nerve. The experimental response connected pieces of the problem and helped guide the identification of the transport machinery.

Later work established the sodium–potassium pump’s role and mechanism. The protein couples a cycle of structural changes to ATP chemistry and ion movement. The maintained ion distributions have consequences for functions such as nerve signalling. Chapter 9 will return to those distributions when an electrical impulse travels along a cell.

For Chapter 3, the important advance is the link between an energy account and a transport account. A concentration gradient can store energy. Passive movement tends to dissipate an available gradient; maintaining one in the face of leakage requires an ongoing process that supplies energy. A living membrane can contain proteins that perform that work.

This distinction also stops a common mistake. A protein that allows an ion through is not automatically an active pump. An open ion channel can permit passive movement down an electrochemical gradient. The pump’s defining feature is its coupling to an energy source that can sustain transport against the otherwise favourable direction.

The root in Chapter 3 uses this principle with different machinery. A root proton pump can use ATP to export hydrogen ions. Their electrochemical gradient can then supply energy for another transporter, which couples proton return to nitrate entry. That is a relay between two proteins. Skou’s crab nerve enzyme should never be relabelled as the root’s nitrate transporter.

Nor should the account quietly become an explanation of water being pumped uphill. Maintaining ion distributions can change the conditions for water movement, but water through a passive channel still follows its water-potential gradient. That distinction is what lets the same chapter explain a root collecting scarce mineral ions and a mangrove taking up water from salty soil.

The story’s useful habit is to ask for two ledgers. What material crosses the boundary, and what supplies the energy associated with that transfer? “There is a protein” answers neither question by itself. Skou’s experiment helped connect them through measurable chemistry.

YS

Yellapragada SubbaRow

The forgotten discoverer of the cell’s battery

1895 to 1948Indian biochemist and physician; co-discovered ATP and phosphocreatine, synthesised folic acid, methotrexate and diethylcarbamazine

Harvard Medical School, Boston, April 1929

In 1923, a twenty-eight-year-old graduate of Madras Medical College named Yellapragada SubbaRow landed in Boston with less than a hundred dollars in his pocket to study tropical medicine at Harvard. He had lost two brothers in India to tropical sprue—a wasting intestinal disease—and had been barred from the British Indian Medical Service after wearing a khadi surgical gown during the freedom movement. To pay his living expenses in Boston while studying biochemistry, he worked the night shift cleaning bedpans and laboratory glassware at the Peter Bent Brigham Hospital.

Joining the biochemistry laboratory of Cyrus Fiske, SubbaRow tackled a problem that was holding back all of cell physiology: how to measure minuscule amounts of phosphorus inside muscle tissue. In 1925, Fiske and SubbaRow invented a rapid colorimetric test—the Fiske–SubbaRow method—that turned phosphate solutions a deep molybdenum blue whose intensity could be read in minutes. It became one of the most cited methods in twentieth-century biology.

Using chemical methods to study muscle extracts, Fiske and SubbaRow identified phosphocreatine in work reported in 1927 and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) in 1929, independently of Karl Lohmann’s ATP work in Germany that same year. Identifying these molecules was a beginning. Later experiments established how ATP reactions are coupled to movement, synthesis and transport. The familiar rechargeable-carrier picture grew from that later work; it was not all established by finding ATP in an extract.

Because SubbaRow was a foreign national on a temporary visa without a formal medical doctorate recognised in Massachusetts, Harvard denied him a permanent faculty position. In 1940 he moved to Lederle Laboratories, where in just eight years before his sudden death at age fifty-three he directed teams that: 1. Isolated and synthesised folic acid (vitamin $\text{B}_9$), curing the very tropical sprue that had killed his brothers; 2. Designed aminopterin and methotrexate (folic-acid mimics that block DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells), giving Sydney Farber the first effective drug against childhood leukaemia; 3. Discovered diethylcarbamazine (DEC), still used by the World Health Organization against elephantiasis (filariasis); and 4. Isolated aureomycin, the world’s first tetracycline antibiotic.

As the writer Doron Antrim remarked after SubbaRow’s death in 1948: “You’ve probably never heard of Dr. Yellapragada SubbaRow. Yet because he lived, you may be alive and well today.”

1997

A pointer too large to miss

Hiroyuki Noji, Ryohei Yasuda, Masasuke Yoshida, Kazuhiko Kinosita Jr, Paul Boyer, John Walker, Peter Mitchell

Yokohama, Japan, a result published in 1997

How would you watch something turn when the moving part is too small to see clearly? A mark on its shaft would be too small as well. One possible solution is to attach a longer pointer and watch the pointer’s changing direction.

In a paper published in Nature on 20 March 1997, Hiroyuki Noji, Ryohei Yasuda, Masasuke Yoshida and Kazuhiko Kinosita Jr reported using that principle with a protein machine. The authors’ laboratories were at the Tokyo Institute of Technology and Keio University, both listed in Yokohama. Their result concerned a component of the machinery that links ion movement and ATP chemistry. It gave an otherwise invisible proposal a visible consequence.

The question had a history. Peter Mitchell’s 1961 chemiosmotic proposal connected energy-releasing electron transfers to ATP formation through a membrane ion gradient. That supplied an energy route, but it did not reveal every moving part of the ATP-making enzyme. Knowing what powers a machine and knowing how its parts move are different questions.

Paul Boyer and colleagues developed a mechanism in which changes in the enzyme’s catalytic sites alter how they bind and release substrates and ATP. Rotation of an internal shaft could coordinate those shape changes. John Walker and colleagues investigated molecular structure, providing a different kind of evidence about the arrangement of the parts. Biochemistry and structure could support a rotary mechanism without being a direct observation of turning.

Step 1: Make the motion report itself

The enzyme has a membrane-associated part and a protruding catalytic part called F₁. Inside F₁, a central component called the gamma subunit forms a shaft within surrounding protein units. If that shaft rotates relative to its surroundings, something attached to it should change direction too.

Noji and his collaborators attached a fluorescent actin filament to the gamma subunit. Actin is a protein that can form filaments; fluorescence made the attached marker visible. The filament served as a longer pointer. Observing its changing orientation supplied evidence about the movement of the part to which it was attached. The pointer did not make the shaft itself grow large enough to inspect with ordinary sight.

Step 2: Ask what supplied the energy

Here is the detail that a quick retelling often loses. The researchers supplied ATP to an isolated F₁ preparation. The turning they observed was driven by ATP breakdown. The paper’s title calls the protein F₁-ATPase: an enzyme breaking ATP down.

This was the reverse energy direction from the mitochondrial synthesis account in Chapter 6. There, an ion gradient supports ion return through the complete membrane-linked enzyme, driving rotation and changes that make ATP available from ADP and phosphate. In the rotation experiment, supplied ATP supported turning in the isolated catalytic component. Reversible coupling makes both directions scientifically connected, but one experiment should not be described as though it directly filmed the other.

Step 3: Keep the conclusion as precise as the observation

The fluorescent pointer demonstrated motion consistent with a rotary shaft. It strengthened the mechanism by making a predicted physical action observable. It did not by itself measure every proton’s route through a mitochondrial membrane, establish one speed for all ATP synthases or calculate the ATP yield of every cell.

The distinction is useful far beyond this protein. A detector records something specific: light from a marker, a gas volume, a change in mass. The explanation connects that signal to a less directly visible event. Good evidence depends on that connection being stated, including what was supplied to the apparatus and which direction the process ran.

Later in 1997, Boyer and Walker jointly received half of the Chemistry Nobel Prize for work elucidating ATP synthesis. Jens Skou received the other half for discovery of a different ion-transporting enzyme. The rotation paper and the prize recognise connected contributions; neither is a reason to replace the collaborators with a story about one lone discoverer.

Return to Chapter 6’s membrane plate and trace its two arrows: H⁺ pumped out, then returning through ATP synthase. The pointer experiment helps explain why rotation belongs in that mechanism. Its ATP-driven reverse direction also gives you a question to carry to any moving apparatus: what went in, what moved, and what does the observation actually establish?

1921–1971

A warm kennel in Toronto and a plastic drum in Bongaon

Frederick Banting, Charles Best, J. J. R. Macleod, James Collip, Leonard Thompson, Sambhu Nath De, Dilip Mahalanabis

Toronto, summer 1921 to January 1922, and Kolkata to Bongaon, 1959–1971

Walk into a hospital ward in 1920 where children with severe Type 1 diabetes lay waiting, or into a border refugee camp in 1971 during a monsoon cholera outbreak. At first glance, the two emergencies look like opposites. In untreated Type 1 diabetes, the blood plasma is flooded with dissolved glucose (15–30 mmol/L) while insulin-dependent muscle uptake is reduced and the liver continues releasing too much glucose, while litres of glucose-containing urine drain away and the child wastes to skin and bone. In cholera, a comma-shaped bacterium in the gut drains so much water and salt out of the bloodstream within hours that the patient’s radial pulse vanishes and the blood turns thick and dark.

Both emergencies made the same question urgent: which signal or transport process has failed, and which still works? Laboratory and clinical investigations supplied different parts of the answers. Insulin treatment replaces a missing signal; rehydration replaces fluid and ions. Neither example means the underlying disease has simply been cured.

Part 1 · Toronto, 1921–1922: rescuing the islet messenger from trypsin

Since 1889, when Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering removed the pancreas from a dog and noticed flies swarming around the animal’s sugar-laden urine, physiologists had suspected that the tiny clusters of pale cells scattered through the pancreas—the islets of Langerhans—secreted an internal chemical messenger that controlled blood sugar. The trouble was that the rest of the pancreas is an exocrine factory packed with powerful digestive proteases such as trypsinogen / trypsin (which you met in Chapter 7). Whenever researchers ground up a whole pancreas to extract the hypothetical islet hormone, the pancreas’s own proteases digested the protein hormone before anyone could test it.

In October 1920, a young Canadian surgeon and war veteran named Frederick Banting sat up late preparing a lecture for medical students and read a pathology report about a patient whose pancreatic duct had been blocked by a gallstone: the enzyme-making acinar cells had shrivelled away, while the islets of Langerhans remained intact. Banting scribbled a three-sentence laboratory plan in his notebook: tie off the pancreatic ducts in dogs for several weeks until the trypsin-making tissue degenerates, then extract the surviving islet cells in cold saline.

In May 1921, physiology professor J. J. R. Macleod at the University of Toronto gave Banting a small upstairs laboratory, surgical facilities, and a twenty-two-year-old student assistant named Charles Best, who had just finished his bachelor’s degree in physiology and biochemistry and knew how to run quantitative blood-glucose and urinary-sugar assays. Through a stifling Toronto summer, Frederick Banting and Charles Best prepared pancreatic extracts and tested whether each batch lowered the blood glucose of diabetic dogs. They soon discovered that they did not even need to wait weeks for tied ducts to degenerate: extracting fetal or adult cow pancreases from the Toronto slaughterhouse with acidified alcohol inactivated the digestive proteases while leaving the hormone intact.

An extract that lowered blood sugar in a dog, however, was still too full of foreign beef proteins to inject safely into a human child. In December 1921, Macleod brought the biochemist James Collip into the team. Collip worked out a fractional alcohol precipitation protocol: at just the right alcohol concentration, most contaminating pancreatic proteins precipitated out while the active hormone stayed in solution; raising the alcohol level further precipitated the purified hormone itself.

On 11 January 1922, at Toronto General Hospital, fourteen-year-old Leonard Thompson—who weighed only 29.5 kg (65 lb), smelled of acetone, and was slipping toward diabetic coma—received an initial injection of Banting and Best’s less pure extract. It lowered his blood sugar slightly, by about a quarter, but caused a sterile abscess at the injection site because of remaining protein impurities. Twelve days later, on 23 January 1922, Leonard Thompson received James Collip’s purified pancreatic extract—now named insulin. Within twenty-four hours, Thompson’s blood glucose dropped from 520 mg/dL (28.9 mmol/L) to 120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L), his daily urinary sugar loss plummeted from more than 100 g to near zero, and he began regaining weight and strength.

Notice what that two-step January 1922 trial teaches about scientific evidence. A crude extract can contain a real biological signal and still fail clinically until biochemical purification separates the active molecule from harmful contaminants. And notice why insulin had to be injected under the skin rather than swallowed as a pill: insulin is a folded protein (two polypeptide chains linked by disulfide bridges, sequenced by Frederick Sanger in the 1950s). Swallowing insulin would expose it to the very stomach pepsin and intestinal trypsin that Banting, Best and Collip had worked so hard to avoid.

Part 2 · Kolkata (1959) and Bongaon (1971): the intact door that cholera forgot to lock

Thirty-seven years after Toronto, in a quiet pathology laboratory at Nilratan Sircar Medical College in Calcutta (now Kolkata), Sambhu Nath De confronted an equally stubborn medical misconception. For decades, standard textbooks taught that Vibrio cholerae killed patients by physically stripping off the epithelial lining of the small intestine so blood plasma simply leaked through raw, denuded walls.

Sambhu Nath De tested that claim directly. He grew Vibrio cholerae in liquid culture, passed the broth through a bacteria-tight filter so zero living bacteria remained in the liquid, and injected that sterile cell-free filtrate into tied-off segments of rabbit small intestine (ligated ileal loops). Within hours, the loops ballooned with clear, watery fluid—yet when De sectioned and stained the intestinal wall under the microscope, the absorptive epithelium and its brush border were completely intact. His 1959 Nature paper established that a bacteria-free culture filtrate could cause fluid secretion. Later molecular work explained how cholera toxin changes epithelial signalling and increases chloride secretion into the lumen. De’s experiment did not itself identify all those molecular steps. Because chloride and sodium ions pour into the lumen, the water potential of the intestinal fluid drops below that of the cells and blood plasma, and osmosis drags litres of water out of the bloodstream into the gut.

De’s discovery contained a hidden clinical lifeline. If the small-intestinal epithelium is still intact during cholera, then the brush-border Na⁺–glucose cotransporter (which you met in Chapter 7 Section 7.4) is still sitting undamaged in the cell membrane. Plain water alone does not replace all the ions lost in severe diarrhoea. A carefully formulated glucose–electrolyte solution can use the still-functioning sodium–glucose transport route: coupled uptake of sodium and glucose supports water absorption even while toxin-driven secretion continues. The concentrations and water volume matter. Standard ORS packets are prepared with safe water according to their directions; this story is not a mixing recipe. Severe dehydration can also require intravenous fluid and clinical care.

In 1968, clinical researchers in Dhaka and Kolkata—including David Nalin, Richard Cash, Norbert Hirschhorn, and Nathaniel Pierce—measured intake and output in hospitalised cholera patients and showed that an oral glucose-electrolyte drink reduced intravenous fluid needs by up to 80 percent. Most senior health officials, however, still insisted that oral rehydration could work only under careful hospital supervision alongside intravenous drips.

Then came the monsoon of 1971. During the Bangladesh Liberation War, millions of exhausted refugees crossed the border into West Bengal. At Bongaon, a frontier town about eighty kilometres north-east of Kolkata, cholera broke out in overcrowded camps where Dilip Mahalanabis, a thirty-six-year-old paediatrician from the Johns Hopkins Center for Medical Research and Training in Calcutta, was running a makeshift two-room field hospital. Supplies of intravenous fluid and trained staff were limited. That made a treatment that could be given by mouth especially valuable, while patients in shock still required urgent parenteral treatment.

Dilip Mahalanabis and his colleagues organised carefully measured glucose–electrolyte mixtures and trained families to help administer them. Their 1973 report describes 3,703 patients admitted at Bongaon, including severe cases initially given limited parenteral fluids and less severe cases treated orally. The overall case-fatality ratio was 3.6 percent. This was a field treatment programme with mixed illness severity and treatments, not a randomised comparison proving that ORS alone changed mortality from a measured 30 percent in an otherwise identical group. Its achievement was showing that oral therapy could be used on a large scale under desperate conditions.

Together, Toronto 1922 and Kolkata–Bongaon 1959–1971 show why cellular mechanisms matter. Insulin signals muscle uptake and storage while suppressing liver glucose production. Sodium–glucose cotransport can support intestinal water uptake during cholera. Careful formulation, testing and organisation turned these physiological connections into treatments that could reach patients. :::

1822–1833

What disappeared from the string?

Alexis St. Martin, William Beaumont

Mackinac and later research stations, 1822–1833

Food disappears from a string. Does that mean it has been chemically digested? It sounds like a small question. In William Beaumont’s published experiments, asking it carefully changes what the evidence can establish.

The investigation depended on Alexis St. Martin, a French Canadian voyageur who survived an accidental gunshot injury at Mackinac in 1822. Beaumont, an army surgeon, treated him. As the injury healed, an opening into St. Martin’s stomach remained. This was a continuing feature of a person’s life, not a window built for a scientist’s convenience.

Beaumont’s introduction says that he began gastric experiments in May 1825 at Fort Mackinac, then continued after transfer to Fort Niagara. Some early results appeared in 1826. His book, Experiments and observations on the gastric juice, and the physiology of digestion, was published at Plattsburgh in 1833. Accident, experimental work and publication are three different events. Calling the whole story “a discovery in 1825” hides how much happened before and afterwards.

Step 1: Notice what the apparatus really measured

In the First Series of the book, Experiment 1 is dated 1 August 1825. Beaumont described attaching several foods to a silk string and introducing them through the opening. The foods included differently prepared meats, bread and thinly sliced cabbage. He withdrew the string at intervals and inspected what remained.

The arrangement let him retrieve material and observe its visible condition. But the result was not a direct count of broken chemical bonds. A piece could lose its structure, soften, melt or come off the string. Those possibilities matter when the observation is “the food is no longer attached”.

Beaumont’s later remarks on this experiment recognise that problem. The cabbage had been cut into thin pieces, exposing much surface. The bread was porous and could admit fluid; it might have fallen away after softening before all its material was chemically digested. Fat becoming oil could also explain disappearance from the string. Comparing such foods did not hold physical form constant.

This is a useful lesson in what scientists call a confounded comparison. Several differences changed together: the material, its preparation, its texture and its exposed surface. The observations were real, but a simple ranking of disappearance times would not isolate one chemical cause. We should not turn that record into a universal timetable for digestion.

Step 2: Move part of the process out of the organ

Other experiments asked a more focused question. Was breakdown caused only by the stomach’s moving wall, or could its secreted juice do chemical work away from the organ?

In Experiments 2–3, Beaumont described drawing off gastric fluid through a tube, placing beef with it in a vial, and keeping the vial warm in a water bath. A similar piece of beef was suspended inside the stomach. He reported breakdown in both settings, with different progress in the two environments.

That comparison separates one part of the system: the collected juice could act without being enclosed by the stomach’s muscular wall. It does not make movement irrelevant. Mixing can renew contact between fluid and food surfaces. Nor does it establish that hydrochloric acid alone causes every digestive reaction. The collected fluid contained several substances; a comparison using that whole mixture does not isolate a single component.

Today’s enzyme account helps distinguish chemical roles. Pepsin catalyses protein hydrolysis under suitable acidic conditions. Acid helps provide those conditions and activate its precursor. Further digestion occurs in the intestine. None of those claims should be credited to one vial as though it measured all the steps, and observing breakdown is still different from measuring absorption into tissues.

Step 3: Read the participant’s experience in the record

The First Series also records St. Martin reporting pain and distress. During Experiment 1, Beaumont eventually withdrew the remaining foods and did not return them. These details prevent a retelling in which the procedures were simply effortless observation through a convenient opening. The investigator’s own record makes clear that participation could be uncomfortable.

St. Martin was essential to the work. He was also someone with employment, a family and decisions about where to live. The research was interrupted when he returned to Canada. Beaumont’s introduction describes his efforts to find him again. A story that treats those interruptions only as lost laboratory time gives us the investigator’s priorities as though they were the whole human situation.

The relationship combined medical care, employment and research. Later agreements tied St. Martin’s experimental service to payment and provisions such as food, clothing and lodging. The Becker Medical Library preserves a catalogue of four articles of agreement from 1832–1833. Scholarship based on that collection reproduces the terms of an October 1832 contract.

A written agreement is evidence of an arrangement. It is not, by itself, proof that someone could freely refuse a procedure without losing essential support. Dependence on an investigator who is also a doctor and employer complicates that freedom. We do not have to invent St. Martin’s private thoughts to recognise the imbalance; the documented roles and contractual obligations are enough to make it a serious question.

The surviving book gives extensive access to Beaumont’s descriptions and conclusions. It does not give equally complete access to St. Martin’s own account. That limit belongs in the history. Scientific value and the acceptability of how evidence was obtained are separate questions, and the first cannot automatically settle the second.

Return to Chapter 7 with two habits. When something disappears, ask what the apparatus actually detected and which alternative explanations remain. When an experiment depends on a person, ask whose contribution made it possible and what freedom that person had over the work.

1616–1628

One drachm a beat, and a finger on a vein

William Harvey, Hieronymus Fabricius, Realdo Colombo, Ibn al-Nafis, Marcello Malpighi

Padua, London and Frankfurt, 1600–1628

How do you follow a river when its smallest channels are invisible to the naked eye? For more than a thousand years, learned physicians inherited a persuasive picture from the ancient Greek physician Galen. In that account, food from the gut was turned into dark nutritive blood by the liver and sent drifting outward through the veins to nourish the tissues, while a separate supply of bright vital blood and spirit moved through the arteries. Most of the blood was thought to be consumed where it arrived, rather than returning to start the journey again.

It is tempting to mock that older view by claiming Galen thought the liver manufactured a person’s entire body weight in fresh blood every hour. He did not: in Galen’s system, blood moved much more slowly, ebbing and seeping to match tissue nourishment. When William Harvey challenged the consumption model, he did not win by inventing a silly version of his predecessors. He combined earlier anatomical discoveries, deliberate underestimate arithmetic and simple mechanical tests on living vessels.

Step 1: Inherit the valves and the lung crossing

Harvey did not work in isolation. Around 1242, the Arab physician Ibn al-Nafis had already argued in his commentary on Avicenna that blood cannot pass through invisible pores in the thick septum between the heart’s right and left ventricles; instead, blood from the right ventricle must travel through the lungs to reach the left chambers. In sixteenth-century Italy, Realdo Colombo (1559) likewise described the pulmonary transit from anatomical and vivisection observations.

When Harvey studied medicine at the University of Padua—graduating in 1602—his anatomy teacher Hieronymus Fabricius of Aquapendente showed him the cup-shaped pockets lining the insides of veins, which Fabricius published in De Venarum Ostiolis (1603). Fabricius thought those venous valves merely slowed blood down to prevent it pooling in the limbs. Harvey noticed something sharper: the pockets all point towards the heart, never away from it.

Harvey began presenting his new lectures on the movement of the heart and blood to the College of Physicians in London from 1616. Twelve years later, his concise Latin book Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus (De Motu Cordis) was printed in Frankfurt in 1628 by the English bookseller William Fitzer. Studying in Padua, lecturing in London and publishing in Frankfurt were distinct stages of a long investigation.

Step 2: Choose an underestimate that no critic can brush aside

In Chapter IX of De Motu Cordis, Harvey asked a quantitative question: how much blood does the left ventricle eject into the aorta over half an hour?

Instead of claiming an exact universal stroke volume, he deliberately chose numbers far smaller than the heart actually holds, so that even a sceptic would have to grant the premise. Suppose, he wrote, the left ventricle holds about two ounces of blood, and ejects only a quarter, a fifth, or a sixth of that—say half an ounce (four drachms), three drachms, or even just one drachm (about 3.9 grams in apothecaries’ weight) at each beat.

In half an hour the heart beats more than a thousand times (and in some people two, three or four thousand times). Multiply even the tiniest assumed ejection—one drachm per beat—by 1,000 beats: that is 1,000 drachms, or 10 pounds 5 ounces Troy (~3.9 kilograms) of blood pumped out of the left ventricle in thirty minutes. If the heart ejects half an ounce (4 drachms) per beat over 1,000 beats, the half-hour total is 41 pounds 8 ounces Troy (~15.5 kilograms).

The larger estimate exceeds a modern adult’s roughly five-litre total blood volume. The smallest estimate, about 3.9 kg, does not. Repeated replacement at even that lower rate would still demand far more material than ordinary food and drink could supply. Arithmetic alone could not show how arteries and veins connect, nor could it prove that flow is steady. What it ruled out was one-way production and complete tissue consumption: unless the vessels burst, the same blood had to return to the heart and be pumped around again.

Step 3: Test direction with ligatures and a finger on a forearm vein

If blood circulates, which vessels carry it outward and which bring it back? In Chapters X and XI, Harvey described seventeenth-century surgical and ligature observations—pinching the great vessels in a live snake and tying bandages of different tightness around a human arm (historical procedures that are never to be repeated on animals or with tight bands at home).

When he compressed a snake’s vena cava just before it entered the heart, the space between his forceps and the heart quickly emptied. When he compressed the artery just beyond the heart, the vessel between the heart and the pinch swelled up purple. In a human arm, a very tight ligature blocked the deep arteries as well as the veins: the hand grew pale and cool, and no pulse beat below the band. Loosening the band to medium tightness let high-pressure arterial blood push past into the hand while still blocking the lower-pressure surface veins: now the hand flushed warm and the veins below the band swelled up—never the veins above it.

Then, in Chapter XIII (illustrated by four famous engravings of a forearm), Harvey described a three-part test on a prominent surface vein of a bound arm:

  1. Pressing one fingertip down on a swollen forearm vein just below a valve node H (near the hand) and sliding a second finger upward (towards the shoulder) past the next valve O emptied the vein segment between H and O, which stayed flat because valve O blocked backward flow from above.
  2. Pushing against the swollen vein above O toward the wrist made the valve puff out as a small knot, refusing to let blood pass toward the hand.
  3. Lifting the lower finger at H allowed blood to refill the empty segment immediately from the hand side, towards the heart.

Step 4: Leave the unseen bridge for the microscope

Even after arithmetic, ligatures and valves converged on a closed loop, one link remained unseen. Without a powerful microscope, Harvey could not see the tiny vessels connecting the finest arteries to the finest veins in the tissues; he had to infer passage through invisible tissue spaces or pores. Nor did anyone in 1628 know about oxygen, which was identified only in the 1770s.

In 1661—four years after Harvey’s death—the Italian physician Marcello Malpighi turned a microscope onto the thin, translucent lung of a living frog (De Pulmonibus). There he saw blood remain inside branching, hair-thin walled channels—capillaries—as it crossed from the smallest arteries into the smallest veins.

Return to Chapter 8 with Harvey’s toolkit in mind. Deliberate lower-bound arithmetic can rule out an impossible supply claim; mechanical experiments with valves and pressure establish direction; and direct microscopy later fills in the structural bridge that calculation had predicted.

1921–1976

Giant squid axons, sleeping frog hearts and the warm-paralysed flies of Colaba

Obaid Siddiqi, Alan Hodgkin, Andrew Huxley, Otto Loewi, Seymour Benzer

Colaba, Mumbai & Pasadena, 1921–1976

For more than a century after Luigi Galvani made a frog’s leg twitch with metal wires in 1791, people pictured nerves as living telegraph cables. It was an easy comparison to make, and a misleading one. In a copper wire (Book 2, The Moving World, Chapter 12), free electrons drift through solid metal while the electric field races along at nearly the speed of light. A nerve fibre, by contrast, is a thin tube of salty water wrapped in an oily lipid membrane. It contains no metal core and no free electrons waiting to run along it. Worse still for a simple wire model, Santiago Ramón y Cajal’s silver-stained microscope slides in the 1880s and 1890s showed that one nerve cell does not even fuse into the next: between every neurone and its neighbour lies an open microscopic gap, named the synapse by Charles Scott Sherrington in 1897.

Two fundamental questions therefore stood in the way of understanding how your brain and spinal cord control your body:

  1. Across the gap: If two neurones do not touch, how does an impulse cross the 20 nm space from one cell to the next?
  2. Along the fibre: How does a leaky membrane tube of sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) ions conduct a fast, non-fading electrical spike without losing strength over a metre of arm or leg?

1. Otto Loewi’s two frog hearts and the chemical courier (1921)

In 1921, at the University of Graz in Austria, the pharmacologist Otto Loewi tested whether a nerve speaks to its target organ by sending electricity across the junction or by releasing a dissolved chemical substance. In a laboratory experiment on isolated amphibian tissue (a historical physiological procedure never to be repeated on animals at home), Loewi placed two beating frog hearts in separate glass chambers filled with Ringer’s salt solution.

Heart 1 still had its vagus nerve attached; Heart 2 had all its nerves removed. Loewi stimulated the vagus nerve of Heart 1 electrically for several minutes, and watched Heart 1’s beat slow down as expected. Then he drew up some of the salty liquid bathing Heart 1 with a pipette and transferred it into the chamber holding Heart 2. Even though no nerve had been stimulated on Heart 2, Heart 2 slowed down as well. When he instead stimulated the sympathetic accelerator nerve on Heart 1 and transferred the bathing fluid, Heart 2 sped up.

Loewi called the vagus-released substance Vagusstoff (“vagus stuff”). Working with Henry Hallett Dale in London, researchers showed that Vagusstoff is the small organic molecule acetylcholine. An electrical impulse arriving at the end of a neurone releases packets of neurotransmitter molecules that diffuse across the synaptic gap and bind to receptor proteins on the next cell.

2. Hodgkin and Huxley’s giant squid axon (1939–1952)

Knowing that a chemical bridges the gap between cells still left the mystery of the electrical impulse travelling along each neurone. Vertebrate nerve fibres are typically only 1 to 20 µm wide—too narrow for 1930s researchers to thread a glass voltage-measuring electrode inside the cell without tearing the membrane.

In 1936, the zoologist J. Z. Young pointed out that the North Atlantic squid (Loligo forbesii) possesses a squid giant axon up to 0.5 to 1.0 mm wide—thick enough to see with the naked eye—which triggers the rapid mantle contraction that jet-propels the squid backwards away from predators. Working at the Marine Biological Association laboratory in Plymouth in the summer of 1939 (again in historical laboratory work on marine tissue), Alan Hodgkin and his student Andrew Huxley slid a fine glass capillary electrode down the inside of a single squid giant axon.

Everyone expected that during an impulse the membrane’s negative resting voltage (about −70 mV inside relative to outside) would simply drop to 0 mV as the membrane briefly became leaky. Instead, Hodgkin and Huxley’s oscilloscope trace shot right past zero to +30 mV before plunging back down to −70 mV in less than two milliseconds.

Returning to Plymouth after the Second World War, Hodgkin, Huxley and Bernard Katz used an electronic feedback circuit called a voltage clamp (published in five landmark papers in The Journal of Physiology in 1952) to hold the axon membrane at any chosen voltage and measure the separate currents carried by sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) ions:

  • At rest (−70 mV), the sodium–potassium pump later identified chemically by Jens Christian Skou in 1957 keeps Na⁺ concentrated outside the cell and K⁺ concentrated inside.
  • When a neighbouring patch of membrane depolarises past a threshold (about −55 mV), voltage-gated Na⁺ channels snap open first. Sodium ions rush in down their steep concentration and electrical gradient, flipping the inside voltage to +30 mV.
  • Within a millisecond, those Na⁺ gates automatically inactivate while voltage-gated K⁺ channels open. Potassium ions rush out down their gradient, restoring the negative inside voltage (repolarisation) and briefly overshooting to −75 mV (refractory period), which guarantees that the domino wave travels forward rather than backward.

3. Obaid Siddiqi and the warm-paralysed fruit flies of TIFR Colaba (1962–1976)

Hodgkin and Huxley’s 1952 equations predicted that the axon membrane must contain distinct molecular gates for Na⁺ and K⁺, yet nobody had seen those protein channels or knew which genes built them. That link was forged with the help of fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster) and a physicist-turned-biologist working on the southern tip of Mumbai.

Born in Basti in Uttar Pradesh in 1932, Obaid Siddiqi studied plant genetics in Aligarh and Delhi before completing his PhD with Guido Pontecorvo in Glasgow and postdoctoral research on the genetic code with Alan Garen in the United States. In 1962, at the invitation of Homi Bhabha (prompted by physicist Leo Szilard), Siddiqi came to Mumbai to establish the Molecular Biology Unit at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in Colaba, right beside the Arabian Sea.

In the early 1970s, Siddiqi turned from bacterial genetics to a bold new question he shared with his friend Seymour Benzer at Caltech: can you dissect the electrical machinery of the nervous system one gene at a time by finding single-gene mutants whose nerves fail under specific conditions?

In 1971, David Suzuki and his colleagues in Vancouver had isolated a remarkable temperature-sensitive Drosophila mutant called para (short for paralytic). At an ordinary cool room temperature of 22 °C, para flies walk, climb and fly just like wild-type flies. Warm the glass vial to 29–32 °C, however, and within five seconds every para fly tumbles to the bottom, completely motionless. Cool the vial back to 22 °C, and within seconds the flies stand up and walk away as if nothing had happened.

Why did warming by a few degrees switch off the nervous system so cleanly? Working between Pasadena and his neurogenetics laboratory at TIFR Colaba, Obaid Siddiqi and Seymour Benzer (published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in September 1976) placed microscopic glass electrodes into the cervical nerve and thoracic flight muscles of living fruit flies while raising and lowering their temperature:

How do we know? Pinpointing axonal versus synaptic failure in a living circuit Siddiqi & Benzer, 1976

Siddiqi and Benzer compared three different temperature-sensitive paralytic mutants—para (paralytic), shi (shibire), and a new mutant they isolated called com (comatose)—by stimulating the neck nerve and recording both the axonal action potential and the flight-muscle response:

  • In para (paralytic): As soon as temperature rose past the threshold (~29–32 °C), action potentials along the nerve axon vanished abruptly, even though stimulating the flight muscle directly still made the muscle contract. When cooled by a few degrees, the axonal action potential reappeared within seconds.
  • In shi (shibire) and com (comatose): By contrast, the nerve axon kept firing normal action potentials above the paralysis temperature, but the signal failed to cross the synapse (neuromuscular junction) because synaptic vesicle recycling and neurotransmitter release were blocked.

Siddiqi and Benzer’s 1976 recordings proved that single genes separately build the axon’s action-potential gates and the synapse’s chemical-release machinery. Thirteen years later, in 1989, Barry Ganetzky’s team cloned and sequenced the Drosophila para gene: it encodes the main pore-forming protein of the voltage-gated sodium (Na⁺) channel itself. Temperature-sensitive changes can impair sodium-channel function on warming and allow recovery on cooling. The physiological recordings located a failure of axonal signalling; identifying the channel protein required the later molecular work. Neither the paralysis observation nor a simple channel drawing establishes the exact structural change for every mutant.

1835–1977

The Finches' Labels, the Fever Letter, the Velveteen Stamp & the Gondwana Leaf

Charles Robert Darwin, John Gould, Alfred Russel Wallace, Salvador Luria, Joshua Lederberg, Esther Lederberg, Bernard Kettlewell, Anthony Allison, J. B. S. Haldane, Birbal Sahni, Carl Woese

In September 1835, when the twenty-six-year-old naturalist Charles Robert Darwin stepped ashore on the volcanic rock of the Galápagos Archipelago from HMS Beagle, he did not experience the cinematic eureka moment that simplified textbooks often invent. Looking at the small, dull-feathered birds hopping among arid thorn scrub and prickly-pear cacti (Opuntia), Darwin did not realise they were all finches, nor did he suspect that each island housed its own species. In his field notes he jotted some down as blackbirds and others as grosbeaks, warblers, or wrens, tossing many skins into shared bags without recording which specific island each bird came from. Only when vice-governor Nicholas Lawson remarked that he could tell from a giant tortoise’s shell which island it inhabited did Darwin begin to wonder whether island isolation mattered.

The real turning point arrived in London in March 1837, when Darwin handed his bird skins to the Zoological Society’s ornithologist John Gould. Within days Gould reported an astonishing anatomical fact: the supposed blackbirds, grosbeaks, and warblers were thirteen closely allied species of a single endemic ground-finch group, differing systematically in the depth, curvature, and mechanical leverage of their beaks. Embarrassed by his missing island tags, Darwin wrote urgently to Captain Robert FitzRoy, servant Syms Covington, and shipmate Harry Fuller, who had labelled their private specimen bags island by island. Once the localities were reconstructed, the pattern locked into place: an ancestral South American flock had colonised the islands and diversified as different beak shapes gave survival advantages on tough seeds, cactus flowers, or wood-boring insects. In July 1837, on page 36 of his private Notebook B, Darwin drew a small branching tree beneath two quiet words: “I think.”

For twenty years Darwin accumulated barnacles, pigeon skeletons, and cross-breeding ledgers at Down House in Kent. Half a world away, in February 1858, the Welsh collector Alfred Russel Wallace—remembered in evolutionary history as Wallace in Ternate—lay wrapped in blankets on the spice island of Ternate in the Maluku archipelago. Shivering through an intermittent malarial fever, Wallace could not go out with his insect nets. His thoughts turned to why closely allied species occupied neighbouring islands, and then to Thomas Malthus’s Essay on the Principle of Population. Disease, famine, and predators killed the vast majority of offspring every year. Between fever chills, Wallace saw the necessary deduction: if any variant possessed even a slight inherited advantage in escaping predators or gathering food, it had to survive in larger numbers and leave more offspring. Over three evenings he wrote “On the Tendency of Varieties to Depart Indefinitely from the Original Type” and posted it to Darwin.

When the packet reached Down House in June 1858, Darwin saw his own unpublished theory mirrored almost word for word. At that very moment his household was in grief: his infant son Charles Waring Darwin died of scarlet fever on 28 June 1858. Rather than let Darwin’s twenty-year priority vanish or suppress Wallace’s breakthrough, Charles Lyell and Joseph Dalton Hooker arranged a joint reading of Darwin’s 1844 sketch, an 1857 letter to Asa Gray, and Wallace’s Ternate essay at the Linnean Society of London on 1 July 1858. Neither author attended—Darwin was burying his child in Downe village, and Wallace was still in New Guinea—yet natural selection was now public, followed in November 1859 by On the Origin of Species.

Darwin and Wallace knew selection required heritable variation, yet neither knew whether the environment caused organisms to mutate on demand. For decades, many microbiologists assumed that pouring an antibiotic or bacteriophage onto bacteria actively taught cells to develop resistance. In 1943, Salvador Luria and Max Delbrück tested that claim with their fluctuation test on Escherichia coli, showing that resistant colonies varied in jackpot bursts across parallel tubes—the statistical signature of random mutations occurring before the selective agent was added. Nine years later, at Wisconsin in 1952, Joshua Lederberg and Esther Lederberg made that proof visible to the naked eye. Pressing a wooden block wrapped in sterile velveteen cloth onto an antibiotic-free master agar plate of bacteria, they stamped exact spatial replicas onto plates containing lethal penicillin or streptomycin. Resistant colonies appeared at identical (x, y) coordinates on every replicate plate. Returning to those matching spots on the antibiotic-free master plate, the Lederbergs isolated pure resistant cultures whose ancestors had never touched a single molecule of the drug. Mutation was a random copying glitch; the antibiotic was merely an environmental filter.

While the Lederbergs worked in Petri dishes, field biologists measured selection in wild populations. Between 1953 and 1955, the Oxford physician Bernard Kettlewell released marked pale (typica) and dark (carbonaria) peppered moths (Biston betularia) into soot-blackened woodland near Birmingham and unpolluted, lichen-crusted woods in Dorset. Filming from hides with Niko Tinbergen, Kettlewell watched robins and hedge sparrows pick off whichever morph clashed with the bark, recapturing twice as many dark moths as pale ones (53.1% versus 27.5%) in Birmingham and nearly three times as many pale moths as dark ones (13.7% versus 4.7%) in Dorset. When critics later noted that Kettlewell had placed moths onto lower trunks in daytime, Cambridge geneticist Michael Majerus repeated the experiment between 2001 and 2007 with 4,864 moths resting naturally on high canopy branches, confirming that bird predation drove both industrial melanism and its reversal after Clean Air laws restored pale lichens.

Simultaneously, selection was traced inside human blood. In 1949, J. B. S. Haldane proposed that infectious disease was a powerful selective agent and that red-cell variants might persist because carriers resisted malaria. In 1954, Anthony Allison tested Haldane’s hypothesis in East Africa, examining blood films from 290 Ganda children near Lake Victoria and mapping 35 tribes. Allison proved that heterozygous sickle-cell carriers (HbᴬHbˢ) suffered far lower rates of dense Plasmodium falciparum parasitaemia (27.9% versus 45.7% in HbᴬHbᴬ children) and rarely died of cerebral malaria—a balancing selection pattern that L. D. Sanghvi independently mapped across malarial forest belts in western and central India.

Finally, how could biologists trace evolution across hundreds of millions of years? In Lucknow, the Indian palaeobotanist Birbal Sahni thin-sectioned silicified Jurassic rocks from the Rajmahal Hills of Bihar and Permian coal seams from Gondwana. In 1948, Sahni described the Pentoxyleae, an extinct gymnosperm order bridging seed-ferns, cycads, and conifers, while showing how Glossopteris leaves linked India, Africa, Australia, and Antarctica. Three decades later, in 1977 at Urbana, Carl Woese showed that every living cell also carries an internal molecular fossil record: by comparing 16S ribosomal RNA base sequences, Woese discovered that “prokaryotes” comprised two distinct domains—Bacteria and Archaea—alongside Eukarya, turning Darwin’s notebook sketch into a sequence-verified tree of life.

1944–1968

A humid X-ray camera in London and a synthetic gene bench from Raipur to Madison

Rosalind Franklin, Raymond Gosling, Erwin Chargaff, James Watson, Francis Crick, Maurice Wilkins, Marshall Nirenberg, Har Gobind Khorana

London and Cambridge, 1950–1953, and Raipur, Lahore, Bethesda and Madison, 1961–1968

Walk into two very different basement laboratories twelve years apart. In the first—at King’s College London in May 1952—a thirty-one-year-old physical chemist named Rosalind Franklin and her doctoral student Raymond Gosling are threading a single microscopic fibre of calf-thymus DNA, no thicker than a spider’s silk, across a pinhole camera while bubbling saturated salt solution through the chamber to hold the relative humidity near 92 percent. In the second—at the University of Wisconsin in Madison in the mid-1960s—an organic chemist born in a tiny village in Punjab, Har Gobind Khorana, is linking nucleotide letters one by one in glass flasks to build artificial genetic messages of exact, repeating sequence.

Between those two benches lies one of the greatest detective investigations in science: first discovering the three-dimensional geometry of the DNA molecule, and then cracking the four-letter triplet cipher that every living ribosome reads to print proteins.

Part 1 · Erwin Chargaff’s chromatogram and Rosalind Franklin’s Photo 51 (1950–1953)

Until the mid-1940s, most biochemists dismissed DNA as a dull structural scaffold inside the nucleus. A widely taught textbook idea—Phoebus Levene’s “tetranucleotide hypothesis”—assumed that DNA was just a monotonous repeating string of the four bases (adenine A, thymine T, guanine G, and cytosine C) in equal 25 percent shares. If a molecule repeats A–T–G–C–A–T–G–C forever, it can carry no more specific information than a page printed with a single repeating word.

That assumption collapsed after Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty proved in 1944 that pure DNA—and only DNA—carries hereditary transformation in bacteria. At Columbia University in New York, the biochemist Erwin Chargaff read Avery’s paper and decided to measure the actual proportions of the four bases in DNA from different organisms using paper chromatography and ultraviolet spectrophotometry. By 1950, Erwin Chargaff had uncovered two striking facts across humans, cattle, salmon, sea urchins, yeast, and bacteria:

  1. DNA is not a monotonous 25-25-25-25 repeat. Human DNA is rich in A and T (~30 percent each, ~20 percent G and C), whereas certain bacteria are rich in G and C. The base composition varies from species to species, giving DNA the freedom to store complex biological instructions.
  2. Yet inside every double-stranded DNA sample from every species, the number of adenine (A) molecules always equalled the number of thymine (T) molecules (%A ≈ %T), and the number of guanine (G) molecules always equalled cytosine (C) (%G ≈ %C).

At the time, Erwin Chargaff did not know why A matched T and G matched C. The physical clue came from X-ray crystallography in London.

When Rosalind Franklin arrived at King’s College London in January 1951 after years of pioneering X-ray diffraction work on coals and carbons in Paris, earlier X-ray images of DNA fibres had been blurry because researchers had unknowingly mixed two different hydration states of the molecule. Rosalind Franklin solved that experimental bottleneck by controlling the water content of the air around the DNA fibre. At lower humidity (~75 percent), the fibre formed a shorter, crystalline A-form; when hydrated at ~92 percent humidity, the fibre lengthened by about a quarter and relaxed into a wet paracrystalline B-form—the conformation DNA adopts inside watery living cells.

Between 1 and 6 May 1952, Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling exposed a single hydrated B-form DNA fibre to a fine-focus X-ray beam for sixty-two hours. The resulting photograph—labelled Photo 51 in their laboratory log—showed a bold, unmistakable X-shaped cross of dark diffraction spots. To a trained crystallographer, that X-cross was the direct mathematical signature of a helix. From the spacing of the layer lines and the dark meridional arcs at the top and bottom of Photo 51, Rosalind Franklin calculated the core dimensions of B-DNA:

  • One complete helical turn repeats every 3.4 nm (34 Å) along the fibre axis.
  • Adjacent stacked bases are separated vertically by 0.34 nm (3.4 Å), meaning exactly 10 base pairs stack in each full turn.
  • The missing fourth layer line on the X-cross showed that two coaxial sugar–phosphate chains are offset from each other along the cylinder, creating an unequal major groove and minor groove.
  • Because the charged phosphate groups avidly bind water molecules when the fibre hydrates, the sugar–phosphate backbones must sit on the outside of the 2.0 nm (20 Å) cylinder, with the less water-soluble bases tucked inside.

At the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, Francis Crick—a physicist who had co-developed the mathematical theory of helical X-ray diffraction—and the young American biologist James Watson were trying to build wire-and-tin molecular models of DNA. An early three-stranded model they built in late 1951 had failed because it placed the phosphate groups on the inside and ignored the water content Franklin had measured. In late January 1953, without Rosalind Franklin’s knowledge or prior permission, Maurice Wilkins at King’s College showed Photo 51 to Watson, and in February 1953 Max Perutz shared an internal Medical Research Council (MRC) progress report containing Franklin’s precise unit-cell measurements and space-group symmetry (C2, which told Francis Crick that the two sugar–phosphate chains run in opposite, antiparallel directions).

One chemical piece remained. When Watson initially tried pairing identical bases (A with A, C with C), the textbook drawings he used showed the bases in a rare enol form, and two large two-ring purines (A or G) bulged wider than two smaller one-ring pyrimidines (T or C). The American structural chemist Jerry Donohue, who shared their Cambridge office, pointed out that in living cells the bases exist in the keto form. The next morning, shifting cardboard cutouts on his desk, Watson saw that a two-ring adenine (A) forms two hydrogen bonds with a one-ring thymine (T) (A=T), and a two-ring guanine (G) forms three hydrogen bonds with a one-ring cytosine (C) (C≡G), producing two rungs of identical 2.0 nm width and identical symmetry.

On 25 April 1953, Nature published Watson and Crick’s model alongside two experimental papers from King’s College—including Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling’s paper presenting Photo 51. Complementary base pairing (A with T, C with G) explained Erwin Chargaff’s ratios at a stroke, left the sequence of bases along one strand completely free to spell out genetic instructions, and showed how each strand could act as a template to build its partner. Tragically, Rosalind Franklin died of ovarian cancer in April 1958 at age thirty-seven—after doing further landmark X-ray studies on tobacco mosaic virus and poliovirus—four years before the 1962 Nobel Prize was awarded to Crick, Watson, and Wilkins.

Part 2 · From Raipur to Bethesda and Madison: Marshall Nirenberg and Har Gobind Khorana crack the 64 codons (1961–1968)

Knowing that a gene is a long sequence of A, T, C, and G bases raised the next great riddle: how do four nucleotide letters specify twenty different amino acids?

Simple arithmetic showed that single letters (4¹ = 4) or pairs of letters (4² = 16) cannot name 20 amino acids, whereas triplets of three bases yield 4³ = 64 combinations. In 1961, Francis Crick, Sydney Brenner, Leslie Barnett, and R. J. Watts-Tobin proved genetically in bacteriophage T4 that the cell reads genes in non-overlapping triplets from a fixed starting point: inserting or deleting one or two bases (+1 or +2) scrambles every triplet downstream, whereas inserting or deleting three bases (+3 or −3) restores the reading frame.

But which of the 64 triplets codes for which amino acid? In May 1961 at the National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, Maryland, Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei prepared a cell-free extract of Escherichia coli bacteria containing ribosomes, transfer RNAs, ATP, and amino acids, added DNase to destroy the bacteria’s own DNA, and fed the ribosomes an artificial messenger RNA (mRNA) strand made purely of uracil bases: UUUUUUUUUUUU... (poly-U). The ribosomes printed a polypeptide chain made purely of phenylalanine (Phe–Phe–Phe...). The first word of the genetic dictionary had been read: UUU = Phenylalanine. Soon CCC was shown to code for proline and AAA for lysine.

Homopolymers like poly-U, however, could only crack the four all-identical triplets (UUU, CCC, AAA, GGG). When researchers mixed two bases at random, they could tell that a triplet contained two Us and one C, but not whether the spelling was UUC, UCU, or CUU.

Solving the exact spelling of all 64 codons required someone who could synthesise nucleic acids of known, repeating sequence letter by letter. That chemist was Har Gobind Khorana. Born in 1922 in Raipur, a village of about a hundred people in Punjab (then British India), Har Gobind Khorana was the youngest of five children of a village agricultural taxation clerk (patwari). His father insisted that all the children learn to read and write, and young Har Gobind studied under a tree with the village teacher before winning scholarships to D.A.V. High School in Multan and Punjab University in Lahore, where Mahan Singh supervised his master’s degree in chemistry. A Government of India fellowship took Khorana to Liverpool, Zurich, and Cambridge—where he worked alongside Alexander Todd on nucleotide chemistry—before he established his own laboratories in Vancouver and then at the University of Wisconsin–Madison.

Har Gobind Khorana combined precision organic synthesis with enzymatic polymerisation. First, he chemically synthesised short DNA segments of exact alternating sequence—such as a two-base repeat TC TC TC TC or a three-base repeat TTC TTC TTC. Next, he used DNA polymerase to copy those short templates into long double-stranded DNA polymers, and RNA polymerase to transcribe them into long messenger RNA (mRNA) strands with an exact repeating sequence. When he added those synthetic mRNAs to cell-free ribosomes, the results were crystal clear:

  • The repeating dinucleotide mRNA (UC)ₙ = UCUCUCUCUCUC... can only be read by a ribosome in triplets as alternating UCU | CUC | UCU | CUC. In Khorana’s tubes, the ribosomes printed a polypeptide of strictly alternating serine and leucine (Ser–Leu–Ser–Leu). Combined with binding assays developed by Marshall Nirenberg and Philip Leder, this proved that UCU codes for serine (Ser) and CUC codes for leucine (Leu).
  • Similarly, (UG)ₙ (UGU | GUG) yielded alternating cysteine and valine (Cys–Val–Cys–Val), (AG)ₙ (AGA | GAG) yielded alternating arginine and glutamic acid (Arg–Glu–Arg–Glu), and (AC)ₙ (ACA | CAC) yielded alternating threonine and histidine (Thr–His–Thr–His).
  • Repeating trinucleotides such as (UAG)ₙ confirmed that UAA, UAG, and UGA do not code for any amino acid at all: they are the stop (nonsense) codons discovered genetically by Obaid Siddiqi, Sydney Brenner, and Alan Garen (which you met in Chapter 9).

By 1966, Marshall Nirenberg and Har Gobind Khorana had completed the entire 64-codon genetic table—and proved that the same dictionary is read by bacteria, plants, fruit flies, and human cells alike. In 1968 they shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Robert Holley, and two years later Khorana’s team went on to achieve the first total chemical synthesis of a complete, functional gene in a laboratory flask. :::
