1856–1970

Twenty-eight thousand pea plants in Brno, a white-eyed fly in New York, and blood-group pedigrees in Mumbai

Johann Gregor Mendel, Reginald Punnett, William Bateson, Nettie Stevens, Thomas Hunt Morgan, L. D. Sanghvi

Brno, 1856–1866, Cambridge and Bryn Mawr, 1900–1905, New York, 1910, and Mumbai, 1948–1970

In the summer of 1856, inside the walled courtyard of St Thomas’s Abbey in Brno (then Brünn in the Austrian Empire, now in the Czech Republic), a thirty-four-year-old Augustinian friar named Johann Gregor Mendel walked down rows of climbing garden peas (Pisum sativum) holding fine forceps and a camel-hair paintbrush. Before a pea flower could open and self-pollinate, Johann Gregor Mendel pried apart the green keel petals, snipped off the immature anthers, and bagged the bud against passing bees. Days later, he brushed the stigma with pollen from a chosen partner plant and logged the cross.

Part 1 · Johann Gregor Mendel’s Brno ledger and Reginald Punnett’s Cambridge grid (1856–1905)

Between 1851 and 1853, Abbot Cyril Napp had sent Johann Gregor Mendel to the University of Vienna, where he studied experimental physics under Christian Doppler and combinatorial mathematics under Andreas von Ettingshausen. There he learned that hidden natural laws emerge only when an experimenter isolates one variable at a time and counts enough trials for random statistical noise to average out.

Most nineteenth-century naturalists assumed heredity worked by blending: parental traits supposedly mixed like red and white paint, producing pink offspring that could never be unmixed. To test whether traits blend or stay discrete, Johann Gregor Mendel spent two years (1854–1856) verifying twenty-two pure-breeding pea lines across seven sharp characters: seed shape (round versus wrinkled), cotyledon colour (yellow versus green), flower colour (purple versus white), pod shape (inflated versus constricted), unripe pod colour (green versus yellow), flower position (axial versus terminal), and stem length (tall 1.8–2.1 m versus dwarf 0.3–0.45 m).

Between 1856 and 1863, across a 35 m × 7 m monastery plot, Johann Gregor Mendel cultivated roughly 28,000 pea plants and scored 19,959 second-generation (F₂) outcomes. Crossing pure round (RR) with pure wrinkled (rr) peas yielded 100% round first-generation (F₁) hybrids (Rr). When those F₁ plants self-pollinated, wrinkled seeds returned unblemished in F₂: out of 7,324 seeds, 5,474 were round and 1,850 were wrinkled (2.96 : 1). Cotyledon colour split 6,022 yellow to 2,001 green (3.01 : 1), and flower colour split 705 purple to 224 white (3.15 : 1). Across all seven characters combined, his ledger totalled 14,949 dominant to 5,010 recessive outcomes (2.98 : 1), converging on 3 : 1.

Crucially, Johann Gregor Mendel raised a third generation (F₃) from 565 round F₂ seeds: 193 plants bred true (RR) while 372 plants segregated 3 : 1 again (Rr), proving the hidden 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr genotype ratio (1 : 1.93). His test crosses (Rr × rr) likewise confirmed a 1 : 1 split.

Published in 1866, the paper was largely overlooked—partly because Carl Nägeli urged Johann Gregor Mendel to test hawkweed (Hieracium), which forms seeds asexually (apomixis) and masked Mendelian ratios. After Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, and Erich von Tschermak rediscovered Mendel’s laws in 1900, Cambridge biologist William Bateson coined genetics, allele, homozygote, and heterozygote. Around 1905, working with William Bateson, Reginald Punnett introduced the 2 × 2 Punnett square, turning Mendel’s binomial algebra (¼ RR + ½ Rr + ¼ rr) into a visual grid where maternal and paternal haploid gametes (n) combine into diploid zygotes (2n).

Part 2 · Nettie Stevens’s mealworm chromosomes and Thomas Hunt Morgan’s white-eyed fly (1905–1910)

Where inside the cell did Mendel’s alleles sit? In 1902–1903, Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri noted that homologous chromosomes segregate during meiosis just like alleles. In 1905 at Bryn Mawr College, cytologist Nettie Stevens provided decisive proof in the mealworm beetle (Tenebrio molitor): females carried 20 matched chromosomes (XX), producing uniform X eggs, whereas males carried 19 large chromosomes and one tiny partner (XY), producing 50% X-sperm and 50% Y-sperm. Sex determination was a Mendelian 1 : 1 chromosome cross.

At Columbia University in New York, embryologist Thomas Hunt Morgan remained sceptical until early 1910, when he spotted a single white-eyed male fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) among thousands of red-eyed flies in his banana-bottle Fly Room. Crossing that white-eyed male to red-eyed females produced 1,237 red-eyed F₁ hybrids. In the F₂ generation (3,470 red : 782 white), every single white-eyed fly was male (XʷY), whereas test-crossing the white-eyed father to F₁ carrier daughters produced both white-eyed females (XʷXʷ) and males (XʷY). That proved the eye-colour gene sat physically on the X chromosome, while the Y chromosome lacked that locus—earning Thomas Hunt Morgan the 1933 Nobel Prize.

Part 3 · L. D. Sanghvi and human genetic pedigrees in Mumbai (1948–1970)

After studying mathematics in Mumbai and completing his doctorate at Columbia University under L. C. Dunn and Theodosius Dobzhansky, Indian geneticist L. D. Sanghvi (1920–1985) founded the Human Variation Unit at the Indian Cancer Research Centre (now ACTREC, Tata Memorial Centre) in Parel, Mumbai.

From the late 1940s through the 1970s, L. D. Sanghvi and his colleagues mapped ABO blood-group alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, Iᴼ), Rh antigens, X-linked red–green colour vision (Xᴮ/Xᵇ), G6PD deficiency, and autosomal recessive haemoglobin variants (sickle-cell Hbˢ and beta-thalassaemia) across communities in Mumbai, Maharashtra, and Gujarat. By combining family pedigree charts with carrier screening, L. D. Sanghvi showed how endogamous marriage patterns concentrate rare recessive alleles (aa) and how Punnett probabilities empower genetic counselling in Indian hospitals.

What to remember

  • Johann Gregor Mendel (1866) proved across 19,959 F₂ pea outcomes (2.98 : 1) and F₃ progeny tests (1 RR : 2 Rr) that alleles are discrete packets that do not blend.
  • William Bateson and Reginald Punnett (1905) established core genetics terminology (allele, homozygous, heterozygous) and the 2 × 2 Punnett square.
  • Nettie Stevens (1905) and Thomas Hunt Morgan (1910) proved that XX/XY sex determination (1 : 1) and X-linked recessive inheritance (XᵇY, XʰY) trace to specific chromosomes.
  • L. D. Sanghvi pioneered ABO codominance (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, Iᴼ), X-linked screening, and autosomal carrier pedigree analysis in Mumbai. :::

1879–2006

Heavy nitrogen in Pasadena, crimson threads in Kiel, and a tadpole nucleus in Oxford

Walther Flemming, Matthew Meselson, Franklin Stahl, John Gurdon, Shinya Yamanaka, Kamal Ranadive

Kiel, 1879–1882, Woods Hole and Pasadena, 1954–1958, and Oxford, Mumbai and Kyoto, 1962–2006

In the spring of 1879, German anatomist Walther Flemming leaned over a brass microscope at the University of Kiel, staring into the translucent tail fin of a fire salamander larva (Salamandra maculosa). For decades, biologists had argued over where new cells came from. Some still suspected that nuclei crystallised spontaneously out of featureless cell sap, like sugar crystals forming in cooling syrup. The trouble was that a living cell nucleus is almost completely transparent; under an ordinary light microscope, its interior looks like clear glass.

Part 1 · Walther Flemming’s crimson threads in Kiel (1879–1882)

Walther Flemming tried a chemical tool from the German dye industry: synthetic aniline stains. When he soaked fixed salamander gill and fin tissues in crimson basophilic dyes, a hidden architecture blazed into view inside the nucleus. One granular substance drank up the red stain so greedily that Walther Flemming named it chromatin—from the Greek khroma, meaning colour. Because aniline fixing and staining froze each cell at a single instant, he reconstructed the sequence of cell division by sorting hundreds of fixed cells into chronological order, like shuffling still photographs back into a film reel.

What his sequence revealed in his 1882 book Zellsubstanz, Kern und Zelltheilung (Cell Substance, Nucleus and Cell Division) astonished every microscopist in Europe. Before a cell divided, the diffuse chromatin condensed into distinct threads. Then—the crucial step—every single thread split lengthwise down its middle into two identical twin threads. Fine spindle fibres radiating from two poles caught those twin threads and pulled one complete set to the left and the other complete set to the right, forming two daughter nuclei that were exact structural copies of the parent nucleus. Walther Flemming named this thread-splitting dance mitosis, from the Greek mitos for a weaver’s warp thread. All cell nuclei, he concluded in a Latin aphorism echoing Rudolf Virchow, arise from pre-existing nuclei: omnis nucleus e nucleo.

Part 2 · Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl’s heavy-nitrogen centrifuge in Pasadena (1954–1958)

Yet Walther Flemming died in 1905 without knowing how a chromatin thread could split lengthwise into two identical copies. That molecular mystery waited until April 1953, when James Watson and Francis Crick ended their Nature paper on the DNA double helix with a quiet sentence: “It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.” Because adenine (A) pairs with thymine (T) by two hydrogen bonds and cytosine (C) pairs with guanine (G) by three hydrogen bonds, unzipping the two strands of a parental double helix should let each old strand serve as a template for a new complementary partner.

Not everyone was convinced that a two-metre tangle of DNA could unzip cleanly without snarling. Biologists debated three rival possibilities. In Watson and Crick’s semi-conservative model, each daughter DNA molecule keeps one intact parental strand paired with one newly built strand. In a conservative model, the original double helix stays intact as a closed master copy while a brand-new double helix is assembled beside it. And in 1954, physicist Max Delbrück proposed a dispersive model: perhaps enzymes chop the parental double helix into fragments during copying, so every daughter strand ends up as a patchwork mosaic of old and new DNA pieces.

In the summer of 1954 at Woods Hole, Massachusetts, a twenty-four-year-old Caltech chemistry graduate student named Matthew Meselson met a twenty-five-year-old biologist named Franklin Stahl while Franklin Stahl sat under a giant shade tree serving gin and tonic to seminar attendees. Matthew Meselson had just heard a lecture by Jacques Monod and was pondering how to weigh newly synthesised molecules using stable heavy isotopes. Before the afternoon ended, Meselson and Stahl agreed to team up at Caltech in Pasadena to test how DNA copies itself.

Their experimental design, published in July 1958, became famous as “the most beautiful experiment in biology.” First, Meselson and Stahl grew Escherichia coli bacteria for fourteen generations at 36 °C in broth where the only nitrogen source was heavy ammonium chloride (¹⁵NH₄Cl). Nitrogen-15 (¹⁵N) is not radioactive; it simply carries one extra neutron (8 instead of 7), making every purine and pyrimidine ring slightly denser. Then they abruptly switched the bacteria into ordinary light nitrogen (¹⁴NH₄Cl) broth and harvested samples every twenty minutes as the cells doubled.

How do you separate DNA carrying ¹⁵N from DNA carrying ¹⁴N when the density difference is less than one percent (1.724 g/cm³ versus 1.710 g/cm³)? Matthew Meselson invented equilibrium density-gradient ultracentrifugation. When concentrated caesium chloride (CsCl) is spun in an analytical ultracentrifuge at 44,770 revolutions per minute—roughly 140,000 × g—for twenty-four to forty-eight hours, the heavy caesium ions settle against diffusion into a smooth density gradient from top to bottom of the tube. DNA molecules float or sink until their density matches the surrounding CsCl solution, forming a sharp band visible under ultraviolet light at 260 nm.

At Generation 0, all bacterial DNA settled in one heavy band at 1.724 g/cm³. After one doubling in light ¹⁴N broth (Generation 1), the 1.724 g/cm³ heavy band vanished; in its place stood a single sharp band halfway up the tube at 1.717 g/cm³—100 percent hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N) DNA. In a single twenty-minute generation, the conservative hypothesis was falsified, because conservative copying predicted two separate bands (50% heavy at 1.724 and 50% light at 1.710) with zero hybrid DNA. Then came the decisive Generation 2 tube after forty minutes: the DNA split into two equal bands—50% hybrid (1.717 g/cm³) and 50% pure light (1.710 g/cm³). That clean split eliminated Delbrück’s dispersive hypothesis, which predicted a single blended band at 1.7135 g/cm³. Semi-conservative unzipping—paired with the proofreading DNA polymerase enzyme isolated by Arthur Kornberg in 1956—was proved beyond doubt.

Part 3 · John Gurdon, Kamal Ranadive, and Shinya Yamanaka (1962–2006)

Yet solving how DNA copies itself in mitosis sharpened a deeper developmental riddle. If mitosis deals an identical copy of all chromosomes to every daughter cell, why does an intestinal cell differ so dramatically from a brain neurone or a pancreatic beta cell? For decades, many embryologists suspected that as embryonic stem cells specialise, they permanently discard or ruin the genes they no longer need.

In 1962 at the University of Oxford, zoologist John Gurdon tested that assumption in the African clawed frog (Xenopus laevis). Using microscopic glass pipettes, John Gurdon destroyed the haploid nucleus of an unfertilised frog egg with ultraviolet light and injected in its place the diploid nucleus from a specialised tadpole intestinal epithelial cell. Earlier experimenters in leopard frogs had failed and concluded that adult nuclei were irreversibly locked. John Gurdon persisted with serial nuclear transfers and watched reprogrammed eggs divide by mitosis into normal swimming tadpoles and fertile adult frogs. A single gut-cell nucleus still held every gene needed to build a brain, a beating heart, an eye lens, and a skeleton. Specialisation had not deleted a single gene; it had merely closed unused chapters of the nuclear library.

In Mumbai during the same era, Indian cell biologist Kamal Ranadive established India’s first mammalian tissue-culture laboratory at the Indian Cancer Research Centre in Parel, cultivating human and mouse cells to investigate how mitotic division and tissue specialisation switches go awry in cancer and leprosy. And in 2006 at Kyoto University, former orthopaedic surgeon Shinya Yamanaka and Kazutoshi Takahashi asked which molecular switches in the egg reset an adult nucleus. Screening twenty-four candidate genes, Shinya Yamanaka discovered that adding just four master transcription-factor genes—Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc—to adult mouse (and in 2007, human) skin fibroblasts rewound them into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) able to form beating heart cells or neurones in a dish. Together, Walther Flemming’s crimson threads, Meselson and Stahl’s spinning caesium tubes, and John Gurdon and Shinya Yamanaka’s reprogrammed nuclei proved that every nucleated body cell carries the same master blueprint—copied faithfully before every mitotic division, and read selectively one tissue at a time. :::

lindeman-chain-boyer-doudna-biosphere-biotech

In the freezing Minnesota winters between 1936 and 1940, a twenty-two-year-old graduate student named Raymond Lindeman chopped holes through the ice of Cedar Creek Bog and hauled up buckets of black mud, pondweed, water fleas, and small fish. Lindeman had lost the sight in one eye to a childhood accident and suffered from a severe chronic liver disorder that repeatedly sent him to hospital, yet whenever he could stand he returned to the bog with his wife and fellow biologist, Eleanor Hall. While he sieved mud cores, she identified every microscopic crustacean and midge larva at the bench beside him.

Fifteen years earlier, in 1927, the English ecologist Charles Elton had noticed that ecosystems are arranged in food chains and what he called a “pyramid of numbers”: a meadow or pond holds millions of tiny herbivores, thousands of small carnivores, and only a handful of large predators at the top. Elton had drawn the shape of the pyramid, but nobody knew the exact physical law that forced every food chain to narrow so steeply.

Lindeman and Hall decided to audit Cedar Creek Bog the way an accountant audits a bank. Instead of merely counting individual pondweeds, water fleas, and sunfish, they dried, weighed, and measured the chemical energy stored in each trophic level across a full year, expressed in calories per square centimetre per year (cal cm⁻² yr⁻¹, equivalent to kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹). When Lindeman added up the numbers, a stark rule emerged. Aquatic plants captured only a tiny fraction of the sunlight striking the bog. When herbivorous water fleas and midge larvae grazed those plants, roughly ninety percent of the chemical energy was lost—burned up in aerobic respiration and dissipated as heat, egested as indigestible faeces, excreted as metabolic waste, or left behind as uneaten dead tissue for mud decomposers. Only about ten percent of the energy at one trophic level was built into new biomass at the level above, and only ten percent of that second level reached the predatory fish.

When Lindeman submitted his manuscript, “The Trophic-Dynamic Aspect of Ecology”, to the journal Ecology in 1941, two senior referees initially rejected it as too theoretical. His advisor, G. Evelyn Hutchinson at Yale, defended the bog data line by line until the editor reversed the decision. Lindeman never held the printed issue. His liver failed in June 1942 at the age of twenty-six, four months before his paper appeared in print and transformed ecology into a quantitative science of one-way energy flow and closed nutrient cycles.

Yet if energy flows through the living world only once before radiating away as heat, why doesn’t life run out of carbon and nitrogen atoms? Half a century before Lindeman’s bog audit, two microbiologists in Europe had uncovered the hidden bacterial engines that recycle nitrogen between air and soil. In the late 1880s, the Russian microbiologist Sergei Winogradsky, working in Strasbourg and Zurich, showed that soil nitrification is a two-step relay run by chemoautotrophic aerobic bacteria in well-aerated soil: Nitrosomonas oxidises ammonium ions into nitrite (NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻), and Nitrobacter oxidises nitrite into nitrate (NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻), the exact ion that plant root hairs absorb by active transport. In the same years in Delft, the Dutch microbiologist Martinus Beijerinck isolated Rhizobium from the pink root nodules of leguminous pea and bean plants (1888) and free-living Azotobacter from garden soil (1901), proving that specialized nitrogen-fixing bacteria crack the triple covalent bond of atmospheric nitrogen gas (N₂ → NH₄⁺).

During the second half of the twentieth century, ecologists realized that human industry was pushing both global nutrient cycles and living food webs out of balance. In March 1958, the American geochemist Charles David Keeling installed a high-precision infrared gas analyser high on the volcanic slopes of Mauna Loa in Hawaii. Within two years, Keeling discovered that the planetary atmosphere breathes once a year—carbon dioxide (CO₂) drops every northern summer as temperate and boreal forests photosynthesise, and rises every autumn and winter as cellular respiration and microbial decomposition return CO₂ to the air. Underneath that annual sawtooth wave lay a relentless upward climb: from 315 parts per million (ppm) in 1958 to over 425 ppm today, driven by fossil-fuel combustion and deforestation.

Four years after Keeling began his Mauna Loa record, in 1962, the marine biologist Rachel Carson published Silent Spring, tracing how persistent synthetic insecticides such as DDT do not get broken down by decomposer bacteria. Instead, they undergo bioaccumulation inside tissues and biomagnification up food chains—from water to plankton to small fish to big fish—until ospreys, pelicans, and bald eagles at the top trophic level lay thin-shelled eggs that crush in the nest. Across India, the same ecological awakening joined field biology with forest conservation. When a hydroelectric dam threatened to submerge the ancient tropical evergreen rainforest of Silent Valley in Kerala during the late 1970s, the cytogeneticist E. K. Janaki Ammal, the ornithologist Salim Ali, and the ecologist Madhav Gadgil marshalled chromosome surveys, bird censuses, and watershed data to show what would be lost if the canopy were felled. In 1983, Silent Valley was declared a protected national park.

While field ecologists were learning how bacteria run the planet’s nutrient loops, biochemists and geneticists were learning how to bring bacteria indoors and rewrite their genetic code. In Oxford between 1939 and 1941, the biochemist Ernst Chain and the pathologist Howard Florey, working with Norman Heatley, set out to purify penicillin from Alexander Fleming’s mould, Penicillium chrysogenum. At first they grew the fungus in hundreds of flat ceramic bedpans, extracting barely enough golden powder to treat a single policeman. To make penicillin for millions of patients, engineers had to invent the modern deep-tank stainless-steel industrial fermenter: sterilized with high-pressure steam, fed with measured glucose and ammonium nutrients, stirred by motor-driven paddles, injected with sterile compressed oxygen through a sparger at the base, buffered to a steady pH, and wrapped in a cold-water cooling jacket so the heat of microbial respiration would not denature the mould’s own enzymes. By 1954, guided by the Indian biochemist Yellapragada SubbaRow, Hindustan Antibiotics Limited opened at Pimpri along the Mumbai–Pune road, running giant aerated fermenters to manufacture affordable penicillin for India.

Even inside the best stainless-steel fermenter, however, a microbe could only synthesize the molecules encoded in its own genome. For fifty years after Frederick Banting and Charles Best treated Leonard Thompson in 1922, millions of people with diabetes depended on insulin extracted from the slaughtered pancreases of pigs and cattle—a protein that differed slightly in amino acid sequence from human insulin and triggered immune reactions in many patients.

Then, in late 1972 and 1973, two California researchers—Herbert Boyer at the University of California, San Francisco, and Stanley Cohen at Stanford—met over corned-beef sandwiches in a Waikiki delicatessen and combined two discoveries. Cohen knew how to coax Escherichia coli bacteria to take up small circular rings of extrachromosomal DNA called plasmids. Boyer had purified a restriction enzyme (EcoRI) that recognizes a specific six-base palindrome in DNA (GAATTC) and makes a staggered cut across the two strands, leaving single-stranded overhanging “sticky ends.” By cutting a human gene and a bacterial plasmid with the exact same restriction enzyme, mixing them so their complementary sticky ends paired up by hydrogen bonding, and sealing the sugar-phosphate backbone with the enzyme DNA ligase, Boyer and Cohen built the first recombinant plasmid (1973). Five years later, in 1978, Boyer’s team inserted the human insulin gene into E. coli plasmids, turning dividing bacteria inside industrial fermenters into living factories that synthesized pure human insulin.

Four decades after Boyer and Cohen’s recombinant plasmids, in 2012, the American biochemist Jennifer Doudna and the French microbiologist Emmanuelle Charpentier uncovered an even sharper molecular tool hidden inside bacteria: CRISPR-Cas9. Bacteria had evolved CRISPR over millions of years as an adaptive immune memory against invading bacteriophage viruses, storing snippets of viral DNA and transcribing them into guide RNA (gRNA) molecules that lead the cutting enzyme Cas9 to matching viral DNA. Doudna and Charpentier proved that by synthesizing a custom twenty-letter guide RNA, scientists can programme Cas9 to locate any chosen address in a plant, animal, or human genome, make a precise double-stranded cut, and repair a single mutated letter—turning four billion years of evolved genetic code into a text that human hands can read, conserve, and responsibly edit.

Try the experiment

  • 3D Atlas: Stirred-Tank Bioreactor Sparging, Cooling & Industrial Fermentation
  • 3D Atlas: Boyer–Cohen Recombinant Insulin Plasmid & Doudna–Charpentier CRISPR-Cas9

The adventure in time

The ideas in this book were not found in the order a textbook teaches them. Here they are in the order they actually happened: two and a half thousand years of people asking how things move, and why.

  1. The 1600s
  2. 1616–1628
    One drachm a beat, and a finger on a vein

    A conservative piece of arithmetic made the old blood-supply model impossible, while valves and ligatures showed which way the river had to run.

  3. 1648
    The doctor who weighed a pot of dirt for five years

    His willow gained far more mass than the dried soil lost, but the missing entries in his ledger made his water-only conclusion incomplete.

  4. 1665
    The rooms in a piece of cork

    A piece of dead plant tissue supplied the name for the living units that build a body.

  5. 1668
    Six jars of meat in the Florentine heat

    By pairing open jars, sealed jars and gauze-covered jars of rotting meat in 1668, he showed how a control group defeats a two-thousand-year-old myth.

  6. 1674
    The cloth merchant who found an invisible kingdom

    A Dutch draper with no university degree ground tiny glass beads that beat every compound microscope in Europe and revealed bacteria in his own teeth.

  7. The 1700s
  8. 1779
    The condition hidden inside “plants improve air”

    Collecting gas made a changing process visible, but the result still depended on what was compared.

  9. The 1800s
  10. 1822–1833
    What disappeared from the string?

    A stomach investigation exposed both a problem with interpreting disappearance and a problem with who controlled the experiments.

  11. 1835–1977
    The Finches’ Labels, the Fever Letter, the Velveteen Stamp & the Gondwana Leaf

    How mislabelled island finches in London, a malarial fever in Ternate, a piece of sterile velveteen cloth in Madison, East African blood films, and petrified Indian Gondwana plants proved how variation and selection drive evolution.

  12. 1859
    The chemist who bent a glass neck and saved millions

    A tanner’s son from the Jura mountains who started with mirror-image crystals and ended by proving that microbes drive fermentation, spoilage and infectious disease.

  13. The 1900s
  14. 1901
    The crescograph and the electrical pulse of plants

    After building the world’s first millimetre-wave radio receivers in Calcutta, he invented instruments that magnified plant growth ten thousand times and proved plants fire electrical action potentials.

  15. 1856–1970
    Twenty-eight thousand pea plants in Brno, a white-eyed fly in New York, and blood-group pedigrees in Mumbai

    How an Augustinian friar trained in physics counted 19,959 pea outcomes in Brno, how Cambridge geneticists invented the Punnett square, how mealworm beetles and a single white-eyed fruit fly tied genes to chromosomes, and how L. D. Sanghvi mapped blood groups and carrier pedigrees in Mumbai.

  16. 1906
    The ten-year-old boy and the yellow-throated sparrow

    A curious ten-year-old from Khetwadi, Bombay, walked into the Bombay Natural History Society with a mysterious sparrow and spent the next eighty years mapping the ecology of Indian birds.

  17. 1921–1971
    A warm kennel in Toronto and a plastic drum in Bongaon

    Two twentieth-century medical emergencies—Type 1 diabetes in Toronto and epidemic cholera on the Bengal border—turned from fatal crises into treatable conditions once researchers traced the exact molecules crossing pancreas islets and intestinal membranes.

  18. 1929
    The forgotten discoverer of the cell’s battery

    Born in Andhra Pradesh, he arrived in Boston almost penniless, helped identify ATP, later understood as a major cellular energy carrier, and created one of the first cancer chemotherapy drugs.

  19. 1934
    The woman who sweetened India’s sugarcane

    Born in Thalassery, Kerala, she earned a doctorate in Michigan, counted chromosomes at the Sugarcane Breeding Institute in Coimbatore, and bred hardy, sweet canes for Indian farmers.

  20. 1944–1968
    A humid X-ray camera in London and a synthetic gene bench from Raipur to Madison

    How humidified X-ray diffraction at King’s College London, paper chromatography in New York, and chemically synthesised repeating RNA messages built by a village clerk’s son from Punjab revealed the double helix and cracked all sixty-four triplets of the genetic code.

  21. 1957
    An ATP reaction at the membrane

    Changing the ions around a nerve-membrane enzyme helped connect ATP chemistry with the maintenance of ion gradients.

  22. 1879–2006
    Heavy nitrogen in Pasadena, crimson threads in Kiel, and a tadpole nucleus in Oxford

    How aniline-stained salamander fins in Kiel, heavy-nitrogen ultracentrifuge tubes at Caltech, and reprogrammed frog and skin nuclei in Oxford and Kyoto revealed how cells copy, divide, and selectively read their chromosomes.

  23. 1954 and 1963
    The drawing that atoms had to fit

    In Madras, a protein-shape puzzle became a way to rule out molecular arrangements that looked possible on paper.

  24. 1967
    A cell with more than one ancestry

    The clues inside mitochondria and chloroplasts connected cell structure with an ancient history of living together.

  25. 1921–1976
    Giant squid axons, sleeping frog hearts and the warm-paralysed flies of Colaba

    How frog hearts in Graz, giant squid axons in Plymouth, and temperature-sensitive fruit flies studied between Caltech and TIFR Colaba in Mumbai revealed the ion gates and chemical relays of the nervous system.

  26. 1992
    The unknown protein and the swelling eggs

    A protein found during other work became a testable explanation for rapid water passage across membranes.

  27. 1997
    A pointer too large to miss

    A glowing filament made molecular rotation visible, but the direction of the energy transfer mattered as much as the turning.

Answers to Check yourself

Try each question before you look. If your answer differs, the reasoning matters more than the words: see whether you used the same idea.

Chapter 0. The detective’s lens

0.1

Suppose a student wants to test whether light is needed for moong seeds to germinate. She puts Dish A on a sunny windowsill in wet cotton wool, and Dish B inside a dark cupboard in dry cotton wool. Only Dish A sprouts, so she concludes that seeds need light to sprout. Why is her conclusion invalid, and how should she fix Dish B?

She changed two variables at once: light and water (wet vs. dry cotton wool). She cannot tell whether Dish B failed to sprout because of the dark or because it had no water. To fix it, Dish B must have the exact same volume of water, number of seeds, and temperature as Dish A, differing only in being kept in the dark. (When you actually run that fair test, moong seeds sprout in the dark just as well as in the light!)

Back to section 0.1

0.4

A photograph of a chloroplast in a textbook measures $36\text{ mm}$ across. The caption says the magnification is $\times 6,000$. What is the actual width of the real chloroplast in micrometres ($\mu\text{m}$)?

Convert the image size to micrometres first: $I = 36\text{ mm} \times 1,000 = 36,000\text{ }\mu\text{m}$. Then rearrange $M = I \div A$ to get $A = I \div M = 36,000\text{ }\mu\text{m} \div 6,000 = 6\text{ }\mu\text{m}$. (A real chloroplast is about $5\text{–}6\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ long—roughly the size of a bacterium, which is a huge clue for Chapter 2!)

Back to section 0.4

Chapter 1. The seed and the flame

1.1

A seed gains wet mass before a root appears. Does that prove it has built new living material? What later observation strengthens the evidence that it was viable?

No. Absorbed water can explain the first gain. Continued root and shoot development supports viability and organised growth. Wet mass alone neither measures new dry material nor proves metabolism.

Back to section 1.1

1.2

Could a non-living chemical reaction release heat and carbon dioxide? Which additional features distinguish the viable seed from the flame?

Yes. Gas and heat alone do not establish life. The seed contains a cellular system with inherited instructions and machinery capable of maintaining and developing it under suitable conditions. The flame lacks that system.

Back to section 1.2

1.3

ATP is hydrolysed in a container beside an isolated motor protein. Must the motor move? Explain the missing connection.

No. ATP’s reaction must be coupled to the motor’s binding and shape-changing cycle. Releasing heat nearby is not equivalent to supplying that organised reaction cycle.

Back to section 1.3

1.4

A dry sponge dropped into a bucket of water swells to twice its size. A crystal of alum hung in a saturated alum solution slowly grows larger over a week. Using the biological definitions of growth and metabolism, explain why neither the sponge nor the alum crystal is carrying out biological growth.

The sponge only absorbs liquid water into existing spaces; its dry mass does not increase at all, and the expansion is reversible when dried. The alum crystal increases in dry mass as ions from the solution stack onto its outer surface (accretion), but it has no cells, no internal metabolism, no ATP, and no genetic code directing the synthesis of new molecules from within. Biological growth builds new cells and protoplasm from the inside using metabolic energy.

Back to section 1.4

1.5

Compare three tiny objects: (1) a dry moong seed, (2) a rod-shaped bacterium (E. coli), and (3) a coronavirus particle. Which of the three contain ribosomes and can make their own ATP when given water and nutrients?

Only (1) the moong seed (whose cells contain ribosomes and mitochondria, with greatly restricted metabolism while dry; viable seeds can resume development when conditions permit) and (2) the bacterium (a single prokaryotic cell containing its own ribosomes and ATP-making enzymes). (3) The coronavirus has no ribosomes, no cytoplasm, and no ATP machinery even when placed in water and nutrients; it can only be copied by hijacking a living host cell.

Back to section 1.5

Chapter 2. The nanocity under the microscope

2.1

A cell has a wall, a membrane, ribosomes and DNA, but no membrane-enclosed nucleus. Is the wall enough to identify it as a plant cell? Explain.

No. Bacteria also usually have walls. The combination described fits a typical bacterial cell: it has DNA and ribosomes, but no enclosed nucleus. Plant walls contain cellulose; typical bacterial walls contain a different material. One feature alone is not enough.

Back to section 2.1

2.2

An unknown compartment has two membranes. Is that enough to conclude that it descended from a bacterium? Name two further tests.

No. Membrane number alone does not establish ancestry. Look for its own inherited DNA and compare relevant gene sequences with bacterial sequences; investigate whether its ribosomes are bacterial-related and whether it divides from existing compartments. Several independent clues make the explanation stronger.

Back to section 2.2

2.3

A moong root grows in darkness. If it has no green chloroplasts, can its growing cells still have a supply problem for respiration?

Yes. Growing root cells use stored or transported nutrients and carry out respiration. A lack of chloroplasts does not remove the requirements for materials and exchange. The seed’s growth in darkness already showed that light capture and respiration are different jobs.

Back to section 2.3

2.3

Eight separate 1 cm cubes have the same total volume as one 2 cm cube. Which arrangement has more exposed surface when all faces touch the surrounding liquid, and by what factor?

The eight separate cubes: each has 6 cm², so together they have 48 cm². The 2 cm cube has 24 cm². Exposed area doubles while total volume stays 8 cm³. If pieces are pressed together, their touching faces are not fully exposed; separation matters.

Back to section 2.3

2.4

A student writes “palisade cell → leaf → palisade tissue → plant”. Repair the order, add the missing level, and explain why a leaf is an organ.

Palisade cell → palisade mesophyll tissue → leaf → shoot system → bean plant. A leaf is an organ because different tissues cooperate within it, including photosynthetic, protective and transport tissues. It is not just one oversized palisade cell.

Back to section 2.4

Chapter 3. The Crowded Train & The Salty Sea

3.1

An equal-volume model starts with 80 particles left and 20 right. You count 17 rightward crossings and 11 leftward crossings. How many particles are now on each side, and has movement been one-way?

The signed net transfer is 17 − 11 = 6 rightward. Left now has 80 − 6 = 74 and right has 20 + 6 = 26; the total remains 100. Eleven crossings were leftward, so movement was two-way even while the net change was rightward.

Back to section 3.1

3.2

A supported cell has a solute contribution of −0.80 MPa. Outside water potential stays at −0.30 MPa. Predict net movement first with no added pressure inside, then with +0.50 MPa inside. In the second case, must every water molecule stop crossing?

Without added pressure, outside is higher (−0.30 > −0.80 MPa), so net entry is favoured. With the pressure contribution, inside total is −0.80 + 0.50 = −0.30 MPa, matching outside. There is no sustained net transfer under these conditions, but water still crosses in both directions. Equal water potential does not require equal solute concentration.

Back to section 3.2

3.3

Does the wall replace the cell membrane in a plant cell?

No. The wall supports the cell; the membrane controls passage. The wall lies outside the membrane, and both remain important when water enters or leaves.

Back to section 3.3

3.3

A plant cell’s membrane-bound contents have visibly pulled away from an intact wall. Which way has net water movement occurred, and what would you need to know before predicting recovery?

The cell has lost water overall and is plasmolysed. Fresh surroundings with higher water potential could favour re-entry, but recovery also depends on the cell remaining sufficiently undamaged. An intact-looking wall alone does not establish a living, functional membrane.

Back to section 3.3

3.4

Does a root cell stop requiring respiration because the leaves can capture sunlight?

No. Root cells require a continuing ATP supply for work such as maintaining transport gradients. The plant’s ability to photosynthesise does not replace cellular respiration.

Back to section 3.4

3.4

A mangrove excludes much salt at its roots. A second plant excludes the same amount, but its absorbing tissues have a higher water potential than the soil water. Will equal salt exclusion guarantee equal water uptake?

No. Salt exclusion restricts one transfer; water uptake requires a favourable water-potential difference. If tissue water potential is higher than the surrounding soil water, that comparison favours net water loss rather than intake. Check the total water potential, not only the salt barrier.

Back to section 3.4

Chapter 4. Carbon’s Lego Set & The Million-Speed Locks

4.1

A sample breaks down to glucose. Does that alone tell you it was starch rather than cellulose? What extra structural feature would help?

No. Both can yield glucose on appropriate chemical breakdown. The orientation of the links distinguishes them; branching and chain arrangement provide further information. A building-unit list leaves out the connections that help determine enzyme action and material properties.

Back to section 4.1

4.2

Would making a membrane protein’s opening larger automatically let it carry every small ion?

No. Chapter 3’s selectivity involved chemical interactions as well as size. Changing the shape may change passage, but charge and the groups lining the route still matter.

Back to section 4.2

4.2

A proposed protein model has plausible local backbone angles. Has its full working structure been proved?

No. It has passed one set of local spatial checks. The full arrangement must also fit experimental evidence and account for interactions across the whole molecule, its partners and its surroundings. Passing a restriction is different from proving a unique solution.

Back to section 4.2

4.3

In the chosen graph, what are the reverse barriers for peaks of 90 and 55 when products are at 10? What changes about equilibrium?

The reverse hurdles are 90 − 10 = 80 and 55 − 10 = 45 chosen units. Both forward and reverse barriers are lowered by 35. The endpoint difference is unchanged, so the enzyme changes how quickly equilibrium is approached, not its position.

Back to section 4.3

4.4

Can the seed’s enzymes assist reactions even though an enzyme molecule does not carry out all the jobs of a living organism?

Yes. Chapter 1 distinguished a living cellular system from one process or component. An enzyme can catalyse a reaction without itself being a living organism; cell-free preparations help demonstrate the distinction.

Back to section 4.4

4.4

Two samples react slowly: one is cold, the other has been strongly heated and then cooled. Why is testing both with fresh substrate at the same temperature and pH useful?

It removes different immediate assay temperatures and pH as explanations for their rate difference. Recovery of the cold sample is consistent with reversible slowing. Continuing loss in the heat-treated sample supports persistent damage, though more evidence is needed to identify the exact structural change. Neither result is an enzyme dying.

Back to section 4.4

4.5

An unknown gives blue-black with iodine and purple with biuret; both sets of controls behave correctly. Does this prove it contains an active starch-digesting enzyme?

No. The results support detectable starch and protein/peptide bonds. They do not identify the protein, establish its fold or show catalysis. Testing enzyme activity would require a separate controlled comparison of reaction rate with an appropriate substrate.

Back to section 4.5

Chapter 5. Solar Power & The Green Engine

5.1

A watered plant becomes heavier overnight. Does that observation alone prove that it made new carbohydrate from carbon dioxide?

No. Increased water content can raise fresh mass. Establishing carbohydrate accumulation requires appropriate measurements and comparisons; weighing a wet plant alone does not identify the source or chemical form of its gain.

Back to section 5.1

5.2

Two leaves each release a net 7 chosen units of oxygen in the same interval. One produces 12 and consumes 5. Must the other have those same two rates? Explain.

No. For example, production of 15 and consumption of 8 also gives 7. A net measurement gives the difference, not each underlying rate. Neither result establishes that respiration has stopped.

Back to section 5.2

5.3

If enzymes lower activation barriers, why does a leaf still require an energy input to synthesise carbohydrate from carbon dioxide and water?

A catalyst provides a lower-barrier route but does not supply the net energy needed for an unfavourable overall transformation. Light-supported processes provide that input; enzymes help the connected reactions proceed.

Back to section 5.3

5.3

Increasing carbon dioxide has no effect in a dim chamber. Increasing light at the same carbon dioxide concentration then increases the measured rate. What does that support, and what would it not establish?

It supports light being limiting in the original conditions. It does not establish that carbon dioxide never limits photosynthesis, that unlimited light will keep increasing rate, or that every plant shares the same response. Further controlled comparisons could reveal a new limit.

Back to section 5.3

5.4

Why would “the spongy layer has spaces because it is called spongy” earn no explanation of gas exchange?

It repeats a label. Interconnecting air spaces provide diffusion routes between stomata and the moist surfaces of internal cells, helping carbon dioxide reach photosynthesising cells. That causal connection is the explanation.

Back to section 5.4

5.5

Does every step of water movement from soil to air count as osmosis? Where does active ion transport fit?

No. Osmosis describes water movement across a partially permeable membrane down a water-potential gradient. Flow through xylem and diffusion of water vapour are different steps. Active ion transport can alter solute conditions and requires energy; that does not make the whole xylem stream an ATP-driven pump.

Back to section 5.5

5.5

A storage organ releases sugars to a growing shoot above it. Name the conducting tissue and explain the direction without saying that food “wants to reach” the shoot.

Phloem carries assimilates from the storage source to the growing sink. Loading, osmotic water entry and unloading/use support a pressure difference that drives bulk flow towards the shoot in this pathway. Gravity does not impose a downward-only rule on phloem transport.

Back to section 5.5

Chapter 6. Burning Sugar in the Dark

6.1

A lit green leaf releases oxygen overall. Does that mean its respiration has stopped?

No. Photosynthesis can produce oxygen faster than respiration consumes it, leaving a net release. The leaf can carry out both processes at once. Roots supplied by the leaf also continue their metabolism without receiving light.

Back to section 6.1

6.1

Explain how a growing root can respire without lungs. Include both a supply route and a cellular job.

Sugars can reach the root through phloem, and molecular oxygen can diffuse towards root cells from their surroundings when available. In aerobic respiration the cells use nutrients and oxygen in linked reactions that support ATP formation. ATP-supported processes include active mineral-ion transport and synthesis for growth. Lungs are one gas-delivery arrangement, not a requirement for the chemistry itself.

Back to section 6.1

6.2

Does an ATP-using enzyme obtain energy simply by breaking one special bond?

No. Breaking an isolated chemical bond requires energy. The whole ATP hydrolysis reaction can release free energy because the resulting products and their interactions in water are more stable under the relevant conditions. Coupling that overall change to another process can support work; the enzyme does not create the energy.

Back to section 6.2

6.2

An inner membrane becomes freely leaky to H⁺. Explain why observing continued electron transfer would not prove that normal ATP synthesis continues.

Electron transfer can still provide energy for pumping, but a leak lets H⁺ return without using ATP synthase. The membrane cannot maintain the usual useful electrochemical difference. The link between oxidation and ATP synthesis is therefore impaired even if some electron transfer continues; glycolytic ATP is a separate contribution.

Back to section 6.2

6.3

Complete oxidation of a 1 kg sample produces about 2.81 kg CO₂ and 1.09 kg water. A pupil says this creates matter. Which input did they omit, and how could you check the claim without knowing where each oxygen atom went?

They omitted incoming oxygen, about 2.90 kg in this representative model. The balanced equation and its unrounded formula-mass ledger give equal input and output totals. Rounded product masses total about 3.90 kg, matching fuel plus oxygen. Tracing each individual atom’s origin is a different question from balancing all the material.

Back to section 6.3

6.4

Two pathways regenerate NAD⁺ after glycolysis. One forms ethanol and CO₂; the other forms lactate. Does seeing no gas prove there was no ATP supply? Explain the shared requirement and the different carbon outcomes.

No. Glycolysis can supply two net ATP per glucose while the lactate route restores NAD⁺ without releasing CO₂. Yeast’s taught alcoholic route restores the carrier too, but splits carbon between ethanol and carbon dioxide. The shared function is carrier regeneration; visible gas depends on the pathway and on collection, so its absence is not a direct ATP measurement. In broader terminology, anaerobic electron-chain respiration is a separate mechanism from these fermentation routes.

Back to section 6.4

Chapter 7. The Chemical Disassembly Line

7.1

A glucose molecule has crossed the intestinal lining and entered the internal tissues. Another piece of food has moved into the colon without being absorbed. Which processes do these observations establish, and what extra event would establish assimilation of the glucose?

The first establishes absorption across the gut barrier. The second establishes movement along the canal, not absorption; if the unabsorbed food later leaves as faeces, that is egestion. Assimilation requires uptake and use by cells, for example using glucose as fuel or incorporating its material into stored glycogen. Arrival inside the body’s outline alone proves none of those later uses.

Back to section 7.1

7.2

If an enzyme helps a bond undergo hydrolysis, does the energy come simply from breaking that isolated bond?

No. Breaking an isolated chemical bond requires energy. The overall reaction also forms bonds and changes interactions with surrounding water. Its complete free-energy change and coupling determine available energy transfer. An enzyme lowers an activation barrier; it does not supply a fresh packet of net energy each time.

Back to section 7.2

7.2

Collected gastric juice breaks down food in a warm vial. A pupil concludes: “Acid alone digests every nutrient completely, and the stomach wall is immune to it.” Give three reasons the observation does not establish that conclusion.

The collected juice contains more than acid, including enzymes, so the comparison does not isolate acid’s contribution. Breakdown in a vial does not establish complete processing of every nutrient or absorption into tissues; further digestion normally occurs in the small intestine. The wall’s protection depends on mucus, bicarbonate, an epithelial barrier, repair and regulated enzyme activation. Its tissues are not immune to acid or proteases.

Back to section 7.2

7.3

A model changes one fat sphere into 64 equal spheres of the same total volume. A pupil claims there are 64 times as many exposed surfaces, so digestion must be 64 times faster and the molecules must already be hydrolysed. Repair the argument.

The radius becomes one-quarter of the original; each sphere has one-sixteenth of its area. Sixty-four such areas total four times the original area. Droplet division does not change triglyceride molecules into hydrolysis products. Lipase, water and suitable conditions are still needed for chemical digestion, and enzyme supply and interfacial conditions prevent geometry alone from establishing a fourfold or a 64-fold biological rate.

Back to section 7.3

7.4

If glucose moves from a low concentration in the lumen into a cell with a higher glucose concentration, can simple diffusion of glucose alone explain that net movement?

No. Simple diffusion alone gives net spreading down a concentration gradient when passage is possible. Glucose can enter by a coupled transporter using the downhill movement of sodium ions. An ATP-driven pump helps maintain the sodium electrochemical gradient. The glucose movement is therefore powered indirectly by ATP-supported ion transport, rather than by diffusion alone or the molecule wanting to enter.

Back to section 7.4

7.4

Trace glucose and material from long-chain dietary fat from the lumen towards the wider circulation. Name one membrane event and the main carrying route for each. Why does neither route show an intact food droplet becoming part of a muscle?

Glucose can enter an epithelial cell through sodium-coupled transport, supported indirectly by ATP-maintained ion gradients. It leaves through a tissue-facing transporter, crosses tissue fluid into a capillary, and travels in portal blood towards the liver before wider circulation. Long-chain fatty acids and monoacylglycerols leave micelles, enter epithelial cells, and are rebuilt and packaged as chylomicrons; those packages leave into tissue fluid, enter lacteals and travel in lymph to blood near the heart. Some shorter-chain fatty acids use portal blood instead. These are selective transfers and molecular processing followed by transport; assimilation into a muscle protein or membrane would require further uptake and cellular reactions.

Back to section 7.4

Chapter 8. The Breath and the Double Pump

8.1

Why does blood returning from working leg muscles to the lungs have a lower oxygen partial pressure and a higher carbon dioxide partial pressure than alveolar air?

In Chapter 6, aerobic cellular respiration inside working muscle cells uses oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor (forming water) and releases carbon dioxide as carbon compounds are oxidised to regenerate ATP. Tissue blood therefore loses oxygen to the muscle cells and picks up carbon dioxide before returning to the right side of the heart and lungs.

Back to section 8.1

8.1

Two students each move 6.0 L of air per minute: Student A takes 12 breaths per minute at 500 mL per breath, while Student B takes 24 shallow breaths per minute at 250 mL per breath. Assuming an anatomical dead space of 150 mL per breath, compare their fresh alveolar ventilation and explain why shallow breathing is less effective at maintaining alveolar gas gradients.

Student A delivers (500 − 150) × 12 = 350 × 12 = 4,200 mL min⁻¹ (4.2 L min⁻¹) of fresh air to the alveoli, wasting 1.8 L min⁻¹ in dead space. Student B delivers only (250 − 150) × 24 = 100 × 24 = 2,400 mL min⁻¹ (2.4 L min⁻¹) to the alveoli, wasting 3.6 L min⁻¹ moving air back and forth in the conducting tubes. Less fresh alveolar ventilation allows alveolar O₂ partial pressure to fall and CO₂ partial pressure to rise, flattening the diffusion gradients across the alveolar-capillary barrier.

Back to section 8.1

8.2

In an exercise test, an athlete’s heart rate is 140 beats per minute and stroke volume is 90 mL per beat. Calculate the athlete’s cardiac output in L/min, and explain why a separate experiment establishing flow direction was still needed after a throughput calculation.

Cardiac output is 140 beats min⁻¹ × 90 mL beat⁻¹ = 12,600 mL min⁻¹ = 12.6 L min⁻¹. A volume-per-minute calculation shows that blood must be recycled rather than made fresh and consumed, because 12.6 L every minute is more than twice the entire blood volume of the body. However, multiplication alone cannot show which way blood travels in a particular vessel; emptying the forearm vein segment between H and O and showing it can refill only from the hand side past one-way venous valves proves that veins carry blood towards the heart.

Back to section 8.2

8.3

A student looks at a heart diagram and writes: “The pulmonary vein is an artery because it carries oxygenated blood, and the ‘lub-dub’ sounds occur when the valves open to let blood through.” Correct both parts of the statement.

Vessel names depend on direction relative to the heart, not oxygen content: the pulmonary vein is a vein because it carries blood towards the heart (from the lungs into the left atrium), even though that blood is oxygenated. The “lub-dub” sounds heard through a stethoscope are caused by the closing of the heart valves as pressure differences reverse—“lub” when the atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves snap shut at the start of ventricular contraction, and “dub” when the semilunar valves snap shut as the ventricles relax.

Back to section 8.3

8.4

In Chapter 2 we saw that a mature mammalian red blood cell has a biconcave disc shape and lacks a nucleus. How do both features suit its job in a capillary?

The biconcave disc shape (thinner in the centre than at the rim) provides a larger surface-area-to-volume ratio than a sphere of the same volume, shortening the diffusion distance for oxygen entering and leaving every part of the cell, and lets the cell flex through narrow 8 µm capillaries. Lacking a nucleus (and mitochondria) leaves more internal room for millions of haemoglobin molecules and ensures the red blood cell does not consume the oxygen it is transporting.

Back to section 8.4

8.4

A blood smear under a light microscope shows three structures: (A) numerous small pink discs paler in the centre with no nucleus, (B) a larger cell with a three-lobed nucleus, and (C) a cell with a single large round nucleus filling most of the cytoplasm. Identify A, B and C, state the main function of each, and state which of them normally passes out through intact capillary walls into tissue fluid during an infection.

A is a red blood cell (erythrocyte), paler in the centre because of its biconcave disc shape and lack of a nucleus; it transports oxygen bound reversibly to haemoglobin. B is a neutrophil, a phagocyte with a lobed nucleus, which engulfs and digests pathogens by phagocytosis. C is a lymphocyte (large round nucleus), B cells can become antibody-producing plasma cells; not every lymphocyte secretes antibodies. During an infection, white blood cells (especially phagocytes) can squeeze between capillary endothelial cells into tissue fluid to reach bacteria, whereas red blood cells remain inside intact capillaries.

Back to section 8.4

Chapter 9. High-Speed Wiring and Chemical Couriers

9.1

During a sudden fright, a student’s heart rate rises within two seconds and stays elevated for five minutes. Explain how both coordination systems contribute to this pattern, and why the student’s leg muscles receive more glucose without the hormone adrenaline itself being an energy source.

Sympathetic nerves from the CNS deliver electrical impulses directly to the heart’s pacemaker and to the adrenal glands within a second or two, causing the immediate rise in heart rate. The adrenal glands secrete adrenaline into the blood plasma, where it circulates for several minutes until broken down, keeping the heart rate high and binding to complementary receptors on liver cells. Liver cells respond by breaking down stored glycogen into glucose, raising blood glucose concentration so contracting leg muscles can take up more glucose for aerobic respiration. Adrenaline is a chemical trigger (signal), not a fuel molecule burned by muscle mitochondria.

Back to section 9.1

9.2

(a) A neuropathy strips away the Schwann-cell myelin sheath from peripheral motor axons while leaving the axons unbroken; what happens to conduction speed and reflex latency, and why? (b) An insecticide inhibits the enzyme acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic gap of an insect’s CNS; using the four-step synapse sequence, explain what happens at the postsynaptic membrane after a single presynaptic impulse arrives.

(a) Loss of myelin increases current leakage and can slow or block propagation. It does not simply convert a damaged fibre into a normal unmyelinated axon with one predictable speed. (b) Acetylcholine persists when its breakdown is inhibited, prolonging receptor activation. This can disrupt normal signalling, including spasms and impaired firing or paralysis. It does not guarantee indefinitely repeated normal impulses.

Back to section 9.2

9.3

Explain why an astronomer trying to spot a very faint star in the night sky sees it more clearly by looking slightly to one side of the star rather than staring directly at it, and state how the astronomer’s iris muscles and lens adjust for viewing the night sky.

Staring directly at the star focuses its light onto the fovea, which is packed with cones (requiring bright light) and contains no rods. Looking slightly to one side shifts the star’s image onto the surrounding retina outside the fovea, where rod cells—which have much greater sensitivity for dim-light night vision—are densely distributed. In the dark night sky, the iris radial muscles contract and circular muscles relax so the pupil dilates to admit maximum light; because the star is at an effectively infinite distance, the ciliary muscles relax, pulling the suspensory ligaments tight so the lens is thin and less convex.

Back to section 9.3

9.4

Two seedlings receive light from a window on their right. Seedling A is stationary. Seedling B rotates slowly around a vertical axis, so different sides face the window over a rotation while gravity remains downward. What difference might you predict, and what must be checked before claiming that B will grow perfectly straight?

A can bend towards the window as unequal auxin distribution causes unequal shoot elongation. Rotation may reduce a persistent one-sided light response in B, but its rate, the plant’s response time and other growth conditions matter. Rotation around a vertical axis does not average gravity’s direction relative to an upright shoot. Record the observed growth; equal illumination over a cycle does not prove equal auxin at every instant.

Back to section 9.4

Chapter 10. Holding the Line in a Mumbai Summer

10.1

If glucose falls, must negative feedback make it fall further?

No. Negative feedback opposes the disturbance; low glucose calls for a response that raises it.

Back to section 10.1

10.1

A student skips breakfast and plays an hour of morning football in Mumbai. Trace the negative-feedback loop that prevents their blood glucose concentration from falling dangerously low: name the stimulus, the receptor/coordinator gland, the hormone secreted into blood, the target effector organ, the chemical conversion inside that organ, and why the hormone secretion slows down again once they eat breakfast.

  1. Stimulus: Blood glucose concentration falls below the normal set point (~4.0–5.0 mmol/L) as working muscle and brain cells respire glucose.
  2. Receptor and coordinator: Alpha (α) cells in the islets of Langerhans of the pancreas detect the lower blood glucose concentration.
  3. Hormone: The pancreas secretes glucagon into the blood plasma (while decreasing insulin secretion).
  4. Target effector and chemical conversion: Glucagon binds to complementary receptors on liver cells, stimulating enzymes to break down stored insoluble glycogen into soluble glucose (glycogen → glucose), which enters the blood and raises blood glucose back toward the set point.
  5. Stopping the correction: Once breakfast is digested and blood glucose rises back to (and above) the set point, alpha-cell glucagon secretion is switched off and beta-cell insulin secretion is switched on—the hallmark of negative feedback.

Back to section 10.1

10.2

A marathon runner finishes a race on a cool 16 °C morning and then stands still in wet clothes in a breeze. Within twenty minutes their core temperature drops to 35.8 °C. State the four corrective actions coordinated by the runner’s brain (hypothalamus) to bring core temperature back to the 37.0 °C set point, being careful to use exact vessel wording.

  1. Vasoconstriction of arterioles supplying skin surface capillaries: smooth muscle in the arteriole walls contracts, narrowing the arterioles so less warm blood flows through the surface capillaries and less thermal energy is lost to the cool air.
  2. Sweating stops (though the runner must also dry off or change out of wet clothes so external water stops evaporating from the skin).
  3. Shivering: rapid involuntary contractions of skeletal muscles increase the rate of aerobic respiration of glucose, releasing thermal energy that warms the blood.
  4. Contraction of hair erector muscles (pulling hairs upright to trap an insulating layer of still air in furry mammals), assisted by the permanent thermal insulation of subcutaneous fatty tissue.

Back to section 10.2

10.3

Does every litre filtered become urine?

No. Most filtered water returns to blood; filtration and final excretion are different rates.

Back to section 10.3

10.3

A healthy student eats a high-protein dinner of grilled chicken and lentils (dal) on a hot evening when they have been sweating heavily. Compared with a cool day on a low-protein diet, predict and explain how the volume of their urine and the concentration of urea, glucose and protein in their urine will change.

  1. If water intake does not replace the extra sweat loss, urine volume tends to decrease (with more concentrated urine), because sweating lost water from the body, so the kidneys reabsorb a higher percentage of filtered water back into the blood in the renal tubules and collecting ducts to preserve blood water potential.
  2. Urea excretion can increase, and a smaller urine volume can raise its concentration: excess dietary amino acids from the chicken and dal cannot be stored, so the liver deaminates them (removing the nitrogen-containing amino part) to form more urea, which is filtered at the glomerulus and concentrated into the smaller volume of urine.
  3. Glucose would normally remain undetected by an ordinary urine test, and protein would remain very low: large plasma proteins are still too big to pass through the glomerulus, and nearly all filtered glucose at ordinary loads is still selectively reabsorbed back into the blood in the renal tubule.

Back to section 10.3

10.4

Does receiving ready-made antibody automatically build immune memory?

No. Passive antibody protection does not itself create the recipient’s specific memory response.

Back to section 10.4

10.4

Compare how cholera toxin causes dehydration with how oral rehydration solution (ORS) supports absorption despite it, and state whether an infant who receives anti-cholera antibodies in breast milk has gained active or passive immunity (giving two reasons for your choice).

  1. Cholera toxin mechanism: Vibrio cholerae bacteria in the small intestine secrete cholera toxin, which causes intestinal epithelial cells to secrete chloride ions (Cl⁻) into the small-intestinal lumen. This lowers the water potential of the gut lumen below that of the blood and cells, causing water to move out of the blood and cells into the gut by osmosis, resulting in watery diarrhoea, dehydration, and loss of ions from the blood.
  2. ORS-supported absorption: Standard ORS supplies water and carefully measured electrolytes and glucose; intact brush-border Na⁺–glucose cotransporters absorb Na⁺ and glucose into the intestinal cells, raising cellular/blood solute concentration so water is drawn back into the blood by osmosis.
  3. Breast milk immunity: Receiving ready-made antibodies in breast milk is passive immunity, because (a) the antibodies were acquired from another individual (the mother) rather than produced by the infant’s own lymphocytes, and (b) antibody transfer itself does not generate the infant’s specific memory response, so the borrowed protection is short-term and fades as the antibodies are broken down.

Back to section 10.4

Chapter 11. The Twisted Ladder & The Protein Printers

11.1

Arrange the following five biological structures in order of size from largest to smallest, and explain how Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty (1944) proved which chemical molecule in a chromosome carries hereditary instructions: gene, eukaryotic cell, DNA base pair, chromosome, nucleus.

  1. Size order from largest to smallest: Eukaryotic cell (~20 µm) → Nucleus (~6 µm) → Chromosome → Gene → DNA base pair (2.0 nm wide, 0.34 nm high).
  2. Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty’s (1944) proof: They took the purified cell-free transforming extract from heat-killed virulent Smooth (S) Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteria and treated separate samples with specific digestive enzymes before adding live harmless Rough (R) bacteria. Treating the extract with proteases (which digest proteins) or RNase (which digests RNA) did not stop the extract from transforming R bacteria into capsule-making S bacteria. Treating the extract with DNase (which digests DNA) completely stopped transformation, proving that DNA—not protein or RNA—carries hereditary genes.

Back to section 11.1

11.2

A short segment along one strand of a DNA double helix has the base sequence A – T – G – G – T – G – C – A – C.

  1. Write down the complementary base sequence along the opposite DNA strand.
  2. State how many hydrogen bonds link these 9 base pairs together across the double helix, and explain why Rosalind Franklin’s Photo 51 showed a vertical spacing of 0.34 nm and a turn repeat of 3.4 nm.

  1. Complementary DNA strand: Using A ↔ T and C ↔ G, the opposite strand reads T – A – C – C – A – C – G – T – G.
  2. Hydrogen-bond count and Photo 51 geometry: - Each A=T pair forms 2 hydrogen bonds (there are 4 A/T pairs: 4 × 2 = 8 H-bonds) and each C≡G pair forms 3 hydrogen bonds (there are 5 G/C pairs: 5 × 3 = 15 H-bonds), giving 8 + 15 = 23 hydrogen bonds across the 9 base pairs. - In Photo 51, the X-shaped diffraction cross showed that B-DNA is a helix that completes one full 360° turn every 3.4 nm along the fibre axis, while the dark meridional arcs at the tenth layer line showed that stacked base pairs sit 0.34 nm apart vertically (3.4 nm ÷ 0.34 nm = 10 base pairs per turn).

Back to section 11.2

11.3

A segment of the coding strand of a human gene inside the nucleus has the base sequence 5'- G T G · C A C · C T G · A C T -3' (and its complementary template strand reads 3'- C A C · G T G · G A C · T G A -5').

  1. Write down the base sequence of the mRNA molecule transcribed from this segment, and state where in the cell this mRNA is made and where it moves next.
  2. Using the genetic code (GUG = Val, CAC = His, CUG = Leu, ACU = Thr), write down the four-amino-acid sequence assembled when this mRNA passes through a ribosome, and explain how DNA controls the function of a synapse (Chapter 9) and active transport (Chapter 3).

  1. mRNA sequence and cellular pathway: - The transcribed mRNA sequence is 5'- G U G · C A C · C U G · A C U -3' (complementary to the 3'→5' template strand CAC GTG GAC TGA, which is identical to the 5'→3' coding strand with Uracil U replacing Thymine T). - The gene remains in the nucleus; the mRNA copy is made in the nucleus and moves through a nuclear pore into the cytoplasm, where it passes through a ribosome.
  2. Amino-acid sequence and control of cell function: - The ribosome reads the mRNA triplets in order (GUG → CAC → CUG → ACU) and assembles the amino-acid sequence Val – His – Leu – Thr (Valine – Histidine – Leucine – Threonine). - DNA controls cell function by controlling the production of specific folded proteins: at a synapse, DNA codes for the postsynaptic receptors for neurotransmitters (whose 3D binding sites match the neurotransmitter); in active transport, DNA codes for the specific membrane carrier proteins embedded in the cell membrane.

Back to section 11.3

11.4

Compare what happens to the mRNA codon, the amino-acid sequence, and the 3D folded beta-globin protein when:

  1. A single-base substitution changes beta-globin Codon 3 on the coding DNA strand from CTG to CTT (given that both CUG and CUU code for leucine, Leu).
  2. A single-base substitution changes beta-globin Codon 6 on the coding DNA strand from GAG to GTG (given that GAG codes for hydrophilic glutamic acid, Glu, and GUG codes for hydrophobic valine, Val).

  1. Codon 3 (CTG → CTT, Silent / Synonymous change): - mRNA codon: changes from CUG to CUU. - Amino-acid sequence: unchanged (Val¹–His²–Leu³–Thr⁴–Pro⁵–Glu⁶–Glu⁷...), because the genetic code is degenerate and both CUG and CUU code for leucine (Leu³). - 3D folded protein: 100% unchanged; because every amino acid along the 146-residue chain is identical (including hydrophilic Glu⁶), the chain folds into normal, soluble adult haemoglobin (HbA).
  2. Codon 6 (GAG → GTG, Missense change): - mRNA codon: changes from GAG to GUG. - Amino-acid sequence: the sixth amino acid changes from negatively charged, hydrophilic glutamic acid (Glu⁶) to neutral, hydrophobic valine (Val⁶). - 3D folded protein: the hydrophobic Val⁶ side chain creates a sticky non-polar patch on the outside of deoxygenated haemoglobin (HbS), causing HbS molecules to stick together into rigid fibres that distort the red blood cell into a sickle shape.

Back to section 11.4

Chapter 12. Copying the Blueprint: Mitosis, Stem Cells & Meiosis

12.1

  1. What happens to the chromosomes inside a nucleus before mitosis begins (0610 17.2.3), and how many chromosomes and how many sister chromatids (DNA double helices) are present in a human body cell (2n = 46) immediately after S-phase replication finishes?
  2. In Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl’s (1958) experiment, E. coli cells uniformly labelled with heavy ¹⁵N (1.724 g/cm³) are transferred to light ¹⁴N medium and allowed to divide through four generations (Gen 4, producing 16 descendant DNA double helices from each original duplex). Calculate how many of the 16 double helices are heavy (¹⁵N/¹⁵N), how many are hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N), and how many are light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N), and state the percentage of DNA in each CsCl band.

  1. Before mitosis, exact replication of chromosomes occurs during interphase (S phase) by semi-conservative DNA replication (A pairing with T, C pairing with G). Immediately after S-phase replication finishes (G₂ phase), the human cell still contains 46 chromosomes (counted by 46 shared centromeres), now composed of 92 sister chromatids (92 DNA double helices).
  2. At Generation 4 (2⁴ = 16 double helices, 32 single strands in total), only 2 single strands are the original heavy ¹⁵N parental strands, and each is paired with a new light ¹⁴N strand. Therefore there are 0 heavy (¹⁵N/¹⁵N) duplexes (0% at 1.724 g/cm³), 2 hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N) duplexes (2/16 = 12.5% at 1.717 g/cm³), and 14 light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N) duplexes (14/16 = 87.5% at 1.710 g/cm³).

Back to section 12.1

12.2

  1. Define mitosis (0610 17.2.1), state its four biological roles (0610 17.2.2), and explain how chromosome number is maintained from parent cell to daughter cells (0610 17.2.3 & 17.2.4).
  2. Strawberry plants can reproduce both asexually (by sending out horizontal stems called runners that grow roots by mitosis) and sexually (by producing insect-pollinated flowers that form seeds). Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of reproducing via runners (a) for a wild strawberry population in a forest clearing, and (b) for a commercial strawberry farmer.

  1. Mitosis is nuclear division giving rise to genetically identical cells. Its four roles are (1) growth, (2) repair of damaged tissues, (3) replacement of worn-out cells, and (4) asexual reproduction. Chromosome number is maintained because exact replication of chromosomes occurs before mitosis (duplicating 2n = 46 chromosomes into 92 sister chromatids), and during mitosis, the copies of chromosomes separate to opposite poles so each daughter nucleus receives a complete diploid set (2n = 46).
  2. (a) In the wild: An advantage of runners is that a single well-adapted strawberry plant can colonise the clearing rapidly without needing a mate or insect pollinators; a disadvantage is that all runner offspring are genetically identical clones with no genetic variation, so a new frost, drought, or fungal pathogen could wipe out the local population. (b) In commercial crop production: An advantage is that every runner daughter plant is a 100% genetic clone that preserves the exact sweet flavour, large fruit size, and uniform ripening time of the parent; a disadvantage is monoculture disease vulnerability—if one cloned plant is susceptible to a fungal wilt or virus, the entire field is equally vulnerable.

Back to section 12.2

12.3

  1. Define a stem cell (0610 17.2.5) and explain why a retinal cone cell in your eye and a beta cell in your pancreas contain the exact same genes on Chromosome 11, yet only the pancreatic beta cell produces insulin (0610 17.1.6).
  2. Explain how John Gurdon’s (1962) frog nuclear-transfer experiment and Shinya Yamanaka’s (2006) induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) experiment prove that cell specialisation does not delete unused genes.

  1. Stem cells are unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised for specific functions. Both the retinal cone cell and the pancreatic beta cell were formed by mitosis from the same diploid zygote, so both contain the exact same 46 chromosomes and the same genes (including the insulin gene INS on Chromosome 11). However, many genes in a particular cell are not expressed because the cell only makes the specific proteins it needs: in the pancreatic beta cell the INS gene is expressed (transcribed into INS mRNA and translated at ribosomes into insulin), whereas in the retinal cone cell the INS gene is not expressed (switched off) and light-sensitive opsin genes are expressed instead.
  2. In 1962, John Gurdon transplanted the nucleus of a fully differentiated tadpole intestinal epithelial cell into a UV-enucleated frog egg, and that single gut nucleus directed the growth of a normal tadpole and frog with working heart muscle, brain neurones, and eyes. In 2006, Shinya Yamanaka added four transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc) to differentiated adult skin fibroblasts and rewound them into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) that could differentiate into heart, nerve, or beta cells. If differentiation had deleted unused genes, neither an intestinal nucleus nor a skin fibroblast could ever build heart or nerve proteins again; their reprogramming proves that 100% of the genome remains intact inside specialised cells.

Back to section 12.3

12.4

  1. Define (a) a haploid nucleus, (b) a diploid nucleus, (c) meiosis (0610 17.3.2), and (d) fertilisation (0610 16.2.2).
  2. A female Indian muntjac deer (Muntiacus muntjak) has a diploid chromosome number of 2n = 6 (3 homologous pairs) in her body cells. State how many chromosomes are present in (a) a muntjac skin cell produced by mitosis, (b) a muntjac egg cell nucleus produced by meiosis, and (c) a muntjac zygote immediately after fertilisation—and explain why both meiosis and fertilisation are necessary in every generation.

  1. (a) A haploid nucleus is a nucleus containing a single set of unpaired chromosomes (n, e.g. 23 in human gametes). (b) A diploid nucleus is a nucleus containing two sets of chromosomes (2n, e.g. 23 homologous pairs = 46 chromosomes in human body cells and the zygote). (c) Meiosis is a reduction division in which the chromosome number is halved from diploid to haploid resulting in genetically different cells. (d) Fertilisation is the fusion of the nuclei of gametes.
  2. (a) Skin cell produced by mitosis: 6 chromosomes (2n = 6). (b) Egg cell nucleus produced by meiosis: 3 chromosomes (n = 3, one from each of the 3 homologous pairs, with 2³ = 8 possible independent-assortment combinations). (c) Zygote immediately after fertilisation: 6 chromosomes (n + n = 3 + 3 = 2n = 6). Both processes are required in every generation because meiosis halves the chromosome count (2n → n) while generating genetic variation, and fertilisation fuses two haploid gamete nuclei (n + n → 2n) to restore the species’ diploid chromosome number instead of allowing it to double (6 → 12 → 24) every generation.

Back to section 12.4

Chapter 13. “The Monk’s Spreadsheet: Mendel, Alleles & Inheritance”

13.1
