  1. Define (a) allele, (b) genotype, (c) phenotype, (d) homozygous, and (e) heterozygous, and state which of (d) or (e) is pure-breeding.
  2. In pea plants, the allele for tall stems (T) is dominant to the allele for dwarf stems (t), where T codes for functional gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase enzyme and t codes for an inactive enzyme. State the genotype, zygosity, relative enzyme dose (100%, 50%, or 0%), and stem-length phenotype of (a) a pure-breeding tall plant, (b) a pure-breeding dwarf plant, and (c) an F₁ hybrid produced by crossing (a) and (b).

  1. (a) An allele is an alternative form of a gene. (b) Genotype is the genetic make-up of an organism in terms of the alleles present. (c) Phenotype is the observable features of an organism. (d) Homozygous means having two identical alleles of a particular gene; two identical homozygous individuals that breed together will be pure-breeding. (e) Heterozygous means having two different alleles of a particular gene; a heterozygous individual is not pure-breeding.
  2. (a) Pure-breeding tall plant: genotype TT, homozygous dominant, 100% active enzyme dose, tall stem phenotype. (b) Pure-breeding dwarf plant: genotype tt, homozygous recessive, 0% active enzyme dose, dwarf stem phenotype. (c) F₁ hybrid (TT × tt): genotype Tt, heterozygous, 50% active enzyme dose (sufficient to synthesise growth hormone GA₁), tall stem phenotype.

Back to section 13.1

13.2

  1. In humans, cystic fibrosis (and beta-thalassaemia) is caused by an autosomal recessive allele (f), while the normal allele is dominant (F). Two unaffected parents (Ff × Ff) are expecting a child. Construct the six-line genetic diagram (parental phenotypes, parental genotypes, gametes, 2 × 2 Punnett square, offspring genotypes/phenotypes, and ratios) and state the percentage probability that the child will (a) have the condition, (b) be an unaffected heterozygous carrier, and (c) be unaffected overall.
  2. A farmer in Nashik buys a black-coated ram. In this sheep breed, black coat (B) is dominant to white coat (b). Explain how the farmer can use a test cross to determine whether the ram is pure-breeding (BB) or heterozygous (Bb).

  1. Genetic diagram for Ff × Ff:
    • Parental phenotypes: Unaffected carrier mother × Unaffected carrier father
    • Parental genotypes: Ff × Ff
    • Gametes: Maternal (F) and (f) × Paternal (F) and (f)
    • Punnett grid (2 × 2): (F) + (F) → FF (25%); (F) + (f) → Ff (25%); (f) + (F) → Ff (25%); (f) + (f) → ff (25%).
    • Offspring genotypes & ratio: 1 FF : 2 Ff : 1 ff (25% homozygous normal : 50% heterozygous carrier : 25% homozygous recessive affected).
    • Offspring phenotypes & ratio: 3 unaffected : 1 affected (75% : 25%).
    • Answers: (a) Probability of having the condition (ff) = 25% (1/4 or 0.25). (b) Probability of being an unaffected carrier (Ff) = 50% (1/2 or 0.50). (c) Probability of being unaffected overall (FF + Ff) = 75% (3/4 or 0.75).
  2. Test cross protocol: Mate the black ram (B_) with several white-coated ewes, which are guaranteed to be homozygous recessive (bb) and produce only (b) ova. If the ram is homozygous dominant (BB), 100% of the lambs will be black (Bb). If the ram is heterozygous (Bb), approximately 50% of the lambs will be black (Bb) and 50% will be white (bb) (1 : 1 ratio); the birth of even a single white lamb (bb) proves the ram is heterozygous (Bb).

Back to section 13.2

13.3

  1. State all six possible diploid genotypes formed by the alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ, and Iᴼ, and group them under the four blood group phenotypes (Group A, Group B, Group AB, Group O).
  2. A woman with Blood Group AB (IᴬIᴮ) marries a man with Blood Group O (IᴼIᴼ). Construct the six-line genetic diagram (including gametes and a 2 × 2 Punnett square) and state the percentage probability that their child will have (a) Group A, (b) Group B, (c) Group AB, and (d) Group O.

  1. Group A: IᴬIᴬ and IᴬIᴼ. Group B: IᴮIᴮ and IᴮIᴼ. Group AB: IᴬIᴮ. Group O: IᴼIᴼ.
  2. Genetic diagram for IᴬIᴮ × IᴼIᴼ:
    • Parental phenotypes: Group AB mother × Group O father
    • Parental genotypes: IᴬIᴮ × IᴼIᴼ
    • Gametes: Maternal (Iᴬ) and (Iᴮ) × Paternal (Iᴼ) and (Iᴼ)
    • Punnett grid (2 × 2): Two boxes are IᴬIᴼ (50%, Group A) and two boxes are IᴮIᴼ (50%, Group B).
    • Offspring ratio: 1 Group A : 1 Group B (50% : 50%).
    • Probabilities: (a) Group A = 50%, (b) Group B = 50%, (c) Group AB = 0%, (d) Group O = 0%.

Back to section 13.3

13.4

  1. Define a sex-linked characteristic (0610 17.4.16) and explain why X-linked recessive conditions such as red–green colour blindness (Xᵇ) and haemophilia (Xʰ) are much more common in males (XY) than in females (XX).
  2. A woman who is a carrier for haemophilia (XᴴXʰ) and a man with normal blood clotting (XᴴY) have children. Construct a six-line genetic diagram (including gametes and a 2 × 2 Punnett square) and state (a) the probability that a son has haemophilia, (b) the probability that a daughter is a carrier, and (c) the probability that any child born to the couple has haemophilia.

  1. A sex-linked characteristic is a characteristic in which the gene responsible is located on a sex chromosome and that this makes it more common in one sex than in the other. X-linked recessive conditions are much more common in males because the gene locus sits on the non-homologous region of the X chromosome and is absent from the shorter Y chromosome. A male (XY) has only one X chromosome, so inheriting a single recessive allele (XᵇY or XʰY) from his mother causes the condition; a female (XX) has two X chromosomes, so a single recessive allele (XᴮXᵇ or XᴴXʰ) is masked by the dominant allele on her second X chromosome (making her an unaffected carrier), and she is affected (XᵇXᵇ or XʰXʰ) only if she inherits a recessive allele from both her mother and an affected father.
  2. Genetic diagram for XᴴXʰ × XᴴY:
    • Parental phenotypes: Carrier mother (normal clotting) × Normal father (normal clotting)
    • Parental genotypes: XᴴXʰ × XᴴY
    • Gametes: Maternal (Xᴴ) and (Xʰ) × Paternal (Xᴴ) and (Y)
    • Punnett grid (2 × 2):
      • XᴴXᴴ (25%): Homozygous normal daughter (normal clotting, non-carrier)
      • XᴴXʰ (25%): Heterozygous carrier daughter (normal clotting, carrier)
      • XᴴY (25%): Normal son (normal clotting)
      • XʰY (25%): Affected son (haemophilia)
    • Probabilities: (a) Probability that a son has haemophilia = 50% (1 in 2 sons). (b) Probability that a daughter is a carrier (XᴴXʰ) = 50% (1 in 2 daughters). (c) Probability that any child has haemophilia = 25% (1 in 4 of all children).

Back to section 13.4

Chapter 14. “The Glitch Engine & Natural Selection: Variation, Adaptation & Evolution”

14.1

  1. Classifying classroom measurements: A botanist in Pune measures two traits across 300 pea plants (Pisum sativum): (A) the mass of each dry seed in milligrams (120 mg to 310 mg), and (B) flower colour (224 purple flowers and 76 white flowers, with zero pale-lilac flowers). Identify which trait shows continuous variation and which shows discontinuous variation, state the genetic and environmental basis of each, and state which graph type the botanist should draw for each.
  2. Evaluating a student’s statement on X-rays and new alleles: A student writes: “When bacteria are exposed to X-rays and penicillin at the same time, the X-rays and penicillin force the bacteria to undergo meiosis and invent a penicillin-resistance allele.” Identify three biological errors in this sentence and rewrite it accurately.

  1. Trait A (seed mass) shows continuous variation because measurements span an unbroken range (120–310 mg) with intermediates; it is controlled by many genes (polygenic) plus environmental factors (water, soil nitrates, sunlight) and should be plotted as a histogram of touching bars (with a bell curve). Trait B (flower colour) shows discontinuous variation because plants fall into two distinct categories (purple vs white, ~3 : 1) with no intermediates; it is controlled by a single gene locus alone with zero environmental shift and should be plotted as a categorical bar chart with spaces between bars.
  2. Error 1: Bacteria are prokaryotes that reproduce asexually by binary fission, never meiosis. Error 2: Even in eukaryotes, meiosis only reshuffles existing alleles; mutation (a random change in DNA base sequence) is the only process that forms new alleles. Error 3: Neither X-rays nor penicillin “force” a directed resistance mutation; X-rays (ionising radiation) are a mutagen that increases the rate of random mutations across all DNA, while penicillin acts only as an environmental selection pressure that kills sensitive cells and allows pre-existing random resistant mutants to survive and reproduce.

Back to section 14.1

14.2

  1. Six-mark exam question — Rat resistance to warfarin: In the 1950s, the poison warfarin was introduced to control brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) populations on farms. Initially, warfarin killed over 98% of rats by blocking vitamin K recycling in blood clotting. Within ten years, farm rat populations were thriving and unaffected by standard doses of warfarin. Using the six steps of natural selection, explain how warfarin resistance evolved in the rat population.
  2. Viral coughs and antibiotic stewardship: A patient visits a Mumbai clinic with a 2-day runny nose and cough caused by a rhinovirus (common cold) and asks the doctor for amoxicillin “just in case”. Give two biological reasons why the doctor must refuse to prescribe an antibiotic.

  1. (1) Genetic variation: Due to pre-existing random gene mutation, a tiny fraction of rats in the original population already carried an allele conferring resistance to warfarin (an altered vitamin K epoxide reductase enzyme). (2) Overproduction: Rats produce large litters (many more offspring than farm food and shelter can support). (3) Selection pressure / struggle for existence: When farmers applied warfarin, the poison acted as an intense environmental selection pressure. (4) Differential survival: Sensitive wild-type rats died of internal bleeding, whereas rats carrying the warfarin-resistance allele survived (and experienced less competition for food). (5) Reproduction and inheritance: The surviving resistant rats bred and passed the resistance allele to their offspring. (6) Allele frequency increase: Repeated over many generations of warfarin application, the frequency of the resistance allele increased until almost the entire farm rat population was warfarin-resistant.
  2. (1) Zero effect on viruses: Rhinoviruses are acellular particles (protein capsid + nucleic acid) with no peptidoglycan cell wall, no cell membrane, and no 70S ribosomes; amoxicillin targets bacterial cell-wall synthesis and therefore cannot kill or inhibit viruses. (2) Selection for antibiotic resistance: Taking amoxicillin unnecessarily exposes the patient’s normal commensal bacteria (in the gut and respiratory tract) to an antibiotic selection pressure, killing sensitive bacteria and selecting for pre-existing antibiotic-resistant mutants, which can multiply and transfer resistance plasmids to pathogenic bacteria.

Back to section 14.2

14.3

  1. Interpreting a transverse leaf photomicrograph: In a practical exam, Kym looks down a light microscope at a stained transverse section (TS) of an unidentified leaf. She observes: (i) the leaf blade is curled into a hollow ring; (ii) the outer epidermis has a thick red-stained waxy cuticle (8.5 µm) and zero stomata; (iii) the inner epidermis has deep grooves containing stomata surrounded by fine hairs; and (iv) vascular bundles contain dense lignified xylem. Identify whether this leaf comes from a xerophyte or a hydrophyte, and explain how features (i), (ii), and (iii) adapt the plant to its habitat.
  2. Explaining submerged pondweed anatomy: A submerged freshwater plant (Elodea) has finely divided, feathery leaves only two cell layers thick, no waxy cuticle, no stomata, and stems packed with large honeycomb air channels (aerenchyma) but almost no woody xylem tissue. Explain why Elodea needs no woody xylem and why large air channels are essential for its survival.

  1. The leaf comes from a xerophyte (such as marram grass, Ammophila arenaria, adapted to dry, windy sand dunes). (i) Curled leaf blade encloses the inner surface away from external wind; (ii) Thick waxy cuticle (8.5 µm) and zero outer stomata prevent waterproof epidermal evaporation on the exposed outside surface; (iii) Sunken stomata in grooves with hairs trap a pocket of moist water vapour outside the stomatal pores, reducing the water potential gradient (ΔΨ) between the internal mesophyll air spaces and the trapped air, which greatly reduces water loss by transpiration.
  2. Elodea needs almost no woody xylem because (1) the surrounding water provides upthrust (buoyancy) that physically supports the stems and leaves, and (2) water and mineral ions can diffuse directly into the thin leaves across the whole surface without needing long-distance xylem transpiration pull. The large air channels (aerenchyma) are essential because they provide buoyancy to hold the feathery leaves upright toward light for photosynthesis and allow oxygen (O₂) produced by photosynthesis to diffuse rapidly down to the roots anchored in low-oxygen mud for aerobic respiration.

Back to section 14.3

14.4

  1. Designing a selective breeding programme for drought-tolerant millet: An agricultural institute in Rajasthan wants to breed a variety of pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum) that produces heavy grain heads under low-rainfall conditions (<250 mm yr⁻¹). Describe step by step how the scientists should carry out this selective breeding programme.
  2. Interpreting a DNA sequence alignment table: Biologists sequence a 200-base segment of a respiratory gene in a newly discovered forest mammal (Species X) and compare the percentage of identical DNA bases against four known mammals: Species P (96.5%), Species Q (82.0%), Species R (91.0%), and Species S (78.5%). State which species (P, Q, R, or S) is most closely related to Species X and which is most distantly related, and explain your reasoning using evolutionary principles.

  1. (1) Grow a genetically varied population of pearl millet plants under controlled low-water (<250 mm yr⁻¹) conditions and select parent plants that produce the heaviest grain heads despite the drought. (2) Cross-breed (cross-pollinate) these selected drought-tolerant, high-yielding parent plants with one another (preventing pollination from unselected plants). (3) Collect the seeds, grow the offspring under the same low-water conditions, and measure their grain yield. (4) Select only the best offspring showing the highest grain mass under drought to be the parents of the next generation. (5) Repeat this cross-breeding and selection cycle over many generations until the entire millet variety breeds true for high grain yield under low rainfall.
  2. Species P (96.5% DNA identity) is most closely related to Species X, and Species S (78.5% DNA identity) is most distantly related. Because random DNA base mutations accumulate gradually over generations after lineages split, a higher percentage of identical DNA bases (96.5%) indicates fewer accumulated mutations and therefore proves that Species X and Species P diverged more recently and share the most recent common ancestor, whereas Species S (78.5%) diverged longest ago.

Back to section 14.4

Chapter 15. “Web of Life & Code Rewritable: Ecology, Nutrient Cycles & Biotechnology”

15.1

  1. SGNP trophic energy calculation: In Sanjay Gandhi National Park, Karvi shrubs trap 20,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ of solar energy into net plant biomass. Assuming a 10% energy transfer efficiency at each step, calculate how much energy (kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹) is incorporated into the biomass of secondary consumers (such as Indian leopards feeding on spotted deer), and state four pathways by which the other 90% is lost at each transfer.
  2. Evaluating pyramid types: Explain one advantage of using a pyramid of biomass rather than a pyramid of numbers, and one advantage of using a pyramid of energy rather than a pyramid of biomass.

  1. Level 1 (Producers — Karvi shrubs): 20,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ → Level 2 (Primary consumers — Spotted deer): 10% of 20,000 = 2,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ → Level 3 (Secondary consumers — Indian leopards): 10% of 2,000 = 200 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. At each transfer step, the remaining 90% is lost via: (1) aerobic respiration and heat loss during movement and body temperature regulation, (2) indigestible egested faeces (cellulose, hair, bone), (3) excreted metabolic waste (urea in urine), and (4) uneaten body parts passing to decomposers.
  2. A pyramid of biomass accounts for the size (dry mass) of organisms, so it is not inverted when a single giant tree feeds thousands of small insects. A pyramid of energy measures the rate of energy production and flow over a full year (kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹) rather than a single snapshot standing crop, so it is never inverted (even in fast-turnover plankton communities) and does not require killing and oven-drying organisms if non-destructive calorimetry/respirometry benchmarks are used.

Back to section 15.1

15.2

  1. Comparing aerated legume soil vs waterlogged soil: A soil scientist analyses two adjacent agricultural plots in Maharashtra: Plot A is well-drained, ploughed, and planted with chickpea (Cicer arietinum, a legume); Plot B is compacted, waterlogged, and unploughed. Compare the rates of nitrogen fixation, nitrification, and denitrification in Plot A versus Plot B, and state which plot will have a higher soil nitrate (NO₃⁻) concentration.
  2. Identifying bacterial guilds: Name the specific type of bacteria that carries out each reaction: (a) N₂ → NH₄⁺ inside pea root nodules; (b) NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻ in aerated soil; (c) NO₃⁻ → N₂ in waterlogged mud.

  1. Plot A (well-drained, ploughed chickpea legume field) has high nitrogen fixation (mutualistic Rhizobium in chickpea root nodules converting N₂ → NH₄⁺), high nitrification (aerobic nitrifying bacteria using soil O₂ to oxidise NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻), and very low denitrification, resulting in a much higher soil nitrate (NO₃⁻) concentration. Plot B (compacted, waterlogged non-legume field) lacks root nodules (low fixation) and lacks soil O₂, which inhibits aerobic nitrification and strongly promotes anaerobic denitrification (NO₃⁻ → N₂ gas escaping to the air), depleting soil nitrate.
  2. (a) Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (specifically mutualistic Rhizobium); (b) Nitrifying bacteria (e.g. Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter); (c) Denitrifying bacteria (e.g. Pseudomonas).

Back to section 15.2

15.3

  1. Restoring a collapsed coastal fishery: A commercial fishing fleet uses fine-mesh bottom trawl nets year-round in a coastal bay. Within five years, the annual fish catch drops by 80%. Explain why the fine-mesh nets caused the population crash, and describe three specific legal regulations that would restore the fishery as a sustainable resource.
  2. Tracing downstream river pollution: Raw sewage is discharged into a slow-flowing river at Point X. Explain why the concentration of dissolved oxygen (O₂) drops sharply 2 km downstream of Point X and then gradually recovers 15 km further downstream.

  1. Why the crash occurred: Fine-mesh nets trap small, juvenile (immature) fish before they have reached reproductive age and bred even once, removing future breeding adults so the removal rate vastly exceeds the birth rate. Three sustainable regulations: (1) Increase minimum net mesh size (and fit escape panels) so juvenile fish slip through, survive to maturity, and reproduce; (2) Enforce legal catch quotas limiting the total mass of each species landed; (3) Establish closed seasons and protected no-take marine reserves over spawning grounds during breeding months.
  2. At Point X, raw sewage introduces abundant organic matter (and mineral ions). 2 km downstream, aerobic decomposer bacteria multiply rapidly as they digest the organic sewage and carry out intense aerobic respiration (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O), consuming dissolved O₂ faster than it can diffuse in from the air (oxygen sag). By 15 km downstream, most of the organic sewage has been broken down, so decomposer bacterial numbers and respiration drop, while diffusion of O₂ from the air (aided by riffles) and photosynthesis by aquatic plants/algae replenish dissolved O₂.

Back to section 15.3

15.4

  1. Cooling-jacket failure in an antibiotic fermenter: Inside an industrial fermenter producing penicillin from the fungus Penicillium, the cold water supply to the outer cooling jacket accidentally shuts off for three hours while the nutrient and oxygen supplies continue. Predict and explain what will happen to the temperature inside the fermenter and to the rate of penicillin production.
  2. Washing powder enzyme temperature: A parent washes a blood-stained cotton shirt in biological washing powder using boiling water at 90 °C instead of warm water at 35 °C, and finds the blood stain is still stuck to the fabric. Explain why the stain was removed at 35 °C but not at 90 °C.

  1. Temperature rises sharply: Billions of Penicillium fungal hyphae are carrying out rapid aerobic respiration (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O), which releases large quantities of thermal energy (heat). Without cold water flowing through the cooling jacket to conduct that heat away, the broth temperature climbs well above the optimum (>45–50 °C). Penicillin production crashes to zero: High temperatures break bonds holding the 3D shape of the fungus’s enzymes; their active sites denature (no longer complementary to substrates), killing the fungus and halting penicillin synthesis.
  2. Blood consists of insoluble proteins (haemoglobin and fibrin). Biological washing powder contains protease enzymes whose optimum temperature is around 35–40 °C, where they rapidly catalyse the hydrolysis of insoluble blood proteins into soluble amino acids that dissolve in the wash water. At 90 °C, thermal agitation breaks internal bonds in the protease molecules, denaturing their active sites so they can no longer bind or digest the protein stain (while boiling heat also coagulates the blood protein onto the cotton fibres).

Back to section 15.4

Words worth knowing

Letter choice in genetic diagrams: Always use the uppercase letter of the dominant trait for the dominant allele (e.g. R for round, B for purple/blue-violet, T for tall) and the matching lowercase letter for the recessive allele (r for wrinkled, b for white, t for dwarf)—never two different letters like R for round and W for wrinkled. Where uppercase and lowercase look similar in handwriting (C/c, S/s, W/w, P/p), write curved or serifed uppercase letters or choose letters with unmistakable shapes (A/a, B/b, D/d, R/r, T/t). 13.1
Absorption
Movement of substances from the intestinal lumen across its lining into internal tissues, followed by transport through blood or lymph as appropriate. 7.1
Activation energy
The energy hurdle involved in reaching a reactive arrangement. An enzyme lowers the activation barrier by providing a different pathway; it does not supply the reaction’s net energy. 4.3
Active site
The region of an enzyme where a substrate binds and the catalysed chemistry takes place. Its shape and chemical groups both matter. 4.3
Active transport
Energy-coupled movement across a membrane against a concentration gradient, or, for ions, against the combined concentration and electrical gradient. ATP may power transport directly or establish a gradient that powers another transport step. 3.4
Alimentary canal
The connected digestive tube from mouth to anus, through which food and unabsorbed remnants pass. Associated glands deliver secretions into it. 7.1
Alveoli
Microscopic air sacs at the ends of the respiratory bronchioles where gas exchange occurs between alveolar air and surrounding pulmonary capillaries. 8.1
Antigen, antibody, and active immunity
  • Antigen: a molecule (usually a surface protein) on a pathogen or foreign cell that has a specific shape and stimulates an immune response by lymphocytes.
  • Antibody: a specialised protein secreted by plasma cells formed from B lymphocytes. Its binding sites recognise particular molecular features of an antigen. Binding can neutralise a pathogen or toxin, support other clearance mechanisms, or mark a pathogen for phagocytes.
  • Active immunity: defence against a pathogen by antibody production in the body, gained either after catching an infection or by vaccination, and accompanied by the production of memory cells that give long-term immunity.
10.4
Arteries
Blood vessels carrying blood away from the heart. Their muscular and elastic walls withstand pressure; large systemic arteries have higher pressure than pulmonary arteries. 8.4
Assimilation
Uptake and use of supplied nutrients by cells, for example using amino acids to make cellular proteins. 7.1
ATP (adenosine triphosphate)
A principal rechargeable energy carrier in cells. Enzymes couple ATP reactions to other chemical changes and cellular work. ATP is not the only energy carrier. 1.3
Auxin
A plant growth hormone (such as indole-3-acetic acid) produced in the shoot tip that diffuses downward and regulates cell elongation during phototropism and gravitropism. 9.4
Bile
A liver-produced mixture delivered to the small intestine. Its components help disperse fat and carry lipid digestion products; it is not a digestive enzyme. 7.3
Capillaries
Microscopic blood vessels with walls one cell thick that link arterioles and venules, allowing exchange of materials between blood and tissue fluid. 8.4
Cell
The smallest unit of life that can carry out all the processes of a living thing, bounded by a membrane and containing genetic instructions and molecular machinery. Coined by Robert Hooke in 1665 after looking at dead cork chambers. 0.2
Cell membrane
The thin boundary around a cell that controls movement of substances into and out of it. A plant’s cell wall lies outside this membrane. 2.1
Cellular respiration
Chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen; moving air into lungs is a separate process. 6.1
Chemiosmosis
Coupling ion movement down an electrochemical gradient across a membrane to ATP synthesis. In this mitochondrial example, H⁺ returns to the matrix through ATP synthase after electron-transfer reactions support outward pumping. 6.2
Chlorophyll
A green light-absorbing pigment in the photosynthetic machinery. In plant chloroplasts it helps transfer absorbed light energy into chemical processes. 5.3
Chromosome, DNA, and gene
  • Chromosome: a thread-like structure located in the nucleus of a cell, made of DNA, which carries genetic information in the form of genes.
  • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid): the giant double-stranded polymer molecule that chromosomes and genes are made of.
  • Gene: a length of DNA that codes for a protein (and therefore helps to determine a characteristic of an organism).
11.1
Chylomicrons
Lipid-and-protein transport particles made by intestinal cells. They carry much absorbed long-chain dietary fat material through lymph before it reaches blood. 7.4
Cohesion
Attraction between molecules of the same substance. In xylem, cohesion helps transmit tension through connected liquid water. 5.5
Complete oxidation
For the carbon fuels modelled here, an overall reaction yielding carbon dioxide and water. It is a material endpoint account, not one reaction step or a measurement of instantaneous body-mass change. 6.3
Controlled experiment
A test in which only one factor (the independent variable) is deliberately changed while all other conditions (controlled variables) are kept the same, so that any difference in the outcome (the dependent variable) has only one possible cause. 0.1
Coronary arteries
Arteries branching from the base of the aorta that supply oxygenated blood and glucose to the heart’s own muscular wall (myocardium). 8.3
Deamination and urea
  • Deamination: the removal of the nitrogen-containing part of excess amino acids to form urea, carried out by enzymes in the liver (while the remaining carbon skeleton is respired or converted to glycogen).
  • Urea: the nitrogenous metabolic waste compound (NH₂)₂CO formed in the liver from excess amino acids, transported in blood plasma, and excreted by the kidneys in urine.
10.3
Denaturation
Loss of a protein’s functional three-dimensional structure. It does not necessarily break the peptide chain, and it can sometimes be reversed under suitable conditions. 4.4
Diffusion
The net movement of particles down their concentration gradient as a result of random movement. Individual particles can move in either direction. 3.1
Digestion
Physical breakdown of food and chemical breakdown of food molecules. Chemical digestion produces smaller substances suitable for absorption; chewing alone does not do all that chemistry. 7.1
DNA double helix and complementary base pairing
  • Double helix: the three-dimensional structure of DNA, consisting of two strands coiled together around a common axis, with sugar–phosphate backbones on the outside and paired bases forming cross-links on the inside.
  • Complementary base pairing: the invariant rule by which DNA bases form cross-links between the two strands: A (adenine) always pairs with T (thymine), and C (cytosine) always pairs with G (guanine).
11.2
Double circulation
A circulatory plan (as in mammals) in which blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body: a low-pressure pulmonary circuit to the lungs and a high-pressure systemic circuit to the rest of the body. 8.3
Dry mass
Mass after water has been removed by a stated drying procedure. It helps distinguish accumulated plant material from changing water content; it is not the same measurement as fresh mass. 5.1
Effector
A body part—specifically a muscle or a gland—that carries out a response when stimulated by a nerve impulse or a hormone. 9.1
Egestion
Removal of undigested food from the body as faeces. It differs from excreting waste made by metabolism. 7.1
Emulsification
Dispersion of one liquid as small droplets in another. In digestion it increases the fat–water interface without itself hydrolysing the fat molecules. 7.3
Endosymbiosis
An association in which one organism lives inside another. The endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts explains their descent from internal bacterial partners. 2.2
Enzyme
A biological catalyst that speeds a chemical reaction without being used up by that reaction. Most enzymes are proteins. 4.3
Enzyme–substrate complex
The temporary association of an enzyme with its bound substrate or substrates. 4.3
Excretion vs. egestion
Excretion is the removal of waste products made by chemical reactions inside cells (such as $\text{CO}_2$ from respiration and urea from amino acid breakdown), plus excess water and salts. Egestion is passing out undigested food (such as plant cellulose fibre in faeces) that travelled through the gut tube without ever entering a body cell. 1.4
Fermentation
Pathways that restore NAD⁺ by passing electrons from NADH to organic recipients. This allows glycolysis to continue without using an oxygen-dependent electron chain; the recycling step itself adds no further ATP in the routes taught here. 6.4
Flaccid
Having little turgor pressure, so the cell is less firm. 3.3
Food test
A chemical procedure used to investigate whether a sample contains a detectable target substance or molecular feature. Controls and the method’s limitations are part of interpreting the result. 4.5
Gas exchange
Net diffusion of oxygen from alveolar air into capillary blood and carbon dioxide from capillary blood into alveolar air across their shared thin barrier. 8.1
Glomerulus, nephron, and selective reabsorption
  • Nephron: one of roughly a million microscopic filtering-and-reabsorbing tubules spanning the cortex and medulla of each kidney.
  • Glomerulus: a high-pressure knot of capillaries sitting inside the cup-shaped renal (Bowman’s) capsule in the kidney cortex; it filters water, glucose, urea and mineral ions out of the blood while retaining blood cells and large plasma proteins.
  • Selective reabsorption: the process in the renal tubule by which nearly all filtered glucose at ordinary loads, most of the water, and some (needed) mineral ions are taken back from the filtrate into the surrounding blood capillaries, leaving urea, excess water and excess ions to pass down the collecting duct as urine.
10.3
Glycolysis
An enzyme-controlled pathway in the cytoplasm that processes glucose into two pyruvate molecules. The usual taught route yields two net ATP and transfers electrons to NAD⁺, forming NADH. 6.2
Gravitropism
A growth response in which parts of a plant grow towards (positive gravitropism, as in roots) or away from (negative gravitropism, as in shoots) the pull of gravity. 9.4
Haemoglobin
The iron-containing protein in red blood cells that binds oxygen reversibly in the lungs (forming oxyhaemoglobin) and releases it in respiring tissues. 8.4
Haploid, diploid, meiosis and fertilisation
  • Haploid nucleus (n): a nucleus containing a single set of unpaired chromosomes (e.g. in gametes, where n = 23 in humans; 0610 17.1 & 16.2.3).
  • Diploid nucleus (2n): a nucleus containing two sets of chromosomes (e.g. in somatic body cells and the nucleus of a zygote, where 2n = 46 or 23 homologous pairs in humans; 0610 17.1 & 16.2.3).
  • Meiosis: reduction division in which the chromosome number is halved from diploid to haploid resulting in genetically different cells, used in the production of gametes (0610 17.3.1 & 17.3.2).
  • Fertilisation: the fusion of the nuclei of gametes (n + n → 2n) to form a diploid zygote (0610 16.2.1 & 16.2.2).
12.4
Homeostasis
The maintenance of a constant internal environment within narrow limits around a norm or set point (such as core body temperature near 37 °C, blood glucose concentration near 4.0–5.5 mmol/L, and blood water potential), despite changes in the external environment or the body’s activity. 10.1
Hormone
A chemical substance, produced by an endocrine gland and carried by the blood, which alters the activity of one or more specific target organs. 9.1
Hydrogen bond
An attraction involving a hydrogen covalently bonded to an electronegative atom, such as oxygen or nitrogen, and another suitable electronegative atom. In water, many such attractions join neighbouring molecules temporarily. 4.1
Hydrolysis
Chemical splitting of a molecule through reaction with water. Digestive enzymes catalyse hydrolysis of particular links in their substrates. 7.2
Ingestion
Taking substances such as food and drink into the digestive system through the mouth. 7.1
Insulin, glucagon, and glycogen
  • Insulin: hormone secreted by the pancreas when blood glucose concentration rises above the set point; it causes the liver (and muscles) to take up glucose and convert glucose into insoluble glycogen, decreasing blood glucose concentration.
  • Glucagon: hormone secreted by the pancreas when blood glucose concentration falls below the set point; it causes the liver to break down stored glycogen into soluble glucose and release it into the blood, increasing blood glucose concentration.
  • Glycogen: the insoluble, branched polysaccharide storage form of glucose kept inside liver and muscle cells (joining many glucose units into glycogen greatly reduces their osmotic effect compared with keeping them all as free glucose).
10.1
Lactate
An organic product formed when pyruvate receives electrons during NAD⁺ regeneration. It can be transported and used metabolically, including oxidation as fuel; its production does not require complete absence of oxygen. 6.4
Limiting factor
A condition that restricts the rate of a process in the conditions being studied. Which factor limits photosynthesis can change as light, carbon dioxide availability and temperature change. 5.3
Lipase
An enzyme that catalyses hydrolysis of lipid molecules. Pancreatic lipase acts on triglycerides at the fat–water interface, producing mainly fatty acids and monoacylglycerols. 7.3
Lumen
The space inside a hollow structure. In the gut, it contains food, secretions and unabsorbed material on the external side of the epithelial barrier. 7.1
Messenger RNA (mRNA) and ribosomes in protein synthesis
  • Messenger RNA (mRNA): a single-stranded nucleic acid molecule that is made in the nucleus as a copy of one gene (using bases A, U, C, G) and moves to the cytoplasm, where it passes through ribosomes to direct protein synthesis.
  • Ribosome: the cytoplasmic organelle through which mRNA passes; the ribosome reads the sequence of bases in the mRNA three bases (one codon) at a time and assembles amino acids into protein molecules in the exact order specified by the mRNA.
11.3
Metabolism
All the enzyme-controlled chemical reactions taking place inside a living cell or organism—both those that break down fuel molecules to release energy and those that build up complex molecules for growth and repair. 1.3
Micrometre and nanometre
A micrometre ($\mu\text{m}$) is one thousandth of a millimetre ($10^{-6}\text{ m}$), the scale of cells and bacteria. A nanometre ($\text{nm}$) is one thousandth of a micrometre ($10^{-9}\text{ m}$), the scale of viruses, ribosomes, membranes and DNA. 0.4
Microvilli
Tiny membrane projections on individual absorptive cells. They add cell-surface area and are distinct from the larger tissue projections called villi. 7.4
Mitosis and asexual reproduction
  • Mitosis: nuclear division giving rise to genetically identical cells (0610 17.2.1), in which replicated chromosome copies (sister chromatids) separate to maintain the chromosome number (2n → 2n) for growth, repair of damaged tissues, replacement of cells, and asexual reproduction (0610 17.2.2 & 17.2.4).
  • Asexual reproduction: a process resulting in the production of genetically identical offspring from one parent (0610 16.1.1) without the fusion of gametes.
12.2
Monomer
A small molecular unit that can be joined with others to build a polymer. 4.1
Myelin sheath
An insulating layer of fatty cell membranes (formed by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves) wrapped around an axon, with narrow gaps (nodes of Ranvier) that greatly speed up the conduction of electrical impulses. 9.2
Negative feedback
A homeostatic control mechanism in which any change away from a set point (norm) is detected by a receptor and triggers an effector response that opposes (reverses) the change, returning the internal condition toward the set point. 10.1
Net gas exchange
The overall gas movement measured after simultaneous production and consumption are combined. A net measurement does not reveal each underlying rate separately. 5.2
Neurone
A specialised nerve cell adapted to transmit electrical impulses rapidly from one part of the body to another along a thin membrane extension (axon or dendron). 9.1
Neurotransmitter
A chemical messenger molecule stored in vesicles in a presynaptic neurone, released into the synaptic gap when an impulse arrives, and able to bind complementary receptor proteins on the next neurone. 9.2
Nutrition
Taking in and using materials that support life, including sources of chemical energy and material for growth and repair. 7.1
Optimum
The condition giving the highest activity in the particular enzyme assay being considered. Change the enzyme or measurement conditions and the optimum can change. 4.4
Osmosis
Net movement of water molecules from higher to lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane. 3.2
Partially permeable
Allowing some substances to pass through while restricting others. A membrane’s permeability depends on both its lipid layer and the proteins present. 3.2
Passive immunity
Short-term defence against a pathogen by ready-made antibodies acquired from another individual (such as maternal antibodies crossing the placenta or transferred in breast milk to an infant, or injected antitoxin/antivenom). Protection is immediate, the antibody transfer itself does not create memory, and protection fades as the borrowed antibodies are broken down. 10.4
Pathogen and transmissible disease
  • Pathogen: a disease-causing organism (or virus).
  • Transmissible disease: a disease in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another.
10.4
Peristalsis
Coordinated waves of contraction and relaxation in the muscular wall of the digestive tube that propel its contents. Local mixing movements also occur. 7.2
Photosynthesis
In green plants, light-supported synthesis of carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water. Released oxygen comes from water; the carbohydrate carbon comes from carbon dioxide. 5.3
Phototropism
A growth response in which parts of a plant grow towards (positive phototropism, as in shoots) or away from (negative phototropism) the direction of a light source. 9.4
Plasmolysis
Separation of the membrane-bound contents from the plant cell wall after sufficient water loss by osmosis. 3.3
Polarity
An uneven distribution of electrical charge within a molecule or bond. A polar molecule can still have zero overall charge. 4.1
Polymer
A large molecule containing many linked units derived from smaller molecules. The units may be alike or differ in their side groups or sequence. 4.1
Protein
A biological molecule made from one or more amino-acid chains. Sequence, three-dimensional arrangement and chemical conditions affect its properties and function. 4.1
Reflex arc
The neural pathway taken by impulses during a reflex action: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in CNS) → motor neurone → effector in the withdrawal example. Reflex circuits can differ. 9.2
Respiration (biological definition)
Cellular chemical reactions that break down nutrient molecules (such as glucose) and release energy for metabolism (recharging ATP). Never confuse it with breathing, which is just the muscular movement of air in and out of lungs. 1.4
Semi-conservative DNA replication and sister chromatids
  • Semi-conservative DNA replication: the mechanism of DNA copying before cell division in which the two parental strands unzip and each strand acts as a template for the synthesis of a new complementary strand (A with T, C with G), so each resulting DNA molecule contains one original strand and one new strand.
  • Sister chromatids: the two identical copies of a replicated chromosome formed during interphase (S phase), joined together at a single centromere until they separate during cell division.
12.1
Sense organ
A group of receptor cells responding to specific stimuli: light, sound, touch, temperature and chemicals. 9.3
Single circulation
A circulatory plan (as in bony fish) in which blood passes through the heart once for each complete circuit of the body, flowing from heart to gill capillaries and directly on to body capillaries before returning to the heart. 8.3
Specialised cell
A cell whose structure suits a particular function, such as moving mucus, absorbing materials or transporting oxygen. 2.4
Spontaneous generation
The old, mistaken belief that living organisms (such as maggots, beetles or microbes) regularly spring to life out of non-living matter like rotting meat, mud or broth. 0.1
Stem cells and selective gene expression
  • Stem cells: unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised for specific functions (0610 17.2.5).
  • Selective gene expression: the principle that most body cells in an organism contain the same genes, but many genes in a particular cell are not expressed because the cell only makes the specific proteins it needs (0610 17.1.6).
12.3
Stimulus
A detectable change in the internal or external environment of an organism, such as light, temperature, touch, sound or chemical concentration. 9.1
Stomata
Small epidermal pores providing routes for gas exchange. Changes in the shape of surrounding guard cells alter the openings and affect both carbon dioxide entry and water-vapour loss. 5.4
Substrate
A reactant that binds to an enzyme and is acted on in its catalysed reaction. 4.3
Surface-area-to-volume ratio
Surface area divided by volume. For the same shape, enlarging all lengths reduces the surface available per unit of interior. 2.3
Synapse
A junction between two neurones, where an electrical impulse in the first neurone triggers the release of a chemical neurotransmitter that diffuses across a microscopic gap to stimulate the next neurone. 9.2
Tissue fluid
The watery fluid formed from blood plasma at capillaries that bathes body cells, supplying them with oxygen and nutrients and receiving carbon dioxide and other metabolic wastes. 8.4
Trachea
The main airway leading from the larynx to the two bronchi, supported by C-shaped rings of cartilage that keep the lumen open during pressure changes. 8.1
Translocation
Movement of assimilated substances, including sucrose and amino acids, in phloem from sources to sinks. The direction depends on the connected source and sink, not a rule that food travels downwards. 5.5
Transpiration
Loss of water vapour from leaves. Evaporation from moist internal surfaces and diffusion through stomata connect leaf water loss to the transpiration stream. 5.5
Triglyceride
A fat or oil molecule containing one glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester links. It is one member of the broader lipid family. 4.1
Turgid
Firm with water and turgor pressure. Turgor is the pressure of the cell contents against the supporting wall. 3.3
Vasodilation and vasoconstriction
  • Vasodilation: relaxation of smooth muscle in the walls of arterioles supplying skin surface capillaries, widening their lumens so more blood flows through surface capillaries and more thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings.
  • Vasoconstriction: contraction of smooth muscle in the walls of arterioles supplying skin surface capillaries, narrowing their lumens so less blood flows through surface capillaries and less thermal energy is lost across the skin.
10.2
Veins
Blood vessels returning blood towards the heart, usually at lower pressure than arteries. Many peripheral veins contain valves that limit backflow. 8.4
Ventilation
Mechanical movement of air into and out of the lungs by bulk flow, driven by pressure differences when respiratory muscles change the volume of the thorax. 8.1
Villi
Small tissue projections of the small-intestinal lining that increase its surface area. A villus contains vessels and is covered by epithelium. 7.4
Virus
An infectious biological particle containing a DNA or RNA genome and a protein coat. Many familiar viruses are tens to hundreds of nanometres across, but sizes vary. Some have a lipid envelope. Viruses lack ribosomes and an independent cellular metabolism; replication requires a suitable host cell. 1.5
Water potential
A measure used to predict net water movement, affected by dissolved substances and pressure. Water moves overall from higher to lower water potential. 3.2

Notes on biological models and numbers

Every diagram and interactive model in this book is a map, not the territory itself. A good map leaves out clutter so you can see how the mechanism works, and states plainly what it simplified:

  1. The crowded cytoplasm. Textbook drawings (and our 2D and 3D cell cutaways) show a few organelles floating in open space so you can see each one clearly. In a real living cell, macromolecules occupy $20\text{–}30\%$ of the volume, packed as tightly as passengers in a rush-hour Dadar train, jostled millions of times a second by water molecules.
  2. Scale inside cell drawings. In a real eukaryotic cell ($20\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ across), the cell membrane is only $7\text{–}8\text{ nm}$ thick and a ribosome is $25\text{ nm}$ wide—more than a thousand times narrower than the cell. To make membranes and ribosomes visible on the same screen as the nucleus, schematic cell diagrams draw them thicker than true scale. Whenever you want true logarithmic ratios, open Powers of Ten in the Living World.
  3. Overall equations vs. multi-step pathways. Writing photosynthesis as $6\text{CO}2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{C}_6\text{H}_2$, or aerobic respiration as its reverse, is like summarising a thirty-station train journey by naming only Churchgate and Virar. The balanced equation strictly tracks the conservation of atoms and energy between start and finish, while the text shows the key intermediate stages (splitting water in thylakoids, the Calvin cycle, glycolysis, and rotary ATP synthase in mitochondria).}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O
  4. Real measured numbers. Cell counts ($\approx 3.0 \times 10^{13}$ human cells, Sender et al. 2016), ATP turnover, enzyme rates, Van Helmont’s willow masses, and Mendel’s pea ratios come from primary scientific literature and are documented in the curriculum and sources registry below.

Further adventures in Mumbai and beyond

The best biology laboratory is not inside a screen—it is right outside your door in Mumbai:

  • Sanjay Gandhi National Park (Borivali) & Maharashtra Nature Park (Dharavi): Walk the trail to Kanheri Caves before the June monsoon and again two weeks after the first rain to watch dormant spores, mosses, Karvi shrubs, and forest food webs wake up in real time.
  • Thane Creek & Sewri Mudflats (November to March): Watch tens of thousands of Lesser and Greater Flamingos filter-feeding on blue-green algae (Spirulina / cyanobacteria) in the tidal mudflats, bordered by salt-excreting Avicennia marina mangroves.
  • Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), Hornbill House, Colaba: Visit the institution where ten-year-old Salim Ali brought his yellow-throated sparrow in 1906, and explore their field guides and natural history collections.
  • Chai and Why? (TIFR Mumbai): Twice a month at Prithvi Theatre in Juhu, Ruparel College in Matunga, or Alexandra Girls’ English Institution in Fort, scientists from the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research run hands-on public science demonstrations where you can look through microscopes, extract DNA, and ask any question you like.
